kgs.name: Counseling theories and philosophy of practice

items.stem: Priya Raman sees performers as healthy learners who struggle mostly because nobody has shown them the right techniques, and she sees her own role as that of an instructor. At a first meeting, collegiate swimmer Tomasz Wójcik says he isn't sure what to expect and asks, "So how does this work?" Which explanation is most consistent with Priya's philosophy of practice?
options: "You'll lead our talks, and my part is to understand your experience as you see it."
"We'll look for races that already go well, and you'll do more of what works in them."
"I'll teach you a set sequence of skills, and you'll practice them between our meetings."
"We'll look at how you interpret your races, and you'll test whether those readings hold up."
rationales: This is a person-centered explanation. It suits a consultant who trusts clients to find their own direction when deeply understood, but Priya sees clients as lacking techniques and herself as the one who supplies them.
Building on existing successes is solution-focused and assumes the swimmer already has workable solutions. Priya's stated belief is that performers have not yet been shown the techniques they need.

An educational, skills-training process follows directly from Priya's beliefs: the difficulty is untaught technique, so the instructor teaches and the learner practices. A consultant's philosophy should show in the process and roles described to a new client.
Examining and testing interpretations is cognitive-behavioral and locates the difficulty in how events are read. Priya locates it in techniques nobody has taught.
items.takeaway: Beliefs about why people struggle and what the consultant is for should show in how the process is explained.

items.topic: Feminist view of the consulting relationship
items.stem: Lena Okafor's practice is grounded in feminist approaches, and she regards a consultant's hidden authority as a problem in its own right. She begins work with Marisol Vega, an elite rugby player who says earlier consultants "acted neutral, so I could never tell where they were coming from or why they picked what we did." Which first-session action best puts Lena's view of the working relationship into practice?
options: State for Marisol the values and beliefs that shape how she works as a consultant
Reflect Marisol's feelings back to her without steering where the session goes
Ask Marisol to describe recent matches in which she performed closer to her hopes
Map the people and settings around Marisol that bear on how she performs
rationales: Feminist approaches reject the idea of a value-free helper and use transparency and purposeful self-disclosure to reduce the power difference. It also answers what Marisol found missing: knowing where a consultant stands.
Nondirective reflection is central to person-centered work. Here it would leave Lena's own position just as hidden as that of the consultants who "acted neutral."
Looking for exceptions is a solution-focused move. It may be useful later, but it does nothing about the concealed authority that Lena and Marisol have both named.
Mapping surrounding settings expresses an ecological view of the performer. The stem asks about the relationship between the two of them, where the concern is the consultant's unstated position.
items.takeaway: In feminist work, openness about the consultant's own values is a way to share power.

items.stem: A youth soccer academy asks Daniel Whitfield to help a 12-year-old whose play has dropped since January. Working from Bronfenbrenner's ecological model, Daniel learns that she gets on well with her coach, teammates, and parents, that her parents and coach talk often and agree, and that local support for girls' soccer is strong. What changed in January was a hospital's decision to move her mother to night shifts, which has upset the family's week. When Daniel explains his thinking to her parents, at which level should he place the origin of this change?
options: The microsystem, the settings she takes part in and the people in them
The mesosystem, the connections among the settings she takes part in
The macrosystem, the customs and beliefs of the culture she lives in
The exosystem, a setting she isn't part of that still affects her life
rationales: The effect is felt in her home, which is a microsystem, but her relationships in each setting are sound. The question is where the change began, and that was in a workplace she is not part of.
Connections between her settings, such as home and club, are working: her parents and coach talk often and agree. The change began elsewhere.
Cultural beliefs form the macrosystem, and the stem describes strong local support for girls' soccer. A staffing decision at one hospital is not a cultural custom.

A parent's workplace is the classic exosystem: the player does not take part in it, yet its decisions reach her through home. Naming the origin helps Daniel focus the discussion on the family's schedule rather than on faults in the girl, her coach, or her parents.
items.takeaway: Ecological levels depend on the person's place in the setting: in it, between settings, outside it, or surrounded by it.

items.topic: Explaining a cognitive model at intake
items.stem: At intake, professional golfer Hiroshi Tanaka says the walk to the first tee is miserable: he is certain he will shank his opening drive in front of the gallery, though he can't recall when he last did. His consultant, Anika Brandt, works from Beck's cognitive model. When Hiroshi asks what they will actually do about the first tee, which explanation is most consistent with that model?
options: "We'll practice letting the dread be there while you commit to the shot in front of you."
"We'll write down what you expect will happen and compare it with what does happen."
"We'll find first tees where you felt steadier and work out what you did differently there."
"We'll build a breathing routine that settles your body in the minutes before you swing."
rationales: Making room for dread while committing to action describes acceptance-based work such as Mindfulness-Acceptance-Commitment. Beck's model works on the content and accuracy of his forecast.

Beck's model holds that appraisals such as Hiroshi's certainty of a shank drive his distress, and treats them as hypotheses to check against evidence. Recording a forecast and comparing it with the outcome is that collaborative empiricism in action.
Searching for times the problem was smaller is solution-focused. It sidesteps the forecast that Beck's model would make the target.
A breathing routine matches bodily tension. Hiroshi describes a prediction rather than physical symptoms, and Beck's cognitive model would address that prediction.
items.takeaway: Cognitive work treats a client's forecast as a hypothesis to check against evidence.

items.stem: Executive Olivia Grant dreads presenting to her board and asks consultant Hollis Penrose how their sessions will run. He replies, "I won't try to talk you out of the dread or wait for it to fade. We'll get clear on the kind of leader you want to be in that room, and you'll practice presenting that way with the dread along for the ride." Which theoretical orientation does Hollis's explanation best reflect?
options: Rogers's person-centered counseling approach
Hayes's acceptance and commitment therapy
Beck's cognitive behavior therapy
De Shazer's solution-focused brief therapy
rationales: Person-centered work would leave the direction to Olivia and rely on the relationship. Hollis lays out a plan of his own: clarify how she wants to lead, then practice it while the dread is present.
Letting the dread remain (acceptance), clarifying how she wants to lead (values), and presenting that way anyway (committed action) are core processes of acceptance and commitment therapy.
Cognitive behavior therapy would examine and test the thoughts behind the dread. Hollis says outright that he won't try to change the dread before she acts.
Solution-focused work would look for times when presenting already goes better and build on them. Hollis mentions no exceptions, scaling, or existing successes.
items.takeaway: Acceptance, values, and committed action together signal ACT: feelings need not change before behavior does.

items.stem: Police sergeant Ray Delgado has told consultant Aisha Mensah about freezing for a few seconds during a standoff. Aisha, who is person-centered, has reflected his feelings several times, and he agrees she has them right. Now he says, "You get it, but you're being careful with me. Straight up, what do you think of me after hearing this?" Aisha feels real respect for him. Which response best offers the facilitative condition Ray is asking for?
options: "It sounds like you feel ashamed, and worn out from doubting yourself since that night."
"What was it like for you to tell your partner about those few seconds?"
"So you've gone from questioning that night to questioning whether you still belong out there."
"I respect you, and hearing how you've faced this has deepened that for me."
rationales: Reflecting feeling conveys empathy, which Ray says he already has ("You get it"). Another reflection would confirm his sense that Aisha is holding herself back.
An open question invites more detail, and nothing in Ray's request calls for that. He has asked Aisha something, and answering with a question would avoid it.
Tying his concerns together shows that Aisha follows his meaning. Ray agrees she already understands; what he lacks is her own honest reaction.

Ray is asking for congruence, or genuineness: the person behind the role. Aisha's respect is real and he has asked for her reaction, so stating it openly is consistent with Rogers's view that the helper should be transparent rather than hide behind technique.
items.takeaway: When a client understands he's been heard and asks where you stand, genuineness may matter more than another reflection.

items.stem: Jordan Avery's written philosophy states that athletes open up to someone who shares their daily world, that lasting change usually starts in unplanned moments, and that formal sessions are a supplement. At a first meeting, a collegiate volleyball coach asks how Jordan will work with the team this season. Which description is most consistent with that philosophy?
options: "I'll be around practice and on trips, and most of my work will be brief chats."
"I'll teach skills early in the season, and players will run them without me by playoffs."
"I'll work mainly with your staff, and players will hear the ideas from their coaches."
"I'll see players by appointment, and each one will choose what we work on."
rationales: Being present in the team's everyday setting and working through short, informal contacts follows from each of Jordan's stated beliefs. Consultants' roles and methods should flow from their core beliefs about how people change.
Teaching early and fading out fits a philosophy of athlete self-reliance. Jordan's philosophy puts formal teaching second and values being there when unplanned moments arise.
Working through coaches suits a philosophy that sees them as the main influence on athletes. Jordan's rests on athletes' trust in the consultant, which this arrangement would give up.
Scheduled, player-led meetings suit a philosophy of private, self-directed work. Jordan treats formal sessions as a supplement to sharing the daily world of the team.
items.takeaway: A consultant's delivery style should be traceable to stated beliefs about how people change.

items.stem: In a video call, professional esports player Malik Haddad says that after a lost round he goes silent or snaps at teammates, as he has done for years with anyone he might disappoint. He asks how working with Ottilie Brekke will help. Ottilie uses an interpersonal process approach, which expects a client's patterns to show up in sessions too. Which explanation is most consistent with that approach?
options: "We'll spot rounds when you shook off a loss, and build on what you did then."
"We'll catch what you tell yourself after a loss, and check how well it fits the facts."
"We'll notice how you deal with people under strain, including how you deal with me."
"We'll practice letting the frustration come and go while you keep playing your game."
rationales: Building on rounds that went better is solution-focused. Ottilie's approach attends to the pattern as it unfolds between people, sessions included.
Checking self-statements against facts is cognitive-behavioral. Ottilie's approach makes his way of relating, rather than the accuracy of his thoughts, the focus.

An interpersonal process approach treats the working relationship as a live sample of the client's patterns, so what happens between consultant and client becomes material for change. Telling Malik this now sets accurate expectations.
Letting frustration come and go describes mindfulness- and acceptance-based work. It targets his inner experience, while Ottilie's approach targets how he relates to others.
items.takeaway: Interpersonal process work uses what happens between client and consultant as material for change.

items.topic: Matching a first session to readiness
items.stem: A high school basketball coach refers 16-year-old Devon Harris to Rachel Kim, saying Devon "refuses to do any pre-game routine." With a parent's permission and Devon's assent in place, Rachel meets him. Devon says that was true last season; since then he has made up his mind that a routine would help, tried a teammate's version once at home, and wants one in place within two weeks. Using the transtheoretical model, which focus for this first session fits Devon best?
options: Ask what he has heard about pre-game routines and what he makes of them
Weigh with him what he would gain and lose by using a routine
Work out how he will keep his routine going on trips and bad days
Help him settle on a routine and pick the game in which he'll start it
rationales: Raising awareness without pressure suits precontemplation, which is the Devon the coach describes. Devon's own account is that he has decided and has already tried a routine.
Weighing pros and cons suits the ambivalence of contemplation. Devon has made up his mind and has a time frame, so this would hold him at a point he has passed.
Protecting an established habit suits later action and maintenance. Devon does not have a routine in place yet.

Intending to act very soon and having taken a small step place Devon in preparation, where a specific plan and start point help most. His own report of readiness, rather than the coach's description, should set the session's focus.
items.takeaway: Let the client's current readiness, not the referral's description, set the starting point.

items.stem: Two consultants serve the same university. Their written philosophies list the same core beliefs about people, both name cognitive-behavioral theory, both describe themselves as collaborators with athletes, and both rely on self-talk and imagery. Yet one counts her work done when competition results improve, while the other counts it done when athletes are thriving in and out of sport. In a hierarchical view of professional philosophy, at which level do the two consultants most clearly differ?
options: Personal core beliefs and values about people
Goals that each intervention is meant to reach
Model of practice and role taken with clients
Techniques and methods used to intervene
rationales: Core beliefs sit at the base of the hierarchy, and the stem says the two lists are the same. The difference appears in the end each is working toward.
One aims at competitive results and the other at the whole person's thriving, so they differ in intervention goals. Beliefs, theory, role, and techniques are each described as shared.
Both describe themselves as collaborators, so the role each takes with athletes is the same. What differs is the outcome that each treats as success.
Both rely on self-talk and imagery, so their methods match. The same techniques are being put to different ends.
items.takeaway: Two consultants can share beliefs, theory, role, and techniques yet differ in what they count as success.

items.stem: Ben Asante works from a structured cognitive-behavioral model and has no training in other approaches. At intake, masters marathoner Ingrid Solberg, 58, asked for open-ended conversations about what running means to her as her racing years end. Ben described how he works, and they talked over whether it would suit her. After a week's thought, Ingrid tells him clearly that she still wants the open-ended kind and doesn't want to try his. What should Ben do next?
options: Give her the names of colleagues who are trained in nondirective work
Explain his structured model and ask how well it suits her aims
Begin his usual cognitive-behavioral program and review the fit with her in two weeks
Set his usual structure aside and let her lead their conversations
rationales: Ben has been transparent, the two have discussed fit, and Ingrid has made an informed choice that lies outside his training. Connecting her with someone competent in what she wants respects both her autonomy and the limits of his competence.
Explaining the model and discussing fit comes first in such cases, and it has been done. Ingrid took a week to think and gave a clear answer.
A short trial with a review is reasonable when a client is curious about it. Ingrid says she doesn't want to try his approach.
Adapting to a client's preference fits a consultant competent in both ways of working. Ben has no training outside his structured model.
items.takeaway: Once fit has been discussed openly and the answer is no, help the client reach someone who fits.

items.stem: A supervisor reviews recordings of virtual sessions between wheelchair tennis player Camila Reyes and Theo Nguyen, who identifies as person-centered. Theo is sincerely fond of Camila and equally warm after wins and losses; Camila says so and feels at ease with him. But when she describes shame at letting her coach down, he restates it as anger about the draw, much as he felt in his own playing days, and she often has to correct him. Which of Rogers's conditions is Theo most clearly failing to provide?
options: Psychological contact between consultant and client
Congruence between what he feels and shows
Accurate empathy for her frame of reference
Unconditional positive regard for her as a person
rationales: Psychological contact means the two are in a relationship in which each registers the other. Camila feels at ease and engages with Theo, so contact is present.
Congruence means the consultant's outward manner matches inner experience. Theo's fondness is sincere, so nothing suggests a front.

Theo hears Camila's shame as anger because he filters it through his own history, and she has to correct him. Empathic understanding requires sensing her experience as if it were his own without letting his experience take over.
Unconditional positive regard means acceptance that doesn't depend on how the client performs. Theo is equally warm after wins and losses.
items.takeaway: Warmth and sincerity don't guarantee empathy, which means grasping the client's meaning rather than one's own.

items.stem: Fourteen-year-old figure skater Corentin Quiroga has begun turning planned jumps into easier ones at the last moment in practice. With his guardian's permission and Corentin's assent, Grace Liu begins her assessment. Grace works from an operant behavioral perspective and wants to find out what might be maintaining the habit. Which assessment question best fits her perspective?
options: "What goes through your mind as you set up for one of those jumps?"
"What happens right after you turn a jump into an easier one?"
"Which recent practices went a little better, and what was different in them?"
"How do the adults at home and at the rink get along about your skating?"
rationales: Asking about thoughts suits a cognitive perspective. An operant perspective explains the habit by what surrounds and follows it, so thoughts are not Grace's first target.

Operant theory holds that behavior is maintained by its consequences, such as relief, praise, or escape from a fall. Asking what follows the switch looks for the reinforcer that keeps the habit going.
Asking about exceptions suits a solution-focused perspective, which builds on what works. Grace wants to know what maintains the habit.
Asking how home and rink connect suits an ecological perspective. Grace's operant perspective focuses on the events tied to the behavior itself.
items.takeaway: An operant assessment asks what follows a behavior, because consequences keep it going.

items.stem: Orchestral trumpet player Nadia Petrova tells consultant Samuel Osei that her hands shake before auditions and that her doctor has found no medical cause. She adds that the shaking has become "a whole thing" at home and in her section. Samuel works from a systems perspective and wants to understand what keeps the shaking going. Which assessment question best fits his perspective?
options: "When your hands shake, who notices first, and how do people respond?"
"When your hands shake, what do you tell yourself that it means?"
"When have your hands shaken less, and what was different that day?"
"When you try to stop the shaking, what does the effort cost you?"
rationales: A systems perspective looks for the pattern of interaction around a problem: each person's response may help maintain it. Asking who notices and how people respond traces that pattern across home and section.
Asking about the meaning she gives the symptom suits a cognitive perspective, which places the maintaining factor in her appraisal. Samuel looks for it in interactions.
Asking when the problem is smaller suits a solution-focused perspective, which looks for exceptions rather than for what maintains a problem.
Asking about the cost of control suits acceptance and commitment therapy, which targets her struggle with the symptom. Samuel's perspective focuses on what happens among people.
items.takeaway: Systems assessment asks how people's responses to one another keep a pattern going.

items.stem: A college athletic department asks Elena Vasquez why many athletes skip the injury-prevention warm-up designed by the sports medicine staff. She is building a survey on the theory of planned behavior. Her draft already asks how worthwhile athletes think the warm-up is, whether they have the time and know-how to do it, and whether they mean to do it this month. Which of the theory's constructs does she still need to cover?
options: How useful and pleasant athletes judge the warm-up to be
How easy or difficult athletes expect the warm-up to be
How strong athletes' intentions are to complete the warm-up
How much athletes sense that teammates and coaches expect it
rationales: This is the attitude component, which her question about how worthwhile the warm-up is already covers.
This is perceived behavioral control, which her questions about time and know-how already cover.
This is intention, which her question about whether athletes mean to do it this month already covers.

In the theory of planned behavior, attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control shape intention. Her draft covers the others, so the perceived expectations of people who matter (subjective norm) are missing.
items.takeaway: Planned behavior needs attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived control to account for intention.

items.topic: Choosing the ACT process to plan around
items.stem: Assessment with collegiate pole vaulter Amara Diallo shows that she can watch thoughts like "I'll balk" come and go without arguing with them, lets herself feel fear on the runway, and has entered every meet on the schedule. Asked why she vaults, she shrugs: "I've done it since I was ten. I couldn't tell you what it's for anymore." Her consultant, Felix Romero, works from acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT). Which focus should the plan take first?
options: Practice treating her thoughts as passing words rather than facts
Practice making room for fear rather than pushing it away
Clarify what she wants her vaulting to be about and stand for
Commit to dates for the meets that she would rather avoid
rationales: This is cognitive defusion, for a client caught up in her thoughts. Amara already lets hers come and go without arguing.
This is acceptance, for a client who struggles against her feelings. Amara already lets herself feel fear.
Amara shows defusion, acceptance, and action but can't say what the action serves. Values clarification is the ACT process missing from the data, and it gives direction to the skills she already has.
This is committed action, for a client who knows what matters but isn't acting on it. Amara already enters every meet.
items.takeaway: Let the data show which ACT process is missing instead of working through them all.

items.stem: Firefighter Owen Gallagher used to play video games until 3 a.m. between shifts. Eight months ago he moved to an earlier bedtime with screens off, and he has kept to it nearly every free night since, sleeping well. He starts at a busier station next month, wants to hold on to what he has, and asks his consultant for a plan. Using the transtheoretical model, what should the plan focus on?
options: Learning how too little sleep affects alertness and decisions on emergency calls
Weighing what he would gain and lose by changing his bedtime habits
Choosing a start date and telling his crew about the coming change
Spotting nights when old habits could return and preparing for them
rationales: Consciousness raising suits earlier stages, when a person hasn't yet seen a reason to change. Owen changed eight months ago and sees the value.
A decisional balance suits contemplation, when a person is torn about changing. Owen has already changed and wants to keep it up.
Setting a date and making a public commitment suit preparation. Owen's new habit is eight months old.
More than six months of sustained change places Owen in maintenance, where the work is consolidating gains and preventing relapse. A busier station makes it timely to plan for high-risk nights.
items.takeaway: After six months of change, planning shifts from starting the behavior to protecting it.

items.stem: Analyst Leah Brooks has gone quiet in her trading desk's strategy meetings. She tells Hana Ito that junior staff get little airtime there, that "one bad idea and I'm finished," that she feels relief each time she stays silent, and that growing up she was praised when useful and ignored otherwise, "so I keep the real me out of it." Hana works from person-centered theory. Which interpretation of Leah's silence best fits that theory?
options: She hides who she is to meet conditions set on her worth
She treats one poor idea as proof that she would fail
She is rewarded with relief when she stays out of discussions
She has adapted to a desk where some people's ideas count less
rationales: Person-centered theory holds that people who learn their worth is conditional come to deny parts of themselves to keep others' regard. Leah's history of praise when useful, and keeping "the real me" out, fit conditions of worth and the incongruence they create.
Her "one bad idea and I'm finished" could be read as a distorted appraisal, which is the focus of cognitive therapy. Hana's theory looks at conditional regard and the hidden self.
Relief that strengthens silence is a negative reinforcement reading, which belongs to behavioral theory. Hana's theory centers on self and worth.
Attention to who gets heard is a power analysis, as in feminist theory. It fits some of the data, but Hana works from person-centered theory.
items.takeaway: The same data support several readings; the consultant's theory decides which one organizes the plan.

items.stem: Raj Patel is helping a tech company plan an employee exercise program. His theory of planned behavior survey shows that employees have paid time for it and know how to use the on-site gym, believe that managers and coworkers want them to exercise, and have weak intentions to do so. Most rate working out during the workday as unpleasant and of little benefit to them. Which planning priority best follows from these results?
options: Shorter workouts and protected calendar time that make exercise easier to fit in
Enjoyable sample classes and messages on what employees gain from exercise
Senior leaders and respected coworkers who visibly encourage staff to exercise
Planning prompts in which staff write down when and where they will exercise
rationales: Removing obstacles raises perceived behavioral control, but employees already have paid time and know-how. Control is not what holds intentions down.

Control and subjective norms are strong, so the weak link is attitude: employees expect exercise to be unpleasant and unrewarding. Positive experience and information on benefits target those beliefs, and through them intention.
Visible endorsement strengthens subjective norms. Employees already believe that managers and coworkers want them to exercise.
Writing when and where helps people who intend to act but don't follow through. These employees' intentions are weak, so there is little yet to carry out.
items.takeaway: Aim a planned behavior intervention at the predictor the data show is weak.

items.stem: Mira Hoffman, who works from a systems perspective, is asked to help a collegiate hockey team. She learns that the head coach and the starting goalie haven't spoken directly about his playing time in weeks. Each takes complaints to the assistant coach instead, who soothes both and carries messages. Tension eases for a few days after these talks, the disagreement stays unsettled, and the assistant is worn out. Which interpretation should guide Mira's plan?
options: Homeostasis, in which a group pulls back toward its usual way of working
Enmeshment, in which members become so involved that their roles blur
Triangulation, in which two people handle their tension through a third person
Circular causality, in which each person's reaction feeds the other's
rationales: Homeostasis explains a system drifting back after someone tries to change it. No one here has attempted a change; the striking feature is who carries the conflict.
Enmeshment describes overly close, blurred boundaries. The coach and goalie are avoiding each other, and their roles remain distinct.

Coach and goalie route their conflict through the assistant, which lowers tension for a while and lets the issue go unsettled. Seeing a triangle points the plan toward direct talk between the two and relief for the assistant.
Circular causality describes reactions that feed each other back and forth. The coach and goalie have little direct exchange; both go through the assistant.
items.takeaway: When two people send their conflict through a third, work toward direct contact between the two.

items.stem: Zoe Adler's written philosophy states that her role in season is that of an expert who supplies tools athletes can use the same day, and that work on how they think belongs in the off-season. In the middle of a playoff run, professional soccer player Luis Ortega reports harsh self-criticism after mistakes and wants something for tomorrow's match. Which plan is most consistent with Zoe's philosophy of practice?
options: Give Luis a short phrase to say to himself after each mistake
Have Luis log his self-criticism and weigh the evidence for it
Train Luis to observe his self-criticism without reacting to it
Help Luis talk through what his self-criticism means to him
rationales: A ready-made self-talk phrase is a same-day tool supplied by an expert, which is how Zoe defines her in-season role. Plans should follow from the consultant's philosophy, including its view of timing and role.
Logging and evaluating thoughts is cognitive restructuring, which takes repeated practice and works on how he thinks. Zoe's philosophy saves that for the off-season.
Training a new stance toward thoughts is mindfulness work built up over weeks. Luis wants something for tomorrow, and Zoe's philosophy calls for same-day tools.
Exploring personal meaning suits a person-centered philosophy. Zoe defines her in-season role as supplying tools rather than exploring how athletes think.
items.takeaway: A philosophy of practice guides not just which techniques to use but when to use them.

items.stem: Collegiate diver Bianca Moretti believed, "If I'm not calm, I'll miss the dive." Over six weeks Isaac Levin, who uses cognitive-behavioral methods, had her record the thought, weigh the evidence for it, and test it by diving while nervous, in practice and at two small meets. Away from competition she now says with conviction, "I can dive well nervous." Just before her dives at meets, though, the old idea crowds in and she "can't call up what we worked out." What should Isaac do next?
options: Have her record the thoughts she has at the pool this week
Have her weigh what supports and contradicts her belief about calm
Have her predict and then test how she dives while nervous
Have her write her conclusion on a card that she reads poolside
rationales: Recording thoughts helps identify what a client is thinking. The thought has been identified, and Bianca reports exactly what crowds in at meets.
Weighing evidence helps when the client still believes the thought. Bianca has done this and is convinced of the new conclusion.
A behavioral experiment tests a belief that talking hasn't shifted. Bianca has run those dives, at meets too, and is convinced; her trouble is recall under pressure.

Bianca has reached and believes a new conclusion but can't retrieve it at meets. A coping card is the cognitive-behavioral tool for bringing a hard-won conclusion into the situation where it's needed.
items.takeaway: If the new belief is sound but hard to recall under pressure, support retrieval instead of repeating the analysis.

items.stem: Wheelchair basketball player Kofi Boateng rates his confidence at the free-throw line 1 out of 10, though the rest of his game and his life are going well. Elif Demir, who uses a solution-focused approach, has asked him to picture the problem solved, to describe one point higher, and to recall any better spell. To each he answers, "I've got nothing." He still stays late to shoot after every practice. Which question best fits the approach now?
options: "What would you notice yourself doing if you were one point higher?"
"How have you managed to keep going through a stretch this hard?"
"When has your shooting been even slightly better than it is now?"
"If this were solved overnight, what would you notice first tomorrow?"
rationales: A next-point question helps a client define a small step. Kofi has just been asked this and could not answer.
When a client can't see exceptions or a better future, solution-focused practice turns to coping questions. Kofi's extra shooting is a strength, and this question draws out what sustains it.
An exception question finds times the problem is smaller. Elif has asked, and Kofi could recall none.
The miracle question helps a client picture a preferred future. Kofi has been asked to picture the problem solved and came up empty.
items.takeaway: When exceptions and future pictures come up empty, ask how the client has coped.

items.stem: Naomi Barrett, who works from a feminist approach, has supported a collegiate women's ice hockey team that gets worse practice slots than the men's team. Last month the players talked through how the program's rules had shaped the way they see themselves, named the inequity, planned their case, and presented it to the athletic director, who will answer in two weeks. Today they say there is nothing more to do until then, and they want to spend the hour on Saturday's opponent. Which response is most consistent with Naomi's approach?
options: Examine how the rules of their program affect how they see themselves
Work out who will raise the practice slots, with whom, and how
Focus the session on what they can control in their upcoming game
Offer to speak to the athletic director about the practice slots
rationales: Consciousness raising helps people connect personal distress to unequal conditions. These players named the inequity a month ago and acted on it.
Planning collective action empowers a team that is ready to act. The case has been planned and presented, and an answer is due.

Feminist practice treats clients as the experts on their own needs and shares power over the agenda. The players have acted on the inequity, are waiting on a set date, and have chosen how to use the hour.

Advocacy with clients' agreement can fit a feminist approach when their own voice has been shut out. These players were heard, and speaking for them now would take over a process that they're leading.
items.takeaway: Empowerment includes honoring a group's own decision about when to act and when to move on.

items.topic: When an automatic thought is accurate
items.stem: Military flight student Rohan Mehta tells Dana Whitaker, "I could wash out of this program." Dana, who uses cognitive methods, goes through his record with him: he has failed two check rides, and one more failure ends his training. They agree the thought is accurate. Rohan doesn't see it as a verdict on himself; he says he just has no idea how to organize the ten days before his next ride. What should Dana do next?
options: Turn to problem solving and lay out his preparation time
Ask him what in his record supports and contradicts the thought
Ask him what the thought would mean about him if it came true
Set up an experiment that tests whether the thought is accurate
rationales: When an automatic thought proves accurate, cognitive therapy moves from evaluating it to solving the problem it points to. Rohan's difficulty is organizing ten days, and he isn't drawing a harsher conclusion about himself.
Weighing evidence suits a thought that may be distorted. Dana and Rohan have gone through the record and agree the thought is accurate.
Tracing the meaning of a thought, as in the downward arrow, helps when a deeper self-judgment drives distress. Rohan says he doesn't see this as a verdict on himself.
A behavioral experiment tests a belief whose truth is uncertain. The record has already shown that this thought is accurate.
items.takeaway: If a worrying thought checks out as true and carries no distorted meaning, solve the problem.

items.stem: Masters triathlete Gwen Holloway, 61, has medical clearance and no injury. Late in races she tenses up and battles the ordinary burn in her legs, trying to make it stop, and her pace drops. She says that her thoughts don't bother her, that her mind stays on the race, and that she knows just why she competes. Pavel Novak uses acceptance and commitment therapy. Which technique best fits what Gwen describes?
options: Saying "I'm having the thought that" before what her mind tells her
Naming three sights and sounds around her at each kilometer
Writing down what she wants to stand for as a competitor
Breathing around the sensations and letting them stay as she runs
rationales: This is a defusion technique for a client caught up in thoughts. Gwen says her thoughts don't bother her.
This is a present-moment technique for a client whose attention drifts. Gwen says her mind stays on the race.
This is a values technique for a client unsure what the effort serves. Gwen knows just why she competes.

Gwen's difficulty is the struggle to get rid of ordinary discomfort. Acceptance, or willingness, means making room for such sensations while continuing to act, which frees the effort that she spends fighting them.
items.takeaway: Pick the ACT technique for the process that's stuck: thoughts, attention, values, or struggle with sensations.

items.topic: Finding the missing process of change
items.stem: Andre Lefebvre began exercising four times a week two months ago. He sets out his gear with phone alerts on, trains with his sister on most days, and buys himself a record after each full week. The workouts he still misses all follow tense work calls, when he turns on the television to settle himself. Lucia Ferraro is using the transtheoretical model's processes of change. Which addition best supplies the process missing from his plan?
options: Post reminders to exercise where he'll see them each evening
Arrange for a friend to join him at his weekly workouts
Swap his usual way of unwinding after work for a brisk walk
Earn a small treat for each workout that he completes
rationales: Reminders are stimulus control, which his gear and phone alerts already provide. The missed workouts come from how he settles himself, not from forgetting.
A workout partner is a helping relationship, which he already has in his sister.

Counterconditioning means substituting a healthier response for the one that competes with the new behavior. Television is how Andre settles after tense calls, and a brisk walk can take its place; cues, support, and rewards are already covered.
Rewards are reinforcement management, which his record for each full week already provides.
items.takeaway: Compare the processes of change already in use with the pattern of slips to see which one is missing.

items.stem: Collegiate rower Imani Carter arrives for a planned imagery session and tears up, saying her father was diagnosed with a serious illness on Monday. Erik Sandberg, who is person-centered, listens, reflects what he hears, and asks what she would like from today. Imani shows no signs of risk. She says she has talked with family and a campus counselor every day, doesn't want to go over it again, and would love "an hour of just rowing in my head." What should Erik do next?
options: Reflect what she is feeling and give her room to talk
Guide her through the imagery session that they had planned
Give her the details of the campus counseling service
Help her work out how to fit family visits around training
rationales: Erik has already listened and reflected, and Imani says she doesn't want to go over it again. Steering her back to it would put his idea of what she needs ahead of hers.
Person-centered work trusts the client to know what she needs. Imani has been heard, has support, and has plainly asked for the imagery, so going ahead with it is following her lead.
Offering a counseling contact helps a client who lacks support or asks for it. Imani is already seeing a campus counselor daily and shows no signs of risk.
Practical planning helps a client who is torn over logistics. Imani raises no such difficulty and has said what she wants from the hour.
items.takeaway: Following the client's lead can mean going ahead with the planned skill when that is what they ask for.

items.stem: Professional softball pitcher Rosa Jimenez says that after walking a batter she falls apart. At their third session, game charts bear her out: across eleven outings there is no exception. Each time she has responded the same way, stepping off the mound, lecturing herself, and throwing harder. Rosa wants a task for this week's games. Will Thornton uses a solution-focused approach. Which task best fits what they know?
options: Do something different after a walk, even if it seems odd
Do more of what she did in outings that went better
Notice what in her pitching she would like to keep happening
Predict before each outing how it will go after a walk, and check
rationales: With no exceptions and the same unhelpful response repeated, solution-focused practice follows the rule that if something isn't working, do something different. De Shazer's "do something different" task breaks the pattern without analyzing its cause.
Doing more of what works needs exceptions that the client can repeat. The charts show none in eleven outings.
Noticing what she wants to continue is the formula first-session task, useful when the complaint is vague. This is the third session, and the complaint is specific.
Prediction tasks help when good outings occur but the client can't explain them. Rosa's charts show no good outings after a walk.
items.takeaway: Solution-focused tasks follow the data: repeat what works, and when nothing has worked, do something different.

items.stem: Freya Lind, an elite cross-country skier, reaches each start through a settled warm-up routine, knows her focus cues for every section of the course, and writes down the lessons after each race. When something unexpected happens, such as a broken pole or a late course change, she stays rattled for several kilometers. Her consultant, Carlos Mendes, builds on Orlick and Partington's mental links to excellence. Which element should they practice next?
options: A pre-race plan for her warm-up and the final minutes before the start
A race plan with focus cues for each section
An evaluation plan for drawing lessons from races
A distraction control plan for getting back on task quickly
rationales: A precompetition plan is one of the elements, and Freya already has a settled warm-up routine. Her difficulty arises during races.
A competition focus plan is one of the elements, and Freya knows her cues for every section. Those cues don't cover what to do when something goes wrong.
Constructive evaluation is one of the elements, and Freya already writes down lessons after each race.

Successful Olympians in Orlick and Partington's study had practiced ways to refocus after distractions. Freya's preparation, focus cues, and evaluation are in place; what she lacks is a rehearsed way back when things go wrong.
items.takeaway: Check which mental link is missing before adding more of those that the athlete already has.

items.stem: Thandiwe Mokoena consults with coaches at a youth club who want players to develop composure. Her observations show that the coaches stay calm on the sideline, give warm support, and expect full effort. Players admire how calm their coaches are but say they have no idea how to do it themselves; the coaches had assumed it would rub off. Drawing on research into how Olympic champions' psychological characteristics developed, which coach action should she help them add?
options: Model the calm behavior that they want to see from players
Give players more encouragement and emotional support after losses
Teach players composure skills directly during regular practice time
Set higher expectations for players' effort and discipline at practice
rationales: Modeling is one route through which coaches influenced champions, and these coaches already do it. Players admire the calm but can't tell how to produce it.
Support from coaches featured in champions' development, and these coaches already give it warmly. It doesn't show players how to become composed.

Gould and colleagues found that coaches and parents shaped champions' psychological characteristics both directly, by teaching, and indirectly, as by modeling. The indirect route is in place here, and players need to be taught how.
High expectations featured in champions' development, and these coaches already expect full effort. Expectations don't tell players how to stay calm.
items.takeaway: Coaches shape mental strengths both by example and by direct teaching; add the route that's missing.

items.stem: Mireille, a collegiate 400 m hurdler, tells the consultant, "One weekend I'm shaking in the call room and sure I'll hit a hurdle. The next weekend, same coach, same teammates, I walk out calm and trusting my legs." The consultant would like to set numbers for these swings beside her finishing times at each of the next six meets. Which questionnaire should the consultant give her?
options: The Sport Anxiety Scale-2 (SAS-2)
The Test of Performance Strategies (TOPS)
The Competitive State Anxiety Inventory-2 (CSAI-2)
The Profile of Mood States (POMS)
rationales: The SAS-2 describes how anxious an athlete tends to be across competitions. Mireille's report differs from one weekend to the next, and a trait score would not follow that.
The TOPS asks how often an athlete uses mental skills in practice and competition. Her swings are in how she feels, not in which skills she uses.
Best. Her shaking, doubt, and trust in her legs change from meet to meet, so a state measure with somatic, cognitive, and self-confidence scores, taken before each race, can be set beside her times.
The POMS covers broad moods such as vigor, fatigue, and anger. It has a tension score but nothing on self-confidence, half of what swings for her.
items.takeaway: Symptoms that change from event to event call for a state measure taken at each event.

items.stem: A professional rugby club's coach sent Casimir, a fly-half, to the consultant after several poor goal-kicking games. Casimir arrived guarded. Half an hour into the intake he has said that the misses are costing him sleep, that he wants to be the one who takes the late kicks again, and that a quiet spell alone on the tee after training used to settle him. "I could pick that up again Monday," he says. "I should have done it weeks ago." Which response best fits motivational interviewing?
options: "How do you see yourself getting started?"
"What bothers you most about how it's been going?"
"It was your coach's idea to come, not yours."
"Would you like to hear what has helped other kickers?"
rationales: Best. Desire, ability, need, and a date have all come from Casimir, signs that he is ready to move from evoking to planning. An open question about starting leaves the plan in his hands.
An evoking question draws out concern when a client has voiced little. Casimir has voiced plenty and has turned toward action; going back would slow him down.
Reflecting the pressure he arrived under helps while he is guarded. He has since moved well past that point.
Offering information with permission suits a client who wants change and has no idea how. Casimir has named something that worked for him.
items.takeaway: Listen for mobilizing change talk: when the client has a reason and a way, move to planning.

items.stem: The coach of a collegiate field hockey team sends Adaeze to the consultant because she "chokes" in penalty shootouts. She has converted 3 of 11 in matches. In training, against the same goalkeepers with nobody keeping score, she has converted 21 of 80. Her teammates manage more than half in both settings. Adaeze, who played defense until August, grins about the misses and says she'll get the hang of it. Her SAS-2 scores are ordinary for college athletes. Which working formulation best fits?
options: Worry that disrupts a well-practiced skill under pressure
Low confidence that has built up with repeated misses
Attention that strays to distractions when stakes rise
A shootout technique that she has yet to learn
rationales: Worry would show up as a gap between training and matches and, most likely, raised worry scores. Her rate is about one in four in both places.
Low confidence would show in how she talks about the next attempt. She shrugs the misses off and expects to improve.
Straying attention tied to the stakes would spare her training attempts. Those fail as often as her match attempts.
Best. She converts about a quarter of her attempts with or without pressure, is new to an attacking role, and is not anxious. "Choking" needs a drop from a level she has shown, and there is none.
items.takeaway: Choking means falling below your own level under pressure; check that the level exists first.

items.stem: At a national selection camp, a judo federation asks the consultant to meet each athlete. Bongani, who is fighting for one of two spots, hands back the ACSI-28 after two minutes. Scored, it gives him a mixed profile, with some subscales at the top and freedom from worry at the bottom. Looking at the sheet itself, the consultant sees that he circled "almost always" for every statement, whether it was about staying calm or about fretting over mistakes. Which reading of the form do his answers best support?
options: He is presenting himself well for the selectors
He answered with little regard to item content
His coping is strong overall, with worry as a soft spot
His answers describe the camp rather than his usual self
rationales: An athlete trying to look good would deny fretting over mistakes. Bongani endorsed the unflattering statements as strongly as the flattering ones.
Best. Agreeing as strongly with opposite statements is a careless or acquiescent response pattern. The mixed profile comes from reverse-scored items, so it says little about his coping.
This is what the scored profile appears to show. The subscale differences come from how items are keyed, since his answer never changed.
Answering about the present week would still yield answers that fit together. Saying he is almost always calm and almost always fretting does not.
items.takeaway: Look at the raw answers before the profile: identical answers to opposite items mean the scores cannot be read.

items.stem: Following the athletic department's intake policy, the consultant gives Marisela, a collegiate softball pitcher, a validated depression screen alongside performance measures. Her score falls in the range the department flags for follow-up. "That sounds right," she says. Sleep and energy have been poor since January, though she has had no thoughts of hurting herself. "We started medication last month and we're still adjusting it. I'm in there every Thursday." What should the consultant do about the score?
options: Walk her over to the counseling center's on-call staff
Give her the names of two clinicians near campus
Ask to send the result to the clinician treating her
Continue the intake and screen her again at midseason
rationales: A walk to on-call staff fits a student whose safety is in doubt. She reports no thoughts of self-harm.
New names help an athlete who has no care. Her weekly visits and recent medication show that she has it, and a second provider could split her treatment.
Best. She is in active treatment that is still being adjusted, so the useful step is to coordinate: with her consent, the result goes to the person who can act on it.
Routine rescreening fits a score in the normal range. Hers is in the flagged range and calls for follow-up now.
items.takeaway: A flagged screen needs clinical follow-up; if care is in place, coordinate with it, with consent.

items.stem: Rhys, a 20-year-old professional esports player, has filled out a performance profile listing fourteen qualities of a top player in his role, with a rating of himself on each for now and for where he wants to be. He and his coach agree that it is a fair picture. Three gaps stand out, each four points wide: aim in late rounds, shot-calling, and patience after early losses. There is time to work on one before the season. Which step would do most to turn the profile into a choice?
options: Rate how much each quality matters in his role
Have his coach rate him on the same qualities
Re-rate himself after reviewing some match film
Add qualities that he sees in players he admires
rationales: Best. The gaps are the same size and the ratings are trusted, so size cannot rank them. Weighting each gap by its importance to his role is the part of profiling that is missing.
A second rater helps when player and coach see him differently. The coach already accepts the picture.
Film can steady ratings that rest on mood or memory. Nobody doubts these ratings, and repeating them could leave the same three-way tie.
Widening the list helps when a player has named few qualities. Fourteen already cover the role, and more would add candidates.
items.takeaway: In profiling, a gap's priority depends on its size and on how much the quality matters.

items.stem: A high school volleyball coach asks the consultant why the team "comes apart" in close sets. Pressed for an example, she laughs. "Honestly? One day they're silent, another day they're all yelling. Sometimes nobody moves, sometimes two girls go for the same ball. I can't tell you what it is. I just know it when I see it." The consultant will watch Saturday's match. Which way of observing best suits this first look?
options: Count each player's calls on a prepared checklist
Time how long the team takes to regroup after errors
Compare calls for the ball in close and lopsided sets
Write running notes on what happens around lost points
rationales: A checklist gives precise counts once the behavior has been defined. The coach cannot yet say which behavior matters, so a checklist might count the wrong thing.
Timing suits a behavior known to drag on. The coach's examples vary, and slow regrouping is not among them.
Comparing conditions tests a specific idea about when a behavior changes. Here the behavior is still unknown.
Best. The problem is undefined and takes many forms, so open narrative notes on what comes before and after lost points can show what is worth defining and counting later.
items.takeaway: Count behaviors once you know which ones matter; until then, start with narrative observation.

items.stem: Esme, an 11-year-old competitive gymnast, has assented to work with the consultant, and her parents have given permission. Her coach says, "State finals, club meet, a pretend meet with six moms watching, it makes no difference. She frets for days, her tummy hurts, and then she blanks on beam." The consultant wants a questionnaire for the initial assessment. Which one best fits?
options: The Competitive State Anxiety Inventory-2 (CSAI-2)
The Sport Anxiety Scale-2 (SAS-2)
The Profile of Mood States (POMS)
The Athletic Coping Skills Inventory-28 (ACSI-28)
rationales: The CSAI-2 captures anxiety at one moment before an event and was developed with older athletes. Esme's pattern is the same at all meets.

Best. Fretting, stomach aches, and blanking at meets of all sizes point to a general tendency involving worry, somatic anxiety, and concentration disruption. The SAS-2 measures these and was developed for children as well as adults.
The POMS tracks general moods such as fatigue and vigor. It is not specific to performing and was not developed for children.
The ACSI-28 profiles coping skills such as coachability and goal setting. It touches on worry but not on stomach aches, and it was developed with older athletes.
items.takeaway: Anxiety that shows up at events of all sizes suggests a trait measure; for children, use one built for them.

items.stem: Nalani, a contemporary dancer, believes that one slip in an audition will finish her. With the consultant she has recalled four slips, her own and her friends', and three of those dancers were hired anyway. "So it's unlikely," she says. "But say it's me. They stop writing, somebody says 'thank you,' and then... I don't know. Lights out." She has stopped at this spot twice before. Which question best helps her think the feared outcome through?
options: "What goes through your mind as you walk into the studio?"
"What have you seen happen to dancers who slipped?"
"What would a slip say about you as a dancer?"
"What would you do in the weeks after a no?"
rationales: This question brings out an automatic thought that has not yet been put into words. Nalani has stated hers clearly.
Asking for evidence is a core Socratic move, and she has just done it. The evidence changed her estimate of the odds but not her dread of the outcome.
The downward arrow looks for the meaning beneath a thought. She is stuck on what happens next, and this would turn her toward judging herself.
Best. The odds have been examined; her picture of the outcome simply ends. Asking what would follow is decatastrophizing, and it lets her see whether she could cope.
items.takeaway: When the odds have been examined and dread remains, ask what would happen next and how the client would cope.

items.stem: Dmitri, a wheelchair basketball player on a national squad, shoots 78% on free throws through three quarters and 55% in the fourth. His coach, who rarely takes him off the court, says he loses focus. On the ACSI-28, Dmitri rates his concentration highly, and he says that late or early he thinks of nothing but his breath and cue word. Over two games the consultant saw the same breath, the same tempo, and the same cue late as early, and most of the late misses hit the front of the rim. What should the consultant do next?
options: Compare late shooting in games with fewer minutes
Code his free-throw routine over several more games
Ask what he is thinking on fourth-quarter attempts
Give the TAIS to see how his attention narrows
rationales: Best. The routine holds up and the misses fall short, so tiring arms are a strong rival to lost focus. Records of games in which he played less are a simple check before a mental formulation is settled.
Coding his routine would help if it seemed to break down or had gone unseen. In two games it did not change.
He has already said what he thinks late in games, and what was seen agrees with it. His account cannot show why the shots fall short.
An attentional profile would suit signs that he is distracted or overloaded. Neither his reports nor his behavior shows any.
items.takeaway: Before settling on a mental explanation, test the physical one that the data suggest.

items.stem: Ezra, a first-year collegiate cross-country runner, says he grew up in a house where nobody hurried to speak. At intake the consultant has twice followed up after a few seconds of quiet, and each time he gave a polite one-line reply. Once, she had to search for a pen; when she looked up, he had begun a long, careful account of what his running means to his family. Now she asks what a good season would be. He looks at the floor, at ease, and says nothing. What should she do?
options: Put the question in simpler words
Tell him they can come back to it
Wait quietly until he speaks
Reflect that the question seems hard
rationales: Rewording helps a client who has not understood. Nothing suggests that, and it would be a third interruption.
Offering to return to a topic respects a client who does not want to discuss it. Ezra is at ease and has talked freely when given time.
Best. His fullest answer came when she happened to leave him time, and her quick follow-ups cut him short. His silence reads as thinking, and waiting adapts her pace to his way of talking.
Reflecting feeling helps when the client shows some. He is at ease, so this would put her discomfort with silence into his mouth.
items.takeaway: The meaning of silence varies; match your pace to the client's before treating it as a problem.

items.stem: A consultant takes over preseason testing at a professional women's basketball club, her only role there. The consent form, which the players signed after a question-and-answer session, says that ACSI-28 scores go to the general manager for use in roster decisions. The consultant has used the inventory for ten years. Reading down her report, the general manager says, "Twelfth and thirteenth are two points apart. That settles our last spot." Which concern bears most directly on this plan?
options: The players have not agreed to this use of their scores
The scores have little evidence behind them for this purpose
The consultant is also the players' confidential adviser
The consultant lacks the training to interpret the inventory
rationales: Lack of consent would be decisive if the players had been promised another use. Here the form named this one.
Best. The ACSI-28 describes coping skills; it was not validated for choosing between two players, and two points means little given measurement error. Consent does not make an invalid use valid.
Dual roles would matter if she also counseled the players. Testing is all she does for the club.
Competence would be the issue for someone new to the measure. She has used it for a decade.
items.takeaway: Even with consent, a score should be used only for decisions its validity evidence supports.

items.stem: Quillon, a collegiate archer, scores high in training and drops at tournaments. He insists that he does "the same mental stuff" everywhere. The consultant leafs through his log. The training pages are full of cue words, pictured shots, and slow breaths between ends. The tournament pages list arrows, scores, and the weather. The consultant would like a questionnaire that could test the pattern the log suggests. Which one fits best?
options: The Athletic Coping Skills Inventory-28 (ACSI-28)
The Sport Imagery Questionnaire (SIQ)
The Test of Attentional and Interpersonal Style (TAIS)
The Test of Performance Strategies (TOPS)
rationales: The ACSI-28 gives a general picture of coping skills. It does not separate training from tournaments.
The SIQ covers what imagery is used for. Imagery is one of several skills that vanish from his tournament pages.
The TAIS profiles attentional tendencies. The log shows a difference in skill use and says nothing about where his attention goes.
Best. The log suggests that he uses several skills in training and few of them at tournaments. The TOPS asks about the use of such strategies in practice and in competition separately.
items.takeaway: When the question is whether skills are used in practice and in competition, the TOPS scores both.

items.stem: A ballet company has hired the consultant to work with Zainab, a soloist, who has agreed in writing that the artistic director may share observations. The director sends a page. It dates three performances and tells what happened in each, describes the coaching she has tried, and notes that Zainab is radiant in studio runs and at matinees. It ends, "I need more presence from her by spring. Then I'll know you two have done it." Which question should the consultant ask the director first?
options: "What would you see if she had more presence?"
"When did you last notice this, and what happened?"
"What have you already tried with her?"
"When do you see her at her best?"
rationales: Best. The director's note is concrete about the past and vague about the target. "Presence" is the standard by which the work will be judged, so it needs to be described in observable terms.
Asking for specific incidents is the remedy for vague complaints. She has given three, with dates and details.
Earlier attempts are worth knowing, and the director has described them.
Exceptions and strengths help balance a list of faults. She has already named studio runs and matinees.
items.takeaway: Find what the stakeholder has left vague; often it is the standard by which success will be judged.

items.stem: Saskia, a professional golfer, is the one her playing partners ask about wind and slope. "She sees the whole hole," her caddie says. Over the ball it is another story: "I've still got the wind going, and the last putt, and my coach, and what if I push it. It all piles up and I swing in the middle of it." The consultant wants a questionnaire whose scores could show both sides of this. Which one fits best?
options: The Athletic Coping Skills Inventory-28 (ACSI-28)
The Test of Performance Strategies (TOPS)
The Test of Attentional and Interpersonal Style (TAIS)
The Sport Anxiety Scale-2 (SAS-2)
rationales: The ACSI-28 has one concentration score. It cannot show that she takes in the surroundings well and is overloaded by her own thoughts.
The TOPS asks about the use of skills such as self-talk and relaxation. Her description is of where her attention goes.
Best. She is strong at broad-external attention and is overloaded by internal thoughts. The TAIS gives separate scores for attentional strengths and for types of overload.
The SAS-2 includes concentration disruption as a part of anxiety. It has no score for her ability to read a hole.
items.takeaway: Match the instrument to the pattern: the TAIS separates attentional strengths from types of overload.

items.stem: The director of a youth soccer academy has noticed that after the same drill, run by the same coach, some 13-year-olds ask, "Did I beat him?" and others ask, "Was that quicker than last week?" Before a coach-education course begins, she would like to know how these two kinds of players are spread across her squads. Parents have given permission and players have assented. Which questionnaire should the consultant suggest?
options: The Athletic Identity Measurement Scale (AIMS)
The Task and Ego Orientation in Sport Questionnaire (TEOSQ)
The Perceived Motivational Climate in Sport Questionnaire (PMCSQ)
The Group Environment Questionnaire (GEQ)
rationales: The AIMS measures how strongly a person identifies with being an athlete. The players differ in how they judge a good performance.
Best. The drill and the coach are the same, so the difference lies in the players: some judge success by comparison and others by improvement. The TEOSQ measures these dispositions.
A climate measure asks what players think their coaches reward. The same coach and drill produce both questions here, so the director's interest is in the players.
The GEQ measures cohesion. How united the squads are is a separate matter from how players judge success.
items.takeaway: Goal orientation belongs to the player; motivational climate belongs to the setting.

items.stem: Callum, a collegiate lacrosse goalkeeper, has rated his confidence on game mornings for five weeks. The numbers run from 3 to 9. Asked about the 9s, he gives a new answer each time: his coach's nod, a sharp warm-up, his brother in the stands, the home crease. Asked about the 3s, he shrugs. Before planning any work, the consultant wants a questionnaire to find out what those numbers hang on. Which measure fits best?
options: The Sources of Sport-Confidence Questionnaire
A self-efficacy scale graded by difficulty of save
The self-confidence subscale of the CSAI-2
The Trait Sport-Confidence Inventory
rationales: Best. The level of his confidence is already recorded; what is unknown is where it comes from. This questionnaire covers sources such as preparation, social support, coach leadership, and environmental comfort.
A graded scale would show which saves he believes he can make. His ratings vary by day, and he has not tied them to kinds of shots.
This would give another reading of how confident he is before games, which his morning ratings already supply.
A trait score shows how confident he usually is in sport. It would not account for ups and downs.
items.takeaway: Knowing how confident an athlete is differs from knowing where the confidence comes from.

items.stem: Katarzyna, a soldier on an army rifle team, pictures shooting every night. The images come when she calls them, she says, in color, with the weight of the rifle and the smell of oil. Asked what she pictures, she says, "Oh, all sorts." Over a month she has mentioned the bolt and breath, a medal ceremony, a quarrel with a range officer, and walking calmly to the line. The consultant wants a questionnaire to help sort this out. Which one fits best?
options: The Movement Imagery Questionnaire-3 (MIQ-3)
The Test of Performance Strategies (TOPS)
The Test of Attentional and Interpersonal Style (TAIS)
The Sport Imagery Questionnaire (SIQ)
rationales: The MIQ-3 measures how easily a person can see and feel imagined movements. Her images already come readily and vividly.
The TOPS could show how often she uses imagery among other skills. It does not sort images by purpose.
The TAIS profiles attention. Nothing here is about what she attends to while shooting.
Best. She images often and well but with mixed content: skills, rewards, and emotions. The SIQ shows how often imagery serves each of its cognitive and motivational functions.
items.takeaway: The MIQ-3 asks how well a person can image; the SIQ asks what the imagery is used for.

items.stem: Since a run of trades, the coach and captains of a professional ice hockey club have watched the 14 forwards and the 8 defensemen drift apart: separate tables, separate cars, separate jokes. Within each bunch, spirits are high. The players are willing to fill out the GEQ if no names are attached, and they want to know, as much as the coach does, whether things are as bad as they look. Which way of giving and reporting the GEQ best serves this purpose?
options: Unmarked forms, reported as team averages
Coded forms, tracked for each player over the season
Forms marked by position, reported as group averages
Named forms, gone over with each player in private
rationales: Team averages are the usual report when a whole team's unity is in question. Here they would blend two groups that may see things differently.
Codes let each player's scores be linked over time. The question is about a divide that exists now.
Best. The concern is a split along position lines, and both groups are large enough for averages to keep individuals hidden. Marking position shows whether the groups see the team differently.
Named forms would support individual talks, but the players have agreed only to nameless ones and the concern lies between groups.
items.takeaway: Report group data at the level where the question lies, with groups large enough to protect individuals.

items.stem: In an intake session, Amadou, a collegiate wrestler, asks for help getting tougher about making weight. He weighs in tomorrow. He has eaten almost nothing for three days and ran in a sweat suit last night. He admits that he panics when he eats these days. Reaching for his bag, he grips the desk until the room stops turning; it happened on the stairs too, he says, and his heart has been skipping since lunch. The team physician is in the sports medicine office across the hall. What should the consultant do first?
options: Arrange a visit with a clinician who treats eating disorders
Take him to the team physician
Arrange a visit with the athletic department's dietitian
Help him plan how to tell his coach that he's moving up
rationales: His panic about eating calls for this, and it should follow. It can be set up once he has been seen for symptoms that could be dangerous today.
Best. Dizzy spells and an irregular heartbeat after fasting and dehydration may be a medical emergency. Prompt medical evaluation comes before any other help he needs.
A dietitian can help plan a safe weight class and fueling. That is for a wrestler who is not in physical trouble today.
Support for that conversation may help later. He has not decided to move up, and his symptoms come first.
items.takeaway: When warning signs include acute physical symptoms, medical evaluation comes first and other referrals follow.

items.stem: In a first video interview, Tadeo, a professional esports player, is asked about the frustration ("tilt") that follows lost rounds. He says, "Am I stuck like this? No. I went a whole year on the academy roster without blowing up at anyone, and we lost plenty. That guy's still in here somewhere." The consultant reflects this back and notes it in the record. In motivational interviewing, what kind of change talk is it?
options: A statement of desire to change
A statement of reasons to change
A statement of ability to change
A statement of steps toward change
rationales: Desire talk tells what a person wants, as in "I wish" or "I'd like." Tadeo does not say what he wants.
Reason talk gives an argument for change, such as what tilt costs him. He gives no such argument.
Best. He answers "Am I stuck?" with proof from his own past that he can stay composed. That is ability talk, one of the preparatory forms of change talk.
Taking-steps talk reports recent action toward the change. His example is from a past season, offered as proof of what he can do.
items.takeaway: Past success offered as proof of what is possible is ability talk; taking steps is recent action.

items.stem: Wren, a masters cyclist, completed the ACSI-28 at intake and is curious about the results. "I hope you won't do what my old boss did with appraisals," she says. "He'd slide the sheet across, we'd go line by line, I'd nod, and on the train home I'd realize I hadn't taken in a word. Then I'd have a hundred questions." They meet again on Friday. What is the best way to give Wren her results?
options: Send her a plain summary to read before Friday
Go through each score with her on Friday
Open with her strengths on Friday, then the rest
Set the results aside and have her retake it Friday
rationales: Best. Her story shows that she takes things in on her own and comes up with questions later. Reading first lets her use Friday to ask them and to say how the results fit.
A line-by-line talk is a common way to give feedback, and it is the experience she says left her nodding and taking in nothing.
Strengths first can ease a client who is braced for bad news. Wren is curious and has a different problem with feedback.
Retesting makes sense when the answers may not be sound. Nothing suggests that hers are not.
items.takeaway: Feedback on results should suit the way the client takes in information.

items.stem: Marte, an elite sprint canoeist, used to lie awake before big regattas. Last season she filled out the CSAI-2 in the team hotel after dinner, on the eve of two national regattas, and her cognitive anxiety scores were high. She has since spent eight weeks practicing a wind-down routine. Two club regattas come up this month, and two national ones next month. Her coach is eager for news. When should the CSAI-2 be repeated to judge whether the routine is helping?
options: An hour before her races at the club regattas
An hour before her races at the national regattas
On the evening before the club regattas
On the evening before the national regattas
rationales: A club regatta and the final hour both differ from baseline. A lower score could come from the smaller stakes.
The stakes would match, but anxiety in the last hour may not resemble anxiety at bedtime, when her problem occurs.
The hour would match and the news would come sooner, but club events would likely stir less worry with or without a routine.
Best. State anxiety varies with the time to competition and with its importance. Matching both lets the new scores be compared with last season's.
items.takeaway: Repeat a state measure under the baseline conditions: the same kind of event at the same time before it.

items.stem: At intake, Nomvula, a collegiate tennis player, built a performance profile and rated herself on ten qualities. Ten weeks later she has met the targets she set, and her coach has moved her from singles to doubles for the rest of the year. Reading down the old sheet at their review, she laughs. "Patience from the baseline? I'm at the net all day now." She and the consultant want to use profiling to plan the next ten weeks. Which approach fits best?
options: Have her re-rate the ten qualities
Have her list new qualities and rate those
Have her coach rate her on the ten qualities
Have her rate how she now thinks she was at intake
rationales: Re-rating the same qualities is the usual way to review progress. She has met her targets, and the sheet no longer describes the game she plays.
Best. A profile's qualities belong to the performer's role as she sees it. Her role has changed, so planning calls for a new list even though it gives up comparison with the old one.
A coach's ratings help when the two see her differently. The trouble here is the list, not the rater.
A look back helps when the player's understanding of a quality has changed what her numbers mean. She plans to look ahead, and the qualities have lost their relevance.
items.takeaway: Re-rate a profile to measure progress; rebuild it when the role it describes has changed.

items.stem: Farah, an executive who meets with the consultant by video, has been learning paced breathing to settle herself before board presentations.
