Her log shows a session every night for six weeks. With her consent, the consultant sees wearable data showing that her breathing slows to the target pace within a minute. Her ratings of stress before presentations have not moved. "On board days I'm on the phone until the door opens," she says. Which reading best fits these results?
options: The skill is learned but is not used where it is needed
The skill is used where it is needed but does not suit her
The skill is helping in ways that her ratings do not show
The skill needs more practice before it can be judged
rationales: Best. She can slow her breathing quickly and practices nightly, yet a board day leaves her no moment to do it. The results show learning without transfer, so the technique has not been tested in presentations.
To conclude this, she would have to be using it before presentations. Her remark about the phone says that she is not.
Other signs of calmer presentations would be needed. There are none here, and she has not used it on those days.
More practice would be needed if she were slow to settle. Six weeks of nightly sessions and a one-minute response show that the skill is there.
items.takeaway: Before judging a technique, separate three questions: was it learned, was it used, and did it help?

items.stem: A consultant has run a team-building program for a collegiate rowing squad: shared dinners, a buddy system, and a service project. On the GEQ, given anonymously, the squad's social scores were low in September and are high in January, in all four boats. The captains have seen the change around the boathouse. "I'm convinced," says the coach. "But I have money and hours for one of the three this spring. Which do I keep?" What would best help the consultant answer?
options: Repeating the GEQ at the end of the season
Observing how rowers mix before and after practice
Holding focus groups with rowers from each boat
Comparing GEQ scores boat by boat
rationales: A later GEQ would show whether the gain lasts. It would come after the choice, and it gives no score for each activity.
Observation would check the scores against behavior. The coach accepts the change, and the captains have seen it.
Best. The GEQ shows that cohesion rose, not which activity brought it about. Rowers' accounts of the three activities speak to the coach's choice.
A breakdown by boat would show who gained. All four did, and they shared the same three activities.
items.takeaway: Outcome scores show whether a program worked; to learn which part helped, ask the participants.

items.stem: Teodor, a professional alpine skier, began working with a consultant in summer and has completed the TOPS three times. From fall to midwinter, his practice scores for self-talk stayed high. In competition, his self-talk score fell by a third and his automaticity score rose by about as much, with other scores steady. He has had his best four results of the season. "I used to talk myself down the whole hill," he says. "Now I just ski." Which next step do these data best support?
options: Adding race simulations so that self-talk carries over
Reteaching the self-talk cues that have slipped
Asking what has been unsettling him on race days
Continuing as they are through the rest of the season
rationales: Simulations help skills move from training to races. His race self-talk was in place and has given way to something that is working.
Reteaching would suit a lost skill. His practice scores show that he still has it.
Race-day trouble would show in other scores, such as emotional control or negative thinking, or in results. Those are steady or better.

Best. Less deliberate self-talk with more automaticity and better results looks like a skill that no longer needs effort. Nothing calls for a change, and asking for more self-talk could get in his way.
items.takeaway: A drop in deliberate strategy use can mean progress; read it beside automaticity and results.

items.stem: Leopold, a firefighter, is working on recovering his composure in the minutes after a serious alarm. Some weeks bring six such calls and some bring none. In the first month the consultant asked each Sunday how the week had gone. "Fine, I think," he said, or, "There was a bad one, or was that the week before?" On the drive back to the station, though, he can describe a call to the minute. Which way of tracking his progress fits best?
options: A five-item rating that he completes on Sunday evenings
A two-item rating that he completes after serious calls
A checklist that his officer completes after each shift
A full skills inventory that he completes each month
rationales: Weekly ratings suit a state that builds or fades over days. His problem is tied to calls, and by Sunday he has lost the details.
Best. The target occurs in single events that come irregularly, and he remembers them well just afterward. Event-based ratings catch each one while it is fresh.
An officer's view helps with signs the client misses. Leopold can describe his own calls well, if asked soon enough.
A full inventory shows broad change in mental skills. It would not show what happens after particular alarms.
items.takeaway: Match the timing of measurement to the target: irregular events call for ratings tied to the event.

items.stem: With his consent, a consultant at a national training center has given Yerlan, an elite long-track speed skater, the POMS every week since spring. Ten days into a heavy block, his fatigue is up and his vigor down, as happened in last year's block, and both ease after rest days. His tension and anger scores have doubled as well. Looking back over the chart, the consultant sees that those two began to climb during his week of leave, before the block. What should the consultant do next?
options: Ask him what has been happening away from training
Talk over with him how the training block is going
Plan with him what to tell his coach about recovery
Help him set up a visit with a licensed clinician
rationales: Best. Fatigue and vigor follow the load, but tension and anger rose while he was resting. Training cannot explain a change that came before it, so the consultant should find out what else is going on.
A talk about the block suits mood changes that follow the load. Fatigue and vigor do, and they ease with rest; the two scores that stand out began to climb before it.
This suits fatigue and vigor that stay poor with rest. His recover after rest days.
Referral fits signs of a mental health concern, such as lasting low mood or loss of interest. Two raised scores with no known reason call for a talk first.
items.takeaway: Line up mood scores with the training calendar; a change that comes before the load has another source.

items.stem: Before teaching Saoirse, a collegiate diver, a pre-dive routine, the consultant coded video of three meets, timing her from the referee's whistle to takeoff. Six weeks into the routine, an intern coded three more meets, timing her from her first step along the board. The second set of times averages four seconds shorter and varies little from dive to dive. The coach is delighted that she has "stopped dawdling." What should the consultant do before drawing a conclusion?
options: Have three more meets timed from the first step
Have her note after each dive which steps she completed
Have the later meets timed again from the whistle
Have practice dives timed from the first step
rationales: More meets help when results are few or scattered. These are consistent, and more of them timed from the first step would leave the problem in place.
Self-report adds what a camera cannot see. The conclusion in question is about time, which video can show.
Best. The two sets start the clock at different points, so the four seconds may come from the rule and not from Saoirse. Applying the baseline definition makes the sets comparable.
Practice video would test use in another setting. It cannot tell whether her meet times changed.
items.takeaway: Before comparing observations, confirm that both sets use the same behavioral definition.

items.topic: Choosing evidence for a final review
items.stem: Talia, a collegiate fencer, asked an online consultant for help with one thing: how nervous she feels in the minute before a bout. They agreed to judge progress on that. She completed the Test of Performance Strategies at intake and has sent a 1-to-10 nerves rating from the strip before every bout since. Her last bout of the season was Saturday, and their closing review is tomorrow. Which evidence should the consultant rely on most to judge progress?
options: Her TOPS scores from intake and from a new administration tomorrow
Her pre-bout ratings from early in the season and from recent bouts
Her scores on the CSAI-2, completed as tomorrow's review begins
Her coach's account of how composed she has looked before bouts
rationales: Repeating the TOPS fits a goal about how often she uses mental skills. Her agreed goal was how nervous she feels, which the TOPS doesn't measure.
Evaluation should use the measure that matches the agreed goal, gathered the same way over time. Her ratings capture felt nerves in the moment that matters, with early and recent points to compare.
The CSAI-2 would fit if she could complete it shortly before a bout. State anxiety at a review meeting says little about how she feels on the strip, and there is no earlier score to compare.
A coach's view helps when the goal is visible behavior. How nervous she feels is a private experience that outward composure can hide.
items.takeaway: Judge progress with the measure that matches the agreed goal and was gathered the same way throughout.

items.topic: Entry with a skeptical head coach
items.stem: A minor-league baseball club has hired a consultant, and the general manager has told field manager Bogdan Dudek why. Over a long breakfast, Dudek talks about how he runs a team and what he wants from his players; when the consultant sums it up, he says, "That's it exactly." Then he shrugs. "The last one had slides and studies. Nice fella. I never saw one of my guys do anything different." Which step would best build a working relationship with Dudek now?
options: Ask how he coaches and what he wants from his players
Give him a short summary of research from professional baseball
Run a brief exercise with a few of his players at practice
Have the general manager go over the program's purpose with him
rationales: Learning a coach's philosophy is usually where entry starts, but he has just laid it out and confirmed the consultant's summary. Asking again would look like not having listened.
A research summary suits a coach who asks what the evidence is. Dudek connects studies with a consultant whose work he never saw make a difference.
Entry should speak to what this coach counts as credible. With his aims understood, his remark shows that he judges by what players do, so a small, visible sample of the work fits him best.
Sponsorship helps when a coach doesn't know why a program exists. Dudek has been told; his doubt is about whether it changes anything on the field.
items.takeaway: Once a coach's aims are understood, build credibility in the currency that coach trusts.

items.stem: Before enrolling, all 30 volunteer coaches at a youth soccer club and the club's director agreed in writing to one rule for a consultant's coach-education program: whatever is used to judge a coach goes to the director, and whatever is meant to help a coach stays with that coach. Twice this season the consultant rated each coach's practice on the form the club uses to assign next year's teams, then met privately with the coach about things to work on. Now the director writes, "What should I expect from you?" What should the consultant send?
options: Each coach's ratings from the two practices, listed by name
Average ratings from the two practices, with names left out
A summary of what each coach discussed in the private meetings
A list of the coaches who completed both of their meetings
rationales: The form decides team assignments, so it is used to judge coaches and, under the rule everyone accepted before enrolling, goes to the director. Roles and information flow agreed at the outset should be honored as written.
Averages would protect coaches if the agreement had limited reporting to group results. Here they would withhold what the coaches knowingly agreed the director would have.
The meetings were about things to work on, so they were meant to help and stay with the coach.
A completion list suits an agreement to report participation alone. This agreement promises the director more than that.
items.takeaway: When reporting terms were clear and accepted at the start, carry them out, no more and no less.

items.topic: Naming the client in joint work
items.stem: A national federation gives each of its adult figure skaters ten hours with a consultant and wants only an invoice in return. The coach of skater Tove, who has trained her for six years, calls to book the hours. "We used to finish each other's sentences," he says. "Now I say one thing, she hears another, and we both go quiet." When the consultant phones Tove, she tells it much the same way: "I could talk to you alone, but then what? It happens when we're both standing there." As roles are set out, whom should the consultant name as the client?
options: The skater, with her coach consulted as needed
The coach, with his skater's views used as feedback
The federation, with skater and coach as participants
The pair, with both taking part on an equal footing
rationales: This suits a skater who wants help with her own skills or concerns. Tove says that the problem lives in what happens between them and that working alone would miss it.
This suits a coach who wants to develop his own coaching. He made the call, but he describes a shared pattern, as does she.
Paying for a service doesn't by itself make an organization the client. The federation has asked for no report and has no stake in the goals.
Both locate the trouble in their interaction and want to address it with the other present, so the relationship is the focus and the two of them are jointly the client.
items.takeaway: Identify the client from whose concern is being worked on, not from who called or who pays.

items.stem: Working from mastery-oriented coach training, a consultant watches an under-11 soccer practice with its coach. Lupe, who has been passing cleanly all week, rushes one and sends it wide. She groans, taps her ankle, and mutters, "Locked it too late." The drill moves on and the next ball is already rolling her way; she glances over at the coach, who says nothing. Afterward he asks the consultant how he might have responded to that pass. What should the consultant suggest?
options: Show her the correct technique once more
Encourage her and let the drill go on
Praise the technique she used on the pass
Remind her of the team's rules for drills
rationales: Corrective instruction helps a child who doesn't know what went wrong. Lupe named the error herself, so a demonstration adds little and slows the drill.
After a mistake, mastery-oriented training calls for encouragement right away. When the player already knows how to fix it, as Lupe's remark shows, encouragement by itself is enough.
Praise for technique fits a well-executed pass with an unlucky result. This one was rushed, she knows it, and praise for it would ring false.
Reminders of agreed rules are for lapses in conduct. Lupe made a playing mistake while trying.
items.takeaway: If a young athlete already knows the fix, encouragement alone is the best response to a mistake.

items.stem: A university women's rowing team rated how often they would prefer, and how often they see, four kinds of behavior from their new coach, Ulrike, on a 5-point scale. The average preferred and perceived ratings were 4.4 and 4.3 for training and instruction, 2.2 and 3.9 for democratic behavior, 3.1 and 3.0 for social support, and 4.2 and 4.1 for positive feedback. Satisfaction has slipped since she arrived, and the staff think the style the rowers want suits the season. Based on the multidimensional model of leadership, which change should the consultant suggest to Ulrike?
options: Teaching more technical detail during practice
Giving rowers more praise for good work
Taking more interest in rowers' lives off the water
Settling more of the training decisions on her own
rationales: Instruction is already within a tenth of a point of what the rowers want, so more of it would open a gap rather than close one.
Preferred and perceived positive feedback nearly match, so it isn't where the satisfaction problem lies.
The rowers see about as much social support as they prefer.

The one large gap is in democratic behavior, where the rowers see far more than they prefer. In Chelladurai's model, satisfaction depends on actual behavior matching preferred behavior, and that can mean doing less of something.
items.takeaway: Congruence cuts both ways: when athletes see more of a behavior than they want, leaders should offer less of it.

items.stem: A consultant is mediating between two esports teammates, Bao and Jasper, who have been blaming each other over voice chat. In the first half hour, each told how the blowups look from his seat, and each put the other's side into words until he heard, "Yeah, that's it." Since then they have been tossing out fixes: one of them always calls, they split the map, whoever has vision calls. There are seven ideas on the whiteboard, and the last two are the first two reworded. What should the consultant have them do next?
options: Choose one idea and decide how they will check it
Describe the problem and how it affects each of them
Restate each other's point of view to show they heard it
Come up with more ideas without judging any of them
rationales: Both sides have been heard, and repeats on the board show that new ideas have run out. Conflict resolution now moves from generating to selecting a solution and planning its follow-up.
Airing each side comes first in a mediation. They did this at the start, and going back risks reopening the blame.
Checking understanding comes before solutions. Each has already heard the other confirm that he was understood.
Brainstorming is valuable until it dries up. Seven ideas with repeats suggest that it has.
items.takeaway: Track where a mediation is in its sequence, and move forward when a stage has done its job.

items.topic: Parents who coach from the stands
items.stem: A consultant helped Coach Hadiya open the age-group swim season with a parent meeting, at which families talked through the roles of coach and parents and signed spectator guidelines they had drafted. Six weeks in, the bleachers are cheerful and the swimmers look to Hadiya before their races, with one exception. Before each of her events, 11-year-old Aino is called to the rail by her father, who whispers a race plan; last week she asked Hadiya, "So which one do I swim?" What should the consultant suggest that Hadiya do?
options: Hold another meeting on roles for all of the parents
Send all families the spectator guidelines in writing
Have a private conversation with the one father
Teach her swimmers a routine for focusing before races
rationales: A group meeting is the right preventive step and the right answer to a widespread problem. Here every family but one is following what was agreed.
Written guidelines help when expectations are unstated or forgotten. Families drafted and signed these, and nearly all keep to them.
Education of the group has worked for the group. A lone, repeated lapse is best raised by the coach in private with the parent concerned, focused on his child's confusion.
A refocusing routine suits distractions that can't be removed. This one comes from a parent whom the coach can speak with, and the other swimmers aren't distracted.
items.takeaway: Use group education for shared problems and a private talk for one parent's lapse.

items.stem: A consultant asks players on a high school girls' basketball team about their coach, Marcus Bell. "First in the gym, and he owns his mistakes." "He's got us seeing ourselves at state, and I actually believe it." "He figured out I learn by watching, so he sends me clips." In games, though, when an opponent switches defenses, five heads turn to the bench. "He'll tell us what to run," a guard explains. "It's his system, and it's a good one." Drawing on transformational leadership, which behavior should the consultant help Bell develop?
options: Living up to the standards he sets for the team
Asking players to question and improve what they run
Painting a picture of what the team could become
Fitting his coaching to what each player needs
rationales: Idealized influence is already present: players see him arrive first and own his mistakes.
Players wait for answers and treat the system as his. Prompting them to challenge assumptions and solve problems is intellectual stimulation, the component their accounts lack.
Inspirational motivation is already present: players picture themselves at state and believe it.
Individualized consideration is already present: he has noticed how a player learns and adapted to it.
items.takeaway: Match the development target to the transformational component that athletes' accounts leave out.

items.stem: Elite judoka Yusuf and his coach each complete a coach–athlete relationship questionnaire twice: once to give their own view, and once to guess how the other would answer. On a 7-point scale, all of their own ratings of closeness, commitment, and complementarity fall between 6.1 and 6.7. Their guesses about the other fall between 3.2 and 4.0 on all three. Training runs smoothly, yet each has privately told the consultant that he is "waiting for the other shoe to drop." Based on the 3+1Cs model, which activity best addresses the main issue?
options: Spending unhurried time with each other away from training
Writing down what they plan to do over the next three seasons
Hearing from each other how they really see the partnership
Agreeing on signals for giving and answering instructions
rationales: Shared time builds closeness, but both already rate their own closeness above 6.
A long-term plan shores up commitment, but both already rate their own commitment above 6.
Each feels strongly about the partnership and badly underestimates the other. The gap is in co-orientation, so the work is to bring their perceptions of each other into line with reality.
Signals build complementarity, but both already rate it above 6, and training runs smoothly.
items.takeaway: High direct ratings with low guesses about the partner point to a co-orientation problem.

items.stem: A consultant is helping a university men's lacrosse team share leadership more widely. Teammates agree that goalie Tevita runs the defense and fixes spacing on the fly, that two juniors lift everyone when the team is down, and that a senior midfielder is where players go to patch up quarrels. Over the fall, a booster dinner took place without a single player, the campus paper printed three players' conflicting accounts of one game, and the athletic director's office complained that it never knows whom to call. Which leadership role should the consultant help the team fill?
options: A task leader, who directs play and gives tactical advice
A social leader, who looks after relationships off the field
A motivational leader, who lifts teammates during games
An external leader, who represents the team to outsiders
rationales: The goalie already provides task leadership by running the defense and fixing spacing.
The senior midfielder already provides social leadership by helping teammates patch up quarrels.
Two juniors already provide motivational leadership.
The dinner, the newspaper, and the athletic director's office all involve people outside the team. Nobody holds the external role, though the task, social, and motivational roles are covered.
items.takeaway: Map athlete leadership roles against what is going wrong, and develop the one nobody holds.

items.stem: A consultant works with the coaches of a youth softball club. One of them, Marjolein, forwards an email she received this morning: "At the weekend tournament, Nell sat two innings of each game. The handbook says half of every game, unless I've misread it. Does that cover tournaments? No rush. I just want to tell her the right thing." The handbook, which Marjolein follows, has a separate line for tournaments. She has had a heated season with two other families and asks the consultant how to handle this one. What should the consultant advise?
options: Reply by email with what the handbook says
Set up a private meeting after a day or two
Cover tournament rules at the next parent meeting
Pass the email along to the club's director
rationales: This is a calm request for information that has a short factual answer. A prompt written reply respects the parent and settles it, whereas a bigger response would make a dispute of a question.
A cooling-off period and a private meeting suit an upset parent. Nell's parent is calm and wants a fact, so a meeting would raise the temperature.
A general explanation suits confusion shared by many families. Only one has asked, and that parent would be left waiting.
The director is the right next stop when a parent contests the rule or a coach's decision after speaking with the coach. This parent is doing neither.
items.takeaway: Match the response to the message: a calm factual question calls for a simple factual answer.

items.stem: A national-league women's ice hockey team gets a new coach midseason. The staff and the league's analysts agree that with a roster this young and a schedule this hard, detailed tactical teaching and firm direction are called for. On a preseason questionnaire, the players asked for loose practices and a large say in tactics. The new coach scripts each practice, stops play to teach, and makes the tactical calls herself, as she has done everywhere she has coached. Players follow her plans. According to Chelladurai's multidimensional model, which outcome is most expected if none of this changes?
options: Good performance and good satisfaction
Good performance and poor satisfaction
Poor performance and good satisfaction
Poor performance and poor satisfaction
rationales: Both outcomes are expected to be high when actual behavior matches what is required and what is preferred. Her style doesn't match what the players prefer.
Her actual behavior fits what the situation requires but not what the players prefer. The model links the first match to performance and the second mismatch to dissatisfaction.
This pattern is expected when the coach gives players what they prefer but not what the situation requires.
Both outcomes are expected to be low when behavior matches neither requirements nor preferences. Hers matches the requirements.
items.takeaway: In the multidimensional model, actual–required fit drives performance, and actual–preferred fit drives satisfaction.

items.stem: Paralympic wheelchair racer Wanjiru and her coach describe their work to a consultant. She says, "He's family. He says a word, I fix it; I ask, he's got an answer." He says, "Couldn't be fonder of her, and sessions run themselves." Each can say, correctly, what the other thinks about tactics, equipment, and training. But he has been answering calls from other squads, she has left his contract for next season unsigned on her desk, and both know it. "We take it a month at a time," she says. Under the 3+1Cs model, which aspect of the relationship most needs attention?
options: Commitment, their intention to stay together
Closeness, their trust in and liking for each other
Complementarity, how well their actions fit in training
Co-orientation, how accurately they read each other
rationales: His calls from other squads, her unsigned contract, and the month-at-a-time talk all point to weak intentions about the partnership's future.
Both speak of each other with affection and trust.
A word brings a fix and a question brings an answer, so their actions in training fit well.
Each knows the other's views, and both know about the calls and the contract.
items.takeaway: Commitment concerns the pair's intentions for the future, even when affection and cooperation are strong.

items.stem: A consultant is preparing a sales company's managers to lead ten-minute team check-ins built around a reset routine after lost deals. The managers have studied a guide and can give its steps and purpose from memory. Over two rounds of paired practice with feedback, they have covered each step, in order, in the flat tone of someone reading terms and conditions. "Is it meant to feel like a meeting?" asks one. "A pep talk? A chat?" Several others turn to the consultant, pens ready. The first real check-ins are in three weeks. What should the consultant do next?
options: Give the managers a fuller guide to the steps
Run another round of paired practice with feedback
Lead a check-in as the managers watch
Sit in on managers' check-ins with their teams
rationales: A fuller guide helps people who are unsure what to do or why. These managers already know the steps and purpose by heart.
More rehearsal helps people who know what they are aiming for. After two rounds the managers still don't know what a good check-in is like.
The managers know the content but have no picture of the performance, as their questions about its feel reveal. A live model gives them a standard to aim at when they practice again.
On-the-job observation suits managers who can lead a sound check-in and need support in carrying it over. These managers aren't there yet, and real check-ins are three weeks away.
items.takeaway: When learners know the steps but not what good looks like, model it before more practice.

items.topic: Family roles in consent with minors
items.stem: Sina, 15, a club soccer player, has been offered sessions on match nerves. Her father has signed the permission form. He says that in their family a new adult is met together, and that he expects to sit in. The consultant usually sees teenagers one-on-one. Talking with Sina at the side of the training field, the consultant asks what she makes of the plan. She shrugs: "My sister did this by herself at school, and she quit after one time. I'm the one who told Dad to come." How should the consultant set up the first sessions?
options: Meet with Sina, and send her father a summary she approves
Meet with her father first, and start with Sina once he is at ease
Meet with Sina and her father together, and review the setup later
Hold off on sessions, and leave the offer open to Sina
rationales: This is a sound arrangement for a teenager who wants private sessions and a parent who wants to be kept informed. Sina asked her father to come, so it would remove something she chose.
This suits a parent who is withholding permission until he understands the work. He has already signed the form and is ready to begin alongside her.

Her father's permission is in place, and Sina's assent turns out to be assent to sessions with him there. The consultant's usual format is a preference rather than a rule, and it can be revisited as the work goes on.
Waiting respects a minor who does not assent. Sina is not declining; she has arranged the condition under which she wants to come.
items.takeaway: With minors, permission and assent can point to a format other than the consultant's usual one.

items.stem: A consultant new to the fire service has spent six weeks riding along with a city department's crews. At first they called her "the campus doctor." Now a senior captain saves her a seat at dinner, and engineers at two stations, separately, have asked how she would keep a clear head on the drive to a call. Last night the captain teased, "So do we get anything out of you, or do you just eat our chili?" What should she do next to build her credibility with the crews?
options: Teach a short skill at shift change
Ride along on more shifts
Survey the crews about their needs
Ask a captain to vouch for her work
rationales: She has been accepted, and crews at separate stations have named the same need. The captain's joke signals that presence has done its work; being useful is now what earns credibility in this setting.
Time on shift is how an outsider learns a tactical culture, and it has worked. The teasing suggests that more of it would start to look like having nothing to offer.
A survey helps when needs are unclear. Two stations have independently raised the same one, and a form would put off what they have asked for.
An insider's backing helps an outsider who is being kept at a distance. The captain already treats her as one of the crew, and nobody has yet seen any work to vouch for.
items.takeaway: Contextual intelligence includes noticing when a group has moved from sizing you up to expecting something of you.

items.stem: Valeria, a professional volleyball player in her second season at a club abroad, asks to see the club's consultant, who speaks only the local language. In a first talk she hunts for words but describes confidentiality and its limits back accurately. The consultant offers to arrange an interpreter. She laughs: "My agent, my doctor, my landlord: every time, somebody in the middle. This year I order my own coffee." Which arrangement for the sessions fits best?
options: Use a trained interpreter from outside the club
Use a trained interpreter by video from another city
Refer her to a consultant who speaks her first language
Speak directly in the local language
rationales: A trained, independent interpreter is the usual safeguard when a client wants one or cannot follow. Valeria follows well enough to consent, and her answer is about doing without a go-between.
Remote interpreting protects privacy where every local interpreter is known to the client. Nobody's identity is her concern; she does not want a third person at all.
Work in a first language can be best when feelings cannot be put into words otherwise. She wants to use the new language and has sought out this consultant.
She can give informed consent in the language, and her remark tells the consultant that managing without a go-between matters to her. Checking meaning protects accuracy while respecting that choice.
items.takeaway: When understanding is adequate, language arrangements follow the client's wishes rather than the provider's default.

items.stem: A consultant is assessing pre-competition anxiety in a national goalball squad. The players, who have visual impairments ranging from partial sight to no light perception, variously use large print, braille, or neither. All of them text and fill in forms on their own phones, set up with screen readers or magnifiers. After a federation survey last year, one told the consultant, "Sighted teams fill theirs in and nobody else ever knows. I had to say mine out loud to a staff member, so I kept it tame." Others agreed. Which way of gathering the players' ratings fits best?
options: Paper copies prepared in large print and braille
A one-to-one interview with the items read aloud
A web form that players fill in on their phones
A group talk about nerves before competition
rationales: Alternative print formats give privacy to those who read them. Some players use neither format, so they would again need to answer to somebody.
Reading items aloud is a fair accommodation for a player who wants it. Having to voice answers to staff is what these players objected to.
Each player already has a phone set up to suit their own vision, so a properly built form lets all of them answer independently and in private, as sighted athletes do.
A group talk can bring out shared experience. It would not yield individual ratings, and it makes answers more public than last year's survey did.
items.takeaway: Accessible assessment means equal privacy and independence, not just access to the items.

items.stem: Idris, a collegiate 10,000-meter runner, is sent to a consultant during Ramadan. His coach writes that he is "flat, probably the fasting." Idris says he has fasted through five track seasons and runs after the evening meal on a plan made with the dietitian. His training log shows steady workout times in those earlier seasons. This year they began to slip in late January, the week the coach split the distance runners into two squads, and Ramadan started a month later. What should the consultant explore next?
options: How he is eating and sleeping during the fast
What keeping the fast means to him this year
How his coach responds to him while he is fasting
What the new training squads have been like for him
rationales: Fueling and sleep would come first if the slump had begun with the fast. It began a month earlier, and the same routine has worked for five seasons.
Asking about meaning is worthwhile if he seems torn or alone in his practice. He describes a settled practice, and the timing points elsewhere.
Strained support would matter if trouble tracked the coach's reactions to fasting. The slip was under way before there was any fasting to react to.

The log ties the start of the slip to the squad change rather than to the fast. Culturally responsive assessment tests a referral source's cultural explanation against the data instead of adopting it.
items.takeaway: Treat a cultural explanation as a hypothesis and check it against the timeline.

items.topic: Locating the strain in a transition
items.stem: Terrence, a first-year rugby player at a university far from home, has missed four early lifts. He has won a starting place and calls the rugby "easier than I thought." His grades are good, and he works the same warehouse hours he worked through high school. Asked about the lifts, he says, "Back home my uncle had the kettle on and Dre was outside with the car. I've been up before six since I was twelve. Here the alarm goes and there's nobody." In Wylleman and Lavallee's developmental model, at which level is his transition strain?
options: At the athletic level
At the psychological level
At the psychosocial level
At the academic–vocational level
rationales: Strain at this level comes from the step up in training and competition. He is starting and finds the rugby manageable.
This level concerns developmental tasks such as forming an identity in late adolescence. He describes missing companions rather than uncertainty about who he is.
The habit of early rising always ran on people: an uncle, a friend with a car. What the move changed is the set of relationships around his sport, which is the model's psychosocial level.
Study and work fall at this level and can crowd out training. His grades are sound and his work hours have not changed.
items.takeaway: The developmental model asks which of several simultaneous transitions is carrying the strain.

items.stem: In a first meeting, Dashiell, a professional contemporary dancer, says he is gay and asks whether the consultant has worked with LGBTQ+ performers. "A few," she says. "I'm still learning, and I'd want you to tell me if I miss something." He leans back. "That's more than the last two admitted. One of them kept me on coming out for a month. I'd come about casting calls." He says he would like to go ahead with her, and casting anxiety is an area she knows well. What should she do next?
options: Begin on what happens to him at casting calls
Ask what being understood would look like to him
Offer names of colleagues with more such experience
Describe what her LGBTQ+ clients have taught her
rationales: He has asked about her experience, had a candid answer, and chosen to go on. His complaint about earlier providers is that they made his identity the topic, so responsiveness here means turning to his concern.
This question suits a client who says that past providers failed to understand his life. His story is of providers who would not leave the subject.
Other names help a client who wants someone with closer knowledge. He has heard the limits of hers and wants to continue, and his concern is one she is competent to address.
Saying more could help if he doubted her answer. He was satisfied with it, and more talk would put off his reason for coming.
items.takeaway: Cultural responsiveness sometimes means answering the question honestly and then getting to work on the client's concern.

items.stem: On the first morning of a camp, a consultant interviewed each member of a visiting national field hockey team through the team's own interpreter. Answers were a few words long, and eyes stayed lowered. Her draft says "low confidence, weak communication." Over the next three days she hears the same players shouting corrections across the pitch and disputing calls with the umpire. At breakfast, two of them tell their physio at length how well they are striking the ball, the same interpreter beside them. Which reading of the interviews fits these data best?
options: The players were short of confidence
The players were reserved with a stranger
The players were deferring to seniority
The players were misunderstanding the questions
rationales: Low confidence should appear in more than one place. The players correct one another, dispute calls, and speak well of their own form.
The quiet appears with an unfamiliar interviewer and disappears with teammates, an umpire, and a physio they know. It says something about the interview rather than about confidence or communication.
Deference would show as looking to, or waiting for, senior members. The interviews were one at a time, and players openly corrected each other.
A language problem would be likely if the interpreting were poor. With the same interpreter they talk freely.
items.takeaway: Before labeling a trait, check whether the behavior follows the person or the setting.

items.stem: A consultant's intake form asks for "mother's name," "father's name," and gender, each with fixed blanks or boxes. Maren, a 24-year-old climber, says the page made her feel she had to account for herself before she had sat down. Going back through two years of files, the consultant sees that she never drew on those answers. What she used came from the first conversation, when she asks every client how they would like to be addressed and who they turn to for support. What should she do about these items?
options: Add a wider set of boxes to each of them
Take both of them off the form
Replace the boxes with open blanks
Mark both of them as optional
rationales: More categories help when answers must be counted in a standard way. Nothing is being counted here, and boxes still ask clients to fit themselves in.
The answers have served no purpose, and what she does need is already gathered from every client in conversation. Intake should ask for information that is relevant to the service.
Open blanks suit information that is used but poorly captured by set categories. This information goes unused, so clients would still be explaining themselves for nothing.
Optional items make sense when the form itself cannot be changed. It is her own form, and skipping an item can still feel like a statement.
items.takeaway: Ask at intake for what the work will use; an unused identity question costs the client something.

items.topic: Framing goals around a client's values
items.stem: Maeve, a collegiate softball pitcher, is setting goals for the spring. Last year's strikeout goal "felt like homework." The team's goal of reaching the conference final moved her, but by April, she says, "I couldn't have told you if I'd had a hand in it." Asked for her best day, she picks a game with no strikeouts, after which the shortstop hugged her and said, "You kept us busy all night." She wants something to work on each time she pitches. Which goal fits best?
options: "Keep my changeup at the knees in bullpen sessions."
"Help us hold opponents to three runs a game."
"Help us get back to the conference final."
"Throw early strikes so my infield gets to play."
rationales: This is a controllable process goal and would suit someone driven by her own craft. Nothing in it touches the teammates who made her best day her best.
A team performance goal ties her to others, but nine players produce the number. She would be back to wondering what her part had been.
The shared outcome stirred her last year and gave her nothing to judge her own part by.
Early strikes are hers to work on every time she pitches, and the goal is framed by what matters to her: giving teammates a part in the game.
items.takeaway: Controllable goals hold better when framed by what the client values, including contribution to others.

items.stem: A community soccer league wants a consultant to help parents of its 10- to 13-year-olds handle the ride home after games, when, players say, "the replay starts." Interviews show that most parents work evenings and weekends and ride shared vans or buses to games. Practices have just been cut to 50 minutes, and parents rarely attend them. When a field changes, the team managers post it in group chats, with English, Spanish, and Vietnamese versions, and nearly every household replies within the hour. Which delivery plan fits best?
options: A weekend workshop with interpreters on hand
Short clips posted to the team group chats
Brief segments built into team practices
Printed handouts sent home with the players
rationales: Interpreters remove one barrier to a workshop. With parents at work on evenings and weekends and dependent on shared transport, few could be there.
The plan has to reach parents, and the chats already do, in the languages they use and on their own schedule. It builds on a working resource instead of fighting time and transport.
Practice segments reach players and coaches without extra travel. The aim is a change in parents, who are rarely there, and practice time has just shrunk.
Handouts help where phones or data are scarce. These households answer messages within the hour, and paper relies on players to pass it on.
items.takeaway: Plan delivery around channels a community already uses.

items.stem: Ignacio, 31, a national-team kayaker, will retire after the world championships in 18 months. His program asks consultants to begin transition goals at that point. Ignacio has a job waiting at the boat workshop where he has spent four off-seasons, coaches his daughter's robotics team, and grins when asked about life after racing. He is healthy and has made every team for six years. Then he shows the consultant video of two finals he lost in the first 50 meters: "That's what wakes me up at night." What should the plan center on?
options: His composure and reactions at the start
His interests and roles outside of racing
His meetings with a career advisor
His coping with an earlier end to racing
rationales: Vocation, roles outside sport, and expectations for retirement are already in place, so transition goals would be planned for the program's sake. His own concern and the performance data point to the start.
Broadening an exclusive athletic identity is important before retirement. Ignacio already has a trade, a parenting role, and things he looks forward to.
Career advising helps an athlete who needs a vocational direction. His job is arranged and he knows it well.
Preparing for an unplanned exit suits an athlete whose place or health is in doubt. Ignacio is healthy and has been selected without a break.
items.takeaway: Transition theory informs the plan; the client's actual readiness decides how much of it is needed.

items.topic: Responding to a microaggression in a workshop
items.stem: In a workshop with a collegiate women's basketball team, one player asks a teammate of Korean descent, "But where are you really from?" The room goes quiet. "Toledo, like I put on the roster," the teammate says. "You can do better than that one." The player reddens: "You're right. That was lazy, I'm sorry." The teammate nods, others murmur agreement, and the two go back to arguing happily over the next drill. It is the first such remark the consultant has heard in this group. What should the consultant do?
options: Name the remark's impact, and restate the group's norms
Pause the activity, and open up a group discussion
Carry on with the activity, and check on the teammate later
Carry on with the activity, and talk to the asker later
rationales: The facilitator should speak when the target is left to carry the moment alone. She has named the remark herself, and the player took it in; repeating it would take the moment away from her.
A discussion fits when remarks like this are a pattern the group has not faced. This was a first instance, and the players have settled it.

The target spoke for herself, the player apologized without defending it, and the group backed her. A private check-in later allows for any impact that didn't show without reopening the matter in public.
A private talk with the asker suits someone who misses the point or keeps doing it. She saw the problem at once and apologized.
items.takeaway: Facilitators make sure impact is acknowledged; when the group has done so, a private check-in may be enough.

items.stem: Two police recruits stay behind before the first class of a breath-focused stress program. "Somebody at our church said these classes have you chanting to something," one says. "We don't do that." The other adds, "If it's just breathing, fine. Nobody's told us what it is." The course, which the academy requires, involves paced breathing and noticing when attention wanders, with no chanting or devotional content. How should the consultant respond?
options: Teach them an attention exercise that uses no breathing
Put them in touch with the academy chaplain to talk it over
Ask the academy to make the course optional for recruits
Tell them what the classes do and don't include
rationales: An alternative with the same aim is right for recruits whose objection stands once they know what the practice is. These two object to something the course doesn't contain.
A chaplain can help recruits who want religious guidance on a practice. They have not asked for guidance; they lack information that the consultant has.
Seeking a change in the requirement makes sense if an informed objection can't be accommodated. There is no informed objection yet.
Their concern rests on a rumor about content, and one says plainly what would make it fine. An accurate description respects their faith and lets them judge for themselves.
items.takeaway: Find out whether a values concern is about the practice itself or about what someone has heard of it.

items.topic: Adjusting imagery for a blind athlete
items.stem: Thandeka, an elite para judoka who has been blind since birth, has rebuilt her imagery script with her consultant around grips, footfalls, and the shift of her opponent's weight. She practices it on the mat in her judogi. "It's all in there," she reports, "and the throw comes off in the time it really takes. But I could be folding laundry. Then Saturday comes and my mouth is dry and my heart's going, and it's like I've never been there before." What should they change next?
options: Add more touch and sound to the throws
Add the nerves and urgency of a match
Rehearse the throws at true match speed
Rehearse on the mat, dressed for a match
rationales: Richer tactile and auditory detail would help if the script seemed thin or relied on sight. She says the content is all there.
The script has the task, setting, and timing but none of the feelings of competition, so match day feels new. PETTLEP's emotion element calls for imaging the emotions and arousal of the real event.
Matching real timing is another PETTLEP element. Her throws already take the time they really take.
Physical and environmental similarity support functional equivalence. She already practices on the mat in her judogi.
items.takeaway: PETTLEP is a checklist: find the element that is missing for this athlete.

items.stem: At season's end, a consultant to a professional women's soccer team reads unsigned evaluation forms, completed in players' own languages and collected by the players' union. Ratings average 9 of 10, with little spread. The comments are just as warm, and nearly every form also objects to something: the Monday slot, a role-play that dragged, the slides. A coach waves the numbers away: "Half of them come from clubs where you'd never criticize staff." How should the consultant treat the ratings?
options: Report the ratings as credible evidence
Report the ratings as inflated by politeness
Report the ratings separately by players' origin
Hold the ratings, and repeat the form in midseason
rationales: The forms were unsigned, independent, and in players' own languages, and the same players criticized freely. The coach's claim about their background predicts something the data don't show.
Politeness could inflate signed forms handed to the consultant. These were unsigned and independently collected, and players criticized specifics freely.
Separate reporting would be useful if ratings differed by group. They have little spread, and splitting them would build the coach's assumption into the report.
Repeating a form helps when it was given before players knew the program well. It was given at the end of the season.
items.takeaway: Cultural knowledge suggests a threat to validity; the data decide whether it is there.

items.stem: A club consultant has worked for a season with Jonas, a 27-year-old hockey forward whose contract will not be renewed. Her role with him ends in two weeks, and he has booked both remaining sessions. He is sad but sleeping well and seeing friends, and a players' association advisor starts with him on the first of the month. "We'll do a proper goodbye in the last one," he says. A club overseas has invited him to a three-day tryout on Tuesday. "I know hockey's been my whole self," he says. "The advisor and I start on that." What should the first remaining session focus on?
options: Who he is and could be outside of hockey
What support he can draw on after the club
What he needs mentally for the tryout
What he has gained over the past season
rationales: Exploring identity is valuable after deselection, and he agrees. He has help arranged for it, with time to do it, and the tryout is days away.
Connecting a client with continuing support is a key part of concluding. An advisor is already in place and friends are close.
Support and a closing session are already arranged, and he is coping. The time-limited need, and the one he raises, is readying himself for Tuesday.
Reviewing gains belongs in a closing session, which he has already placed in the last meeting.
items.takeaway: Concluding well means using the remaining time for what isn't already covered.

items.topic: Revising a plan for acculturation stress
items.stem: Seo-yeon, a first-year collegiate golfer who moved from overseas for school, is six weeks into work on her pre-shot routine. Video shows the routine complete on nearly all shots, in practice and in tournaments alike. Her classes are going well. Her scores at home events match her practice rounds, but on road trips they climb after the first day. Her journal for those weekends reads: "Ate in my room. Thought up a joke in English, and they'd moved on. Didn't sleep much." Which change to the plan fits these data best?
options: Add crowd and scoring pressure to routine practice
Arrange support for her coursework in English
Shorten the routine to spare effort late in rounds
Add goals for connecting with teammates on trips
rationales: Simulated pressure helps a routine that breaks down in competition. Hers holds in tournaments, and her home scores show it.
Academic language support would fit if study demands were wearing her down. Her classes are going well.
A shorter routine suits a player whose steps fall away as she tires. The routine is complete on nearly all shots.
The routine is intact, and scores slip where she is isolated and losing sleep. Reassessment points to acculturation stress on road trips, so the plan should grow to address connection there.
items.takeaway: When a skill is intact and scores still vary, look at the context in which they vary.

items.stem: A consultant leads mental skills for a running program for adults resettled after fleeing conflict. On feedback forms, runners say she asks rather than assumes, owns her mistakes, and reworks exercises that don't suit them. One writes, "I'm glad you ask me. But you are the fourth one to ask, and I am tired of explaining what an asylum hearing is." Two others say much the same. Which next step in her development best fits this feedback?
options: Keep a journal of the assumptions she brings
Study the circumstances that her clients live with
Practice adapting techniques with a supervisor
Invite clients to say more about their backgrounds
rationales: Self-reflection builds awareness of her own assumptions, one of the multicultural competencies. Runners already see her questioning them.

Her awareness and flexibility are evident. What is missing is knowledge of clients' worlds, and leaving clients to supply it has become a burden. Multicultural competence includes learning on one's own time.
Supervised practice builds culturally appropriate skills. Runners say she already reworks exercises that don't suit them.
Asking clients reflects cultural humility, and she does it well. More asking would add to the load they describe.
items.takeaway: Humility means asking about the person; competence includes not making clients teach you what you could look up.

items.stem: Reviewing two years of case notes, a consultant sees that Dante, a 19-year-old boxer, is "not really committed." He had moved three sessions because his delivery shifts changed, and had made up each one. She had used the phrase for two other athletes, both of whom moved sessions for work. Athletes who moved as many for exams or family trips are "busy" or "juggling a lot." She recalls her own college years, when her parents paid her way. She enjoys Dante and leaves sessions with him energized. What does her phrase most likely reflect?
options: A standard set by an advantaged upbringing
A reaction carried over from a past relationship
A sign that her caseload is wearing her out
A fair reading of his readiness to change
rationales: The same behavior earns a different label depending on whether a paid job caused it, and paid work is what she never had to fit around sport. Seeing how one's social position shapes judgment is the work of self-reflexivity.
Countertransference would show as feelings tied to a particular person from her past. The phrase spans several athletes, and she enjoys Dante.
Strain would show across clients and in her energy. Her sessions with Dante leave her energized, and the label follows one kind of reason.
The phrase would be fair if Dante were avoiding the work. He has made up each session.
items.takeaway: Compare how you label the same behavior in different clients; the pattern may be about you.

items.topic: Competence and choice for a Deaf client
items.stem: Nerys, a collegiate wrestler who is Deaf and uses American Sign Language, asks the athletic department's consultant for help with pre-match nerves. The consultant doesn't sign and has not worked with Deaf athletes; a colleague on the same staff signs fluently and has openings. The consultant lays out several ways they could work. Nerys says she has no tie to either of them, adding, "In the training room it's me, the trainer, and an interpreter. Same with my professors. I'd love one conversation with just two people in it, in my language." What should the consultant do?
options: Arrange a qualified interpreter, and seek consultation
Hold sessions by typed chat, and review how it goes
Invite the colleague to co-lead, and learn from her
Refer Nerys to the colleague, and help with the handoff
rationales: An interpreter plus consultation is a sound way to extend competence when a client chooses this consultant or no signing provider exists. Nerys wants a conversation without a third person, and a signing colleague is free.
Typed chat leaves two people in the conversation and suits a client who prefers it. English on a screen is not the language Nerys asks for.
Co-leading helps a client who wants to stay with a consultant still building competence. It would put a third person back in the room.
The colleague alone can offer what Nerys describes: direct conversation in ASL between two people, with fitting competence. She has no tie to this consultant that would weigh against it.
items.takeaway: Extending competence is one ethical path; a better-placed colleague the client would prefer is another.

items.stem: A consultant with a collegiate football program hears the linebackers coach call an injured player "soft" and praise another for "never bothering the trainers." The other position coaches talk about injuries matter-of-factly, as the head coach has asked them to. The athletic trainer's figures show steady early reports of minor injuries from every position group except the linebackers, whose reports have stopped. After practice the linebackers coach, who respects the consultant, asks, "You've been watching me. What am I doing that I can't see?" Which step should the consultant take first?
options: Raise the program's injury culture with leadership
Lead a session with all players on reporting injuries
Tell the coach how his remarks may affect reporting
Urge the linebackers to get injuries checked early
rationales: Going to leadership fits a pattern that runs through the staff. Here leadership has set the tone and one coach departs from it, and he has just asked for feedback.
A team session fits if players in general keep injuries to themselves. Every other group reports early, so the players' general attitude is not the problem.

The figures place the problem with one group and one coach's remarks, and he has opened the door. Direct, respectful feedback to the person who can change it is the smallest step that addresses the risk.
Encouraging players to seek evaluation is right whenever one is known to be hurt. It leaves in place the remarks that make reporting costly, and no particular injury has come to light.
items.takeaway: Let the pattern show where a culture problem sits, and intervene at that level.

items.stem: On a video call, a consultant told Emilio, a professional esports player born and raised in Texas, "Your English is really good." At the next session Emilio said that people often assume he isn't American. The consultant acknowledged having made that assumption and apologized without explaining it away. "Appreciate it. Most people get weird," Emilio said. Two sessions on, he is as frank as ever, and he has sent a clip of a scrim he "choked" for today. The consultant still loses sleep over the remark. How should the consultant open today's session?
options: Apologize again, naming the assumption it carried
Turn to the scrim clip that he sent for today
Ask how the remark has affected their work together
Ask if he would rather work with another consultant
rationales: A fuller apology would be due if the first one had been vague or defensive. It named the assumption, and Emilio accepted it; repeating it asks him to tend to the consultant's guilt.

The impact was acknowledged, Emilio accepted the apology, and his openness suggests the repair has held. What remains is the consultant's own distress, which belongs in supervision rather than in his session.
Checking on the alliance suits signs of lingering strain. Emilio is frank and is bringing hard material.
Offering a change respects a client who doubts that he can go on. He has shown no such doubt.
items.takeaway: After a repair is accepted, don't make the client look after your guilt.

items.stem: Harper, a newly certified consultant, has spent six weeks with a professional baseball organization and has an idea for between-pitch routines. Her notes on staff meetings record that two suggestions from newer staff met silence. One came back a week later from the hitting coach, to nods all around. An analyst who arrived when she did "gets everything through"; Harper has seen him in the hitting coach's office most Friday afternoons. Papers from the general manager's office are read out and not mentioned again. What should she do with her idea?
options: Talk it over with the hitting coach first
Present it at the next staff meeting
Put it in writing to the general manager
Try it out with a few interested players
rationales: Her notes show that ideas are taken up when the hitting coach carries them and stall when newer staff or the front office put them forward. Acting on unwritten rules like this one is contextual intelligence.
Presenting openly suits a staff that takes up ideas from whoever raises them. Newer staff who tried it met silence.
A paper to the general manager would fit if decisions came from that office. Its papers are read out and dropped.
A small trial suits a staff that is won over by seeing results. Nothing in her notes suggests that ideas travel up from players.
items.takeaway: Contextual intelligence means reading how things get done here before choosing how to act.

items.topic: Scope in responding to a bias incident
items.stem: A technology company retains a consultant for leadership and team communication. After an employee complains that a manager mimicked his accent in a meeting, an executive calls: "You know that team, and everyone trusts you. Could you talk to the two of them and to whoever was in the room, find out what was said, and tell me whether it crosses the line? We'd act on whatever you conclude." The company has a human resources department, which has not yet been told. What should the consultant do?
options: Lead a conversation between the two of them
Direct the executive to human resources
Lead a workshop with the team on its communication
Recommend a specialist in inclusion to train the staff
rationales: A facilitated conversation can help repair a working relationship when both want it and any complaint has been resolved. This complaint hasn't been looked into, and the executive wants a finding.

The executive is asking for an investigation and a judgment on alleged discriminatory conduct. That is the organization's formal process, and taking it on would conflict with the consultant's trusted role with the team.
A communication workshop is within the consultant's role. It would not answer an unexamined complaint and could seem to spread the responsibility around.
Specialist-led training fits a wish to build inclusion across the company. The request concerns what happened in one meeting.
items.takeaway: Trust with a team doesn't make a consultant its investigator.

items.topic: Third-party requests: who is the client
items.stem: A professional women's soccer club has engaged a consultant to review how decisions about selection, rehab, and contracts get passed along inside the club. The written agreement calls for interviews across departments and a summary for the sporting director, with nothing attributed to a person. Her first interview is with Ifeoma, a striker who read the invitation and came willingly. Ifeoma sits down and says, "I've been dying for someone to work with. So this is my time?" Which reply describes the arrangement most accurately?
options: "The club is my client here, and what you tell me will feed my report, without your name."
"You're my client here, and the club will hear that we met and nothing more."
"Your coaches are my clients here, and what you tell me will help me advise them on working with you."
"You and the club are both my clients here, and you'll both approve what I write."
rationales: The club commissioned a review and receives the report, so the organization is the client and Ifeoma is an informant in it. Saying so before she shares anything is the third-party clarification the Ethics Code calls for.
This fits individual sessions arranged for a player. The agreement here calls for a report built from interviews, so telling Ifeoma nothing goes back would mislead her.
This fits a contract to advise the coaching staff. The agreement covers the whole club's communication and reports to the sporting director.
This fits a joint development plan with shared sign-off. Nothing in the agreement gives interviewees approval over the report.
items.takeaway: Who commissioned the work, for what purpose, and who gets the product tell you who the client is.

items.stem: For two years a consultant has seen university rowers one at a time. Now the head coach asks her to lead a weekly discussion series for the varsity crew at the boathouse, where rowers will talk about how they handle pressure and one another. She plans to reuse the written sheet from her individual work, which explains what coaches receive, how her notes are kept, and when safety overrides privacy. Which statement most needs to be added before the first meeting?
options: "Your parents may ask about our work, and I'll talk with you before I answer them."
"I'll keep what I hear private, and I can't promise that others who hear it will."
"Our connection is secure, and someone near you could still overhear or see your screen."
"A trainee will sit in with us, and I'll discuss our meetings with the trainee's mentor."
rationales: Parents' questions matter when clients are minors. These are university rowers, and nothing suggests parents have a part in the services.

The change from individual to group work adds a limit her sheet never needed: other participants hear every disclosure, and the consultant can't vouch for them. Group members need to know that before they share.
Overhearing and visible screens are limits of remote sessions. The crew is meeting face to face at the boathouse.
Clients should know about a trainee and supervision. No trainee is involved in this series.
items.takeaway: Moving from individual to group work adds a limit: the consultant can't guarantee other members' discretion.

items.stem: Wen, a 14-year-old figure skater, comes to a second meeting with her father, who signed the permission form last week. At the first meeting the consultant described sessions in plain terms, and Wen asked sharp questions about what her coach would hear. She took a week to think. Today she says, politely, "I get what it is. I don't want to do it." Her father says she'll warm up once things get going, and Wen shakes her head. What should the consultant do now?
options: Describe the work to Wen in plain terms, and ask whether she would like to take part
Ask her father for written permission, and go over with him what it covers
Start with an easy interview about skating, and ask at the end what she would like from the work
Put the work on hold for now, and let them both know that Wen can come back to it
rationales: Plain explanation and a request for assent come at the first meeting. Wen's questions and her week of thought show she already understands what is on offer.
Guardian permission is already in hand. What is missing is the young person's own agreement.
A light first interview is a sensible start once permission and assent are both present. Wen has understood the work and declined it.
Work with a minor rests on guardian permission plus the minor's assent. Wen gave an informed, considered no to an elective service, so the consultant respects it and leaves the way open.
items.takeaway: A minor's informed, considered refusal of elective work counts, even when a parent has signed.

items.stem: A consultant at a U.S. soccer academy wants a first picture of match nerves in an under-11 squad. Most of the boys came from Brazil with their families this fall. They joke freely in Portuguese during warm-ups and are in their school's beginner English class. Her shelf holds several questionnaires, all in English, and she can find no Portuguese version that has been tested with children. Which source of information should she rely on for now?
options: Interviews through a trained interpreter, with observation at matches
The SAS-2, completed by each player before an ordinary training session
The CSAI-2, completed by each player in the hour before a match
Short rating forms completed by the parents and the coach after matches
rationales: With no instrument supported for these children's language, the boys' own accounts through a trained interpreter, checked against observation, give the soundest information. Measures should suit both population and language.
The SAS-2 suits children who read English comfortably. Beginner English readers may not understand the items, so scores couldn't be trusted.
The CSAI-2 assesses state anxiety near competition, in English, and was developed with older competitors. It suits neither these boys' language nor their age.
Adult ratings help when children are too young to describe what they feel. These boys talk readily in Portuguese, so relying on outside impressions would skip the best source.
items.takeaway: When no instrument fits the client's age and language, interview and observe rather than score a poor fit.

items.topic: Assessment results and consent for use
items.stem: Before players on a junior hockey team (ages 18–20) filled out a mental skills inventory, each signed this: "My profile belongs to me. After my feedback meeting I'll decide what, if anything, goes to the player development coach." By November the consultant has finished the feedback meetings. Nineteen players wrote a page with her for the coach, and four preferred to keep theirs. The coach asks, "What can I have?" Which of these does the signed form let her hand over?
options: The team average for every scale, with no player identified
The scored profile for each player, marked for development use
A list of players who have finished the inventory and feedback
The pages written by the players who chose to pass one along
rationales: Group averages would be right if the form had promised staff team-level results. This form says nothing about averages and leaves each player to decide what goes out.
Full profiles would be right if players had agreed at testing that staff would receive them. Here the profile belongs to the player.
A completion list would be right if the form let staff know who took part. This one leaves what reaches the coach to each player, and no player chose to send that.
The form makes each player the one who decides, and nineteen decided to send a page. Sharing exactly that, and no one else's, matches what players consented to.
items.takeaway: Share assessment information in the form, and from the people, that the consent specifies.

items.topic: Intake: ordinary setback or clinical concern
items.stem: At intake with a consultant who isn't a licensed clinician, Desmond, a 52-year-old masters cyclist, says that dropping out of nationals last month "flattened" him. He skipped Sunday's club ride, slept badly for two nights, and told his wife he should take up lawn bowling. On Wednesday he joined the midweek group, got teased about it, "and gave it right back." He has slept fine since, has entered a race in May, and wants help with his nerves before long climbs. What is the best next step?
options: Recommend an evaluation with a licensed mental health professional
Continue the intake, and ask what he'd like from the work
Ask him directly whether he has had thoughts of suicide
Request a release to speak with the clinician who is treating him
rationales: An evaluation would be called for if low mood had lasted or spread through his life. A couple of bad days after a letdown, followed by a full return, is an ordinary reaction.
Desmond's reaction was brief, tied to one event, and has resolved; he is riding, sleeping, and planning. Nothing signals a need outside CMPC scope, so intake moves on to his goals.
A direct question is right whenever there is a sign of hopelessness or danger. His joke about bowling and quick return to friends and racing give no such sign.
A release is the way to coordinate with a treating clinician. Nothing in his account indicates that he has one or needs one.
items.takeaway: Brief, resolved distress after a setback is not a referral signal; watch duration, spread, and impairment.

items.stem: Halle, a 15-year-old swimmer at a club in the U.S. Olympic and Paralympic movement, has been quiet for two weeks. Today, sitting with the consultant on the bleachers in view of the pool deck, she pulls her towel tighter and says, "There's something about one of the grown-ups here. I want to tell you. But first swear it stays with you, or I'm not saying it." She looks at the consultant and waits. What should the consultant do at this moment?
options: Report to child protective services or police, and to the U.S. Center for SafeSport
Stay beside Halle, and call 911 so that an officer can come to the pool now
Check how Halle has been since the reports were made, and what support would help her
Tell Halle that some things can't stay secret, and that she is still welcome to talk
rationales: This is the prompt report required once there is reason to suspect abuse. Halle hasn't yet said what happened or who is involved; the question in front of the consultant is her request for a promise.
Emergency help is for immediate danger. Halle is in view of others and has described no present threat.
Follow-up support belongs after a report. No disclosure or report has been made.

An adult who may have to report can't promise secrecy. Saying so now, warmly and before Halle decides what to tell, is honest and keeps the conversation open; if she then discloses abuse, prompt reports follow.
items.takeaway: Never promise a minor secrecy; explain the limit before the disclosure, then report promptly if abuse is suspected.

items.stem: Thiago, a professional golfer on a developmental tour, wants to start weekly work in February. His money is tied up in entry fees, so he offers the consultant 5% of his winnings instead of her hourly rate. She explains that she can't tie her pay to his results. He nods and says, "Understood. My equipment company's check comes in July whether I win or not. I want to pay what your other clients pay. I just can't do it yet." Which arrangement fits best?
options: A lower fee, set by his current income and reviewed in the off-season
A set number of sessions without charge, agreed before he begins
Her usual fee, billed on fixed dates once he is able to pay
Her usual fee, billed to a sponsor under a written agreement
rationales: A sliding-scale fee is ethical and suits a client whose income is low for the foreseeable future. Thiago's shortfall ends in July, and he wants to pay the normal rate.
Pro bono sessions are ethical and suit someone who can't pay at all. Thiago can pay in full later in the year.
His difficulty is timing: guaranteed money arrives in July. Deferring a fixed fee answers that and keeps payment independent of results, as the Ethics Code requires.
Third-party payment is ethical when the payer agrees and roles are clear. The equipment company hasn't offered to pay for services; it simply pays Thiago.
items.takeaway: Fees can be reduced, waived, or deferred, as long as they don't depend on results.

items.stem: Harriet Blaise is ordering cards for a practice that opens on Monday. She finished a master's degree in counseling two years ago and earned the CMPC in the spring. Her state licensing application is in, and the board tells her that a decision usually takes three months. The last chapter of her doctoral dissertation is with her committee. Which line should she print?
options: Harriet Blaise, PhD, Certified Mental Performance Consultant
Harriet Blaise, MS, Licensed Professional Counselor, CMPC
Harriet Blaise, MS, Licensed Professional Counselor
