Harriet Blaise, MS, Certified Mental Performance Consultant
rationales: The doctorate hasn't been awarded while the dissertation is still under review, so listing it would misstate her degree.
The certification and degree are accurate, but the license is still an application. Claiming it before it is granted would be a false public statement.
This line also claims a license she doesn't hold yet, and leaves off the certification she has earned.
A master's degree and the CMPC are what Harriet holds on the day the cards are printed. Public statements describe earned credentials, not pending ones.
items.takeaway: List only credentials you hold today; pending degrees and licenses wait.

items.stem: Cordelia, an airline executive, finished a year of work with a consultant three years ago and hasn't been in touch since. Reading that the consultant is opening a new practice, she emails a few unprompted lines for the website: the sessions "changed how I walk into a boardroom." She wants her name and job title on them, "because people in my world should know they can ask for this kind of help." What should the consultant do with the lines?
options: Publish them with her name, once she has approved in writing how they will appear
Thank her, and keep them off the website for the time being
Publish them without her name or title, once she has approved the wording
Ask her to take out the line about boardrooms before they are published
rationales: The bar is on soliciting testimonials from current clients and others open to undue influence. Cordelia's work ended long ago, the offer was hers, and she wants to be named; written permission for the exact use completes it.
Holding the lines back would be right for someone still receiving services. Cordelia hasn't been a client for three years.
Leaving her name off suits a former client who wants to stay private. Being identified is the point Cordelia is making.
Editing would be needed if her words claimed or promised outcomes for others. She describes only her own experience.
items.takeaway: Testimonials: none from current clients; a former client's freely offered words need written permission and accuracy.

items.stem: A consultant at a small university sees most of the volleyball squad individually and enjoys the work. The head coach is adding a fourth vote to the staff meeting that picks each week's travel squad and tells him, "You know them better than any of us. Just give me your vote; you don't have to say why." The consultant is the only mental performance provider on campus and hopes to stay in that job. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Take it on, and explain the new duty to the athletes in writing
Take it on, and send the one athlete it affects to a colleague
Turn it down, and carry on with the consulting he does now
Turn it down, and hand the squad's consulting to someone else
rationales: Openness about a second role is enough when that role doesn't put anyone at risk. Judging his own clients for selection would compromise trust and objectivity however clearly it was announced.
Transferring a client can manage an overlap that touches one person. Most of the squad sees him, and no colleague is on campus to receive them.

Voting on clients' selection would draw on what they told him in confidence and make it risky for them to speak. A second role likely to impair the work or cause harm should be avoided, so he declines it.
Passing the squad to another consultant would help if his objectivity or the athletes' trust were already damaged. He hasn't voted, the work is going well, and nobody else on campus can do it.
items.takeaway: Some second roles can be managed openly; one that evaluates your own clients should be declined.

items.stem: In August the sports dietitian gave Tomás, a collegiate soccer player, an eating plan for adding muscle. He likes it, and at their November review she was pleased with his numbers and left it unchanged. On weekends he follows it easily. On days with back-to-back classes the afternoon snacks don't happen: "I pack them, I'm thinking about my lab, and at six they're still in my bag." He asks the consultant what to do. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Connect him with the sports dietitian about changing the plan
Work with him on goals and cues for following the plan
Connect him with the team physician for an evaluation
Connect him with a campus counselor for an evaluation
rationales: The dietitian would set or change what he eats. She reviewed the plan and Tomás likes it; what breaks down is remembering it on crowded days.

Forgetting an agreed behavior on busy days is a self-regulation problem, and goal setting, cues, and implementation plans are squarely within CMPC scope. The content of the plan stays with the dietitian.
A physician would be needed for physical symptoms or unexpected changes. His numbers pleased the dietitian, and he reports no symptoms.
A counselor would be needed for warning signs of a disorder. A snack forgotten while thinking about a lab, with no distress about food, isn't one.
items.takeaway: What to eat belongs to the dietitian; helping a client follow through on it is mental skills work.

items.stem: In March, Rosamund, a CMPC, told another CMPC over coffee that his podcast had given away a client's identity. He thanked her and cut the segment. In summer he told two more recognizable client stories, and she went back to him with the passages marked. He said listeners love them and he would go on telling them. He works alone. Yesterday's public episode gives a client's team, jersey number, and medical history. What is Rosamund's most appropriate next step?
options: File a written complaint with the AASP Ethics Committee
Raise the episode with him privately, and ask him to take it down
Describe the situation to a mentor without names, and ask whether it breaches the Code
Bring it to the person who supervises him
rationales: Informal resolution comes first, and she has tried it twice. He refuses and the disclosures are growing more serious, so a formal route to the Ethics Committee is now appropriate.
A private talk is the usual starting point. Two of them have already taken place, and after the second he told her he would continue.
A mentor's view helps when it is unclear whether a standard was broken. Identifying clients with medical details on a public show is clearly a breach.
A supervisor is the right contact when the colleague is a trainee or employee. He is an independent practitioner with nobody over him.
items.takeaway: Try informal resolution first; when it fails and harm continues, go to the Ethics Committee.

items.stem: A consultant (CMPC, not a licensed provider) drafts a plan for Ana, 13, at a gymnastics club in the U.S. Olympic and Paralympic movement. Text reminders will go to a thread with Ana and her mother. On Thursdays they'll talk in a staff room off the back hallway during practice, blinds drawn so that teammates don't stare. Ana will ride to regionals in the team van with two coaches and the squad. They'll debrief over the team breakfast at the hotel. Ana's mother approves it all in writing. Which part needs to change?
options: The text reminders during the week
The ride to regionals in the van
The Thursday talks during practice
The debrief at the team hotel
rationales: Messages to a minor are fine when they are professional and a parent is on the thread, as Ana's mother is.
A van carrying two coaches and the whole squad isn't a one-on-one situation, so this travel is appropriate.

A room off the back hallway with the blinds drawn can't be observed, and a parent's signature doesn't waive the MAAPP expectation that one-on-one meetings be observable and interruptible. A spot in view but out of earshot would protect both privacy and safety.
Breakfast with the team present is in plain view and easy to interrupt, so the hotel setting isn't a concern here.
items.takeaway: One-on-one time with a minor athlete stays observable and interruptible, whatever a parent has signed.

items.stem: Lorna, 61, took up trail running for her health and would like three sessions on race-day nerves. She is short of cash until spring. A potter, she suggests that the consultant pick a piece off her shelf at the county gallery, where one she likes is tagged at the price of three sessions. People in their valley commonly settle bills this way. The two women know each other only by sight, and Lorna says it makes no difference to her if the consultant prefers cash in spring. What is the best response?
options: Take the piece as a thank-you gift, and make a note of it in the file
Turn it down, and offer her a reduced fee until spring
Take the piece as payment, with the terms in writing
Turn it down, and refer her to a colleague in town
rationales: A small token at the end of paid work can be accepted as a gift. This is payment for services, and recording it as a gift would disguise the fee.
Offering another fee arrangement is right when a trade would be unfair or would entangle the work. Here the value is public, the exchange is single, and Lorna is free to pay otherwise.

Barter is acceptable when it isn't contraindicated or exploitative. A posted price equal to the fee, one completed exchange, local custom, and no pressure on Lorna meet those conditions, and written terms make the agreement clear.
Referral fits when an existing relationship would compromise the work. They know each other only by sight.
items.takeaway: Barter isn't banned: it must be fair, non-exploitative, harmless to the work, and clear.

items.stem: A mother calls a consultant who holds the CMPC and no license. Her 16-year-old son, Emrys, is a pole vaulter. In practice he clears his heights; at big meets his hands go cold, he hurries his run, and he passes early. "The rest of the time he's just Emrys," she says: grades steady, friends in and out of the house, asleep by ten. He laughs about it himself. His sports physical was clean. She asks, "Is this a psychologist's job? A doctor's? Yours?" Which answer is most accurate?
options: "I can help him with that directly; it's the kind of work I do with athletes."
"A licensed psychologist should see him first and assess what's behind it."
"His doctor should see him first and look for a physical cause."
"He should stay with his therapist, and I can add performance work alongside."
rationales: Nerves confined to big meets in a teenager who is otherwise doing well are a performance concern, which mental performance consulting addresses. The consultant can say so plainly and describe what the work does and doesn't include.
Assessment by a psychologist would come first if distress had spread into school, sleep, or friendships. All of those are going well.
A doctor would come first if symptoms were new, unexplained, or happening outside meets. The physical was clean, and cold hands come only with big meets.
Work alongside treatment suits a client who is already in therapy. Emrys has no therapist, and nothing his mother describes suggests that he needs one.
items.takeaway: Competition-bound nerves in a well-functioning client are within CMPC scope; say so without over-referring.

items.stem: A consultant ran a program for club swimmers aged 10 to 13 last spring. Her folder from it holds the attendance sheets and a survey that parents completed after the final session, in which 41 of 48 families said they'd enroll again. The studies she draws on were carried out with university and national-team swimmers. Her brochure for this year's parents has room for one line about how the program has done or what supports it. Which line could she print as it stands?
options: "Most of last spring's families told us they would enroll again."
"Last spring's swimmers were racing faster by the end of the program."
"Studies with swimmers your child's age support the skills we teach."
"Last spring's swimmers were using more mental skills by the end."
rationales: The survey supports exactly this and no more, so the claim is accurate. Public statements should go no further than the data behind them.
Race times would support this line. Her folder holds attendance and a parent survey, neither of which measures speed.
Research with children would support this line. The studies she uses tested university and national-team swimmers.
A measure of skill use before and after would support this line. Nothing in the folder measured what swimmers did.
items.takeaway: Advertise what your data show, even when the true claim is the modest one.

items.stem: Florian, an adult triathlete, worked weekly with a consultant for one season. They held a final review and said goodbye three years ago. Since then he has booked two single sessions to rework his swim start, the more recent of them fourteen months ago, and he has none planned. He writes now to say that he thinks about her and would like to take her to dinner, as a date. She is single and likes him. Which limit settles her reply?
options: The bar on intimacy with someone who is a client at present
The waiting period that runs from the end of services
The duty to show that intimacy would not be exploitative
The bar on consulting with a past intimate partner
rationales: This would govern if services were continuing. Florian has had no session for fourteen months and has none planned, so he is a former client.
Services last took place fourteen months ago, not three years ago, because the single sessions were services. Intimacy with a former client is barred for at least two years, so she declines.
Showing that a relationship wouldn't exploit him becomes the question only after at least two years have passed since services ended.
This would govern if the two had once been partners and he now wanted to be a client. The order here is the reverse.
items.takeaway: The two-year minimum runs from the last service, including a one-off session.

items.stem: Tamsin, a high school basketball player, strained her hamstring five weeks ago. Her athletic trainer cleared her on Tuesday and, when Tamsin asked for another check this morning, found full strength and no pain. She can't wait for Friday's game. "I know it's fine. I ran full length for an hour," she tells the consultant. "Then I go to cut hard and my brain hits the brakes." What is the most appropriate response?
options: Ask her to have the athletic trainer check her leg again
Rehearse hard cuts with her in imagery before the game
Help her weigh whether she wants to play on Friday
Suggest that she talk with her coach about shorter minutes
rationales: Another check would be needed if she reported a new sensation. The trainer found nothing this morning, and what stops her happens in her head.
The medical decision has been made by those who own it. What remains is fear of reinjury on one movement, and rehearsing it with confidence is mental skills work within scope.
Weighing the decision would help a player who was torn about returning. Tamsin can't wait to play.
Shorter minutes would make sense if her conditioning were lagging. She ran full length for an hour.
items.takeaway: Once medical staff clear an athlete, the remaining fear of reinjury is within the consultant's scope.

items.stem: A professional symphony asks a consultant to coach its string players for a round of chair auditions that begins in eleven days. Her entire career has been in team sports. She has never attended an audition, doesn't know how playing-related injuries show up, and has no mentor in the performing arts. Two members of her peer group have worked with orchestras for years, and one of them mentioned being free this month. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Accept, and prepare with reading and a performing-arts mentor
Accept, and adapt her existing program
Pass the request to the colleague who works with orchestras
Accept the general workshop, and leave the coaching to others
rationales: Building competence through study and mentoring is how to enter a new field when there is time. Eleven days before players' jobs are at stake leaves none.
Adapting an established program suits a consultant with experience of this work. Her career has been in team sports.
She lacks the competence, can't gain it in eleven days, and knows a qualified person who is free. Competence and concern for the musicians' welfare both point to handing this one over.
Taking only the part she can do well works when the request has such a part. The symphony asked for audition coaching.
items.takeaway: When there's no time to build competence and a qualified colleague is available, pass the work on.

items.stem: Ilya plays tennis in a U.S. Olympic and Paralympic movement program. Since he was 16 he has exchanged pre-match messages with the consultant on a thread that includes his father. The two of them have always kept it short and professional. Last month Ilya turned 18 and signed his own consent form. He now asks, "Can we take my dad off? Some of what I'd like to say before matches is just for us." How should the consultant handle the messages?
options: Move to direct messages, with limits on timing and content
Keep his father on the thread, and explain why
Move his reminders to the squad thread, with the coaches included
Stop messaging between sessions, and go over reminders in person
rationales: Copying a parent protects minors. Ilya is 18 and has signed for himself, so he is an adult client, and messaging can be private between them under agreed professional limits.
Keeping a parent copied, with an explanation, is right for a minor. Ilya's birthday and signature show that he isn't one any longer.
A squad thread suits reminders meant for everyone. He wants to say things that are for the consultant alone.
Ending messages would fit if the program barred them or if they had become a problem. They have been brief and professional.
items.takeaway: MAAPP's transparency rule for messages protects minors; adult clients get private, professional channels.

items.stem: In September a consultant who isn't a clinician noticed that Simone, a collegiate diver, was losing weight and skipping meals. She told Simone, and Simone went to sports medicine. Since then a physician, dietitian, and therapist have treated her, with releases signed for all three. This week the physician cleared her for full training, and the therapist wrote that she is doing well. Simone comes in smiling, mentions the breakfast she cooked, and says she keeps balking on her inward dives. What should the consultant do in this session?
options: Tell Simone privately what she has noticed about her eating
Help Simone set up a visit with sports medicine
Work with Simone on the balk in her inward dives
Ask Simone for a release to speak with her therapist
rationales: Voicing concern in private was the right step in September. Today there is nothing new to notice: she is eating, cleared, and doing well.
Connecting her with sports medicine was the right step once the concern was raised. She is already under its care.

The disorder is being treated by those qualified to treat it, and they have cleared her. Balking on a dive is a performance concern she has brought herself, so the consultant works on it and leaves eating to the treatment team.
A release was needed before coordinating care. It has been signed, and the therapist is already writing to the consultant.
items.takeaway: When clinicians are treating the disorder and the client is cleared, do the performance work you were asked for.

items.stem: A technology company's leadership office has sent a consultant a list of four requests. She was a licensed psychologist in a hospital mood clinic for nine years, where she also ran stress groups, and her license is current. She then retrained, earned the CMPC, and has spent three years preparing surgeons and athletes for high-pressure days. Which of the requests lies furthest outside the competence her background supports?
options: Evaluating a manager who has asked whether he is depressed
Preparing a vice president for a series of hostile investor calls
Recommending how to combine three overlapping departments
Leading a small group on recovering between long workdays
rationales: Evaluation for depression is beyond most mental performance consultants. This one holds a current psychology license and nine years of experience with mood disorders.
Preparing someone for high-pressure events is what she has done for surgeons and athletes since earning the CMPC.

Nothing in her clinical or performance training prepared her to redesign an organization. Competence is judged against the individual's own education and experience, so this is the piece to pass to a specialist.
She has led stress groups and knows recovery, so a small-group session on it fits both parts of her background.
items.takeaway: Competence is individual: check the request against this consultant's training, not against a job title.

items.stem: Three weeks before a qualifying event, an elite wheelchair tennis player brings her consultant a study: 18 college basketball players improved at free throws with a new visualization method, and there was no comparison group. The consultant has read the paper closely and found nothing that follows it up. The player has held her serve well all spring with the routine they built together. "Should we switch?" she asks. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Switch to the new method, and drop the routine they built
Add the new method to the routine, and track her serve
Keep the routine, and explain what the study can't show
Read the study's methods, and bring her an answer next week
rationales: A switch would be reasonable if her routine were failing and the method were well supported for players like her. Neither is so.
A tracked addition is a reasonable off-season experiment. Three weeks before a qualifier, with serves holding, it puts a working routine at risk on thin evidence.

An uncontrolled study of 18 college players in another task can't show that the method works, still less that it beats what is working for her now. Evidence-informed practice weighs research against this client's results and timing.
Reading the paper first would be responsible if she hadn't. She has read it and looked for follow-ups.
items.takeaway: Weigh a new finding against its design, its fit, and how well the current plan is working.

items.stem: A consultant is employed by a university athletic department. The consent form tells athletes that the department may review records "to the extent needed to confirm that services were provided." An internal auditor writes that she is checking whether the 212 hours charged to the mental performance budget last year actually took place, and asks for "whatever you have." Which records should the consultant send?
options: Session dates and lengths, listed by client code
A summary of common themes, with nobody named
Notes from the sessions listed in a signed release
The complete file, sent by a secure transfer
rationales: The consent form ties review to confirming that services happened. Dates and lengths answer that, and codes keep identities out, so this is the least disclosure that serves the purpose.
Unnamed themes would inform planning. They reveal what athletes talk about and don't show whether 212 hours took place.
Released notes are what an athlete's chosen recipient would receive. No athlete has signed one here, and content isn't needed to count hours.
A whole file might go to a new provider at the athlete's request. The auditor's question doesn't require it, and the form doesn't allow it.
items.takeaway: Disclose the least that the stated purpose and the consent allow.

items.topic: Release of information to another provider
items.stem: In March, Liam, a 27-year-old professional rugby player, signed a release good through September. It names his grief counselor and covers "what we're aiming for in rugby and how often we meet." In July the counselor calls the consultant. Liam seems worn out, she says, but he isn't in any danger; she hears little from him about match nights and wonders what he has been saying on that subject. What may the consultant share on this call?
options: What Liam has said in their sessions about match nights
Nothing about the work until Liam signs a fresh release
Details about the risk to Liam, as far as safety requires
The purpose of the performance work and its schedule
rationales: Session content would be open if the release had covered it. Liam's covers aims and frequency, and the counselor's interest doesn't widen it.
Silence would be right after September or if Liam had withdrawn the release. In July it is still in force.
Disclosure to protect safety is a separate exception. The counselor reports no danger, and nothing suggests one.
The release is current, names this counselor, and covers these two things. The consultant shares what it authorizes and can tell Liam about the counselor's question.
items.takeaway: Read a release for who, what, and until when, and share exactly that.

items.stem: A consultant whose softball career ended when knee surgery failed sees that her first client today, Xiomara, has the same injury. She feels her throat tighten over the intake form. In the session Xiomara, a collegiate shortstop recovering well, goes silent and then says, for the first time to anybody, "I don't think I'll trust it again." Her eyes fill, and she looks away. Which response is most appropriate?
options: "I had that surgery too, and I remember that feeling."
"You're not sure you can rely on it the way you did."
"On which rehab days has it felt most like yours?"
"What has your surgeon said about how it's holding up?"
rationales: A brief disclosure can help when it serves the client and the story is settled for the teller. The consultant's is still raw and ended badly, so it risks shifting the focus to her.
Xiomara has just voiced something new and painful. Reflecting it lets her stay with it, and keeps the consultant's unresolved experience from entering the session to meet her own need.
Looking for better days can build hope once a client feels heard. Asked at the moment she first says this aloud, it moves past the feeling.
The surgeon's view would matter if she were asking about the graft. She is telling the consultant how she feels.
items.takeaway: Before disclosing, ask whose need it meets; if the experience is still raw, stay with the client's.

items.stem: A professional baseball organization invites its consultant to sit in on contract meetings and comment on players' "mental toughness." She sees a problem, marks the Ethics Code standards and contract clauses that bear on it, and talks it over with her mentor without naming players. Between them they come up with three responses: turn the invitation down, attend for staff matters only, or propose a separate education session. Following a structured ethical decision-making model, what should she do next?
options: Work out how each response would affect those concerned
Talk the situation through with a trusted mentor
Establish which standards and agreements apply
Write up how it turned out and what she learned
rationales: She has identified the issue, checked the standards, consulted, and generated responses. Weighing the likely consequences of each for players, staff, and the organization comes before choosing and acting.
Consultation is an early safeguard in these models. She has had that conversation.
Identifying standards comes near the start. She marked the Code and contract passages before talking to her mentor.
Documenting the outcome closes the process. No response has been chosen or carried out.
items.takeaway: Identify, check standards, consult, generate options, weigh consequences, act, evaluate.

items.stem: Maribel, 14, figure skates at a club in the U.S. Olympic and Paralympic movement. Near the end of a meeting at the rink she says that an assistant coach has been touching her under her costume after evening practices, most recently last week. She and the consultant are in view of the front desk, the coach is away at a competition until Sunday, and her mother is due to collect her in ten minutes. She asks, "What happens now?" Once she has been listened to and is with her mother, what should the consultant do?
options: Report to child protective services or police, and to the U.S. Center for SafeSport
Call emergency services and stay beside her until officers reach the rink
Report to the U.S. Center for SafeSport, which will decide whom else to involve
Give the club's director a written account, as the club's conduct policy asks
rationales: Sexual abuse of a minor must be reported promptly to child protective services or law enforcement, and in the Olympic and Paralympic movement to the U.S. Center for SafeSport as well. The consultant reports what she said and leaves investigating to them.
Calling emergency services first fits a child in immediate danger. She is with her mother and the coach is out of town, so the prompt reports are the next step.

A report to the Center alone can fit misconduct that isn't child abuse or a crime. Suspected child abuse also goes directly to civil authorities, and reporting to one body doesn't replace reporting to the other.
The club's own procedure may be enough for a breach such as lateness or rude conduct. For suspected abuse, telling the club doesn't satisfy the duty to report to the authorities.
items.takeaway: Suspected child abuse goes promptly to civil authorities and, in Olympic and Paralympic sport, also to SafeSport.

items.stem: Torvald, a professional cellist, stays seated when his session ends. He says he has been thinking about dying for months. Asked directly, he says that he has been saving up his sleeping pills, that they are in the bag at his feet, and that he means to take them when he gets home tonight. He lives alone and has an appointment with his therapist on Thursday, two days away. The consultant isn't a licensed clinician. He thanks her for asking and reaches for his coat. What should the consultant do?
options: Ask his consent to let his therapist know before Thursday what he has said
Ask him to wait while she contacts emergency services, and stay with him
Help him find a clinician who can see him within the next few days
Ask him whether he has thought about how he would do it, and when
rationales: Coordinating with his therapist, with consent, fits distress without immediate danger. A plan for tonight with the means at hand can't wait for consent or for Thursday.

A stated intent, a plan for tonight, and the means within reach are imminent risk. The consultant follows the emergency plan, stays with him, and brings in emergency help; protecting life is a limit of confidentiality.
Connecting him with a clinician soon fits serious distress without a plan or intent. He has both, and may act in hours.
Asking directly about a plan and timing is the right step when someone mentions thoughts of dying. He has already answered those questions.
items.takeaway: Intent, a plan, and access to means is an emergency: stay with the person and get emergency help now.

items.stem: Ilan, a collegiate golfer, rushes his short putts. Before teaching a pre-putt routine, his consultant has been charting pre-stroke time and short-putt makes, the two measures Ilan and his coach agree matter most. Across the last eight practices, both have stayed within a narrow range with no trend. His next event is five weeks away. The consultant wants to be able to show later whether his putting changed once the routine began. What should the consultant do next?
options: Chart several more practices, and introduce the routine after that
Wait until his next event is over, and introduce the routine then
Introduce the routine at the next practice, and keep charting
Choose a new target measure, and chart a fresh baseline for it
rationales: A longer baseline is warranted when data are trending or scattered. Eight practices within a narrow range with no trend already give a steady standard for comparison, so more charting only delays the work.

Holding off would make sense if an event were days away and changes to his putting were unwelcome. With five weeks before he competes, waiting gives up practice time and improves nothing about the comparison.

In a single-case A–B design, the baseline has done its job once the target measures are stable. His are, the measures are agreed, and the calendar is open, so the intervention phase can begin with the same measures continued.
New measures are needed when the charted ones miss what the client cares about. Ilan and his coach agree that these two matter most, so starting over would discard a usable baseline.
items.takeaway: End the baseline when the agreed measures are stable; extend it only if the data are trending or too variable.

items.topic: Matching a measure to the goal
items.stem: A consultant is planning an eight-week program with a professional esports team. The agreed goal is for players to feel safe admitting mistakes and disagreeing during match reviews. Recordings show that the reviews are already full of lively talk, yet several players say they voice what they think the coach wants to hear. The organization wants one primary progress measure, chosen before the program starts. Which measure fits best?
options: Players' own ratings, gathered anonymously every two weeks
Counts of how often each player speaks, from recorded reviews
The coach's weekly ratings of each player during reviews
Match results, adjusted for the strength of each opponent
rationales: The goal is a perception, so the people who hold it are the direct source. Players already tailor what they say in front of the coach, so anonymity protects the accuracy of brief, repeated psychological-safety ratings.

Comment counts suit a goal of getting more players to talk. These reviews are already full of talk that does not reflect what players think, so counts would look good whether or not players felt safer.
Coach ratings suit behavior the coach can see firsthand. Here, players are shaping what they show the coach, so the coach's view is the one most distorted by the problem itself.
Match results suit a goal about performance. They are far removed from whether players feel able to speak honestly in reviews and have many other causes.
items.takeaway: Choose the primary measure from the goal: a goal about how people feel is best tracked by protected self-report.

items.stem: A consultant is planning the evaluation of a voluntary arousal-regulation course for an infantry company. The commander says, "The last provider taught sound material and taught it well. But soldiers decided in the first hour that it wasn't made for infantry, and they quit coming. Before I look at anything else, I want to know after session one whether yours lands differently." Which measure fits the commander's request?
options: A scenario test of when and how to use each technique
Squad leaders' checklists of technique use in the field
The company's scores on its next timed qualification
Soldiers' ratings of the session's relevance and value
rationales: A scenario test shows learning. The commander has no doubt that such material can be taught and is asking first how soldiers receive it.
Field checklists capture behavior, the level for asking whether soldiers apply the skills on exercises. They cannot answer a question to be settled after one session.
Qualification scores sit at the results level. They come later and have many causes, and they would not show whether soldiers see the course as made for them.

Whether a session lands with participants as relevant and worth attending is Kirkpatrick's reaction level. It is the right level here because attendance is voluntary and the last course failed at that point.
items.takeaway: No Kirkpatrick level is best in general: the stakeholder's question picks the level, and sometimes that level is reaction.

items.topic: Locating where a program is failing
items.stem: A consultant ran four performance-anxiety workshops for a professional ballet company. Dancers rated them as highly relevant. The artistic staff set aside ten minutes of every rehearsal for skills practice, and observation shows most dancers using it to try the techniques. In a midseason skills check, however, most dancers could not pace their breathing as taught or produce a workable refocusing cue. Their performance-anxiety ratings have not changed. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Ask the artistic staff to build more practice time into rehearsals
Reteach the techniques with demonstration and coached repetition
Redesign the workshops around the topics that dancers request
Continue the program as it is, and track anxiety ratings for longer
rationales: More time would help if dancers could perform the skills but had no chance to practice. They already have daily time and use it, so extra minutes would mean rehearsing the techniques incorrectly.

Reaction is good and the setting supports practice, but the skills check shows that learning did not happen. Demonstration and coached repetition address that level, on which later behavior and results depend.
New topics would be the answer to low ratings of relevance. Dancers see the content as highly relevant; they have not mastered it.
Waiting is reasonable when skills are being performed correctly and outcomes simply need time. These dancers cannot yet do the techniques, so later ratings would tell the consultant little.
items.takeaway: Trace the evaluation chain to the first level that fails, and revise the program there.

items.stem: With his assent and a parent's permission, a consultant charts an adolescent swimmer's weekly 100-m freestyle time trials, held under the same conditions with a steady training load. His six baseline times, in seconds, were 62.2, 62.1, 62.3, 62.2, 62.1, and 62.2. Imagery training then began, and the next six times were 62.2, 62.0, 61.7, 61.4, 61.0, and 60.7. Which reading best fits these data?
options: The baseline trend carried on, giving no sign of an added effect
The level shifted at the switch, consistent with a rapid effect
The times vary too widely within phases to support a judgment
The slope changed at the switch, consistent with a gradual effect
rationales: This reading fits a baseline that was already improving and went on improving at the same rate. These baseline times are flat, so there was no downward trend to carry on.
A shift in level would show up as a drop at the first imagery data points. The first imagery time, 62.2, equals baseline, and the improvement builds week by week.
Wide, overlapping scatter would prevent a judgment. Baseline times fall within 0.2 seconds of each other, and the imagery times follow an orderly path.

A flat baseline followed by steady improvement after imagery began is a change in slope, the pattern expected of a skill that builds with practice. A single A–B sequence does not prove the cause, but this is the reading that fits.
items.takeaway: In single-case data, compare level, trend, and variability across phases; a slope change can signal an effect that builds.

items.stem: Folasade, a collegiate softball pitcher, is two weeks into an eight-week plan to regain composure after walks. Video coding shows her completing a reset routine after most walks, up from none at baseline, and she and her pitching coach both describe her as steadier. Her walk and strikeout numbers are unchanged; all three agreed at the outset to weigh those at week eight. The coach, eager for results, now suggests trying something else. What should the consultant do?
options: Continue the plan as designed until the scheduled review
Explore with her why her view differs from the coach's
Replace the reset routine with another composure strategy
Add a structured measure of her behavior between pitches
rationales: The process measure is moving as intended, the sources agree, and the performance numbers are not due to be judged for six weeks. Changing course now would abandon a plan that is on track because of impatience.
Exploring a mismatch is the step when athlete and coach see different things. Here both describe her as steadier, so there is no gap in their views to explain.
A replacement is justified when a strategy has been used as planned for long enough and has not helped. After two weeks, with composure improving, it has had neither a full trial nor a failure.
Structured observation would fill a gap if impressions were the sole evidence. Coded video of her routine already does that job.
items.takeaway: When process data are on track and outcomes are not yet due, keeping the plan is the evidence-based decision.

items.topic: Choosing a source of consultant feedback
items.stem: A consultant has worked for two seasons with a professional string quartet. On an anonymous evaluation form, all four musicians recently rated her support as useful but not well fitted to them individually, and none gave details. They have long been comfortable disputing her ideas in sessions. They declined her offer to have someone else gather their views, and two do not want sessions recorded. She wants to learn what to change for each musician. Which method best fits?
options: A second anonymous form with more open-ended questions
A mentor's review of recorded sessions with the musicians
A one-to-one conversation with each musician, led by her
An interview of each musician, led by a trusted colleague
rationales: Anonymity helps when clients fear speaking frankly, but these musicians do not. An unnamed form also cannot show her which change belongs to which musician.
Recordings show what she does in sessions, which would help with a question about her technique. Two musicians object to being recorded, and what each needs is better heard from them.
She needs individual detail from clients who already disagree with her openly and do not want a go-between. Talking with each of them directly supplies exactly that.
An independent interviewer reduces pressure to please when clients would hold back with the consultant. These musicians have turned that arrangement down and do not hold back.
items.takeaway: Match the feedback method to the question and to the clients' candor; direct conversation can be the best source.

items.stem: After a goal-setting session with a high school track team, a consultant writes a journal entry. It recounts the session step by step, judges the goal cards a success and the group discussion a flop, and reasons that a crowded room and a recent loss kept athletes quiet. It ends with two things he could have done instead and a detailed outline for next week. His mentor remarks that it reads as if someone else had led the session. Under Gibbs's reflective cycle, what should he add?
options: A weighing of what worked and what did not
An account of what he thought and felt
An explanation of why it unfolded as it did
A plan for how to lead the next session
rationales: This is Gibbs's evaluation stage, and it is in the entry: he judged the goal cards a success and the discussion a flop.

The entry covers description, evaluation, analysis, conclusion, and action plan, but he is absent from it. Gibbs's feelings stage, what he was thinking and feeling, is the missing part the mentor noticed.
This is the analysis stage, and it is present: he linked the quiet group to the crowded room and the recent loss.
This is the action plan stage, and it is present in the detailed outline for next week.
items.takeaway: Gibbs's cycle moves from description through feelings, evaluation, analysis, and conclusion to an action plan; check which stage is missing.

items.stem: Rosalind, a masters triathlete, has met her goals for race-morning worry, and two sessions remain before the agreed end. She has written up the skills that helped, has rehearsed what she will do if travel or an unfamiliar course unsettles her at her overseas race, and wants no later check-ins so she can see how she manages alone. But whenever the consultant mentions finishing, she changes the subject, and last week she joked, "Don't make me say goodbye." Which focus best serves the final sessions?
options: Rehearsing responses to situations that could bring worry back
Compiling the skills that helped her into a written plan
Setting the date and purpose of a check-in after her race
Talking about what their work and its ending mean to her
rationales: Relapse prevention matters near the end of a consultation, and she has already done it for the race most likely to test her.
Consolidating useful skills is a sound closing task, but she has already written them up.
Planned follow-up supports some clients after the work ends. She has considered it and prefers to manage alone.

Her skills and plans are in place; the unfinished business is the goodbye she keeps sidestepping. Acknowledging the relationship and its ending is part of a good conclusion and lets her leave on purpose rather than by avoidance.
items.takeaway: A good ending covers the relationship as well as the skills; look for whichever part is unfinished.

items.stem: After a season-long refocusing program with a collegiate volleyball team, a consultant drafts an annual report. Players' ratings of the program were high. On a practical skills test given before and after it, they improved sharply, while a similar team without the program did not change. Nobody recorded what players did between rallies in matches. The team, which had added a transfer setter, won its conference. What is the strongest claim these data support?
options: The players learned the refocusing skills that were taught
The players found the program relevant and worth their time
The players used the refocusing skills in their matches
The program contributed to the team's match results
rationales: Improvement on a before-and-after skills test, with no change in a similar team, is evidence at Kirkpatrick's learning level. It is the highest level for which the consultant has sound data.
High ratings do support this claim, but it rests at the reaction level. The skills-test data support a stronger claim about what players gained.
This is a behavior-level claim. Nobody recorded what players did between rallies, so there is no evidence of use in matches.
A results claim needs a chain of evidence running through match behavior. That link is missing, and the new setter offers another explanation for winning.
items.takeaway: Claim as much as the data reach and no more: name the highest evaluation level with sound evidence.

items.stem: Stellan, a conservatory violist, has worked on a pre-performance routine with a consultant, who messages him a cue before each mock audition. His tension ratings dropped well below baseline and have stayed there. Video shows him completing every step, and he and his teacher both call the routine natural and worthwhile. Sessions and messages end next week; real auditions come in the spring. He asks, "Is this mine now, or is it you nudging me?" Which evaluation step best answers him?
options: Score videos of his mock auditions for routine steps completed
Interview him and his teacher on how acceptable the routine is
Repeat his measures some weeks after support has stopped
Compare his current tension ratings with those at baseline
rationales: Scoring steps checks whether the routine is carried out as designed. Video already shows that it is, and while the messages continue it cannot show what he does without them.
Acceptability interviews are social validation. He and his teacher have already said that the routine is natural and worthwhile.
He is asking whether the change lasts without help, which is maintenance. Repeating the same measures after sessions and messages have stopped is the step that can show it.
The comparison with baseline shows that tension changed, which is already known. It cannot separate his own command of the routine from the consultant's prompting.
items.takeaway: To learn whether gains belong to the client, measure again after support is withdrawn.

items.stem: Midway through an Olympic cycle, a consultant to a national rowing team reads anonymous evaluation forms. Rowers praise her feel for the sport, say the strategies she gives them are personal and work on the water, and mention that she circles back to see how each one is going. The criticisms run along one line: "Tuesdays in the meeting room and that's it," "Hard to catch," "Still a guest here." Based on research on consultants' effectiveness with elite athletes, which change should she prioritize?
options: Tailor her strategies more closely to individual rowers
Spend more of her time around training and camps
Follow up more often on strategies already introduced
Deepen her knowledge of rowing's technical demands
rationales: Individualized, practical strategies are a mark of effective consultants, and rowers already credit her with them.
Elite athletes value consultants who fit in with the team and are accessible. The criticisms are about being absent and an outsider, and regular presence in the team's own setting addresses both.
Follow-up is a recognized strength of effective consultants, but rowers say that she already circles back.
Sport knowledge supports credibility, but rowers praise her feel for the sport. More of it would not make her easier to find or less of a guest.
items.takeaway: Elite athletes value consultants who fit in, are accessible, individualize, and follow up; let the feedback show which one is missing.

items.stem: A consultant led a new trust-building activity with a youth hockey team, and players joked their way through it. That evening he went over his notes and saw that the joking began when he asked 12-year-olds for personal stories. Over the weekend he read about group development and early adolescence, and decided that light, low-risk sharing needs to come before personal disclosure. According to Kolb's experiential learning cycle, what comes next?
options: Looking back over what he noticed in players' reactions
Working out a principle for when such activities suit a group
Taking part in a trust activity to gain firsthand experience
Trying out a revised activity at an upcoming practice
rationales: Looking back on an experience is reflective observation, which he did that evening with his notes.
Forming a general idea is abstract conceptualization. He did that over the weekend when he drew on theory to decide what should come before disclosure.
Kolb's cycle includes concrete experience, but leading the activity already supplied it. Seeking another experience now would leave his new idea untested.
He has had the experience, reflected on it, and formed a general idea. The next stage is active experimentation: putting the idea to the test in practice.
items.takeaway: Kolb's cycle runs experience, reflection, conceptualization, experimentation; place the consultant on it to find the next step.

items.topic: When a client chooses to stop
items.stem: A consultant has met by video for eight sessions with Annika, an adult elite figure skater. She has reached two of her three goals and is halfway to the third. Annika says she has what she came for and would like to handle the rest on her own. She likes the approach, has time for sessions in any part of the year, and shows no signs of distress. The consultant thinks four more sessions would secure the third goal and says so once; she thanks the consultant and repeats her wish. What should the consultant do?
options: Close the work after a final review
Help her move to another consultant
Revise the third goal and continue
Pause now and resume in the offseason
rationales: Participation is voluntary, and an informed adult with no signs of risk may stop before every goal is met. The consultant has given an honest view; informed consent rests on voluntariness, so reviewing her gains and ending well honors her choice.
A transfer fits a client who wants more help but finds the approach a poor match. She likes the approach and wants no further consulting.
Revision fits a client who wants to go on but is stuck. She has said twice that she wants to work on the rest alone.
A pause fits a client who wants to go on but lacks time. She has the time and has chosen to finish rather than postpone.
items.takeaway: A client's informed choice to stop is reason enough to end well, even when the consultant sees more to gain.

items.stem: A consultant who works with executives at a financial firm is moving abroad and closing her practice. One client, midway through his plan, has decided to continue with a colleague she recommended. He has agreed in writing that the colleague may know he has been her client, and he would like her to make the first contact because he tends to put such things off. He wants the colleague to hear about his goals from him, in a first meeting with no one else present. Which handoff is most appropriate?
options: Send the colleague a short summary of his goals and progress
Introduce the two by email, and leave the work undescribed
Give him the colleague's details, and leave the contact to him
Hold a joint closing session with him and the colleague
rationales: A summary supports continuity when the client has authorized it. His permission covers the fact that he has been a client, and he wants to present his goals himself.

Under the Ethics Code's confidentiality standard, what is shared follows the client's consent. He has authorized the relationship to be known and asked her to start the contact, and he has kept the content for himself.
Leaving contact to the client suits someone who has not agreed to be identified. He has agreed, and he asked her to make the first move because he might not.
A joint session can ease a transfer for a client who wants one. He wants the first meeting to be between himself and the colleague, and it would expose content he has not agreed to share.
items.takeaway: At a handoff, share as much as the client has authorized: the relationship, its content, or neither.

items.stem: A wheelchair basketball player on a national squad wonders whether a warm-up playlist lifts her effort, which staff already chart at practice as pushes per minute. No one else will use the playlist, and it will be played in practice warm-ups alone. She and the consultant expect any benefit to fade as soon as the music is off. Her baseline is stable, and she is happy to go without music for stretches. Which design would give the most convincing evidence that the playlist makes the difference?
options: Start the intervention with several players on different dates
Start the intervention in one setting, and add others later on
Introduce the intervention, withdraw it, and reintroduce it
Raise the target level in steps as each step is reached
rationales: Staggered starts make a multiple-baseline design across people, which suits a skill that cannot be unlearned and is taught to several athletes. Here, one player will use the playlist.
Staggering across settings is also a multiple-baseline design, but the playlist will be used in a single setting.

An A–B–A–B withdrawal design suits an effect expected to reverse when the intervention stops, with a client who accepts going without it. If effort rises and falls with the music, rival explanations are unlikely.
Stepped targets make a changing-criterion design, which suits behavior being shaped gradually toward a goal. The question here is whether the presence of music matters.
items.takeaway: Use a withdrawal design when the effect is reversible and withdrawal is acceptable; stagger starts when learning cannot be undone.

items.stem: In a virtual stress-management series for fire recruits, a consultant saw cameras switching off and swapped her slides for a chat about the recruits' own stressors. That night she watched the recording to work out why the slides had lost them. She began the next session with a redesigned exercise to see how it would go. When the series ended, she asked recruits and their captains whether the skills were worth the hours and whether the next class should get them. Which concept best describes this last step?
options: Reflection-on-action, as described by Schön
Reflection-in-action, as described by Schön
Active experimentation, as described by Kolb
Social validation, as used in applied evaluation
rationales: Reflection-on-action is looking back at one's practice afterward, as she did when she watched the recording that night. The last step gathered other people's judgments of the program's worth.
Reflection-in-action is adjusting while practice unfolds, as she did when she dropped her slides. The last step took place after the series ended.
Active experimentation is testing a revised approach, as she did with the redesigned exercise. The last step tested no change in delivery.
Asking participants and stakeholders whether the goals, methods, and effects of a program were worthwhile to them is social validation.
items.takeaway: Reflection examines the consultant's practice; social validation asks clients and stakeholders whether the work was worthwhile.

items.stem: A consultant's contract with a collegiate lacrosse team ends in three weeks, and the head coach wants the assistants to run the pre-practice focus routines without her next season. The assistants watched her lead the routines in the fall and co-led them over the winter. For the past month they have led alone while she observed, and her last several reviews found nothing to correct. They ask her to keep coming, "just in case." How should she handle the routines in her final three weeks?
options: Let the assistants run them without her, and check in weekly
Watch the assistants lead them, and give feedback afterward
Share the lead with the assistants, and debrief each routine
Lead them while the assistants watch, and explain each step
rationales: The assistants have moved through observing, co-leading, and leading under observation, and nothing is left to correct. Stepping back while she is still available tests the independence the coach wants and limits reliance on her.
Observation with feedback fits assistants who are leading alone for the first time. A month of it now turns up nothing to correct, so staying would feed the "just in case" reliance.
Co-leading fits assistants who have watched but not yet led. They passed that point over the winter.
Modeling fits assistants who have not seen the routines led well. They did that in the fall.
items.takeaway: Before concluding, fade support in stages, and leave room for staff to work independently while help is still available.

items.stem: On evaluation forms from three teams, athletes say that a consultant's strategies help but that she "talks more than she listens." On client-approved recordings she finds the same pattern with every athlete: closed questions, few reflections, quick advice. She feels at ease in her sessions, and no athlete or topic stands out as hard for her. Her graduate program offered nothing on interviewing. When she shadowed a seasoned colleague last year, she could see that it worked but could not name what the colleague was doing. Which development step best fits?
options: Code more of her recordings for talk time and question types
Take a course in counseling and interviewing skills
Explore her reactions to certain athletes with a mentor
Sit in on an experienced colleague's individual sessions
rationales: More coding fits a consultant who does not yet know what she does in sessions. Her recordings have already shown a clear pattern, so further counts would confirm it without changing it.

The pattern holds across athletes, she is at ease, and she was never taught these skills. That points to a gap in knowledge and skill, which structured instruction fills; the same gap kept her from learning by watching.
Exploring reactions with a mentor fits a problem that flares with particular clients or feelings. Hers is uniform and comes with no discomfort.
Observation fits a consultant who knows the skills but has not seen them used well. She has shadowed a colleague and lacked the concepts to recognize what she saw.
items.takeaway: Diagnose the gap first: knowledge, modeling, self-monitoring, and personal reactions each call for a different development step.

items.topic: Revising a plan from monitoring data
items.stem: Darnell, an office manager, is working with a consultant on keeping up a running habit before a charity 10K. He set his own target of four runs a week and met it for six weeks, then dropped to two in weeks seven and eight. Talking it over, he explained that year-end reporting and his mother's care now take up every hour he used to have free, and will for another month. He is as keen as ever and says that two runs are what he can manage. What should the consultant suggest now?
options: Reviewing his logs to find out what preceded the drop
Retaking the exercise motivation questionnaire from intake
Reducing his weekly target for a limited period
Shifting his runs to a different time of day
rationales: A log review is the step when the reason for a change is unknown. He has already explained what happened and how long it will last.
Reassessing motivation would fit an unexplained loss of interest. He is as keen as ever, and the limit is time.
The cause is known, temporary, and out of his hands, and his motivation is intact. A smaller, time-limited target keeps the goal attainable and the habit going until his schedule opens up.
Rescheduling would help if one part of his day were blocked and another were free. He has no free hours left this month.
items.takeaway: Once the reason for a decline is known, adjust the plan to fit it rather than assess again.

items.topic: Matching evaluation level to a decision
items.stem: An esports organization's consultant finished a two-day workshop on a new in-match call system yesterday. The five players now leave for a three-week break, with no scrims or matches until the day before their season opener. The general manager must decide today whether to pay for a refresher session on the final day of the break. He says it depends on whether players know which call to make in which situation. Which evaluation step best informs his decision?
options: Ratings from each player of how useful and engaging the workshop was
A scenario quiz asking each player which call fits each situation
Coding of the team's voice comms for use of the new calls in matches
The team's match results from before and after the workshop
rationales: Ratings show Kirkpatrick's reaction level. They would fit a decision about whether players value the workshop, not whether they know the calls.
The decision turns on knowledge, Kirkpatrick's learning level, and the players can be tested now. A scenario quiz shows directly whether each knows which call fits.
Coding comms addresses the behavior level and would be the choice if the question were whether players use the calls in competition. There are no matches to code before the decision.
Results address the fourth level. They come too late for this decision and depend on much more than knowing the calls.
items.takeaway: Choose the Kirkpatrick level that answers the decision at hand and can be measured in time.

items.stem: Collegiate sprinter Temitope Ibekwe is describing meets to her consultant. Of a personal best she says, "By warm-up my hands shook so hard I couldn't pin my number on, and I thought, good, here we go." Of last week's poor race she says, "By warm-up there was a little tremble, like when you're cold, and I thought, good, here we go." Four more meets she recalls follow the same lines. Which rating, added to her pre-meet log, is most likely to show what separates her fast meets from her slow ones?
options: Whether she expects each symptom to help or hurt
How early in the week each symptom comes on
How strongly she feels each symptom on race day
How often each symptom comes back during the day
rationales: Direction is worth logging when an athlete reads the same symptom as helpful at some meets and harmful at others. Temitope greets the shaking the same way before good and poor races.
Onset would matter if slow races followed days of symptoms. Her symptoms appear at warm-up in both accounts.

Her accounts match in timing and in how she reads the symptom. What differs is strength: violent shaking before fast races, a slight tremble before slow ones. Intensity is therefore the dimension to track.
Frequency is a real dimension of the anxiety response, but neither account suggests the shaking returned more often on one day than the other.
items.takeaway: Anxiety symptoms vary in intensity, frequency, timing, and direction; assess the dimension on which good and poor performances differ.

items.stem: A rowing federation report flags sculler Tomasz Wierzbicki as "over-anxious" because his pre-race scores ran well above the average for elite rowers all last season. His results that season ranged from a title to a last place. It is now the off-season, his plan for next year is due in two weeks, and he recalls his races vividly. He asks the consultant, "Is that too high for me?" Which information would best help the consultant answer him?
options: How he recalls feeling before his best and worst races
How he feels before each race in the season ahead
How other elite scullers score on the same questionnaire
How he feels on ordinary training days away from racing
rationales: Hanin's model defines optimal intensity within the person, by comparing states recalled before successful and unsuccessful performances. Recall also works in the off-season, before the plan is due.
Tracking upcoming races is a sound way to refine a zone, but no races fall before the plan is due.
Scores from closer peers would show whether his level is unusual for a sculler. They can't show whether it is too high for him.
Training-day ratings would show whether racing brings the anxiety on. That is a different question from whether the level suits his racing.
items.takeaway: Whether an intensity is too high is answered by comparing a performer's own best and worst performances.

items.stem: A ballet company's director wants to know why twelve teenage apprentices avoid difficult variations and cover up mistakes. Records from a summer residency at another school show the same twelve volunteering for hard roles and asking for corrections. Within two weeks of returning, nearly all had stopped, including those who are cast most often. The consultant's questionnaire packet has room for one more measure. What should it assess?
options: How able each dancer feels compared with her peers
How each dancer tends to define success for herself
How strongly each dancer's identity rests on dance
How dancers see success being judged in company classes
rationales: Low perceived ability can lead to avoiding challenge, but the same group sought challenge over the summer, and even the most-cast dancers withdraw now.
Goal orientation is a fairly stable personal tendency. It would help explain differences among dancers in one setting better than a change in nearly all of them between settings.
Identity bears on reactions to injury, deselection, or leaving. It travels with the dancer and can't explain a change that follows the setting.
When the same people seek challenge in one place and hide mistakes in another, the likely difference is the perceived motivational climate: what people there seem to value, reward, and punish.
items.takeaway: If behavior changes with the setting, measure the perceived climate; if it differs among people in one setting, measure the orientation.

items.stem: Collegiate golfer Diego Fuentes has CSAI-2 scores from nine tournaments. At all nine his cognitive anxiety was low and his self-confidence high. His somatic anxiety varied. At three small local events it was very low and he averaged 76; at three conference events it was moderate and he averaged 71; at three televised qualifiers it was very high and he averaged 77. The consultant's plan for this month is aimed at a fourth qualifier. According to multidimensional anxiety theory, what should the plan aim to do before that event?
options: Raise the level of his bodily activation
Lower the level of his bodily activation
Reduce the amount of worry he carries
Strengthen the confidence he has in his game
rationales: Raising somatic activation would suit the small events, where it sat below his best range. The plan is for a qualifier, where it has been too high.

The theory predicts an inverted-U for somatic anxiety, and his scores show one: best at moderate levels, worse at both ends. Qualifiers put him on the high side, so the aim is to come down toward the middle.
The theory links rising worry to steadily poorer performance, but his worry is low throughout and can't account for the swings.
The theory expects confidence to relate positively to performance, but his is already high at good and poor events alike.
items.takeaway: In multidimensional anxiety theory, target the component whose changes track performance, in the direction that moves toward its best level.

items.topic: Matching an anxiety model to data
items.stem: Five professional basketball players, Keisha Morrow among them, rated their anxiety before forty games, and a consultant has set the ratings beside their free-throw percentages. Plotted together, the ratings bear no relation to shooting. Plotted one player at a time, Keisha shoots best when her ratings are high, two teammates when theirs are low, and two near the middle, with a gradual fall on either side. The pattern repeats from month to month. Which account should guide plans for these players?
options: The inverted-U hypothesis of arousal and performance
The catastrophe model of anxiety
The multidimensional theory of competitive anxiety
The individual zones of optimal functioning
rationales: The inverted-U allows a gradual fall on each side, but it places the best level near the middle. Three of the five shoot best well away from it.
The catastrophe model describes a sudden, large drop when arousal rises while worry is high. Here the falls are gradual and depend on each player's own level.
Multidimensional theory separates worry from bodily anxiety and gives one shape to each. These are single ratings whose best level differs from player to player.
Best levels that are high for one player, low for another, and stable over time for each are what the individual zones model describes. Pooling the players hid the pattern.
items.takeaway: When best levels are stable within people but differ between them, plan with individual zones.

items.stem: Collegiate rower Kazuki Matsuda has not missed one of his crew's optional 5 a.m. ergometer sessions. His coach assumes he loves them or fears for his seat. Kazuki laughs at both ideas. "Nobody checks who comes, and I count the minutes until it's over. But I decided last year I want to find out how far I can go in this sport, and that room is how you find out." According to self-determination theory, what should the consultant's plan treat as the main driver of his attendance?
options: Identified regulation of the behavior
External regulation of the behavior
Introjected regulation of the behavior
Intrinsic motivation for the behavior
rationales: Kazuki doesn't enjoy the sessions; he attends because they serve an aim he has chosen and personally values. That is identified regulation, an autonomous though not intrinsic form of motivation.
External regulation rests on rewards or punishments from others. The sessions are optional and unchecked.
Introjected regulation runs on guilt, shame, or pride. Kazuki speaks of an aim he chose, with no sense that he would feel bad about himself for missing.
Intrinsic motivation means doing something for its own interest or enjoyment. He counts the minutes until these sessions end.
items.takeaway: Autonomous motivation need not feel fun: valuing what an activity serves is identified regulation.

items.stem: Firefighter recruit Lena Brandt has completed the full aerial ladder climb six times in training, cleanly and with energy to spare. Two weeks before the graduation test she watched two other recruits, both about her height, lose their reach near the top and fail. Her confidence rating has since gone from 9 to 3. "It's always the short ones who come off that thing," she says. In terms of self-efficacy theory, which support would most directly counter what lowered her confidence?
options: Another set of supervised climbs that start low and go higher
An instructor's detailed account of why her technique is ready
A visit from recent graduates of similar build who passed
Practice in treating a racing heart as a sign of readiness
rationales: Mastery experience is usually the strongest source, but she has six clean climbs and they did not prevent the drop. Her doubt came from what she saw happen to others.
Credible feedback can help, especially when someone's words have shaken a performer. Nobody has questioned her technique.
Watching similar others fail lowered her efficacy: a vicarious source. Seeing people like her succeed supplies the opposite information from the same source.
Reinterpreting arousal suits a performer who takes bodily signs as proof of weakness. Lena reports no such signs.
items.takeaway: Trace a loss of efficacy to its source; seeing similar others fail or succeed is vicarious information.

items.stem: Tennis player Zara Khoury, 15, has lost five matches in a row to opponents she beat last year. After each loss she adds practice time and is now on court more than anyone at her academy. Her coach's video shows her hitting nearly every second serve to the same corner, where opponents stand waiting. "I've doubled my hours and nothing changes," she tells the consultant. "Maybe that's my level." Which understanding of her losses should the plan help Zara reach?
options: She has not yet put in enough work
She has been relying on the wrong tactics
She has had a run of poor luck on big points
She has drawn some unusually strong opponents
rationales: Effort is a controllable cause and often a helpful one. When effort is already high, blaming effort invites the conclusion that ability must be lacking, which is where Zara is heading.
The video points to a predictable serve pattern. A strategy attribution is accurate, controllable, and changeable, and it explains why extra hours have not helped without implicating her ability.
A temporary, external cause can protect expectations when it is accurate. The video shows a repeated pattern that opponents exploit.
Task difficulty would be an accurate account of losses to better players. She beat these opponents last year.
items.takeaway: When effort is high and results still lag, guide attributions toward strategy rather than more effort.

items.stem: Elite figure skater Mei-Lin Zhou rated her confidence before eight competitions. The highest ratings came at her home rink and at a small arena abroad where she had once spent a training camp. The lowest came at three larger arenas. Of one she says, "The boards looked miles away and I couldn't find my marks." Of another, "I went left off the ice and the dressing rooms were right." Her next event is in a city she has never visited. Drawing on Vealey's work on sources of sport confidence, which plan best fits her ratings?
options: Keep a log of elements she has improved
Record messages from her coach to play before she skates
Watch training mates skate the same elements cleanly
Arrive early to learn the arena and its ice
rationales: A log builds confidence from mastery. Nothing in her ratings tracks how her elements are coming along.
Coach support is a recognized source, but her ratings rise and fall with the venue.
Vicarious experience is a source of confidence. Her accounts of good and poor events don't involve what she saw others do.
Her confidence is high in places she knows and low in places she doesn't. Environmental comfort is one of the sources Vealey's work identified, and early visits can build it before a new venue.
items.takeaway: Match a confidence plan to the source the performer's own pattern reveals, including comfort in the competition setting.

items.stem: Masters swimmer Gloria Esposito logs her anxiety three times a day in the week before a championship. Her worry stays at 1 or 2 out of 10 from Monday until her race on Saturday. Butterflies and muscle tension are just as low until Saturday's warm-up, when they reach 8, and they are 9 behind the blocks. Her starts are sluggish, and her pace recovers once she is under way. Which strategy should her plan for the next championship call for, and when?
options: Body-focused relaxation on race day
Body-focused relaxation throughout race week
Worry-focused strategies on race day
Worry-focused strategies throughout race week
rationales: Her only marked anxiety is bodily and it climbs shortly before racing, as multidimensional theory expects of somatic anxiety. A somatic technique used on race day fits both its type and its timing.
The technique fits the type of anxiety, but there is little bodily anxiety to reduce before Saturday.
Race day is the right time, but her worry is low then. A cognitive strategy would miss the bodily symptoms.
Cognitive anxiety is often raised for days before competing, and early cognitive work would then make sense. Gloria's log shows little worry all week.
items.takeaway: Let the type of anxiety choose the technique and its time course choose when to use it.

items.stem: Judoka Rafael Moreira, a national team member, rated his recalled feelings before ten matches from 0 to 10. Before his best matches, tension was 7 to 9 and irritation 2 to 4. Before his worst, tension was 3 to 5 and irritation 7 to 9. Before the two matches he lost last weekend he rated both at 8. His coach asks the consultant for a plan that gets him to "relax and stop being so wound up." Based on Hanin's model, what should the pre-match plan aim to do?
options: Lower his tension and keep his irritation
Lower his tension and lower his irritation
Keep his tension and lower his irritation
Keep his tension and keep his irritation
rationales: This would move both emotions toward the levels that went with his worst matches.
This is what the coach's request implies, but a tension of 8 is within the range of his best matches and a fall would take him toward his worst.
A tension of 8 sits in the range of his best matches, unpleasant as it is, while an irritation of 8 sits in the range of his worst. In the IZOF model each emotion has its own individual zone.
An unpleasant emotion can be part of an optimal profile, and his tension is. His irritation, though, is at the level that went with poor matches.
items.takeaway: In IZOF planning, each emotion is compared with its own zone; an unpleasant one may belong there while another doesn't.

items.stem: At stoppages, professional point guard Ondine Caldwell can say where every defender stood and which of them were switching. Once a play begins, her passes and shots are crisp. Yet she calls the same two sets whatever the defense shows her. "I see it," she tells the consultant. "Then the whistle goes, and I've called the usual before I've thought about what it means." In Nideffer's terms, which kind of attention should the plan have her practice at stoppages?
options: Attention that is broad and external
Attention that is broad and internal
Attention that is narrow and external
Attention that is narrow and internal
rationales: This focus takes in the surroundings. She already reads where defenders stood and what they were doing.
