Ondine takes the information in but doesn't stop to work out what it means or weigh her options. Analyzing and planning call for a broad-internal focus.
This focus locks onto a target, as in shooting. Her execution once the play starts is sound.
This focus suits settling oneself or rehearsing a movement. Nothing suggests she is unsettled or unsure of a movement.
items.takeaway: Locate the point where attention breaks down: taking in, working out, settling, or executing.

items.stem: A youth wrestling club is about to move several athletes up an age group, and its consultant is reviewing notes on one of them, Sven. On days with scored bouts he asks for the strongest partners, expects to beat them, and works harder than anyone. During technique weeks, when nothing is scored, he drifts between mats and asks a coach, "So who's ahead?" Shown that his takedown has become quicker, he shrugs. Which achievement goal profile should the consultant's plan assume?
options: High task orientation, low ego orientation, low perceived ability
High task orientation, high ego orientation, high perceived ability
Low task orientation, high ego orientation, low perceived ability
Low task orientation, high ego orientation, high perceived ability
rationales: A highly task-oriented wrestler would care that his takedown had improved. Sven also expects to beat strong partners, which points to high perceived ability.
His confidence and interest in rank fit, but work without scores leaves him cold, so there is little sign of a high task orientation.
The orientation fits, but an ego-oriented wrestler who doubted his ability would tend to steer clear of strong partners on scored days.

He comes alive when he can be compared with others, expects to come out ahead, and shows little interest in improvement. The profile works while he wins, so the plan should build task involvement before the move up.
items.takeaway: Read orientation from what engages a performer and perceived ability from the challenges the performer seeks.

items.stem: A collegiate volleyball coach tells a consultant that his players compete hard for one another and share the blame when they lose, but something "feels thin." In interviews every player names two or three teammates among her closest friends and says leaving them would hurt. On road trips, though, the team eats at three separate tables, and no one can remember an evening when all sixteen were in one room by choice. In terms of the Group Environment Questionnaire, which dimension should the plan target?
options: Individual attraction on the task side
Group integration on the task side
Group integration on the social side
Individual attraction on the social side
rationales: This is each player's own draw to the team's goals, productivity, and her part in them. Players are competing hard for the team.
This is the team's unity around its goals. The coach describes a team that competes for one another and shares responsibility.
Individual friendships are strong, yet the team as a unit splits into three and does not gather. Closeness of the group as a whole in social life is group integration–social.
This is each player's own sense of acceptance and friendship in the group. Every player names close friends she would hate to leave.
items.takeaway: Cohesion has task and social sides, each seen from the individual's bond to the group and from the group's unity as a whole.

items.stem: A police academy asks a consultant to plan a resilience program. Interviewed after the hardest training scenarios, cadets come across as able and sure of themselves. Those who had a bad week describe getting through it alone. Asked about the peer mentors down the hall, one says, "They're not there for somebody like me," and many agree. The mentors say they wish more cadets would come; they have turned no one away. Drawing on Fletcher and Sarkar's theory of psychological resilience, what should the program target first?
options: Cadets' belief that support is there for them
The number of mentors the academy provides
Cadets' confidence in handling hard scenarios
Cadets' ability to focus during hard scenarios
rationales: Perceived social support is one of the protective factors in the theory. Support exists, yet cadets don't see it as available to them, so the perception is the thing to change.
More mentors would help if there were too few. Those in place have room and turn no one away.
Confidence is a protective factor, but the cadets already come across as sure of themselves.
Focus is also a protective factor. The gap in the interviews appears after bad weeks and concerns support.
items.takeaway: Support protects through being perceived as available; having it on site isn't enough.

items.topic: Tuckman's stages in a new roster
items.stem: An esports organization assembled a five-player roster ten weeks ago. The first scrims were polite; then came three weeks of shouting over who makes the calls. Since then the players have written down a shot-calling order. In scrims they stop to ask, "Whose call is this?" and remind anyone who speaks out of turn. They have also begun eating together. Results are middling, and the general manager wonders about changing the roster. Which stage of Tuckman's model should the consultant's plan assume?
options: The forming stage of group development
The norming stage of group development
The storming stage of group development
The performing stage of group development
rationales: Forming is marked by politeness and uncertainty about roles. The roster passed through that in its first scrims.
Conflict has given way to agreed rules that players remind one another to follow, along with growing closeness. They still have to stop and check, so the rules are not yet second nature.
Storming is the open conflict over calls that ended some weeks ago.
In performing, roles are settled enough that energy goes into the task. This roster still pauses to work out whose call it is.
items.takeaway: Norming shows in newly agreed rules being used and enforced, before they run smoothly.

items.stem: Paramedic Oluwaseun spent four years on a helicopter crew until the service closed in the spring. He now works ambulance shifts. "The shifts are fine; I could do them half asleep," he tells his consultant. "But that crew was the best thing I ever built, and it's finished. Every time a helicopter goes over, I fly the last call again." He is sleeping well and sees friends often. In Lazarus's terms, which appraisal should the consultant's plan address?
options: A primary appraisal of threat
A primary appraisal of challenge
A secondary appraisal of too few coping resources
A primary appraisal of harm or loss
rationales: Threat concerns harm that may still come. Oluwaseun speaks about something that has already ended.
Challenge concerns a chance to gain or grow. He describes nothing ahead of him in that way.
Secondary appraisal weighs what one can do about the situation. He says the new work is well within his abilities.
His stress centers on damage already done: a crew that mattered to him is gone. Lazarus calls that harm/loss, and it is worked with differently from a threat that might be prevented.
items.takeaway: Harm/loss looks back at damage done, threat looks ahead to possible harm, and challenge looks ahead to possible gain.

items.stem: Conservatory pianist Anaya Deshpande practices an audition script every evening: "My pulse quickens and my palms are damp. I let my shoulders drop. My fingers sink into the opening chord and I feel it in my forearms. This is what four years were for, and I play as though I belong." Walking into the real hall for a rehearsal, she tells her consultant, she felt as if she had never imagined it at all. Drawing on Lang's bioinformational theory, what should the revised script add?
options: The panel's table, the stage lights, and the piano
The dryness in her mouth, the warm arms, and the slow breath out
The reasons the audition matters to her and her family
The real length of the pauses between her pieces
rationales: Lang holds that effective imagery links features of the situation (stimulus information) with the person's responses. Her script is rich in responses and meaning and contains almost nothing of the scene that should call them up.
Response details are often what a script lacks. Hers is made almost wholly of them already.
What the scene means to her belongs in a script, and hers has it: this is what four years were for.
Matching real timing is a PETTLEP concern. Her trouble was failing to recognize the situation.
items.takeaway: In bioinformational terms, a script joins the situation's features with the performer's responses; add whichever is missing.

items.stem: Gymnasts at a youth club seem to like the place. They pick among stations, know what each is for, and linger afterward to talk. Attendance has slipped since winter all the same. "I've been on my kip for five months," one tells the consultant. "Coach says 'nice work' to all of us every time, so I guess it's the same as it was." Others make similar remarks. Based on self-determination theory, what should the coach training in the consultant's plan focus on?
options: Offering gymnasts choices within clear limits
Showing personal interest in each gymnast
Giving gymnasts information about their progress
Explaining the purpose of each drill in practice
rationales: Choice supports autonomy. These gymnasts already choose among stations, and the remark is about not knowing where they stand.
Personal warmth supports relatedness, and the gymnasts already stay to talk.
Uniform praise tells a gymnast nothing about whether she is getting better, so the need for competence goes unmet. Specific information on progress is the support that is missing.
A rationale supports autonomy and internalization. The gymnasts already know what the stations are for.
items.takeaway: Competence needs information: praise that is the same for everyone doesn't tell anyone she is improving.

items.stem: An aquatics program's 9- to 11-year-olds can't wait for the deep end. At the signal they run to the edge and leap, laughing, and nearly all land flat on their stomachs or backs. None has yet landed feet first, and the instructor's explanations of arm and leg position have changed nothing. The consultant is helping her plan one short demonstration for the next class. Based on social cognitive theory, which demonstration best fits what these children need?
options: A child their age who hesitates at the edge, then jumps
A child their age who is cheered for jumping well
A video that shows each child's own best jump so far
An instructor who jumps with correct form, slowed down
rationales: A similar model who copes with fear raises efficacy in fearful children. These children aren't afraid.
Seeing a model rewarded adds an incentive. The children are already eager.
Viewing one's own best attempts suits a learner with successes to show. No child has landed one yet.
The children lack a clear picture of the movement. A skilled model shown so that the form can be seen conveys how to do it, which is what observation must supply here.
items.takeaway: Choose a model for what the learner lacks: form, confidence, incentive, or belief in repeating success.

items.stem: Distance runners Kwabena and Anders missed a national final by the same margin. Both went out too fast, and both say so. "I got carried away that day," says Kwabena, who expects to qualify next year. "I know how to hold back, and nobody's stopping me," says Anders. "I just don't, and I've raced that way since I was twelve." He expects to miss again. For the consultant's planning, which feature of their explanations best accounts for the difference in what they expect?
options: The locus of the cause
The stability of the cause
The controllability of the cause
The globality of the cause
rationales: Locus bears mainly on pride and self-esteem. Both runners place the cause in themselves.
Kwabena describes a lapse on one day; Anders describes a habit that does not change. In Weiner's theory, expectancy of future success depends mainly on how stable the cause is seen to be.
Controllability bears on guilt and responsibility, and both runners describe something they could have done differently.
Globality concerns whether a cause spreads to other areas. Neither speaks of anything beyond racing.
items.takeaway: Stability drives expectations; locus and controllability bear more on pride, shame, and guilt.

items.stem: Collegiate diver Lachlan Reid's CSAI-2 intensity scores for worry and bodily symptoms have been the highest on his team at four straight meets. His coach forwards them to the consultant and asks for a plan to settle him. The form also included direction ratings, on which Lachlan marked nearly every symptom as helpful, and he set personal bests at three of the four meets. What should the consultant plan for Lachlan's pre-dive preparation?
options: Keep the preparation he already uses
Teach him to read his symptoms as readiness
Teach him relaxation to reduce his symptoms
Add an energizing routine to build his intensity
rationales: From a directional perspective, high intensity is not a problem in itself. He reads his symptoms as facilitative and is diving better than ever, so there is nothing here to settle.
Reinterpretation suits an athlete who reads symptoms as harmful. Lachlan already marks his as helpful.
Lowering intensity may suit someone whose symptoms disrupt performance. His go with personal bests.
Energizing suits a performer who is below his best level. Lachlan's intensity is already high and serving him well.
items.takeaway: High anxiety intensity calls for no change when the performer reads it as helpful and performs well.

items.stem: Eight officers on a police tactical team practice searching a warehouse for hidden items. When the floor is split into marked zones and each officer's finds are recorded, they work quickly and miss little. When all eight share the whole floor for one team score, they spread out smoothly and rarely cross paths, yet they cover a third less ground and miss twice as much. Afterward they agree that the team is a good one and the exercise worthwhile. Which concept best explains the drop and should guide the consultant's plan?
options: Low cohesion around the task
Gaps in shared mental models
Social loafing in the group
Low collective efficacy for the search
rationales: Low task cohesion would show in disagreement about the exercise or a lack of commitment to it. They agree that it is worthwhile and the team is good.
Differing pictures of who does what would produce collisions, repeated searching, and overlooked areas. They move smoothly and rarely cross paths.
Individuals do well when their finds are recorded and do less when the work is pooled into one score. Reduced effort when contributions can't be identified is social loafing.
Low collective efficacy would show as doubt that the team can do the job. They call the team a good one.
items.takeaway: When coordination is smooth but output falls as individual contributions disappear from view, suspect social loafing.

items.stem: Tennis professional Sofia Lindqvist had fretted all week about her ranking. Leading 5–1 with her heart pounding, she went within one game from striking the ball cleanly to barely finding the court, and she lost five games in a row. At the 5–6 changeover she took slow breaths until she felt, she said, "about how I felt at 5–1." The next game went the same way, and the set was gone. In case it happens again, which changeover plan should the consultant teach her?
options: Ease her activation to just under its current level, then hold it
Lift her activation with quick movement, then hold it there
Bring her activation far down, then build it up gradually
Hold her activation steady, then change her shot selection
rationales: A small reduction suits a gradual slide past a moderate peak. Her play collapsed at once, and coming back to the earlier level did not restore it.
Energizing suits a player who has gone flat. Her heart was pounding when her play collapsed.

High worry, a sudden drop, and no recovery on returning to the earlier level fit the catastrophe model. Because of hysteresis, arousal has to fall well below the point of collapse before performance returns, and then be raised again with care.
A tactical change suits a player whose state is unchanged and whose opponent has found an answer. Sofia could barely find the court with any shot.
items.takeaway: After a catastrophic drop, returning to the pre-drop level isn't enough; come well down before building back up.

items.topic: Matching support to an unmet need
items.stem: Attendance at a collegiate soccer team's optional mental skills sessions has slid from twenty to eight. Players pick their own skill each week, and their refocusing times in practice keep improving. "Oh, it works," a midfielder says of the sessions. "You put your headphones in, do your recording, and go. Half the reserves are in there and I couldn't tell you one of their names." Others describe it in much the same way. Based on self-determination theory, which change should the consultant make?
options: Have players practice skills in pairs and compare notes
Let players choose when, where, and how long they practice
Show players charts of how their skills are improving
Explain how each skill applies to match situations
rationales: The players choose freely and see results; what they describe is sitting alone among teammates they don't know. Working in pairs gives the sessions a chance to meet the need for relatedness.
More choice supports autonomy, which the sessions already respect: attendance is optional and players pick their skills.
Progress charts support competence. The players already say the sessions work.
A rationale helps players value an activity whose point is unclear. These players see the benefit.
items.takeaway: Find which need the setting leaves unmet before choosing a support; an effective activity can still lack connection.

items.stem: After calm runs of a police scenario, recruit Dana Kowalczyk can list the wall posters, the observers on the catwalk, and both armed role players. After the most stressful run, with her heart rate near its peak, she could describe both role players, their hands, and the exit she had covered, and her decisions were rated excellent. She recalled no posters and no observers. Her instructor calls it tunnel vision and asks what the consultant will change before the next stressful run. Based on cue utilization theory, what should the consultant do?
options: Teach her breathing that brings her arousal down
Teach her a routine that brings her arousal up
Have her repeat calm runs until scanning is automatic
Continue her present training at this intensity
rationales: Lowering arousal fits once narrowing has begun to cost relevant cues. She caught every cue that mattered.
Raising arousal fits when attention is so broad that irrelevant cues get in the way. In the stressful run they didn't.
More scanning practice fits a recruit who misses people in calm conditions too. She sees them all.
Narrowing first drops irrelevant cues, which helps. Posters and observers are irrelevant; she kept the relevant cues and decided well, so nothing needs correcting at this intensity.
items.takeaway: Arousal-driven narrowing is a problem only once relevant cues begin to drop out.

items.stem: A youth basketball coach asks a consultant for help keeping slower learners engaged. In practice, mixed groups of players choose among stations, and the coach quietly tells players how their own skills are coming along. A whistle moves every group on after four minutes. "I nearly had the left-hand layup," one girl says, "and then it was passing." Several players have stopped attempting new moves. Which change should the consultant help the coach make?
options: Let players decide more of what they practice
Let players stay longer with a skill they are learning
Recognize players in private for improving on their own marks
Group players of differing ability together
rationales: Sharing authority supports a mastery climate, and players already choose their stations.
Time is one of the structures that shape climate. A fixed whistle cuts slower learners off before they can improve, so varying the time lets effort pay off for them.
Private, self-referenced recognition is already part of the coach's practice.
Mixed grouping reduces social comparison, and the groups are already mixed.
items.takeaway: Climate is built from tasks, authority, recognition, grouping, evaluation, and time; change the one that is failing.

items.stem: Renée Dubois, 52, has finished every workout of a six-week supervised exercise program for which she has medical clearance. The program ends in two weeks. Asked by her consultant how sure she is that she could train by herself, she says, "Two out of ten. Of course I finish here. My instructor sets the machines, counts for me, and keeps a hand on the bar." Based on self-efficacy theory, which step would do most to raise her confidence for training alone?
options: Have her watch members her age who train by themselves
Have her instructor talk with her about how capable she has become
Help her read heavy breathing as a normal response
Have her run a workout with her instructor standing by
rationales: Similar models help when someone doubts that people like her can do it. Renée's doubt is about who deserves credit for her workouts.
Persuasion is a weaker source, and more words from the person she credits would not show that she can manage without help.
Reinterpreting bodily signs suits someone who takes them as proof of weakness. She mentions no such signs.
Success builds little efficacy when it is credited to outside help. Managing a workout without aid, with the instructor still in the room, is mastery she can credit to herself.
items.takeaway: Success raises efficacy most when performers can credit it to themselves; withdraw aids so that they can.

items.stem: Attendance in an adult exercise class is falling, and its instructor asks a consultant for help. Members wear the class's own shirt and chat readily with whoever is nearby. Each session, though, opens with people hunting for floor space. Newer members end up at the edges, doing moves too hard or too easy for them, and several leave partway through. "I never know where I belong in there," one says. Drawing on Carron and Spink's team-building work, which strategy should the consultant suggest?
options: Have members choose a class name and slogan
Mark areas by fitness level where members keep a spot
Have members agree on a goal for class attendance
Have members pair up for partner exercises
rationales: A name builds distinctiveness. The class already has an identity of its own, and the trouble lies within the room.
Individual positions are part of group structure in Carron and Spink's approach. Areas matched to fitness, in which members keep a place, meet the trouble these members describe.
Shared goals and norms help when coming and going is taken lightly. Newer members want a place in the class.
Partner work builds interaction, and members already chat with those nearby.
items.takeaway: Carron and Spink's strategies include distinctiveness, positions, norms, and interaction; choose by what the group lacks.

items.stem: Field hockey player Nia Achterberg has scored on nearly every penalty stroke this season. At breakfast before a collegiate final, the assistant coach, a former national-team striker, joked to her, "Let's hope it doesn't come down to your nerve." Nia's confidence rating went from 9 to 3. In warm-up she scored ten out of ten, and the rating stayed at 3: "She's seen hundreds of strikers. She'd know." The coach, mortified, asks the consultant how to help in the last half hour. Based on self-efficacy theory, which step fits best?
options: Have the coach tell Nia what she sees in her play
Have Nia score on one more set of strokes
Show Nia clips of a similar player scoring in finals
Help Nia read her pounding heart as readiness
rationales: A credible person's words lowered Nia's efficacy, and she weighs that judgment above her own results. Sincere, specific feedback from the same person works on the source that did the damage.
Mastery is usually the strongest source, but ten straight goals changed nothing, because Nia gives the coach's judgment more weight.
Vicarious information fits a doubt that came from watching someone like her fail. Hers came from a remark.
Reinterpretation fits a player who takes arousal as a sign she will miss. She mentions no bodily signs.
items.takeaway: Persuasion carries weight through the credibility of the source, for harm and for repair.

items.stem: In a company's virtual walking challenge, employees earn a badge for reaching weekly targets that they set themselves. An executive who has read that rewards undermine motivation asks the consultant running it for a redesign. In surveys, employees say things like "The badge shows me I'm getting fitter." Walking and enjoyment ratings rose during the challenge. During a two-month break without badges, both stayed where they were. Based on self-determination theory, what should the consultant recommend?
options: Phase out the badges and help employees find their own reasons
Keep the badges and add groups in which employees walk
Keep the badges and give employees a say in targets
Keep the badges and the way that they are earned
rationales: This would suit rewards that had become the reason to walk. Walking and enjoyment held up without them.
Groups would support relatedness. Nothing suggests that employees feel alone in the challenge.
A say in targets supports autonomy, and employees set their targets already.

Cognitive evaluation theory holds that rewards undermine intrinsic motivation when they are felt as controlling. Here badges inform employees about progress toward self-set targets, and motivation lasted without them.
items.takeaway: A reward's effect depends on whether it is experienced as controlling or as information about competence.

items.stem: In close games, collegiate center fielder Mateo Ruiz gets an instant jump on fly balls and couldn't say who was in the stands. Late in lopsided games he picks the ball up a beat late. Afterward he can repeat the bullpen's jokes, the song between innings, and the score on the next field. His coach wants something he can do before each pitch in those innings. Based on cue utilization theory, what should the consultant have him practice?
options: Slow, deep breaths with a long exhale
Quick foot taps with a sharp exhale
A scan of the runners and the outs
An image of his route to the wall
rationales: Calming fits arousal so high that relevant cues drop out. In lopsided games he is taking in too much.
When arousal is low, attention is broad and takes in irrelevant cues along with relevant ones. A brief activating routine raises arousal so that the irrelevant cues drop away.
Scanning fits a fielder who misses the situation. He is already taking in more than he needs.
Rehearsing a route fits errors of movement. His trouble is how late he picks up the ball.
items.takeaway: Too little arousal leaves attention broad enough to let irrelevant cues in; activation can narrow it.

items.stem: A professional rugby team beat the league leaders by two points and will meet them again in the final. The leaders had rested seven starters, who will return. Video shows the winners missing more tackles than in any loss this season. In the changing room, players say they have the leaders figured out. The head coach asks the consultant to help with a debrief that leaves players with accurate expectations for the final. Based on attribution theory, which account of the win should it draw out?
options: The lineup their opponents chose
The preparation that the squad did
The ability that the squad has
The effort that the squad gave
rationales: The evidence points to an external, unstable cause that will be gone in the final. Crediting it keeps players from expecting the same result against a stronger side.
Crediting controllable preparation after a win is often wise when it is accurate. The video shows one of their poorer defensive games.
A stable, internal cause raises expectations. That would fit a run of good wins; here it would feed an inflated view.
Effort would be an accurate account if they had worked unusually hard. Nothing in the video suggests it.
items.takeaway: Accurate attributions set useful expectations; after a flattering win the accurate cause may be external.

items.stem: Collegiate gymnast Yolanda Pires has added two elements to her bars routine. She has hit the release move in 47 of her last 50 tries. She has hit the dismount in 11 of 50, and no two misses look alike. Her team holds closed practices, with only the event coach present, and open practices, where teammates, parents, and donors watch. The coach asks the consultant where she is likely to perform each element better over the next two weeks. Based on Zajonc's social facilitation theory, which schedule fits?
options: Both the release move and the dismount in closed practices
Both the release move and the dismount in open practices
The release move in open practices, the dismount in closed ones
The dismount in open practices, the release move in closed ones
rationales: Closed practice suits elements on which errors are likely. The release move is well learned and would gain from an audience.
An audience helps when the dominant response is correct. On the dismount, errors are still far more likely than hits.
Zajonc held that an audience raises arousal, which strengthens the dominant response. That response is correct for the release move and wrong for the dismount.
This exposes the less learned element to an audience and shields the one that would benefit.
items.takeaway: An audience strengthens the dominant response: show what is well learned and protect what is not.

items.stem: Startup founder Priscila Navarro pitched to investors on Tuesday. They vote in nine days and have asked founders to stay out of touch until then. "Either way we'll be all right; we have a second offer," she tells her consultant. "But I reread my slides at midnight, I snap at my team, and every email makes me jump." Drawing on Lazarus's work on stress and coping, which focus best fits their session?
options: Weighing what the vote will mean for the company
Preparing answers to questions the investors may ask
Finding another source of funds in case of a no
Finding ways to settle herself through the wait
rationales: Reappraising the stakes helps when they are being magnified. Priscila already sees that the company will be all right.
Problem-focused preparation fits a demand she can still act on. The pitch is over and contact is closed.
Problem-focused coping would fit if a no left a gap that she could work to fill. She has a second offer.
For nine days nothing she does can change the outcome. When a stressor can't be acted on, emotion-focused coping, which eases the distress itself, is the better fit.
items.takeaway: Problem-focused coping fits what can be changed; emotion-focused coping fits what can't.

items.stem: Esports professional Jae-won Park wants one cue word for the start of a duel. Replays show that he reaches duels from good positions, having read the opponents' route correctly. As the duel opens, eye tracking shows his gaze flicking to the minimap and his teammates' health bars, and his first shots go wide. When a coach covers those displays in practice, he wins most duels. Using Nideffer's model, which cue should the consultant help him practice?
options: "Map" as he checks where everyone is
"Plan" as he picks his next move
"Dot" as he fixes on his crosshair
"Loose" as he feels his grip soften
rationales: This cues a broad-external focus, which he has already used well by the time the duel opens.
This cues a broad-internal focus for deciding. His decisions on the way to the duel are sound.
His attention stays broad and external when the duel calls for one external target. A cue that moves him to a narrow-external focus fits the moment his aim fails.
This cues a narrow-internal focus, which suits settling tension. His shots go wide because his eyes leave the target.
items.takeaway: A refocusing cue should shift attention to the width and direction the moment demands.

items.stem: Players at a youth soccer academy say they can go to their coaches with anything, and coaches sit down with each player after every match. Practice stops when a drill becomes frustrating, matches are arranged against weaker sides, and starting places are never in doubt. At an outside tournament the players fell apart after conceding first, as they had the year before. Drawing on resilience research in sport, how should the consultant advise the coaches to adjust the environment?
options: Raise the demands on players and keep the support as it is
Keep the demands on players as they are and raise the support
Raise the demands on players and raise the support
Keep the demands on players and the support as they are
rationales: Support is strong and challenge is slight, a comfortable setting in which players seldom practice dealing with difficulty. Raising demands within that support gives them the practice.
More support fits an environment whose demands outrun it. Here support is the stronger of the two.
Raising both fits a setting in which players are neither stretched nor backed. These players are well backed.
Leaving things alone fits a setting that is working. Two tournaments suggest players are not ready for setbacks.
items.takeaway: Resilience grows where challenge and support are both high; adjust whichever is low.

items.stem: Para swimmers training alone in different cities must swim the same 40-minute test set each Monday so that results can be compared. On a group call the consultant asks how it is going. "We get why it has to be that set, and they ask nicely," says one. "But it's forty minutes, alone, the same thing, and then everybody tells us how exciting the data are." The others laugh and groan. Motivation for Mondays is falling. Based on self-determination theory, which step should the consultant suggest to their coach?
options: Explain what the set shows and how results are used
Invite swimmers to pick from several versions of the set
Replace pressuring phrases in the weekly messages
Acknowledge that the set is dull to swim alone
rationales: A rationale supports autonomy when the reason is unclear. The swimmers understand it.
Choice supports autonomy where there is room for it. Here the set must be the same for everyone.
Noncontrolling language supports autonomy. They say they are already asked nicely.

With choice unavailable and the reason understood, what remains is that nobody recognizes how it feels. Acknowledging feelings is an autonomy-supportive behavior that helps people internalize tasks that aren't interesting.
items.takeaway: Autonomy support includes choice, rationale, noncontrolling language, and acknowledging feelings; the last works even when the task is fixed.

items.stem: Alpine skier Lukas Brenner is healthy, and his training times are the best of his career. His coach of nine seasons retired last month. "I used to push out of the gate knowing he'd read the course right for me," Lukas tells his consultant. "Now I stand up there going over the line myself." His confidence before races has fallen, and a world championship is three weeks away. Using Vealey's sources of sport confidence, which step should the consultant take?
options: Go back over his training log and times with him
Have his new coach take him through course decisions
Have him watch teammates ski the course cleanly
Arrange for his family to be with him at the start and finish
rationales: Evidence of preparation helps an athlete who doubts his preparation. His training is going well and he doesn't question it.
Trust in a coach's decisions is one of the sources of sport confidence, and Lukas lost it with the retirement. Seeing how the new coach reads a course can begin to rebuild that trust.
Seeing others succeed is another source. Lukas's doubt is about whose course reading he can rely on.
Encouragement from family is social support, another source. He describes missing a judgment he trusted.
items.takeaway: Trust in a coach's leadership is its own source of sport confidence and may need rebuilding after a change.

items.stem: Junior track cyclist Ayesha Rahman took up the Madison, a relay event, a month ago and is still working out its hand-sling exchanges. Her coach set a specific, demanding lap-time target; she signed on eagerly, and she sees her time after every run. Her times have stopped falling. On video she makes the same late reach in each exchange and pedals harder out of it. Based on goal-setting theory, what should the consultant suggest to the coach?
options: Set a faster lap time for the next block
Set a goal of finding three ways to exchange
Give her lap times partway through each run
Talk through why the lap-time target matters to her
rationales: A harder target helps when a goal is too easy for someone who has the skills. Ayesha is short of an effective way to make the exchange.
On a complex task that is still new, a specific, hard performance goal can lead people to press harder with poor strategies. A learning goal directs effort to finding better ones.
Feedback moderates the effect of goals, and she gets her time after each run. Earlier times wouldn't show her how to exchange.
Commitment moderates the effect of goals. She signed on eagerly and rides hard.
items.takeaway: For complex, unfamiliar tasks, set learning goals before performance goals.

items.stem: Amateur triathlete Minh Tran has spent three weeks learning to question his race worries. "My head's quiet now," he tells his consultant after the season's first race. "But I'm in the start pen with my shoulders up by my ears and my jaw locked, and my arms are gone by the second buoy." His swim time was unchanged. Which technique should the consultant teach him next for use in the start pen?
options: Brief progressive relaxation of his shoulders and jaw
Written evidence for and against his worries
Energizing self-talk with quick, sharp movements
An external cue to focus on, such as the first buoy
rationales: His worry has eased and what remains is muscle tension, a somatic symptom. The matching principle points to a somatic technique.
Restructuring is a cognitive technique for cognitive anxiety. It has done its work: his head is quiet.
Energizing suits a flat start. Minh is too tense.
An external focus suits a swimmer whose mind wanders or turns inward. His trouble in the pen is muscle tension.
items.takeaway: As symptoms change, change the technique: somatic methods for bodily tension, cognitive methods for worry.

items.stem: A professional ice hockey team's penalty kill has slipped, and the consultant interviews the unit's six regulars. About the unit they sound alike: "This group has always killed penalties. We'll sort it out." About their own jobs, four of the six say something like, "I'm not getting into lanes the way I was. The other guys are covering for me." Based on Bandura's work, which practice change should the consultant suggest first?
options: Drills in which the unit gets stops as a group
Drills in which each player gets stops in his role
Video of a similar unit that turned its season around
A talk in which the coaches voice faith in the unit
rationales: Group mastery builds collective efficacy. The players' belief in the unit is intact.
The doubt is about individual capability while belief in the group holds. Mastery experience at each player's own task matches the level at which efficacy is low.
A similar group's success is vicarious information about what a group can do. Their belief in the group isn't in question.
Persuasion about the unit addresses a belief the players hold already.
items.takeaway: Check whether doubt is about oneself or the group; build efficacy at the level where it is low.

items.stem: A regional theatre cast has worked together happily through a five-month run. In its final week, actors who had been close begin bickering over dressing-room space, two skip the usual warm-up circle, and another has gone quiet. When the stage manager offers to sort out the rooms, an actor says, "Why bother? On Monday there's no 'us' left to argue." The director asks the consultant to run one session with the cast. Drawing on Tuckman's expanded model, what should it focus on?
options: Helping cast members get to know one another
Airing and settling disputes over space and duties
Looking back on the run and marking its close
Agreeing on ground rules for backstage life
rationales: Getting acquainted belongs to the forming stage. This cast has been together for months.
Working through conflict belongs to the storming stage. The squabbles have appeared as the group is about to end, and the actor's remark shows what they are about.
Friction, withdrawal, and low investment at the end of a group's life fit adjourning. Acknowledging the ending and what the group achieved meets what the cast is reacting to.
Setting shared rules belongs to the norming stage. Rules would be of little use to a cast that disbands on Monday.
items.takeaway: When a settled group frays near its end, the ending may be the issue.

items.stem: Vitali swam, ran, and played soccer and tennis until he was 12, kept soccer and tennis until he was 15, and gave up soccer last year because, he says, "I'd rather be on court." Now 17 and in good health, he hopes to play on the professional tour. His parents have read about the risks of specializing too early, and they ask a consultant whether his plan for the coming year should bring back other sports. Under the Developmental Model of Sport Participation (DMSP), which plan best fits him?
options: Several sports, with most time given to playful games
Two sports, with playful games and focused practice balanced
Regular activity for fun and fitness, without performance targets
One sport year-round, with most time given to focused practice
rationales: Sampling with plenty of deliberate play fits roughly ages 6 to 12, a stage that Vitali has already been through.
A balance of play and practice in one or two sports fits the specializing years, about 13 to 15. Vitali went through those with soccer and tennis.
The recreational path suits adolescents who want to stay active without pursuing elite performance. Vitali is aiming for the tour.
At about 16 and older, a young person who has sampled, specialized gradually, and chosen elite performance enters the investment years, marked by one sport and a high amount of deliberate practice.
items.takeaway: The DMSP warns against early specialization, not against investment by a committed older adolescent.

items.stem: Marit, a retired college gymnast now in graduate school, took up golf this month. Her teacher has read that mixed practice is best and has her change clubs and targets after each ball. In her second week, she makes solid contact on perhaps one ball in six, no two swings look alike, and she says, "I can't tell what I did, so I can't do it again." She has no plans to compete, and her body feels fine. She and her teacher ask a consultant to help plan her next few range sessions. Which plan best fits her stage of learning?
options: Switching clubs and targets from one ball to the next
Hitting one shot with one club in short blocks
Playing scored practice holes against a partner
Rehearsing the swing in her mind at home
rationales: Random practice strengthens retention and transfer once a learner can produce the movement. Marit can't yet, and this is the schedule she is lost in.
Marit is in the cognitive stage and has no basic pattern yet. Repeating one shot lets her form it; variety can be added once she makes fairly consistent contact.
Scored practice prepares a skill for pressure. Marit doesn't compete and has no stable skill to test.
Imagery works best with a clear model of the movement, and it can stand in when a player can't train. Marit is able to hit balls but can't yet tell what she did.
items.takeaway: Contextual interference helps once a learner has the basic pattern; absolute beginners may first need repetition.

items.stem: Collegiate dance major Nkechi has six weeks to prepare a 40-second solo. She learned its few steps in an afternoon. To polish it, she has been rehearsing it in three chunks, and each looks clean. Joined up, the solo dies: every turn has to spill into the next leap, and from a standing start at a chunk's edge she has nothing to spill. At half tempo she simply tips over. She asks a consultant to help her organize her rehearsals. Which plan best fits this task?
options: Dance the solo from beginning to end at tempo
Dance each chunk until it is secure, and then join them
Add one chunk at a time to those already joined
Dance the solo slowly, and then raise the tempo
rationales: The solo is simple but highly organized: each movement's momentum creates the next. Tasks that are low in complexity and high in organization are best practiced whole.
Part practice suits a long task whose sections are largely independent. Her chunks are already clean, and cutting the solo up is what breaks it.
Progressive-part practice suits a long sequence whose order or links are hard to remember. Her solo is short and well remembered, and stopping at a chunk's edge still kills the momentum.
Slowing a task simplifies it when it keeps its form at low speed. Hers depends on momentum and falls apart at half tempo.
items.takeaway: Practice whole when a task is simple and its parts depend on one another; use parts when it is complex and they don't.

items.stem: A consultant and a high school volleyball coach are planning a six-week program in which setters learn a refocusing routine at one session each Monday. In a trial run, the setters used every step well by the close of each session. "And then by the next Monday we're back to zero," the coach says. "Or it feels like that. I can't tell." Before they change anything, the two of them want one measure that will settle whether she is right. Which should they use?
options: How well setters use the routine as each session closes
How well setters use it in a match situation new to them
How well setters use it as each session opens, before review
How well setters believe they have learned it, rated weekly
rationales: Performance at the close shows acquisition. It was already strong in the trial and says nothing about what lasts until the next week.
A new situation tests transfer, and would fit if the question were whether the routine carries over to matches.
Best. The coach's doubt is about retention: what remains after a week without help. A check at the opening, before review, measures learning and not the temporary effect of practice.
Learners' judgments can show confidence, but they are a weak guide to retention, because ease during practice tends to inflate them.
items.takeaway: Learning is what remains after a delay: test retention before review, not performance at the end of practice.

items.topic: Planning for the stage of learning
items.stem: Halvard, a 52-year-old recreational triathlete, has been learning freestyle for three months. His stroke now looks much the same from length to length, and he no longer asks his coach what to do. Some lengths go better than others; after a poor one he often says, "Elbow dropped, I think," and looks to the coach to confirm it. If she chats with him as he swims, his timing slips. He asks a consultant to help him plan what to work on mentally in his next block of practice. Which plan best fits his stage of learning?
options: See the stroke shown again, and follow one or two main cues
Hold the stroke as he thinks through race tactics
Give his attention to each part of the stroke to rebuild it
Judge each length himself, and adjust on the next one
rationales: Demonstrations and a few simple cues serve the cognitive stage, when a learner is working out what to do. Halvard knows what to do and swims consistently.
Tactical thinking during movement needs the spare attention of the autonomous stage. Conversation still upsets his timing.
Conscious reworking is for a well-learned movement that has to be changed. His stroke needs refining, not taking apart.
A consistent stroke, growing awareness of errors, and attention still partly needed mark the associative stage. Practice there should sharpen the learner's own error detection and correction.
items.takeaway: In the associative stage, plan practice that builds the learner's own ability to detect and correct errors.

items.stem: A fire academy gives a consultant six hours to teach stress-management skills to its recruits. Last year all six fell on one day in week one, and the day went well: that evening recruits listed the skills without notes, matched them to sample calls, and used them in full gear in the training tower. At graduation, 12 weeks later, most couldn't say what the skills were. The academy can't add hours, but the consultant may arrange them in any way. Which change should the consultant plan for this year?
options: Have recruits pick among the skills on mixed sample calls
Split the teaching into short sessions across the course
Have recruits do more of their practice in full gear
Have recruits list the skills from memory as the day ends
rationales: Mixing skills builds the ability to choose among them, which recruits could already do on the day.
Recruits learned everything on the day and lost it over the weeks. Distributing the same hours over time produces far better retention than massing them.
Practice in gear helps skills carry over to working conditions. Recruits used the skills in gear on the day; what failed was memory.
Retrieval strengthens learning, but these recruits already listed the skills from memory that evening, and it didn't last.
items.takeaway: When learning is good on the day and gone weeks later, spread the same practice time out.

items.stem: Elite javelin thrower Chidi spent the off-season rebuilding his technique. By spring his coach no longer has to prompt him: film of his last 30 throws shows the new pattern each time, including when he is tired. Heading into the season, Chidi still goes down the runway reciting checkpoints. He tells the consultant, "I know it looks right. I have no idea whether it's doing anything." His early meets range from a small local event to a field of Olympians. Which goals would best serve him at those meets?
options: Distances to reach, set from his own recent throws
Technical points to carry out on each throw
Places to finish, set for each of the meets
An open aim of doing his best, with no numbers
rationales: The pattern is stable, and what he lacks is evidence that it pays. Self-referenced performance goals supply it whatever the field, and they move his attention off the checkpoints.
Process goals suit a pattern still being secured. His is secure, and more checkpoints would feed the recital on the runway.
Outcome goals can add drive, but with fields ranging from local throwers to Olympians, a placing would say little about his technique.
A do-your-best aim can protect someone learning a complex new task. Chidi is past that, and it would leave his question unanswered.
items.takeaway: Let the goal type follow the learning stage: once technique is stable, self-referenced results become useful.

items.stem: Collegiate swimmer Siobhan has done heart rate variability biofeedback for five weeks. With the on-screen display she holds her slow breathing pace for ten minutes. Last week her consultant hid the display. For the first two minutes she kept the pace and judged it within a breath of the sensor; then she sped up without noticing until the screen came back. No screens will be allowed on deck at her meets, which begin in six weeks. How should the consultant plan to use the display in the next few weeks?
options: Turn it off, and check her against the sensor at the end
Let her decide when she wants to look at it
Show it on some stretches and hide it on others
Keep it on through most of her breathing practice
rationales: Working without it is the aim, and would fit if she held the pace with the screen hidden. She still drifts after two minutes, so she would practice long stretches off target.
Learner-chosen feedback works when the learner can tell that she needs it. Siobhan drifted without noticing.

Best. She can feel the pace for a short time and loses it later, so feedback should be faded: enough to correct the drift, with growing stretches in which she must rely on herself. The guidance hypothesis warns that constant feedback would leave her dependent on the screen.
Frequent feedback suits the very start, before a learner has any inner sense of the target. After five weeks she has one, and more of the same would build dependence.
items.takeaway: Fade feedback as an internal sense of the skill develops: neither constant display nor sudden removal.

items.stem: For six weeks a consultant has stood behind elite archer Ilse in training and commented after each arrow on her pre-shot routine. Before each comment, Ilse gives her own verdict, and the two almost always agree. She says she enjoys the sessions and leaves them confident. Last week a late train kept the consultant away for the first half of practice. Her coach says that Ilse kept turning to look behind her and lost her place in the routine on nearly a third of her arrows; at Saturday's tournament, the same thing happened. What should the consultant change in training?
options: Comment in more detail on each arrow
Comment on fewer and fewer of her arrows
Comment mainly on the steps she does well
Ask for her verdict before commenting on each arrow
rationales: Detail helps an athlete who can't tell what is wrong. Ilse's verdicts match the consultant's, so she has the information already.
Her routine holds up only when a comment is coming. The guidance hypothesis explains this as dependence on frequent feedback, and the remedy is to fade it.
Positive feedback builds motivation and confidence. Both are in good supply.
Self-evaluation builds error detection, but she is already doing it, and accurately.
items.takeaway: If a skill holds up only when feedback is expected, reduce how often it comes.

items.topic: Explaining breathing to a young group
items.stem: A consultant taught slow breathing to a squad of 16- and 17-year-old gymnasts last week. They did it well, watched their heart rates drop on their wrist monitors, and agreed that it felt calming. None has used it since. "It's fine," says one. "It's what my grandma does in yoga." Another, who is taking advanced biology, adds, "I get that it did something. But breathing's breathing. Why would letting air out slowly do anything to nerves?" Heads nod around the circle. What should the consultant do next?
options: Make it a game, such as blowing out pretend candles
Have them breathe quietly and report what they notice
Show them their heart rates as they breathe
Explain briefly how long exhales act on the nervous system
rationales: A concrete image and a game suit young children. These are older adolescents who find the exercise a little childish already.
Guided noticing helps those who haven't felt an effect. They have done it and felt calmer.
A demonstration convinces those who doubt that anything happens. They have watched their heart rates drop and accept that it did something.
They accept the effect but can't see how it could work, and that question is keeping them from using it. Older adolescents can reason about mechanisms, and a brief rationale makes the skill credible.
items.takeaway: Pitch the explanation to the learners' development and to the question they are asking.

items.topic: Getting team skills onto the field
items.stem: In September a consultant taught a university women's soccer team several refocusing skills in weekly meetings. In November, with no warning, she asks players to write down what they remember. Nearly all of them explain every skill, and when she describes match situations, they choose sensible ones. Yet in matches she sees hardly any of it. "I know this stuff cold in here," says the goalkeeper. "Then I'm out there with my lungs burning and it's like I've never heard of it." Which change to the sessions is best supported by learning research?
options: Open with unannounced recall of skills from earlier weeks
Come back to each skill some weeks after teaching it
Move some of the practice to the field, at match intensity
Work on choosing the right skill for described situations
rationales: Retrieval practice strengthens memory, and their memory is strong: they explained every skill two months later.
Spacing guards against forgetting. They haven't forgotten.
The skills are well remembered in the room but don't appear under match conditions. Practicing under conditions like those of use, physical strain included, supports transfer.
Practice in choosing helps players who mix up the skills. They already choose sensibly.
items.takeaway: If skills are remembered but not used, make the practice conditions more like the performance conditions.

items.stem: The coach of a club wheelchair basketball team asks a consultant why his free-throw comments aren't helping the newest players. At practice, the consultant hears him speak up on about one shot in five, when something is well off: "Elbow's out." "Late release." He is just as quick to name what a good shot had in it. Players nod at the comments and repeat the fault. During a break, a newcomer demonstrates to a friend: "See, late. It felt late, too." She makes the same motion again and shrugs. What change should the consultant suggest to the coach?
options: Say what to do differently on the next shot
Comment on a smaller share of the shots
Point out more of what players do well
Show players video of their own shots
rationales: The newcomers can recognize the fault but don't know how to change it. Beginners need prescriptive feedback, which gives the correction as well as the error.
Cutting back helps when comments are so frequent that players depend on them. He speaks on one shot in five, and only for large errors.
Positive feedback is already there, and the trouble is a fault that persists.
Video helps players who don't believe or can't feel what the coach describes. The newcomer saw and felt it.
items.takeaway: Descriptive feedback names the error; beginners usually also need to be told what to do about it.

items.stem: A consultant has been teaching tactical breathing to police recruits. Three weeks ago they counted aloud and lost the rhythm if a door slammed. Since then they have kept it going while answering a radio, then with sirens playing and a stopwatch running, and, this week, in walk-through scenarios with role players. On the instructors' checklists, 22 of the 24 recruits held the rhythm in every walk-through, most of them talking as they did so. The training officer, remembering the slammed door, wonders what should come next. What should the consultant recommend?
options: Return to classroom practice until it is second nature
Use it in the full-speed use-of-force scenarios
Add a mild stressor, such as noise or a time limit
Switch to a simpler cue, such as a single word
rationales: Calm practice serves recruits who are still counting. These can breathe, talk, and act at the same time.
Recruits have kept the skill through progressively harder conditions, and with little conscious effort. The next step in a graded progression is the demanding setting it is meant for.
Mild stressors were the right step a couple of weeks ago, and recruits have since gone beyond them.
Simplifying helps when a technique is too much to manage. Nearly all of the recruits manage this one while talking.
items.takeaway: Raise the stress of practice in steps, and take the next step when the skill holds up.

items.stem: At a coach's request, a consultant looks into a high school volleyball team's serving. In practice, players hit 40 float serves to one zone, then 40 to another, and land about 90 percent. In matches the coach signals a zone before each serve. Going through match video, the consultant finds that players who are signaled the same zone twice running land nearly all of their second serves; after a change of zone, they miss close to half. Crowd size and score make no difference. Which change should the consultant suggest for practice?
options: Serving longer runs to a single zone
Serving with noise and a penalty for misses
Serving with a comment after each attempt
Serving to a different zone from ball to ball
rationales: Long runs help beginners get the movement. These players have it and perform at 90 percent in runs; it is the change that beats them.
Pressure practice helps players who falter in tense moments, but crowd size and score make no difference here.
Frequent comments help players who can't yet find the right form. Their form is good enough to land repeats.
Blocked practice lets players repeat a solution, but matches require building a new one for each serve. Random practice brings in that demand and improves retention and transfer.
items.takeaway: If a skill fails when the task changes, practice with the task changing from trial to trial.

items.stem: A youth hockey association asks a consultant to help coaches in its house league for 15- and 16-year-olds. Nearly all of the players left rep hockey a year or two ago, most of them after being told they would go no further. They skate on Friday nights; several also run or lift with friends. "I just like being out there," one tells the consultant. Yet the players have begun drifting away, and a typical session looks like a rep practice. Drawing on the Developmental Model of Sport Participation, which kind of session should the coaches run?
options: Playful games, drawn from several different sports
An even mix of hockey games and hockey drills
Mostly games and fitness, with few skill targets
Mostly drills on weaknesses, with close feedback
rationales: Sampling many sports through play fits children of about 6 to 12.
A balance of play and practice fits the specializing years, when players of about 13 to 15 are narrowing to a sport in which they hope to progress.
These players have chosen participation over elite performance. The model's recreational years stress enjoyment, activity, and health, with a good deal of deliberate play.
A high share of deliberate practice fits the investment years of players who have committed to elite performance. These players have left that path.
items.takeaway: In the DMSP, adolescents who aren't pursuing elite sport are best served by play, activity, and enjoyment.

items.stem: Professional concert pianist Sakura learned a concerto at 17 and has played it easily for 20 years. A conductor points out that she has been blurring two notes in one passage all along, because she crosses two fingers early. She agrees, and can play it cleanly if she stops to think. But as soon as she plays in her usual way, with her mind on the line of the music, the old crossing comes back, at home or onstage, rested or tired. The performance is seven weeks off. How should she practice the passage over the next few weeks?
options: Slowly, with her attention on each finger
At tempo, with her attention on the musical line
After a breathing exercise that settles her nerves
Within full run-throughs of the whole movement
rationales: Her automatic movement is the error. Changing it means bringing it back under conscious control for a time, and seven weeks leaves room for the new version to become automatic.
A holistic focus protects a correct automatic skill. Here it calls up the old crossing.
Calming down helps when anxiety disrupts a skill. The wrong note turns up at home and onstage alike.
Run-throughs help a passage that works by itself but not in context. This one goes wrong in both.
items.takeaway: Attention to mechanics disrupts a sound automatic skill, but it is needed for changing a faulty one.

items.stem: Professional esports player Tariq feels stuck and shows a consultant his practice log. Each block has a stated purpose ("hold angles after trades"), chosen from his most common errors. A coach reviews clips with him as each block ends, and the drills are set so that he fails about a third of the time. He practices from ten in the morning to ten at night with a sandwich at his desk, six days a week. The log shows reaction times creeping up from midafternoon, and by evening he is repeating errors he had fixed before lunch. Which change best fits deliberate practice principles?
options: A specific weakness to work on in each block
Feedback that comes sooner after each block
Tasks that go further beyond his present level
Fewer hours, with rest between the blocks
rationales: Each block already has a purpose chosen from his errors.
A coach already reviews clips as each block ends.
Failing about a third of the time already keeps him at the edge of his ability.
Deliberate practice takes full concentration, which can be kept up only for limited periods and depends on recovery. His decline through the day shows that he has gone past that limit.
items.takeaway: Deliberate practice is limited by concentration and recovery; beyond that limit, more hours add little.

items.stem: A professional handball club books four sessions meant to get players talking openly with one another about losing a starting place. The head coach says he'll help in whatever way is most useful. In individual meetings with the consultant, players had plenty to say. The coach then sat in on the first session: the room went quiet, the captain answered for everyone, and several players watched the coach before speaking. Which role should the consultant propose to the coach for the remaining sessions?
options: Leading the sessions himself, after briefings from the consultant
Joining the sessions as one voice among the players
Staying away from the sessions, which the consultant runs
Sitting in on the sessions, and cueing their skills in practice
rationales: Coach-led delivery can work when players look to the coach for guidance on the topic. These players fell silent merely because the coach, who decides who starts, was in the room.
Taking part as one voice assumes players will speak freely around the coach. In the first session they watched the coach before speaking and let the captain answer.

The sessions depend on open talk about selection, and the contrast between the individual meetings and the first session shows that the coach's presence shuts it down. A defined role outside the room best serves the program's aim.
Cueing skills in practice helps transfer when the program teaches a skill such as a reset. This program is about open conversation, and sitting in has already stifled it.
items.takeaway: Fit the coach's role to the aim of the sessions: presence that aids skill transfer can shut down open talk.

items.stem: At an intake meeting, Haruto, an elite golfer, describes a year with a former consultant: "I never missed a week. Within a month I had the breathing and the imagery down cold, and I did them in my room every night. Then I'd stand on the first tee of a tournament and have nothing. He told me to keep going, so I did the same thing for eleven more months." Which expectation about the new work is most important to set with Haruto?
options: His practice will move into harder and harder conditions
His gains will depend on work he does between sessions
His skills will need weeks of repetition to become steady
His nerves will remain, and he will learn to play with them
rationales: Haruto mastered the skills quickly in a quiet room and never practiced them anywhere else, so they didn't transfer. Skills need to be rehearsed under conditions that come to resemble competition, and he should expect that from the start.
Work between sessions is essential, but Haruto already did it every night for a year. Effort outside sessions wasn't what was missing.
This is the message for someone who quits after a few days. Haruto had the skills within a month and then repeated them for eleven more.
This expectation suits a client who judges a skill by whether nerves vanish. Haruto's complaint is that the skills themselves were unavailable on the tee.
items.takeaway: Mental skills learned in calm conditions must be practiced under pressure before they can be counted on there.

items.topic: Fitting a one-off workshop to its aim
items.stem: A logistics company's vice president asks a consultant for a single 90-minute workshop on mental performance for 200 employees. Asked what she'd like to be different afterward, she says, "We already fund individual sessions with your colleague, and the people who go rave about them. But most staff have never heard of it, or think it's therapy. I'd like them to walk out knowing what it is and how to book." How should the consultant respond to her request?
options: Propose a six-session series in place of the single workshop
Propose training for supervisors in place of the staff workshop
Suggest a needs survey of employees ahead of the workshop
Accept the workshop in the single-session form requested
rationales: A series is right when the aim is new skills that staff will use at work. The aim here is awareness of an existing service, which one session can deliver.
Training supervisors fits when the change depends on how supervisors act. The vice president wants staff themselves to know about a service and how to book it.
A survey is useful when nobody can say what employees need. She has named a clear gap in knowledge and a clear result she wants.
Her goal is informational: staff should know what a service is and how to book it. A single session is well matched to that goal, so the request needs no redesign.
items.takeaway: Match the format to the goal: a single workshop can build awareness, though it rarely builds skills.

items.stem: A high school athletic director is planning mental performance training with a consultant and describes last year's yoga program: "We made it mandatory, and attendance was perfect. The volleyball team had been asking for it, and they still do it on the bus. Football and wrestling lay on the mats and counted ceiling tiles until it ended. So I've already printed your sign-in sheets, every team, every Tuesday." Which point about mental performance training does the director most need to hear?
options: It serves performers of any level, including those doing well
It takes hold best with athletes who choose to take part
It builds skills gradually, through practice across a season
It teaches performance skills and is separate from clinical care
rationales: This point helps a director who reserves training for athletes in trouble. This director is already enrolling every team.

The same program lasted with the team that had asked for it and left no trace with those who were made to come. Willing participation drives learning and use of mental skills, so perfect attendance is the wrong target.
Gradual skill building is the message for someone who wants a quick fix. The director has planned weekly sessions, and the yoga failed with some teams and lasted with others.
This would matter if the director were confusing the training with counseling. The account of the yoga program raises no such confusion.
items.takeaway: Mandated attendance fills seats; voluntary commitment builds skills.

items.stem: A professional volleyball club hires a consultant for six hours a month, and the head coach expects a mental performance plan for each of 18 players. The consultant meets them all. Fourteen describe routines built over years, which match records show holding up in tight sets, and ask for nothing. The others each raise something: a server who rushes, a libero who dwells on bad passes, a setter new to starting, and a blocker who goes quiet in big arenas. How should the consultant propose to use the hours?
options: On team sessions for the full roster
On team sessions plus brief individual check-ins
On individual work for the players who ask
On a wider contract that gives each player a plan
rationales: Team sessions suit a need that players share. The four concerns differ from one another, and the rest of the roster is doing well.
A mixed model fits when there is a shared need alongside individual ones. The meetings turned up no shared need, so team time would draw hours from those who can use them.

The needs are individual, varied, and held by four willing players, while the others have routines that work. Matching delivery to assessed need makes good use of limited hours and resets the coach's expectation.
More hours would be worth requesting if most players wanted help. Fourteen don't, and their routines are holding up.
items.takeaway: Let assessed need, rather than roster size, decide how limited hours are spent.

items.topic: Agreeing on an aim for audition nerves
items.stem: Isabela, a professional violist, tells a consultant at intake that she wants her shaking dealt with before auditions. She has kept a diary of nine auditions. In four, her hands were fairly steady and she played well. In five, they shook hard and her bow skipped on the string. Her frame of mind didn't separate the two groups: before two of the five she had written, "Buzzing, can't wait, this one's mine," and after two others, "Let it shake and just played. Still skipped." Which aim should the consultant propose for their work?
options: Reading the shaking as a sign that she is ready
Letting the shaking be there as she commits to the music
Making auditions more familiar through mock panels
Lowering the intensity of the shaking
rationales: Reinterpreting symptoms helps when the reading of them does the harm. Before two of the poor auditions she already read her state as excitement, and the bow skipped anyway.
Making room for symptoms suits a performer who plays well with them present. She let the shaking be there twice, and her bow still skipped.
Mock panels build familiarity when the setting is what unsettles a performer. Nothing in the diary ties the shaking to unfamiliar auditions.
Performance followed how hard her hands shook and not how she felt about it. For a fine motor task in which the symptom directly disrupts execution, lowering its intensity is the sensible aim.
items.takeaway: Interpretation matters, but when a symptom physically disrupts execution, reducing it is a sound aim.

items.stem: A collegiate men's basketball team learned a breathing-and-cue reset from its consultant in the fall. At the four road games the consultant attended, sitting quietly a few rows back, players came over before tip-off and again at halftime to be walked through it. At the five the consultant missed, video shows the same players using it without help at the same points. The coach offers a seat on the conference tournament trip and leaves the role open. Which role should the consultant propose?
options: Remaining at home, reachable by phone if needed
Staying near the team, available if players want to talk
Leading players through the reset ahead of each game
Helping coaches on the bench cue the reset in timeouts
rationales: Players run the reset themselves when the consultant is away and lean on the consultant when one is present. Staying home protects the independence the training was meant to build, and a call is still possible.
Being quietly available suits players who use their skills either way. These players come to the consultant whenever one is there, so being nearby invites the dependence.
Leading the reset would help players who forget it or can't manage it alone. Video from five games shows that they can.
Coach cues help when players miss the moments to use a skill. These players use it at the right points without prompting.
items.takeaway: Consulting aims at self-regulation; sometimes the most useful place to be is somewhere else.

items.stem: A mother signs the permission form and books ten sessions for Anselm, a 14-year-old figure skater, whose coach thinks he could be steadier in competition. At a first meeting the consultant described the work, and Anselm asked what a session would be like, who would hear about it, and whether he could have a week to think. Today he says, "I thought about it, and I get what it is. I don't want to do it." What should the consultant do next?
options: Explain to Anselm what the sessions would involve
End the intake without starting the sessions
Ask Anselm what he'd like to improve in his skating
Ask his mother what she has noticed in his skating
rationales: An explanation comes before a decision. Anselm asked good questions last time, got answers, and says he understands.
A minor's assent is sought alongside a guardian's permission. Anselm gave an informed, considered no to performance training, so the consultant respects it and can say that he is welcome back.
Exploring his goals suits a reluctant teenager who hasn't made up his mind. Anselm took a week and decided.
A parent's observations inform an assessment. There is no assessment to conduct until Anselm agrees to take part.
items.takeaway: For minors, guardian permission doesn't replace assent; a considered no should be honored.

items.stem: Moira, a 52-year-old triathlete, opens a video session by saying, "I need help with my race nutrition, and I know that isn't your department." She goes on: "In training I take a gel every half hour, the amounts my dietitian set, and they sit fine. In races, somebody passes me, I start chasing, and I find the gels in my pocket at the finish. My coach says I hold my pace well up to that point." How should the consultant handle the request?
options: Suggest she take it to her dietitian
Suggest she take it to a sports physician
Suggest she take it to her triathlon coach
Take it on in the sessions they have
rationales: A dietitian sets what and how much she eats, and that plan works in training. The trouble is that she forgets to follow it once she is chasing.
A physician would be the contact for symptoms such as dizziness or stomach pain. She reports none, and the gels sit fine.
A coach would handle pacing and training plans. Her pacing is sound until her attention goes to a rival.
The label is nutrition, but the pattern is a lapse in attention under competitive pressure. Helping her hold to an existing plan, with a cue or routine, is mental performance work.
items.takeaway: Judge scope by what is going wrong and not by the label a client gives it.

items.stem: A fire chief meets a consultant about mental performance training for the department. "I've paid for three of these," the chief says. "Crews signed up, they liked them, and nobody told me anyone's private business, which suits me fine. Each trainer said it had gone great. And I couldn't tell you one thing that was different at a fire the next month. I suppose you'll want six sessions as well?" What should the consultant settle with the chief first?
options: What the chief will hear about individual firefighters
How crews will learn that taking part is voluntary
What the chief would see if the training had worked
Where training ends and counseling would take over
rationales: Reporting limits come first when a chief expects to learn about individuals. This chief is content not to.
Voluntary participation would need settling if crews were being ordered to come. They signed up for the earlier programs willingly.
