options: The group's structure, an input
The group's environment, an input
The group's processes, a throughput
The group's cohesion, an output
rationales: Giving members regular positions of their own is a group structure strategy, alongside roles and norms, and structure is one of the framework's inputs.
The group environment covers distinctiveness, such as a group name or shirts, and closeness. A spot of one's own concerns a member's position within the group.
Group processes cover interaction, such as partner work, shared goals, and sacrifices. Keeping a spot doesn't involve members' working together.
Cohesion is the result the framework aims to produce. Strategies act on the inputs and throughputs that lead to it.
items.takeaway: In Carron and Spink's framework, positions, roles, and norms belong to group structure.

items.stem: Six weeks into an imagery plan for composure, Anjali, a collegiate pianist, asks her consultant for something different because her jury was "a mess." Her log shows four imagery sessions a week, as agreed. The jury fell in the second week. In weekly studio class, where she plays for about thirty students and faculty, her composure ratings have run 3, 3, 4, 5, 5, 6. Her next jury is a month away. What should the consultant recommend?
options: Keep the imagery plan as it is until the next jury
Replace the imagery with a cue-word strategy
Work out what has kept her from imagery sessions
Move her imagery into rehearsals with an audience
rationales: The one poor result came before the plan had had time to work, and ratings in front of an audience have climbed steadily since. With practice on track and a fair test a month off, the evidence supports staying the course.
Changing strategies makes sense when a well-practiced plan shows no benefit. Her studio class ratings have doubled.
Barriers need exploring when practice is being missed. Her log shows every agreed session.
Adding pressure helps when gains stop short of performance settings. Hers already appear when she plays for an audience.
items.takeaway: Judge a plan on adherence and the trend, not on one result from its first days.

items.stem: Corwin, a collegiate swimmer, set a goal of holding a target stroke rate on 8 of 10 repeats in Thursday's set. Over five weeks he has managed 8, 10, 10, 10, and 10. "Best part of my week," he says. "I'd like to keep it just like this, it's great for my confidence." His coach mentions that Corwin has started chatting between repeats and that his attention drifts in the second half of the set. What is the most appropriate adjustment?
options: Leave the stroke-rate goal at its current level
Ease the stroke-rate goal to a smaller step
Make the stroke-rate goal harder to reach
Pair the stroke-rate goal with a race-time goal
rationales: Keeping the goal would suit a swimmer still working to reach it. Four perfect weeks and wandering attention show that it no longer asks much of him.
A smaller step helps a swimmer who keeps falling short. Corwin has met his goal every week.
Challenging goals draw more effort and attention than easy ones. He reaches this one with little effort and his attention drifts, so raising the standard restores its value.
Linking it to race times helps a swimmer who can't see the point of the goal. Corwin values it; it has simply become easy.
items.takeaway: A goal that is met without effort has stopped directing effort; raise it.

items.stem: After a six-week stress-management program, paramedics rate the sessions highly, and nearly all perform the breathing and refocusing techniques well in the drills that open each shift. On ride-alongs, supervisors see the techniques on about one call in ten. "I believe in it," one medic says, "I've felt it work. I just think of it when I'm restocking the rig." Which revision to the program fits these findings best?
options: Reteach the techniques with closer demonstration and feedback
Pair one technique with a step crews take on each call
Add time for technique practice to the start of shifts
Have respected medics describe how the techniques helped
rationales: Reteaching addresses weak skills. Crews perform the techniques well in drills.
Crews can use the techniques and want to, but they remember too late. Tying one to a step already in every call, such as pulling on gloves, puts a reminder at the moment of use.
More practice time helps when skills have gone rusty. Crews already practice at the start of each shift and perform well.
Testimony from peers helps when crews doubt the techniques. The medic already believes in them and has felt them work.
items.takeaway: When skill and belief are present but use is not, build a cue into the job itself.

items.stem: For six weeks Emre, an elite judo athlete, has used slow diaphragmatic breathing at competitions. He now sleeps well before tournaments, and his activation ratings as he bows in are where he likes them. Yet he has lost three matches early on grips. On video he is a beat late to each opponent's first reach. "I keep the breath low and slow the whole way through," he says, "just like we practiced." How should the consultant adjust the plan?
options: Add a cognitive strategy for the night before tournaments
Lengthen the breathing he does before each match
Confine the breathing to the time before he bows in
Replace the breathing with an activating routine
rationales: A cognitive strategy would address pre-tournament worry. He sleeps well before tournaments.
Longer breathing would suit an athlete who is still too keyed up at the start. His ratings are where he wants them.

The breathing does its job before matches, but he carries it into the fight, where it holds his attention on his own body as the opponent moves. Keeping it to the preparation period preserves the benefit and frees his attention.
Activation would help if the breathing had left him flat. He reaches the mat at his preferred level, and the trouble begins once the match does.
items.takeaway: A well-learned technique can hurt when it takes attention at the wrong moment.

items.topic: Recognizing warning signs in a runner
items.stem: In an initial assessment, collegiate distance runner Astrid asks for help with mental toughness because her times have slipped since fall, when her mileage went up by half. She has had two stress fractures since then, has not had a period for five months, and catches every cold. She is in bed by ten and wakes at seven, laughs easily, and looks forward to practice. "I'm not dieting," she says. "I eat exactly what I've always eaten." With her consent, the consultant arranges a visit to the team physician. Which concern do these signs most suggest?
options: Too little sleep for the training she is doing
Too little energy intake for the training she is doing
A depressed mood affecting how well she trains
A fear of racing that shows up in her body
rationales: Nine hours in bed, regularly kept, makes short sleep an unlikely explanation.

Missed periods, bone stress injuries, frequent illness, and falling times after a rise in mileage with no change in food suggest low energy availability (RED-S), which needn't involve dieting. A physician must evaluate it.
Easy laughter and looking forward to practice don't suggest low mood.
Race anxiety can produce bodily symptoms and falling times, but it wouldn't account for stress fractures and months without a period, and she looks forward to practice.
items.takeaway: RED-S can occur without dieting when training rises and intake doesn't; recognize the pattern and refer.

items.stem: A 17-year-old soccer player, Cormac, says he can't concentrate in class on Wednesdays and Fridays. The two-week sleep log he kept for a consultant shows lights out at ten and alarm at seven every day, weekends included, with his phone in the kitchen. He falls asleep within minutes except on Tuesdays and Thursdays, when he lies awake past one. Those are the days of evening training. "I'm dragging by then," he says, "so I grab a can of something at the station on the way. Gets me through." He doesn't snore and wakes rested after other nights. What should the consultant ask about next?
options: How much his bedtime shifts across the week
What he does on screens before lights out
How much caffeine he takes in, and when
How he breathes at night, and what his family hears
rationales: The log already shows the same bedtime and wake time every day.
His phone is in the kitchen every night, including the five on which he falls asleep quickly.
The trouble follows the evenings on which he has a can of something to get him through training. Late caffeine is the first thing to ask about before planning any change.
Loud snoring or gasping would call for a medical evaluation, but he doesn't snore and wakes rested after most nights.
items.takeaway: Let the pattern in a sleep log point to the next question before planning an intervention.

items.topic: Urgent signs after a head impact
items.stem: University rugby player Declan arrives for a first session an hour after a match in which he took a knee to the head. He tells the consultant that he was checked at the sideline, sent to rest, and felt "okay, just a headache." As they talk, the headache gets worse. He vomited twice on the way over, he answers more and more slowly, and he lays his head on the desk, saying he needs to sleep. The athletic trainer's office is a ten-minute walk away. What should the consultant do first?
options: Call emergency services and stay with him
Walk with him to the athletic trainer's office
Ask the team physician how to pace his sessions
Ask medical staff which return-to-play step he is on
rationales: A worsening headache, repeated vomiting, and increasing drowsiness after a head impact are red flags for a serious brain injury. The emergency plan comes first.
Prompt handover to the athletic trainer suits a suspected concussion in someone who is stable. Declan is getting worse by the minute.
Adapting sessions with medical guidance suits an athlete whose concussion has been diagnosed and is being managed.
Checking progress suits an athlete who is recovering under medical supervision.
items.takeaway: Worsening headache, repeated vomiting, or growing drowsiness after a head impact is an emergency.

items.stem: In early autumn, national-team swimmer Pilar, her coach, and a consultant map out a season that peaks at championships in August. General preparation runs through winter; specific preparation, with race-pace sets and small meets, fills the spring; a taper follows in July, and a transition period in September. Pilar learned a pre-race routine last season and can run it alone on an empty deck without a thought. At last season's one meet with it, she says, "there were people everywhere and a whistle, and it came out in pieces." Which phase should the plan make the main time for working on it?
options: General preparation, as volume builds
The taper, as the training load drops
Transition, once the season is over
Specific preparation, as racing begins
rationales: Early preparation is the time for learning a skill's basics. Pilar has them, and the phase offers few of the conditions that upset her.
In the taper, skills should be steady and familiar. Reworking the routine then would leave uncertainty just ahead of the championships.
Transition is for recovery and review, and it falls after the championships she is preparing for.
Her routine is learned but breaks down in racelike surroundings. Race-pace sets and small meets supply those conditions with time left to refine it.
items.takeaway: Learn skills early, adapt them to competition conditions in specific preparation, and leave the taper for rehearsal.

items.topic: Planning mental work in a taper
items.stem: Collegiate 800-meter runner Jamal and his coach are planning a two-week taper with a consultant. His log from the last three championship tapers reads much alike: heavy legs, fidgety, "can't sit through class," sleeping fine, imagery and routine done daily and enjoyed. Beside each he wrote a version of "here we go, right on time," and each ended in a season's best. The coach, who has just read an article on the psychology of tapering, asks what the consultant would like to put into this one. What should the consultant plan for the two weeks?
options: Keeping his present imagery and routine as they are
Teaching him what a taper feels like, and why
Adding a relaxation exercise to do in the evenings
Cutting back his imagery until the week of the meet
rationales: Jamal expects the sensations and reads them as a good sign, sleeps well, and has raced well on this preparation three times. A taper is for holding what works, so nothing new is needed.
Education helps an athlete who takes taper sensations for lost fitness. Jamal's notes show that he already reads them as normal.
An evening exercise would address trouble settling at night, and he sleeps fine.
A lighter mental load suits an athlete who is worn out by it. Jamal enjoys his daily practice.
items.takeaway: In a taper, keep what is working; normal sensations read well don't need an intervention.

items.stem: Elite biathlete Sigrun shoots nearly perfectly in dry practice. In races she skis hard into the range, and by her monitor her heart is at 90 percent of its maximum as she lies down; her best rivals' are, too. She means to get five shots away in about 30 seconds and can't afford longer. Video shows the rifle rising and falling with her chest as she fires. She sleeps well, starts races feeling sharp, and hits the first target as often as the last. Which skill should the consultant plan to build with her and her coach for the range?
options: Slow breathing at about six breaths a minute
A short pause after exhaling, timed to each shot
Progressive muscle relaxation from head to toe
Quick, deep breaths with an energizing cue word
rationales: Slow-paced breathing suits moments when the body is at rest. Six breaths would use a full minute and wouldn't meet the oxygen demand of near-maximal effort.
The rifle moves with her breathing, and neither her heart rate nor the time can change much. Firing in a brief pause at the end of an exhale steadies the rifle within both limits.
Progressive relaxation takes minutes and targets lasting muscle tension, which isn't what the video shows.
Psyching up suits an athlete who starts flat. Sigrun starts sharp, and her heart is at 90 percent of maximum.
items.takeaway: Fit arousal and breathing skills to the event's physiological demands and the time available.

items.stem: Snowboarder Kai, 15, rides carefully in training. When his friends film him, he goes for tricks that his coach hasn't cleared, and he has fallen hard. He and a consultant wrote if-then plans for those moments, and he rehearsed them daily. The coach cleared him a new set of tricks, which he lands easily and calmly. Three Saturdays later he recites the plan word for word and explains just how a bad landing can break a wrist. He also reports that he dropped it all three times: "Phones came out and I was already going." His friends say they are happy to film whatever. What should the consultant try next?
options: Going over the injury risks of the uncleared tricks
Rehearsing more if-then plans for when filming starts
Having friends film the runs his coach has cleared
Practicing a calming breath to take before dropping in
rationales: Information helps a rider who misjudges the danger. Kai can explain it in detail.
If-then plans are a good first approach, but he knows his by heart, and in the moment it has failed three times out of three.

In adolescence, peers heighten the pull of reward faster than self-control can answer it. Kai knows the risks and the plan, so the lever left is the situation, which his friends are willing to change.
A calming breath helps a rider undone by nerves. Kai is drawn in by the moment and rides calmly otherwise.
items.takeaway: When an adolescent's knowledge and plans give way in front of peers, change the situation.

items.stem: Over video, a consultant is teaching slow-paced breathing to Rosalie, a healthy sales executive, with a pacer set at six breaths a minute and a sensor showing her heart rate. She sits back with her shoulders low, and her belly moves gently. She doesn't feel dizzy. But near the end of each exhale her jaw tightens, and she snatches the next breath ahead of the pacer. "I'm running out of road," she says. When she slips ahead of it for a few breaths, the heart rate wave on the screen grows larger and smoother. What is the best adjustment?
options: Smaller, softer breaths at the present pace
Belly breathing in place of chest breathing
A break from practice until her physician is consulted
A pacer set slightly faster than the present one
rationales: Smaller breaths correct overbreathing, which shows up as large, forceful breaths with lightheadedness or tingling. Her breaths are gentle and she isn't dizzy.
Her shoulders are low and her belly is moving, so she is breathing that way already.
Medical advice comes first if there is chest pain, fainting, or a relevant condition. Straining at the end of an exhale is a matter of pace.
She strains at this pace, and her heart rate pattern improves when she speeds up. Best breathing frequency differs among individuals, so the pacer should move toward hers.
items.takeaway: Resonance breathing rates are individual; set the pace by comfort and heart rate response.

items.stem: Swimmers of 15 and 16 on a high school team get about six hours of sleep and nod off in class. At their coach's request, a consultant had them log two weeks. In nearly every log, the phone is out of the room by nine and the lights are off at half past; sleep comes around eleven, and the alarm goes at a quarter to five for practice. On Sundays, with no alarm, they sleep from about eleven until nine and wake rested. The coach has the pool from five until eight in the morning and may use any part of it. Which step is most likely to help?
options: Teaching the swimmers a wind-down routine for bedtime
Showing their coach how practice times fit teen sleep
Asking parents to have the house quiet by half past nine
Suggesting a medical evaluation of the swimmers' sleep
rationales: A wind-down routine helps teens who are on their phones late. These already put screens away and lights out in good time.

In adolescence the body clock shifts later, so sleep comes at about eleven whatever time lights go out. The wake time is what cuts sleep short, and the coach is the one who sets it and has room to move it.
Parents can help when evenings at home run late. The lights are already off at that time, and the swimmers don't fall asleep until eleven.
An evaluation suits a swimmer who is unrefreshed after plenty of sleep or who shows signs of a disorder. These sleep soundly and wake rested when allowed to.
items.takeaway: Teens' body clocks run late; when bedtime habits are sound, look at the wake time and who sets it.

items.stem: A consultant tracks professional cyclist Lucas with weekly mood and confidence ratings out of 10. Before a hard three-week block in February, his mood stood at about 8. It went to 7, 6, and 5 during the block, 5 after the recovery week, and 4 or 5 in each of the six weeks since, though his coach has kept rides short and easy. He still does his imagery and routine daily. His power is down, his sleep is broken, and he says, "Everything's fine at home, the contract's signed, and I'm just flat." Which reading of these data should guide the review?
options: A prolonged response that calls for medical evaluation
A planned dip that should lift with the next easy week
A reaction to events elsewhere in his life
A sign that the mental skills need to be changed
rationales: Mood, power, and sleep haven't recovered after weeks of light load. Planned overreaching should have cleared by then, so prolonged maladaptation or illness has to be considered, and that is for a physician to evaluate.
A dip in a hard block is expected and normally rebounds with recovery. He has had seven easy weeks without a rebound.
A mood drop that tracks life events would point here, but he describes home and contract as settled, and the drop began with the block.
A skills problem would show in how he uses them or in specific situations. He keeps up his practice, and the decline is general and physical.
items.takeaway: Mood and performance that stay low through weeks of light training call for a medical evaluation.

items.topic: Reviewing a plan during hard training
items.stem: At a quarterly review, masters rower Beatriz tells her consultant, "Maybe we need to rethink everything." She is 16 days into a three-week block that is her heaviest of the year. Her ergometer times are down by about 2 percent, her legs feel heavy, and she has been snapping at her crewmates. Her mental skills practice is as regular as ever, and she sleeps and eats well. Leafing through her log, the consultant finds nearly the same entry from the same week last spring, followed ten days later by "Legs back. Best piece of the year." What should the consultant suggest?
options: Seeing her physician about the drop in her times
Setting lower goals for the rest of her season
Keeping the plan, and looking again after the block
Trading some of her mental skills for new ones
rationales: A medical evaluation is called for when a decline goes on despite rest or comes with worrying signs. She is mid-block, hasn't rested yet, and has recovered from this before.
Goals should be revised when circumstances change. A short dip in a heavy block isn't a reason to expect less of the season.
A brief drop in performance and mood fits planned overreaching, as her log from last spring shows. The time to judge the plan is after she has recovered.
Skills are changed when a fair trial shows that they aren't working. Nothing here points to them; the cause is the training load.
items.takeaway: Don't judge a mental skills plan by data from the middle of a planned overload.

items.stem: A consultant has spent a season with a professional women's soccer team and wants to interview players about which parts of the program they used and why, to help decide what to offer next year. The last match, on a Sunday in October, will decide the title, and the coach wants nothing new asked of players before it. Four weeks of rest follow, during which staff are in the office; preseason opens in January. Eleven of the 24 players are on loan and fly back to their own clubs on the Wednesday after the match; by the team's habit, others leave for places without much signal. Staff won't have time to read the interviews until November. When should the consultant hold them?
options: In the week before the last match
During the four weeks of rest
In the opening days of preseason
In the first days after the last match
rationales: Interviews then would go against the coach's request before the title match and would miss the season's final test. The players will still be there afterward.
The transition is usually the time for analysis and revision, and staff will do that part then. By that point nearly half of the players will have gone to other clubs.
Preseason suits questions about the coming squad's needs. Loan players won't be back, and memories will have faded.
The whole season can be covered, all players are still there, and memories are fresh. Analysis can wait for the transition, but access to nearly half of the players can't.
items.takeaway: Collect perishable data while the sources are available; analysis can wait for the transition period.

items.stem: Liv, an elite alpine skier, is nine weeks past ACL reconstruction. For six weeks she completed 95% of her rehab sessions; since then, about half. "It's the same knee, only better built," she said at week three, and she says it still. Her mood ratings have stayed steady and high. She rehabbed back from two earlier injuries without missing a day. In week seven her rehab moved to a clinic across the city, where she sees a different therapist each visit, at hours that overlap her team's video meetings. Using the integrated model of response to sport injury, which part should the plan address first?
options: How she appraises the injury and her recovery
How she responds emotionally to the injury
Personal factors she brought to the injury
Situational factors surrounding her rehab
rationales: Appraisal drives emotion and behavior in the model and is often the target. Hers is realistic, hopeful, and unchanged across the drop in adherence.
Emotional response would be the target if low mood were eroding adherence. Her mood has stayed steady and high.
Injury history, personality, and coping skills are personal factors. Hers carried her through two earlier injuries and the first six weeks of this one.
Adherence fell when the setting changed: a distant clinic, rotating therapists, and clashing hours. In the integrated model these are situational factors that shape behavioral responses.
items.takeaway: In the integrated model, find what changed when the behavior changed.

items.stem: A ballet company asks a consultant to help reduce injuries during its audition season. In interviews, dancers call auditions "the fun part" and expect to do well. They lean on one another, and it has been a settled year for most of them. Accident reports have a theme: "Didn't see her coming from the side." "My shoulders were up by my ears and I landed stiff." Based on the stress–injury model, which component should the prevention program start with?
options: Relaxation and attention-control training
Restructuring of audition-related thoughts
Team building to widen social support
Help with moves and other life changes
rationales: The reports describe the stress response itself, muscle tension and narrowed peripheral vision. The model's interventions target that physiological and attentional side as well as appraisal, and appraisal is favorable here.
Changing appraisals is the model's other intervention target. These dancers see auditions as enjoyable and expect to do well.
Social support is a coping resource in the model, and building it helps isolated dancers. These dancers already rely on one another.
A history of stressors raises vulnerability in the model. It has been a settled year for most of the dancers.
items.takeaway: Match injury-prevention work to the part of the stress–injury model that the data point to.

items.stem: Curtis, a firefighter, is eight weeks past shoulder surgery. His exercise log shows each prescribed set ticked, then a column he has added himself: ten more, twenty more, a run of push-ups. "The guys are covering my shifts," he says. "I'm not going to sit around." His physical therapist reports that the joint is irritated most Mondays and that his progress has stalled. With Curtis's consent, she and the consultant are planning goals with him. Which goal fits best?
options: "Complete my prescribed sets, and tick each one off."
"Stop at my prescribed sets, and log my rest days."
"Gain a set number of degrees of motion each week."
"Return to my engine on a date we fix together."
rationales: A completion goal helps someone who skips exercises. Curtis already ticks off every set; the trouble starts after that.
The log and the Monday irritation point to over-adherence. A process goal that counts stopping and resting as success turns his drive toward what recovery needs.
A weekly target makes progress visible when rehab seems endless. For someone already overdoing it, a number to beat would feed the problem.
A date can sustain someone who has lost sight of the purpose. Curtis has purpose in plenty, and a deadline would add to his hurry.
items.takeaway: Over-adherence is an adherence problem too; goals can reward restraint.

items.stem: Odessa, a collegiate lacrosse player, is rehabbing a dislocated shoulder. Her log shows every set done except the last two, small rotations with a light band. "Those are the warm-up ones for old people, right?" she says. "I do the ones that make me strong." She feels good about her progress, finds the band work easy, and is happy for the consultant to speak with her athletic trainer about this. Which step should the consultant take first?
options: Teach Odessa self-talk for the final sets
Set completion goals for the final sets
Ask the trainer to explain the final sets to her
Ask the trainer to alter the final sets for her
rationales: Self-talk can help an athlete who doubts she can finish or gives up from fatigue. Odessa finds these sets easy and leaves them out on purpose.
Goals and tracking help an athlete who means to finish and loses track. Odessa is leaving out sets she sees no use in.
She skips the sets because she misjudges what they are for. Explaining an exercise's purpose is the athletic trainer's role, and Odessa has agreed to the contact.
Altering exercises is the trainer's call and worth raising if she can't do them safely or comfortably. She finds them easy.
items.takeaway: Find the reason behind a skipped exercise, and go to the professional whose role covers it.

items.stem: Rosalba, a 58-year-old triathlete, is recovering from knee surgery. Twice a day she wears a brace that holds a gentle stretch for half an hour; it sets itself, and she has nothing to do but sit. Her physical therapist has told her to expect a dull, harmless ache. "My leg's loose and I'm breathing fine," she tells the consultant. "I just sit there staring at my knee, and after ten minutes the ache is the only thing in the world." Which strategy should the consultant suggest for these half hours?
options: Get absorbed in a story or music
Follow the sensations in her knee closely
Breathe slowly and let the leg go loose
Take the brace off and call the therapist
rationales: The ache is expected and harmless, the task asks nothing of her attention, and dwelling on the ache magnifies it. Dissociative strategies suit exactly that kind of pain.
Associative attention helps when sensations must guide effort or form. The brace does the work, and watching the knee is what makes the ache grow.
Paced breathing and muscle release suit someone who braces against pain. Her leg is loose and her breathing easy.
Stopping and contacting the therapist is right for new or sharp pain. This is the ache the therapist described.
items.takeaway: Choose a pain strategy by what the pain signals and what the task needs from attention.

items.stem: In a session at school before hockey practice, Ronan, 16, mentions that since a hard hit two days ago he has had headaches, can't concentrate in class, and wears sunglasses indoors. He is alert, walks steadily, and says it is no worse than yesterday. He has told no one, because Friday is a playoff game, and asks the consultant to keep it between them. The athletic trainer is in the training room down the hall, getting ready for practice. What should the consultant do first?
options: Call emergency services, and stay with him until they arrive
Phone his parents, and ask them to arrange a medical visit
Continue the session, within the limits he has been given
Walk him to the athletic trainer, and explain why on the way
rationales: Emergency care is right for red flags such as worsening headache, repeated vomiting, or growing drowsiness. He is alert and steady, and his symptoms are not worsening.
His parents need to know, and they would be the route if no medical staff were at hand. With the athletic trainer down the hall and practice about to start, this is slower.
Mental skills work can go on alongside medical management. No one has evaluated him, so there are no limits to work within.
A suspected concussion in a minor needs medical evaluation before any further play, and confidentiality does not extend to withholding this risk. The professional responsible is steps away.
items.takeaway: Suspected concussion goes to the medical team the same day, whatever the game schedule.

items.stem: Brigid, a collegiate volleyball setter, is three months into rehab for a torn Achilles tendon. She eats with the team, travels to matches, and charts opponents' serves. Her roommate hears about the bad days. Her therapist has walked her through each stage. She has missed four of her last ten rehab visits; the clinic is two buses away, and on crutches, she says, "it eats the whole afternoon." She would be glad for the consultant to talk with her coach. Which strategy should the consultant suggest?
options: Give her a part in team meetings
Help arrange rides to her clinic
Set aside time to hear how she is
Go over what her return will involve
rationales: A team role supports belonging for an injured athlete who feels cut off. She is with the team at meals and matches and already has a job to do.
Belonging, emotional, and informational support are all in place. What keeps her from rehab is the journey, so tangible support is the kind that is missing.
Emotional support helps an athlete who has nobody to talk to. Her roommate fills that role.
Informational support eases uncertainty. Her therapist has explained each stage.
items.takeaway: Social support works when its type fits the need.

items.stem: Yuna, an elite figure skater, has six weeks left in a boot after an ankle fracture. Her surgeon is pleased with the bone, she has had no pain for weeks, and she hasn't missed an exercise. She keeps pulling up old videos of her triple Lutz. "I used to know the edge without thinking," she tells her consultant. "Last night I tried to feel the takeoff and it was blurry." Her physical therapist has no objection to imagery work. Which imagery should the consultant introduce?
options: Imagery of the bone knitting together
Imagery of soothing warmth in the ankle
Imagery of her jump takeoffs and edges
Imagery of working through her exercises
rationales: Healing imagery can give an athlete a sense of involvement in recovery. Healing is going well and isn't on her mind.
Pain-management imagery suits discomfort during rehab. She has had no pain for weeks.
Her concern is losing the feel of a skill she can't practice. Rehearsal imagery keeps the skill mentally active while the ankle heals.
Imaging rehab tasks supports motivation and adherence. She hasn't missed an exercise.
items.takeaway: In rehab, imagery can serve healing, pain, adherence, or skill; choose by the athlete's need.

items.stem: Femi, a professional soccer midfielder, was medically cleared nine months after ACL reconstruction and has spent five weeks in full-contact training. Since clearance his readiness scores have risen from 48 to 91 of 100. The performance analyst's video shows him tackling and cutting at his pre-injury rates. "Yesterday I had to think which knee it was," he laughs. His head coach, whose last player back from this injury "came apart in a month," urges more sessions, twice a week. What should the consultant propose to Femi?
options: Confirm that his goals are met, and space out the sessions
Add confidence work that is built around contact
Return to the medical team before any further sessions
Keep the present plan, and repeat the scale in a month
rationales: Scores, video, and his own account agree that he is confident and playing freely. The coach's worry comes from another player, and the evidence supports tapering the work.
More confidence work is needed when clearance outpaces readiness. Femi's scores and his tackling show that the two have come together.
New physical signs call for the medical team. None are reported, and they have cleared him.
Waiting is sensible while readiness is still developing or hasn't been tested by contact. He has had five weeks of contact with clear gains.
items.takeaway: Clearance and readiness can differ; when they converge, let the plan wind down.

items.topic: Recognizing a clinical concern in rehab
items.stem: At a progress review three months into rehab for a back injury, Carmen, a collegiate gymnast, says rehab itself is on schedule. For the past several weeks, though, she has felt hopeless nearly every day, sleeps badly, and has stopped answering friends and going to class. "I can't see the point anymore." Asked directly, she says she has had no thoughts of suicide or of harming herself and has no plan. She isn't seeing anyone else for support. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Adjust her rehab goals, and keep an eye on her mood
Follow the crisis plan, and stay with her until help comes
Ask her consent to coordinate with her current therapist
Help her connect with a licensed mental health provider
rationales: Setbacks often bring brief dips in mood that goals and support can help. Weeks of near-daily hopelessness, withdrawal, and poor sleep while rehab goes well are beyond that.
The crisis plan is for imminent risk. Asked directly, she reports no suicidal thoughts and no plan, so this is urgent to refer but not an emergency.
Coordinating is right when a client already has licensed care. She isn't seeing anyone.
Persistent hopelessness, sleep problems, and withdrawal need evaluation by a licensed professional, which is outside a CMPC's scope. With no imminent risk, the step is a prompt, supported referral.
items.takeaway: Persistent, wide-ranging low mood calls for referral; imminent risk calls for the emergency plan.

items.stem: Rodrigo, an elite wheelchair basketball player, had met every weekly goal since shoulder surgery. He arrives for his progress review straight from his surgeon's office. A complication has added eight weeks, and he will miss the world championships. He understands the new protocol and starts it Thursday. When the consultant takes out the goal sheet, he pushes it back across the table, jaw tight. "I've been counting down to that tournament for two years," he says, and stares out of the window. What should the consultant do now?
options: Reset his weekly goals to the surgeon's timeline
Hear what losing the tournament means to him
Go over the gains he has made since surgery
Help him list questions to take back to the surgeon
rationales: New short-term goals will be needed, and in a few days they will probably help. He has just had the news and has pushed the sheet away.
The loss is minutes old and large. Attending to his emotional response comes before planning, which can wait until he is ready and the new protocol begins.
Reviewing gains helps someone who believes that nothing has been achieved. He is grieving a tournament, and progress charts would speak past that.
Preparing questions helps a client who is unsure what the news involves. He understands the protocol.
items.takeaway: After a fresh setback, the emotional response comes first and the goal revision follows.

items.stem: Rin, a professional esports player with chronic wrist pain, was offered surgery or a longer course of conservative treatment. On a video call she tells her consultant, "I'm having the surgery. I asked two surgeons everything on my list, and I've slept on it." The consultant would have expected her to wait until after a tournament in the spring. Rin goes on, "My manager's going to go quiet on me. I've written the message four times and deleted it." What is the most appropriate response?
options: Help her think through which option matters more to her
Help her draw up questions about the two treatments
Help her prepare to tell her manager what she decided
Help her set up another medical opinion on her wrist
rationales: Clarifying priorities is useful, and within scope, for a client who is torn. Rin has decided; reopening the choice would reflect the consultant's doubts rather than her need.
Preparing questions supports a client who lacks information. She has put hers to two surgeons.
The treatment choice belongs to Rin and her medical team, and it is made. Her difficulty is the conversation ahead, which is squarely within mental performance work.
Encouraging another opinion is reasonable when a client doubts the advice she was given. She has had two and is settled.
items.takeaway: Medical choices belong to the client and the medical team; help with what the client is facing around them.

items.stem: Yusra, an injured collegiate soccer player, signed a release letting her consultant share her attendance and mental skills plan with the sports medicine staff. At the staff's weekly meeting, the physical therapist turns to the consultant: "How's Yusra's plan going? Is she showing up?" Around the table are two athletic trainers, the team physician, and, as of this month, an assistant coach and an academic adviser who sit in to hear about availability. How should the consultant handle the request at this meeting?
options: Share nothing about Yusra's sessions
Share her attendance and her plan
Share her attendance, not her plan
Share her attendance, plan, and concerns
rationales: The release covers the sports medicine staff, and two people now at the table are outside it. The consultant can give the authorized information to the staff separately.
This is what the release allows, to the people it names. The coach and the adviser are not among them.
A limited disclosure needs a release that covers it for everyone present. Attendance is as protected from the coach and adviser as the plan is.
Concerns could be shared with the medical staff if Yusra had agreed to it. Her release doesn't mention them, and others are present.
items.takeaway: A release specifies both what may be shared and with whom; check who is in the room.

items.stem: An athletic trainer asks a consultant about Corbin, a wrestler three weeks into recovery from a broken forearm. He was miserable the Saturday he missed a meet and back to joking by Monday. He comes to rehab, does his work, and can recite his timeline, including the two meets still to miss. He sleeps fine and eats with the team. "He never got angry," the trainer says. "I was taught that they go through stages, and I keep waiting for the rest." Based on research on responses to sport injury, what should the consultant suggest?
options: Help Corbin voice anger that he might be holding in
Help Corbin see a licensed mental health provider
Carry on with his rehab and her usual check-ins
Go over his recovery timeline with him once more
rationales: Making room for anger helps when there are signs of it. There are none, and research doesn't support a set sequence that an athlete must complete.
A referral fits persistent distress or changes in sleep, eating, or functioning. He had one hard day and is doing well.
Fixed stage models are poorly supported; responses vary with appraisal and circumstances. Corbin's appraisal is realistic and he is adherent, so nothing more is called for.
Reviewing the timeline helps when cheerfulness rests on a misunderstanding. He can recite his, with the meets he will miss.
items.takeaway: Athletes don't have to pass through set stages; watch how this one appraises and copes.

items.stem: At intake, 15-year-old golfer Odette and her father agreed in writing that he would be told about attendance and that what she says would stay private unless safety was at risk. A month later he calls: "I've been dropping her at the clubhouse every Tuesday. Has she actually been coming in?" Odette has come to two of four sessions. Before each of the others, she texted the consultant that she'd rather hit balls that day. What should the consultant do?
options: Get Odette's permission first, and call him back with the answer
Explain that sessions are private, and suggest that he ask Odette
Tell him that she has come to two of the four sessions so far
Tell him how many she has missed, and what she gave as the reason
rationales: Odette gave her assent to this disclosure at intake, so a second permission isn't needed and only delays an answer he was promised. It would fit if the agreement had left attendance open.
What she says in sessions is private, but his question is about attendance, which the written agreement says he will be told. This would fit if he had asked what she talks about.

Attendance is exactly what Odette and her father agreed he could have, and he has asked for it. Keeping to the terms set during informed consent serves both the guardian's permission and the minor's assent.
The number of missed sessions falls within the agreement, but the reason is something Odette told the consultant, and nothing in it raises a safety concern. The agreement keeps it private.
items.takeaway: A sharing agreement cuts both ways: give what it promises, and hold what it protects.

items.stem: Henrik, a collegiate rower, comes to a first meeting at his coach's suggestion. "Coach told us straight out that you don't report to him, so that's fine," he says. "And I know what I want. I rush the first ten strokes of every race. I just can't picture this part. With the physio, I lie on a table and he works on me. Do I just start talking?" What is the best way for the consultant to begin?
options: Explain how sessions work and what each of them will do
Ask what Henrik hopes will be different by season's end
Explain what the coach will and won't hear about the sessions
Reflect how odd it may feel to be sent here by a coach
rationales: Henrik has a goal but no picture of the process or his part in it. Clear, direct information about roles and tasks is what he asked for, and it builds the agreement on tasks that a working alliance needs.
Goals matter early, but he has just named one. Asking again would pass over the question he actually put: what happens in a session?
Reporting lines must be covered during consent, but he raises them only to say he is satisfied. It would be the place to begin if he had wondered what gets back to the coach.
Reflecting feeling would help if he had shown resentment at being sent. He treats the coach's suggestion matter-of-factly; what he lacks is information.
items.takeaway: Begin with the gap the client shows you; sometimes that is plain information about the process.

items.stem: Before a fall workshop series, every athlete on a collegiate track and field team fills out an intake form for the consultant. Under "name and pronouns you use," one athlete, listed on the team roster as Rebecca, writes, "Rowan, they/them. I'm telling my teammates and coaches after the indoor season. Right now it's just my roommates and, I guess, you." The first workshop is on Thursday, with the full team and staff. How should the consultant handle names there?
options: Use Rowan and they/them, as the athlete wrote on the form
Open with a round in which everyone gives a name and pronouns
Tell the coaches beforehand that Rowan is the name to use
Use the roster name, and keep Rowan for private conversations
rationales: Using the name and pronouns an athlete gives is usually right, but doing so on Thursday would announce to teammates and coaches something Rowan plans to tell them months from now.
A round can be welcoming when athletes are ready to share. Here it would push Rowan to disclose early or to give a name they don't use, in front of the whole team.
Alerting staff helps when an athlete asks for it. Rowan has told the consultant and means to tell the coaches later, so this would disclose private information.
Rowan's note sets a limit: the consultant knows now, and the team will know after indoors. Following that limit respects confidentiality and leaves the timing of the disclosure with Rowan.
items.takeaway: The client decides who knows what and when; use a disclosed name as widely as they have asked.

items.stem: Five professional esports players begin weekly sessions with a consultant. Management will receive a one-page monthly update, and the players wrote the template themselves. When the consultant asks the group how they handle tilt, nobody answers. Then the support player says, "Last split we did one of these. I said I'd choked in the semifinal, and by dinner I had a nickname." Two teammates laugh; the others study their keyboards. What should the consultant do next?
options: Go over what the monthly updates to management will contain
Have the players settle how they'll treat what is said in sessions
Offer individual meetings for what players won't say in a group
Tell a story of the consultant's own tilt, then ask again
rationales: Reporting limits are essential in organizational work, but the players wrote the template. The story is about what teammates did with a disclosure, not what management did.
The support player spoke up and was ridiculed by teammates, so the interpersonal risk lies inside the group. Norms for how members treat what is said are the starting point for psychological safety.
Individual meetings suit topics that are personal to one player. The whole group has gone quiet, and moving talk elsewhere would leave the cause in place.
Modeling can help a group that doesn't know how to begin. These players know how; one of them did it and paid for it, and a story from the consultant doesn't change what teammates do.
items.takeaway: Find out where the risk of speaking lies before choosing how to lower it.

items.stem: Marguerite, 52, books a single video session nine days before her first full-distance triathlon, which she says will also be her last. "I don't want a project," she says. "Training has been lovely. It's the wait on the beach that undoes me. My heart pounds, I breathe like a train, and I've burned half my matches before the horn." What should the consultant offer her?
options: A set of mental skills, added one at a time over coming weeks
An assessment to find out which skills need the most attention
One breathing technique to practice between now and the race
A start date after the race, with time to build skills properly
rationales: Skills usually do take weeks to build, and a staged program would suit an athlete with a season ahead. Marguerite has nine days, one session, and no races after this one.
Assessment guides the work when the problem is unclear. She has described when it happens and what her body does, which is enough to choose a simple somatic technique.

Her concern is narrow and physical, and she has nine days for it. A single somatic technique, with an honest word about how much it can do in that time, fits what she asked for and the time available.
Waiting makes sense for an athlete who wants lasting change. This race is her last, so help that begins afterward is no help.
items.takeaway: Scale the offer to the time and the request; a small, honest offer can be the right one.

items.stem: A consultant has been contracted to provide voluntary performance support to a fire department; the chief receives attendance totals with no names. Individual meetings happen only if a firefighter asks for one. Opening the twenty-minute kickoff with an engine company, the chief says, "This person's here to figure out which of you is cracking under the pressure," and takes a seat in the front row. Arms fold around the room. What should the consultant do?
options: Tell the crew now what the work involves and what the chief sees
Give the planned talk, and clarify the role in individual meetings
Talk with the chief later about correcting it at the next briefing
Ask the crew what they've heard about the program so far
rationales: The crew has just been told that the program screens them, and they must choose to come back. Correcting the role and reporting lines now, in front of the chief, clears it up for everyone at once.
Individual meetings happen only on request. After that introduction, few are likely to ask, so most would never hear the correction.
Speaking privately with the chief is worthwhile, and would be enough if the crew hadn't heard the remark. Until the next briefing, though, the crew would believe they are being screened.
Asking is useful when the source of a crew's wariness is unknown. Here it is plain, and the question would invite them to repeat the chief's version with the chief looking on.
items.takeaway: When a third party misdescribes your role to the people you serve, correct it where they heard it.

items.stem: Before starting with a professional women's soccer club, a consultant turned down the head coach's request for "toughness" reports on players. The coach accepted this, and both signed terms under which individual sessions are private and the consultant has no part in selection. At the first squad meeting, a midfielder says, "Word is you'll be telling them who can handle the big games." Several players nod. What should the consultant do next?
options: Return to the coach to settle what will be reported
Tell the squad what the signed terms say about reporting
Ask the squad what they would be willing to have reported
Follow up with the midfielder in private about her worry
rationales: Settling reporting with the coach is the first move in third-party work, and it has been done. The terms are signed; the players just don't know them.

The question has a settled answer that the squad hasn't heard. Stating the limits of confidentiality and the consultant's role openly, to all who share the worry, is what the Ethics Code asks for at the outset of team work.
Asking players would fit if the terms were still open. Inviting their views on a settled matter suggests that reports are on the table.
A private talk suits a personal concern. Several players nodded, so an answer to one would leave the rest with the rumor.
items.takeaway: Once reporting terms are set, the people they protect need to hear them.

items.stem: Linnea, a conservatory pianist, self-referred for "stage nerves." As the consultant describes a biofeedback program, she leans in, tries on the sensor, and asks how soon it shows results. "I can see it working," she says. "What I keep wondering is what I'd be calm for. The audition forms have been on my desk since March. Some days I'd like to find out I don't have to send them." In terms of Bordin's working alliance, what should the consultant do next?
options: Explain more fully how biofeedback would ease her nerves
Offer a different method for easing her nerves on stage
Ask her how comfortable she feels with the consultant
Work out with her what she wants the sessions to achieve
rationales: More rationale strengthens agreement on tasks when a client doubts a method. Linnea expects biofeedback to work; she doubts what it would be in aid of.
A new method would help if she disliked this one. She is curious about the sensor, and any other method would serve the same uncertain goal.
Checking on the bond fits a client who has turned guarded. Linnea is engaged and has just confided something she finds hard to say.
Calming nerves assumes she wants to audition, and she isn't sure that she does. In Bordin's terms the method is acceptable and the goal isn't settled, so agreement on goals comes next.
items.takeaway: A task the client likes is no use until the goal it serves is agreed.

items.topic: Preparing for a new sport culture
items.stem: A consultant who is new to para sport will begin next month with a national wheelchair rugby squad. On a welcome call the captain, Tavita, says, "Ask us whatever you like, nobody here is shy. The only thing is, we've had nine new staff in six years, and we've sat down with every one of them and explained classification from scratch." How should the consultant prepare for the first team meeting?
options: Study the published rules on how players are classified
Plan questions for the players about how classification works
Arrange for the coach to explain how the lineups are built
Develop an opening session on reclassification
rationales: The captain is openly tired of teaching new staff the basics, and the basics are published. Arriving with that homework done shows respect and saves the players' time for what only they can tell.
Curiosity about athletes' experience is valuable, and Tavita welcomes questions. Asking how classification works would make the consultant the tenth newcomer to need the same lesson.
The coach's thinking on lineups may be useful later, but it isn't what the captain raised, and it depends on knowing classification in the first place.
Nothing on the call suggests that players are struggling with reclassification. Planning a session on it before meeting them assumes a need that no one has assessed.
items.takeaway: Learn on your own what is public; save clients' time for what only they know.

items.stem: Ximena, an 11-year-old gymnast, comes to a first session with her mother, who has signed the consent forms and explained by phone that Ximena cried at a meet. Ximena stands half behind her, eyes moving from the consultant's desk to a closed cabinet. "Is it going to be like when I got the stitches?" she whispers. What should the consultant do first to begin a relationship with Ximena?
options: Bring out markers and invite her to draw her favorite skill
Ask her mother to tell the two of them about the meet
Tell her in plain words what they will and won't do here
Suggest that her mother sit just outside the open door
rationales: Drawing is a fine way in for a child who has trouble finding words. Ximena has found them: she has asked what will happen to her, and an activity leaves that unanswered.
The mother has already described the meet by phone. Retelling it would turn attention to an upsetting day while Ximena is still worried about this one.
She fears that this will hurt, like an earlier visit. Honest, simple information answers that fear and gives her what she needs in order to assent, which is where trust with a child begins.
Some children talk more easily when a parent sits a little farther off, in view. Ximena is using her mother as shelter, so separating them now would add to her fear.
items.takeaway: With a worried child, start by answering the question about what is going to happen.

items.stem: A consultant joins a collegiate men's ice hockey team with open access to practices and road trips. In the first week a veteran explains why the players seem cool: "Last guy was slick. Great slides. After that you never saw him, and when he did come by, he'd check his phone for our names. That was in February." Which approach to the early weeks is most likely to build trust with these players?
options: Give an opening talk on how strong players use mental skills
Be around the rink and the road trips, offering no services yet
Set up short individual meetings to explain what is available
Have the captains tell teammates how the service helped them
rationales: An opening talk can win over players who like the consultant and doubt the content. This team's complaint is about a person who talked well and then wasn't there.
The veteran's story is about absence and not being known. Consultants describe building a connection, often by being present and informal before offering anything, as the base of effective work.
Individual introductions suit players who are curious about services. Booking them now puts the offer ahead of the relationship, much as the last consultant did.
Peer endorsement helps once players have used the service. No one on this team has anything to endorse yet.
items.takeaway: Presence often earns the trust that services later depend on.

items.stem: During an intake, professional boxer Bilal mentions that his next camp falls during Ramadan and asks, "Ever worked with somebody fasting through a camp?" The consultant has not. Before there is time to answer, Bilal adds, "Last consultant hadn't either. Went home, read a bunch of articles, and spent the next session telling me what my fast is about." He waits. Which reply is best?
options: "I haven't. Let me read up on it before our next session."
"I haven't. I could connect you with a colleague who has."
"Before I answer, what has you asking about that?"
"I haven't. What should I know about how you do it?"
rationales: Preparing between sessions is often a good sign of respect. It is also the very thing Bilal has just described as having gone wrong.
Offering a colleague would fit if Bilal wanted someone with experience. He faults the last consultant for lecturing him rather than for being new to it.
Asking about the reason for a question helps when it is unclear. Bilal has explained himself and is waiting for a straight answer.

It answers truthfully and treats Bilal as the authority on his own practice. Honesty about limits with an other-oriented, humble stance is what cultural humility looks like, and it is what the last consultant left out.
items.takeaway: Answer honestly, then let what the client says about past help shape how you learn.

items.stem: At a ballet company's season-opening reception, the newly hired consultant is introduced to the dancers. Aroha, a soloist, comes over with a plate of food; two colleagues and the artistic director are chatting within earshot. "I read that you do imagery with dancers," she says. "I've always pictured people lying in the dark listening to whales. What is it, really?" What is the best response?
options: Tell her in a sentence or two what imagery involves
Offer a private meeting, and answer then
Suggest a quieter corner of the room before answering
Explain the limits of confidentiality before saying more
rationales: She has asked about the field and disclosed nothing about herself. A short, friendly answer is ordinary public education and a natural start to rapport.
A private meeting is the right offer when a dancer starts describing her own difficulties. Putting off a general question would make the consultant seem guarded for no reason.
Moving away would protect something personal. Nothing personal has been said, and drawing her aside in view of the director might make it look as if something had.
Limits of confidentiality belong at the start of services. Aroha hasn't asked for services, and nothing she said needs protecting.
items.takeaway: Not every question is a disclosure; a general question can simply be answered.

items.stem: A technology company's HR director engages a consultant to work with Soraya, a new vice president, on presenting under pressure. In a call, the HR director mentions looking forward to "the session summaries." At a separate get-acquainted meeting, Soraya says how relieved she is that "HR told me it all stays with you. That's just how I want it." No sessions have been held, and nothing is in writing. What should the consultant do next?
options: Draft confidentiality terms, and send them to each for signing
Meet with HR to agree on what the company will receive
Meet with Soraya to agree on her goals for presenting
Meet with both at once to settle what will be shared
rationales: Written terms are needed, but there is nothing yet to write down. The two hold opposite expectations, and a document sent to each would settle by mail what they haven't discussed.
Agreeing with HR alone would add another private version of the terms. Separate conversations are how the two versions came about.
Agreeing on goals is early work with any client, once the terms are settled. Going ahead now would let her speak freely under a promise that HR doesn't share.

Each party has been told something different, and neither knows it. In third-party work the limits of confidentiality are clarified at the outset, and a joint conversation lets both hear the same terms.
items.takeaway: When parties hold different versions of the terms, get them to one version in one conversation.

items.stem: Reviewing a stalled case, a supervisor tells a trainee consultant, "Anyone can see that this archer likes you and trusts you. What your notes don't tell me is whether the two of you are after the same result, or whether the archer sees the point of that breathing log you keep assigning." Which framework is the supervisor most likely using to examine the relationship?
options: Rogers's core conditions of a helping relationship
Bordin's model of the working alliance
Jowett's 3+1Cs model of relationships
Ryan and Deci's basic psychological needs
rationales: Rogers's conditions are empathy, congruence, and unconditional positive regard. The supervisor asks about shared aims and the purpose of an assignment, which those conditions don't address.
The supervisor covers a bond (liking and trust), agreement on goals (the same result), and agreement on tasks (the point of the log). Those are the three parts of Bordin's alliance.
Jowett's model, built for coaches and athletes, concerns closeness, commitment, complementarity, and co-orientation. It has no counterpart to seeing the point of an assigned task.
Basic needs are autonomy, competence, and relatedness. Liking and trust touch on relatedness, but shared results and the purpose of a log aren't needs.
items.takeaway: Working alliance: agreement on goals, agreement on tasks, and a bond.

items.stem: Devraj, a collegiate esports player, says at the end of a first video session that the consultant "seemed kind of distracted." On the recording, the consultant looks at the camera, nods, and speaks warmly. An excerpt: "My duo's been off since qualifiers," Devraj says. "Kind of cold with me." "And how many hours are you sleeping?" "Six-ish? Anyway, I don't know if she's mad." "Got it. Do you have a warm-up routine?" Which change would most improve the consultant's attending?
options: Look toward the camera for more of the session
Let tone of voice follow what is being said
Stay longer on the topics that Devraj brings up
Give more visible nods and facial responses
rationales: Eye contact is one part of attending and is easily lost on video. The recording shows the consultant looking at the camera.
Vocal qualities carry attention too, and a flat tone would matter. The consultant's voice is warm; it is the questions that miss him.
Twice Devraj brings up his duo partner, and twice the consultant asks about something else. Verbal tracking, staying with the client's topic, is the missing part of attending.
Visible body language helps on a small screen. The consultant is already nodding, yet the next question still leaves his topic behind.
items.takeaway: Attending includes verbal tracking: warm delivery can't make up for changing the subject.

items.stem: Aaliyah, a softball player, books a consultant employed by her university's athletic department after seeing a poster in the weight room. "Do you report to Coach?" she asks. "Because if you do, I'm not telling you anything." Under department policy, a coach who refers an athlete is told whether the athlete attended, an athlete may sign a release for a coach to receive a summary of skills covered, and everything else stays private unless safety is at risk. Which answer is accurate for Aaliyah as things stand?
options: "Short of a safety concern, Coach won't hear that you came or what you say."
"Short of a safety concern, Coach will hear that you came but not what you say."
"Short of a safety concern, Coach will hear which skills we cover but not how often you come."
"Short of a safety concern, Coach will hear that you came and what we cover."
rationales: Aaliyah booked on her own and has signed nothing, so neither exception for coaches applies. An accurate statement of the limits of confidentiality is the most useful answer to her question.
Attendance goes to a coach who made the referral. She came because of a poster.
A summary of skills goes to a coach only with the athlete's signed release, and she hasn't signed one.
Both pieces would reach a coach only if the coach had referred her and she had signed a release. Neither is the case.
items.takeaway: Tell each client how the reporting rules apply to them, not just what the policy says.

items.topic: Acting on a stated access request
items.stem: Emeka, an elite swimmer, emails a consultant about race-day focus. "I'm Deaf and I sign," he writes. "Typing is fine for arranging things, but not for talking about racing. An agency called Harborline sent interpreters for my knee surgery consults, and they were excellent. I'm free Thursdays after two." The consultant, who doesn't sign, is open on Thursdays. What should the consultant do next?
options: Ask Emeka how he would prefer to communicate in sessions
Set up text-based sessions, and send him the link
Give him the names of consultants who can sign
Offer to book a Harborline interpreter, and propose a Thursday time
rationales: Asking is the usual first move and would be right if he hadn't said. His email names how he wants to talk, who he has found good, and when, so asking again shows it wasn't read closely.
He is content to type for scheduling and says it won't do for talking about racing. Text sessions would meet the consultant's convenience.
Some clients want a consultant who signs. Emeka chose this one and points to interpreters who have worked well for him.

He has made a clear and reasonable access request. Acting on it, by arranging an interpreter from the agency he trusts at a time he is free, respects his stated preference and removes the work from him.
items.takeaway: When a client has told you what access they need, arrange it rather than asking again.

items.stem: A consultant travels with a collegiate women's volleyball team. After the first season, athletes' anonymous comments on the pre-match team meetings are warm. On the rest of the consultant's time on trips, typical comments read: "Getting asked how I was doing at breakfast made me start wondering," and "My Tuesdays on campus cover it. On the road I just want to play." The coaches will support whatever format the consultant proposes. Which travel plan fits best?
options: Hold drop-in hours in the hotel lobby on each evening of a trip
Lead the team meetings, and see individuals only on campus
Reserve a meeting room, and post times for individual sessions
Check in for a few minutes with each athlete on every trip
rationales: Drop-in hours suit athletes who want a quick word and can't find the consultant. These athletes are asking for fewer such contacts on the road.
The team meetings are valued, and the individual contact is unwanted on trips and met at home. Doing less on the road, with that made clear beforehand, fits the feedback.
Booked private sessions would answer a need for longer talks while traveling. Athletes say that their regular campus sessions cover this.
Reaching out to each athlete helps when quiet ones go unnoticed. Here, being asked how they are doing is the thing athletes found unhelpful.
items.takeaway: Being available isn't the same as being helpful; let feedback set how present to be.

items.stem: Under a collegiate water polo program's agreement, a consultant keeps individual sessions confidential, has no part in selection, and may facilitate talks between athletes and coaches when both sides want one. Zofia, a junior, has gone to her head coach twice about her minutes; both talks ended in raised voices. Last week the coach told the consultant, "I'd try again if there were somebody in the room to slow us down." Today Zofia says, "I can't do that alone a third time." What should the consultant do?
options: Help her rehearse what she'll say to the coach next time
Pass her concerns to the coach, with her written permission
Offer to arrange a meeting and facilitate it for the two of them
Help her cope with her minutes, and leave the coach out of it
rationales: Rehearsal would build the skills of an athlete who hasn't yet raised the matter. Zofia has tried twice, and what she and the coach both describe is a need for someone in the room.
With a release, a consultant might pass on a fact that a coach needs. Her concerns have reached the coach already; the talks break down when they discuss them.
The agreement allows facilitation when both sides want it, and each has said so. Guiding the conversation, with no voice in selection, stays within the consultant's role.
Working on coping would respect an athlete who has accepted the decision. Zofia still wants to talk with the coach and only says she can't do it alone.
items.takeaway: Whether to step between athlete and coach depends on the agreed role and on both parties wanting it.

items.stem: Tendai, a high school basketball player, says, "I miss late, Coach pulls me, and then I'm on the bench with the whole gym looking." "So you miss at the end and then come out of the game," the consultant says. "That's what happened, yeah." Tendai pulls his hood forward until it covers his eyes. "That's not what it's like, though." Which response fits best at this moment?
options: "When you miss late in a game, that's when Coach takes you out."
"You sound ashamed, sitting out there in front of all of them."
"What do you tell yourself at the line late in a game?"
"Being a player they can count on means a lot to you."
rationales: A paraphrase shows that the facts were heard, and the consultant has just given one. Tendai confirms the facts and says they aren't the point.
He hides his face and says the facts leave out what it is like for him. Naming the emotion he is showing, a reflection of feeling, answers that.
An open question about self-talk could start useful work later. It would move him to the free-throw line while he is still on the bench, trying to be understood.
Reflecting meaning fits when a client speaks of what matters to him and why. Tendai is showing a feeling, and nothing he has said is about the kind of player he wants to be.
items.takeaway: When the facts are understood and the client still isn't, reflect the feeling.

items.stem: In their fifth session, a consultant urges Aiko, a professional ballet dancer, to trade her usual pre-performance routine for a new one. "I like mine," she says, "but all right." She arrives for the sixth session fifteen minutes late. The new routine, she reports, was "fine." To two questions about it she answers, "You're the expert," looking toward the window. Until now she has done most of the talking. What should the consultant do next?
options: Shorten the new routine so that it suits her better
Ask what has been tiring her out in rehearsals
Go on as planned, and see whether the mood lasts
Own having pushed last time, and ask how that was
rationales: Adjusting the routine would help if she had used it and found it too long. Her replies say little about the routine and a good deal about the relationship.
Outside strain could explain a flat session if she had mentioned any. The change began with her reluctant agreement and shows up when the routine is discussed.
A single off day needn't be examined. Late arrival, minimal answers, and 'You're the expert' just after she was overruled form a withdrawal that waiting would let harden.
She complied against her preference and has since withdrawn. Bringing the rupture into the conversation, beginning with the consultant's own part in it, is how an alliance is repaired.
items.takeaway: Compliance followed by withdrawal is a rupture; name your part in it and ask.

items.topic: Protecting psychological safety in a debrief
items.stem: In preseason, a collegiate women's lacrosse team agreed that mistakes would be discussed without ridicule. Midway through a film session the consultant is leading, a sophomore says she froze on the play that led to a goal. "Shocking," a senior mutters, loudly enough that people laugh. Across the room a freshman, whose hand was half up, lowers it and closes her notebook. There are six clips left to review. What should the consultant do?
options: Point the room back to its own agreement right away
Take the senior aside when the film session is over
Ask others to describe mistakes of their own on that play
Check on the sophomore privately later in the day
rationales: The whole room heard the remark, and the freshman has already decided not to speak. Upholding the team's own norm now, in front of everyone, keeps it safe to own up to mistakes in the clips that remain.
A private word suits something the rest of the room didn't catch. Everyone heard this, and six more clips would go by with the norm broken and no response.
Inviting others to speak can spread the risk in a room that is kind but quiet. In this one it asks players to step into ridicule.
Care for the sophomore is worthwhile, but a later talk with her alone does nothing for the freshman or for the rest of the session.
items.takeaway: A norm broken in front of the group needs to be upheld in front of the group.

items.stem: Three weeks ago Dariusz, a professional esports player, decided to be asleep by 1 a.m. to sharpen his reactions. He and the consultant have worked together for a year and speak frankly. "Sleep plan's great, I'm all in," he says cheerfully, then describes a winning streak that had him in ranked matches until 4 on five of the last seven nights. "Anyway," he says, "what's next on our list?" Which response fits best at this moment?
options: "What could you do on nights when you feel like queuing up?"
"You've stuck to a hard change, and it took real discipline."
"You're all in on one o'clock, and you played until four."
"You sound worn down by how hard this has been to keep up."
rationales: Planning helps a client who knows he has a problem to solve. Dariusz thinks the plan is going well, so a question about how to fix it runs ahead of him.
Affirmation would suit a week in which he had kept to the plan. Praising it here would confirm a picture that his own report contradicts.
He states one thing, describes another, and moves on without seeing the gap. Setting the two side by side without judgment is a supportive confrontation, which a strong relationship can bear.
Reflecting weariness would fit if he seemed discouraged. He is cheerful, so this names a feeling he doesn't show.
items.takeaway: When words and actions diverge unnoticed, place them next to each other and wait.

items.stem: Sam, a collegiate fencer who uses they/them pronouns, has met with a consultant for months. They once described a coach who got their pronoun wrong: "He was so upset that I spent the rest of practice telling him he was a good person." Today, talking through Sam's last bout, the consultant says "she" for the first time. Sam blinks, then waits to hear the rest of the point. What should the consultant do?
options: Say "sorry, they" and go on describing the point
Leave the bout for now, and ask how that was to hear
Finish the session, and bring it up at the end
Ask what Sam would like done when slips occur
rationales: A short apology and correction owns the mistake without making Sam look after the consultant, which is what went wrong with the coach. Sam is ready for the conversation to go on.
Asking about the impact would be called for if slips had added up or Sam had withdrawn. After one slip, it would make the consultant's mistake the subject of the session again.
Waiting leaves the wrong pronoun standing for the whole session and makes more of it at the end than a correction now would.
Asking for a preference makes sense when the client hasn't shown one. Sam's story shows it clearly enough.
items.takeaway: Match the repair to the slip and to what the client has shown about repairs.

items.stem: Brynja, an elite cross-country skier, wants help with her fear of repeating a poor championship. In the second and third sessions, as the talk neared the final climb, she asked about the consultant's own racing days; the consultant answered briefly, and the hour drifted there. Today she gets as far as "So, the climb," stops, and asks, "Did you ever completely fall apart in a big race?" The consultant did, twice. How should the consultant respond?
options: Answer briefly from experience, then bring the talk back to her
Tell her that many elite skiers have had races like that
Ask what she would like to know about the consultant's racing
Say they can come back to that, and stay with the climb
rationales: Brief disclosure with a return to the client is the usual guideline. It is also what was tried twice, and both times it led away from the climb for the rest of the hour.
