Normalizing would comfort an athlete who feels alone in this. Here it supplies another way off the subject just as she reaches it.
Curiosity about a first question of this kind might be useful. This is the third at the same moment, and inviting more about the consultant's racing continues the detour.

Each time she nears the climb, a question about the consultant takes them off it. Self-disclosure should serve the client's work, so gently keeping it out and staying with what she began serves her better.
items.takeaway: Judge a self-disclosure by what it does for the client's work, including what past ones did.

items.stem: Jun, a 14-year-old tennis player, has spent fifteen animated minutes telling a consultant about a lost match, game by game, and has just reached the three double faults in the tiebreak. Which of two serving drills Jun should take to tomorrow's practice depends on whether the serve routine held up on those points. Jun's mother has pulled into the parking lot. What should the consultant say?
options: "What was the tiebreak like for you out there?"
"Did you go through your routine on those serves?"
"Tell me more about how you were feeling then."
"It sounds like the match slipped away from you."
rationales: An open question gets a reluctant client talking. Jun is already talking freely, and there are only moments left.
One specific fact decides the next step, and the session is nearly over. A closed question gets a particular piece of information quickly.
A prompt for elaboration helps when a story is thin or the feeling needs room. It would open a new topic as Jun's ride arrives.
A reflection would show understanding and might be welcome earlier. It doesn't yield the fact needed to choose the drill.
items.takeaway: Closed questions earn their place when one specific fact is needed now.

items.stem: Over fifty minutes of a video session, Captain Otieno, an Army helicopter pilot, has talked about ragged sleep since a rotation began, a new crew member who gets under his skin, and a check ride he is dreading. The consultant now says, "So you're sleeping badly, you're irritated with the new guy, and the check ride fills you with dread. Have I got that right?" Which microskill is the consultant mainly using?
options: Paraphrasing what he has just said
Reflecting the feelings he has shown
Summarizing what he has talked about
Reflecting what his work means to him
rationales: A paraphrase restates one recent statement in fresh words. The consultant reaches back across the session and gathers three separate topics.
Two emotions are named, but as parts of a longer recap that also includes facts about sleep. The purpose is to draw the session together.
Gathering several topics from a stretch of conversation, feelings and facts alike, and checking accuracy is a summary.
Reflecting meaning would bring out the values or significance behind his experience. Nothing is said about why any of this matters to him.
items.takeaway: A summary gathers content and feeling over time; a paraphrase or reflection takes one piece.

items.stem: A consultant whose gymnastics career ended after years of competing hurt works with Brielle, a 19-year-old gymnast whose mild back tightness the medical staff is monitoring. Twice the consultant has urged her to "stand up to" her coaches about training load; she looked puzzled, said she likes her coaches, and went on with her imagery. Reading over old notes, the consultant finds the same advice given to two other gymnasts with sore backs. Which reading of the pattern fits best?
options: Countertransference that arises mainly from the consultant
Countertransference that Brielle tends to evoke in others
Transference, with Brielle reacting as if to a past coach
A rupture, with Brielle pulling back from the work
rationales: The advice follows sore backs rather than anything Brielle has asked for, and it matches the consultant's own history. That is countertransference originating in the consultant, a matter for reflection and supervision.
Client-evoked reactions tell you how others may respond to the client too. The consultant had the same reaction with other gymnasts, so Brielle isn't the common factor.
Transference would appear as Brielle relating to the consultant as to someone from her past. The out-of-place reaction here is the consultant's.
A rupture would show in strain or withdrawal on her side. She was puzzled, and she went on with the work.
items.takeaway: Look at when a reaction recurs: across clients, it points to the consultant.

items.stem: Lior, a collegiate diver, drops into the usual chair, laughing. "Three weeks, no journal entries. I know. And I'm still hanging on to bad dives, it's driving me nuts. But I sit there with the notebook and nothing comes. I don't think in sentences. Ask me about a dive and I could stand up and show you where it went." In terms of Bordin's working alliance, what should the consultant do next?
options: Talk about how comfortable Lior feels in sessions
Revisit whether quicker recovery is what Lior wants
Set a regular time and place for the journal entries
Try another way for Lior to review missed dives
rationales: Attention to the bond fits a client who has grown guarded. Lior is relaxed enough to laugh about the missed entries.
Reworking the goal would fit if Lior no longer cared about it. Hanging on to bad dives still bothers Lior a great deal.
A set time and place would help someone who means to write and forgets. Lior sits down to write, and nothing comes.
Lior still wants to let go of bad dives, and the writing is what doesn't fit. In Bordin's terms the disagreement is about the task, so change the task and keep the goal.
items.takeaway: Locate an alliance problem in goals, tasks, or bond before changing anything.

items.stem: Kalani, an elite wheelchair racer, is deciding whether to race for another four years. "If there were no medals in it," the consultant asks, "what would racing be for?" Kalani starts to speak, stops, and looks down at her gloves. "Hang on," she says slowly. "There's something." Fifteen seconds pass, and she is still looking at the gloves. What should the consultant do?
options: Reflect the feeling that shows in her face
Stay quiet and wait until she goes on
Put the question to her in simpler words
Turn to a topic that's easier
rationales: Reflecting feeling would fit if emotion had welled up and she looked to the consultant. She is searching for a thought, and naming a feeling would interrupt.
She has asked for time and is plainly working something out. Silence is an attending skill, and here the most helpful thing is to do nothing more.
Rewording helps when the question wasn't understood. 'There's something' shows that she understood it and has the start of an answer.
Changing topics would respect a client who didn't want to go there. Kalani has asked the consultant to wait, not to move on.
items.takeaway: Silence while a client is thinking is work under way; leave it alone.

items.topic: A small gift at the end of services
items.stem: After two seasons, Alejandro, a professional cyclist, has met the goals he set with a consultant in private practice, and today is their last scheduled session. On his way out he hands over a jar of quince jam with a card thanking the consultant for "a good two years." He has never given the consultant anything before. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Decline it warmly, and explain the trouble with such gifts
Ask what it means to him before deciding
Accept it with thanks, and leave it at that
Accept it on the employer's behalf, and report it
rationales: Declining is right when a gift is costly or could sway the work. A jar of jam at the close of finished work has no such power, and refusing it could hurt for no reason.
Exploring the meaning helps when gifts recur or come with something the client wants. A single token of thanks at a planned ending explains itself.

The gift is small, offered freely, and tied to a natural ending, so it is neither exploitative nor likely to affect the work. Gracious acceptance respects the client and the Ethics Code's conditions on gifts.
Reporting gifts fits a consultant whose employer requires it. This consultant is in private practice, with no employer to report to.
items.takeaway: Weigh a gift's value, timing, and pattern; a small closing token can simply be accepted.

items.stem: On trips, a collegiate field hockey team's players are in their rooms by 10:30 p.m., and the team's agreement with its traveling consultant puts individual meetings between 8 and 8 except in an emergency. At 10:50 one night, Destiny, a junior, taps on the consultant's hotel room door. "I saw your light. I'm fine, just annoyed about getting benched, and I figured you'd be good to vent to." The next match is tomorrow at four. What should the consultant do?
options: Offer her a time to talk tomorrow after breakfast
Talk with her now in a quiet part of the lobby
Walk with her to the athletic trainer on call
Stay with her, and call the team's crisis contact
rationales: She is annoyed, not in distress, and there is a whole morning before the match. Keeping to agreed hours and the team's rule, with a definite time offered, holds the boundary and still meets her need.
A public spot is the right place for a late talk that can't wait. This one can, and going ahead would set aside both the curfew and the agreed hours.
The trainer is the right contact for a physical complaint. She describes none.
Staying and calling for help is required when someone may be at risk. Nothing she says or does suggests it.
items.takeaway: Hold agreed hours for ordinary upset, and break them for risk.

items.topic: Client invitation to a public event
items.stem: A consultant has worked for five years in a university athletic department, with an office beside the pool, and sees many of the swimmers individually. Each year on Senior Day the whole support staff lines the deck and shakes hands with the graduating swimmers as they are introduced. Riley, a senior and a regular client who often tells teammates about their sessions, stops by the office and asks, "You'll be out there Saturday, right?" What is the most appropriate response?
options: Decline, and mark the milestone with Riley in a session
Say yes, and take part along with the rest of the staff
Ask how Riley wants to handle being seen together
Suggest that Riley check with the head coach about it
rationales: Marking a milestone in session suits a personal invitation, such as a family party. This is a work event where the consultant has an ordinary staff role.
Standing with the other staff is part of the job, singles out no one, and reveals nothing about who is a client. Not every contact outside sessions is a multiple relationship.
Planning for being seen together protects a client when the contact would reveal the relationship. A handshake that every senior gets reveals nothing, and Riley talks about the sessions openly.
The coach's approval would matter for someone who had no standing place at the event. The support staff attends each year.
items.takeaway: Ask what role you'd hold at an event: a staff role differs from a personal one.

items.topic: Conflict of interest in a small community
items.stem: A consultant in a town of six thousand gets a call from the parents of Ethan, a 16-year-old club pitcher. "He's fighting one other boy for the last spot in the rotation, and it's eating him up," his mother says. "We thought of you because you know everybody." The consultant does know the other boy: he is upstairs doing his homework, and he will want dinner soon. What should the consultant do?
options: Take the case, with regular consultation from a colleague
Take the case, after agreeing on how to handle chance meetings
Meet with Ethan first, to hear whether he wants the help
Turn down the case, and give them names of other consultants
rationales: Consultation with a colleague supports a consultant who is competent and new to some part of a case. It can't remove a parent's stake in the rival's success.
A plan for chance meetings manages the light overlap that small towns bring, such as sharing a church. Here the consultant's own child gains if Ethan loses out.
A minor's assent matters in any case that can be accepted. Meeting Ethan would begin a relationship that the consultant shouldn't enter.

The rival is the consultant's own child. Wanting one's child to win a spot that the client also wants is a multiple relationship likely to impair objectivity, so it is better to decline and point the family elsewhere.
items.takeaway: Some small-town overlap can be managed; a stake in the outcome calls for declining.

items.stem: At intake, Noor, a 26-year-old professional squash player, agreed that texts with the consultant are for scheduling and that other matters wait for sessions. She has kept to this for two months. At 11:40 on Saturday night, after a tournament loss, she texts, "Lost to her AGAIN. Why do I rush the third game every time?? Anyway. Drowning my sorrows in noodles." Their next session is on Tuesday. What should the consultant do?
options: Raise the growing reliance on texts in Tuesday's session
Call her tonight, and follow the safety steps set at intake
Reply on Monday that they can take it up on Tuesday
Suggest on Tuesday that she see a counselor
rationales: Exploring reliance in session suits a run of late-night messages. One text in two months is a slip after a hard loss, and treating it as a pattern would be out of proportion.
A call and safety steps are needed when a message hints at risk. Frustration about a third game, followed by noodles, doesn't.
A brief reply in working hours that moves the topic to the session keeps the agreed boundary, acknowledges her, and makes no more of it than it is.
Suggesting a counselor would follow signs of a clinical concern. Disappointment after a loss is ordinary, and it is a performance topic that belongs in their sessions.
items.takeaway: Answer a single slip with a light, consistent return to the agreement.

items.stem: Folake, a professional surfer and current client, wins her first major event and posts, "Couldn't have done it without my mental performance coach!" with the consultant's name. She is now on a long flight home. A sports reporter phones: "She's told the world already, so I just need a line from you. How long have you two worked together?" Folake has signed no release. What should the consultant do?
options: Confirm that she is a client, and say nothing more
Describe in general terms how the consultant trains surfers
Give a short comment that Folake can approve before it runs
Explain that the practice doesn't discuss who its clients are
rationales: A bare confirmation would be acceptable if Folake had released that much. Her own post is hers to make; it doesn't free the consultant to confirm the relationship.
General education suits a reporter writing about mental training. In answer to a question about Folake, a description of work with surfers would all but confirm it.
Approval after the fact comes too late: in giving the comment, the consultant would already have discussed a client with a reporter.
Confidentiality belongs to the client, and only she can release it. A standard reply that neither confirms nor denies protects her until she decides, and it is the same one any client would get.
items.takeaway: A client's public post doesn't waive the consultant's duty of confidentiality.

items.topic: One-on-one with a minor while traveling
items.stem: Zdenek, 15, wrestles for a club covered by the Minor Athlete Abuse Prevention Policies. At a national championship, an hour before his semifinal, he approaches the club's consultant. "Can I ask you about something? I don't want the guys hearing it. Or the coaches." The team is camped out in a block of seats above the mats, and his parents, who have approved his meetings with the consultant, won't arrive until evening. Where should the two of them talk?
options: In the team's block of seats, among teammates
On an empty row across the aisle, in view of the team
In the warm-up room, with an assistant coach beside them
On a video call that evening, with a parent in the next room
rationales: Talking among teammates is observable, and it would do for a quick reminder. It puts his teammates in earshot, which he has asked to avoid.
Others can see and interrupt, so the one-on-one policy is met, and they can't overhear. It protects him and his privacy, and it happens before he wrestles.
A second adult beside them meets the policy and would suit an athlete who wanted the coach there. He has asked that coaches not hear.
A call with a parent close by can meet the policy for electronic communication. It would come hours after the semifinal that he faces within the hour.
items.takeaway: Observable and interruptible doesn't have to mean overheard.

items.stem: A consultant is starting a first video session with Arjun, a firefighter in another state. His signed forms give his home address, a neighbor as his emergency contact, and his cell number, which she has just called to help him log in. She matched his ID on the screen. He isn't at home: he is in the cab of his parked truck, alone, on the way back from a wildfire deployment, and he is eager to begin. What does the consultant most need to ask before the intake?
options: "What is your exact location right now?"
"Is there anybody close enough to hear us?"
"Could you hold your ID up to the camera?"
"What number should I use if we get cut off?"
rationales: Emergency help has to be sent to where the client is. The address on file is no longer where Arjun is sitting, so the consultant needs his actual location before starting.
Privacy would be the concern if others were around. Arjun is alone in a closed cab.
Identity should be verified at a first session. She has already matched his ID.
A backup number is part of the disconnection plan. She has his cell number and has just reached him on it.
items.takeaway: Confirm the client's physical location at every remote session; the address on file may not be it.

items.stem: A consultant wants intake information from 30 university athletes who are spread across the country for the summer and report to campus in two weeks. Her questionnaire covers injury history, sleep, and mood. She'll use it to decide whom to call in the first days and to plan each athlete's opening session. The department gives her an encrypted platform that only she can open. Which way of collecting the information fits best?
options: An anonymous questionnaire filled out on the platform
A paper questionnaire completed in a private room
A video interview based on the questionnaire
A named questionnaire filled out on the platform
rationales: Anonymous answers encourage candor when only group patterns matter. She needs to know whose mood or sleep calls for a prompt contact.
Paper in a private room works when athletes are on campus. They are scattered across the country.
Interviewing each athlete would give depth in a small group. With 30 athletes and two weeks, it would delay learning whom to call first.

She has to connect answers to people in order to follow up and plan, and has to reach them remotely. Named responses in an encrypted system that only she can open meet both needs with protection suited to sensitive data.
items.takeaway: Let the purpose decide whether data need names, then protect them accordingly.

items.stem: Before he has met the players, a consultant for a professional basketball team gets a file from the performance staff with each player's sleep and heart-rate variability. The consent form players signed in preseason reads: "My nightly data go to the performance staff and the mental performance consultant for planning my support. I can opt out of either by checking a box." Two players checked the consultant's box; their rows are in the file as well. First meetings begin on Monday. What should he do?
options: Set the file aside until players have been asked about his access
Have the staff resend the file without the two players, and use the rest
Use the team averages to prepare, and leave individual rows unopened
Send the file back, and collect his own sleep ratings on Monday
rationales: Waiting would be right if players hadn't known about his access. The form named the consultant and the purpose, and players had the chance to refuse.

Players who left the box blank agreed to his access for this purpose; the two who checked it did not, and their rows should not have come. A clean file lets him prepare with the data he may see, and it tells staff about the error.
Averages alone would be right if the form had limited him to group data. It speaks of planning each player's support.
Collecting his own ratings would help if the device data were doubtful. Nothing suggests that they are.
items.takeaway: Consent defines the use of wearable data: honor both the yes and the opt-out.

items.stem: A consultant leads weekly video sessions on handling pressure for a sales team that works from home. Members join by personal links from a waiting room, and at the first session they settled how to treat one another's stories. After the third session Iolanthe, a member, forwards an email from the company's meeting service: "Here's your recap!" It contains much of what she said, word for word. The sales director, who scheduled the series, is copied. What should the consultant do first?
options: Have members revisit what they settled about repeating stories
Shut off the automatic notes, and have the saved copies removed
Have members confirm at the start of each session that they are alone
Give each member a new link, and admit members one by one
rationales: Revisiting group norms fits when a member has passed something along. No member did; the software sent the email.
The meeting service is recording what members say and delivering it to someone outside the group. Stopping it and removing what it has saved closes the actual leak.
Checking for others in the room fits when somebody has overheard. A verbatim text sent to the director didn't come from a listener at home.
New links fit when an uninvited person has got in. Members already use personal links and a waiting room.
items.takeaway: In online groups, check what the platform itself records and who receives it.

items.stem: When they began, the consultant and Camille, an elite fencer, put in writing that messages on the secure app are for training notes, that he answers by ten the next morning, and that anything urgent means a call. Camille has used it well for months. At 11:40 tonight she sends a long, cheerful account of a new parry, with questions, and at midnight adds, "Sorry, I know you're asleep! Couldn't wait to get this down." The consultant happens to see both. What is the best response?
options: Answer in the morning, as he would another training note
Talk with her about what messages are for and how soon he replies
Call her now, and ask how she is and whether she's safe
Suggest that she keep these notes in a journal
rationales: The message is a training note sent late at night, and the agreement already says when it will be answered. Keeping to it maintains a boundary that has been working.
That conversation sets expectations when none exist or when they've stopped working. They are in writing, and one late, excited message after months isn't a breakdown.
A call is right when a message hints at danger. Camille is excited about a parry.
A journal suits reflections that don't need a reply. She is asking questions, which is what the app is for.
items.takeaway: A messaging agreement works when you keep to it; an eager note isn't an emergency.

items.stem: Midway through a video session Corinne, a police officer, speaks of a call that went badly last week. "I don't see the point of any of it anymore," she says, and her picture freezes and drops. She has never spoken this way before, and the consultant hasn't yet been able to ask what she means. Thirty seconds pass. The plan they wrote at intake lists her cell number, her sister's number, and the emergency services where she takes her sessions. What should the consultant do first?
options: Contact emergency services where Corinne takes her sessions
Call Corinne's sister, and ask her to go over
Call Corinne on the number she gave for dropped sessions
Send Corinne a new link, and stay in the session until she joins
rationales: Emergency services are the step for stated intent, or for a worrying call when she can't be reached. Nobody has yet tried to reach her, and her meaning isn't known.
Her sister is a next contact if Corinne doesn't answer. Going to her first would disclose the situation before the direct route has been tried.
Corinne's words need a prompt safety conversation, and the quickest way to have one is the backup number. If she doesn't answer, the plan moves on to others and to emergency services.
Resending a link and waiting suits an ordinary session. After what she said, the consultant should actively reach her.
items.takeaway: After a worrying drop, call the backup number at once, and escalate if you can't reach the client.

items.stem: Before the season, a consultant plans how to evaluate her work with a university lacrosse team online. Last year she used the same ratings in August and May, saw the team average stay flat, and couldn't tell whether nobody had changed or whether some had climbed while others had slid. Several players also told her, kindly, that they'd rated her higher than they felt because their names were on it. Which design for this year best addresses both problems?
options: Surveys in both months with no identifying information
Surveys in both months linked by a code only the player knows
Surveys in both months with names, seen only by the consultant
Group discussions in both months led by a colleague from elsewhere
rationales: Dropping all identifiers would bring candor. It would leave her again with averages and no way to follow a player from August to May.
A self-made code lets each player's two sets of ratings be matched without revealing who the player is, so she sees individual change and players can be frank.
Names would show who changed. They are also what led players to soften their ratings last year.
An outside discussion leader can draw out frank, detailed views. It wouldn't show how far each player's ratings moved.
items.takeaway: Self-generated codes give matched data and anonymity when you need both.

items.stem: Gustavo, a masters rower, has used slow-paced breathing for six weeks to manage race nerves. The app shows that he practiced on 40 of 42 days. His watch's overnight heart-rate variability hasn't moved. At both regattas in that time, a chest strap worn on the dock showed a heart rate well below last year's at the same events, and his nerves rating fell from 8 to 4. His training and fitness are about what they were. Which reading fits these data best?
options: The breathing has calmed how he feels and left his body's response as it was
The breathing hasn't been practiced enough for its effects to be judged
The breathing has improved his recovery, which has made races feel easier
The breathing has eased his response before races, with recovery unchanged
rationales: This would fit a lower rating with no physical change on the dock. The strap showed a markedly lower heart rate there.
This would fit a sparse practice log. He practiced on nearly every day.
This would fit a rise in overnight variability alongside calmer races. Overnight variability stayed flat.

Ratings and dock heart rate both changed at the moment he was targeting, and the overnight measure, which reflects recovery, didn't. Each measure speaks to its own situation, so a flat overnight line doesn't cancel the race-day change.
items.takeaway: Match the measure to the target: overnight HRV says little about arousal on the start line.

items.stem: A new consultant recorded a video session with Osgood, a collegiate wrestler, under a consent form that says the recording is for review with her mentor and will be erased within 30 days. She and the mentor went through it on day nine. It is now day 29. She thinks it is the best session she has done and would love to study it again. Osgood graduated last week and hasn't replied to the note she sent him about it. What should she do with the recording?
options: Ask Osgood to agree to a longer period, and keep it until he replies
Move it to encrypted storage, and keep it with his other records
Erase it by the end of tomorrow, and note the date in his client record
Send it to her mentor by secure link, and ask for a second review
rationales: Asking for a longer period is reasonable while the agreed time is still running. She has asked, had no reply, and can't extend the consent by waiting.
Secure storage with the file would be right if the form had promised that the recording would be kept. It promised the opposite.
The form set purpose and time limits. The review is done, the time is nearly up, and no new consent has come, so she keeps the promise he agreed to.
A secure transfer for mentor review would fit if the review hadn't taken place. It took place on day nine.
items.takeaway: Recording consent includes an end date; honor it even when the recording is useful.

items.stem: Matthias, a 22-year-old professional esports player, is a current client. On his public stream he tells viewers that he has been working on his nerves "with a really good mental performance coach" and tags the consultant's professional page. He mentions nobody else, and he never told her he was going to do it. Fans start asking under the clip whether it's true. What should the consultant do?
options: Reply under the clip with a short thank-you
Repost the clip on her page with his written permission
Ask him to take the clip down before more people see it
Leave the clip alone, and talk with him about it next session
rationales: A public thank-you would be fine for something that involves no client, such as praise for a talk she gave. Here it would confirm a confidential relationship.
A former client's freely offered praise may be shared with permission. From a current client, promoting it would turn his remark into a testimonial.
Removal would be worth asking for if the clip exposed someone else's confidences. His own story is his to tell.
Clients may disclose their own consulting; the consultant's duty of confidentiality still holds. She neither confirms nor uses the clip, and they discuss what it means for him and the work.
items.takeaway: A client may go public about your work; you still don't confirm it or use it.

items.stem: A consultant with an office in Colorado hears from Maja, a professional golfer from Sweden who wants weekly video sessions for twelve weeks, starting in January. Maja plays a European schedule most of the year, keeps her apartment in Gothenburg, and will pay from her Swedish bank. Each winter, from New Year until April, she rents a house in Arizona and trains there. The consultant will work from her office throughout. Whose rules on practice and titles should the consultant look into first?
options: Those of Colorado and Sweden
Those of Arizona and Sweden
Those of Colorado alone
Those of Colorado and Arizona
rationales: This pairing would apply if Maja were at home in Gothenburg during the sessions. Residence and bank account don't place her there from January to April.
This pairing would apply if the consultant were working from Arizona and Maja from Sweden. The consultant stays in her Colorado office.
A single state's rules would apply if both were in Colorado during the sessions. Maja will be in Arizona.
Remote services are governed by the law where each party is located when they take place. For these twelve weeks that means a consultant in Colorado and a client in Arizona.
items.takeaway: For remote work, check the law where both parties are physically located during sessions.

items.stem: A clip of a quarterback's outburst on the sideline goes viral. A radio host who has had a consultant on air twice before to talk about pressure invites her back: the segment will play the clip and ask her, step by step, what was going on with him. The quarterback has been seeing her privately since spring and has told no one. The host knows nothing about this and needs an answer within the hour. What is the most appropriate reply?
options: Accept, and speak about pressure in general without mentioning him
Decline, and pass along the statement that he has approved
Accept, and ask the host to correct how she was introduced last time
Decline, and leave the reason for it unspoken
rationales: General education is a good use of a media invitation when the topic is general. This segment is built around his clip, so anything she says will be heard as about him, from what she knows in confidence.
A client can authorize a specific statement. He has told nobody about the work, there's no sign that he has approved anything, and passing it along would reveal the connection.
Correcting a misstatement of one's credentials is a duty when one has been made. Nothing like that has come up here.
He is a client, so commenting would draw on confidential knowledge, and explaining why she can't would reveal it. A plain no protects both the relationship and the fact of it.
items.takeaway: When the subject is secretly your client, decline without a reason; the reason itself is confidential.

items.stem: A consultant's newsletter goes to coaches throughout a small national track program. For the next issue she wants an example of a routine that settled panic about lane draws. She has seen it once in her career, with Rurik, a 24-year-old 400-meter hurdler who is a current client and keeps that private. When she asked him about it he said, "I'd rather not be in there. Even as a mystery guy, they'd know in a second." Which example should she use?
options: A composite drawn from several clients, with details altered
An invented athlete, labeled for readers as made up
Rurik's story, with the wording he has signed off on
Rurik's story, with his name and event left out
rationales: Composites protect people when many clients share an experience. Only Rurik has had this one, so a composite would still be him.
Rurik declined and would be recognized in any version of his story. A clearly labeled fictional example teaches the same lesson and discloses nothing about him.
His story would be usable with specific written consent. He was asked and said no.
Removing identifiers can be enough when readers couldn't work out who it was and the client is content with it. Rurik isn't, and these readers would know.
items.takeaway: If a client declines or would be recognizable, teach with fiction and label it.

items.topic: HIPAA: when it reaches a consultant
items.stem: For years a consultant has had a self-pay practice and, after checking with an attorney, treated it as outside HIPAA. A hospital's sports medicine clinic, which bills insurers, now hires her as an outside contractor. The clinic will send her its patients' confidence questionnaires and rehab charts, and she'll analyze them and report which rehab groups improve most. She won't meet the patients. Which rules should she expect to govern this information, in addition to the Ethics Code?
options: The same rules as her own practice, since HIPAA doesn't reach this work
HIPAA, through a business associate agreement with the clinic
HIPAA, as a covered provider that bills insurers electronically
A school's student-records rules, through a written agreement
rationales: This describes her self-pay practice. The clinic's charts are protected health information held by a covered entity, and they don't lose that status when sent to a contractor.
A contractor who analyzes identifiable patient information on behalf of a covered entity is acting as a business associate. HIPAA's safeguards follow the data to her through a written agreement.
Electronic billing of insurers is one way that a provider becomes covered. The clinic bills; she sends no claims.
School rules would be relevant if she handled records for a school. These are a hospital clinic's patients.
items.takeaway: HIPAA can reach a consultant through the data she handles for a covered entity, even if she never bills.

cards.title: Cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) in performance consulting
points: Cognitive model: interpretation → emotion, physiology, behavior
Structured, collaborative, goal-directed, with between-session practice
Cognitive restructuring through guided discovery (Socratic questioning)
Behavioral experiments: predict, test, compare
cards.examNote: Look for agendas, homework, "what went through your mind?" questions and evidence-weighing. Changing thought content is CBT; changing the relationship to thoughts is ACT.
body: CBT rests on the cognitive model: it is not a situation by itself but how a person interprets it that shapes emotions, body reactions and behavior.

A diver who reads a racing heart as "I'm about to fail" feels and acts differently from one who reads it as "I'm ready." CBT work is structured and collaborative. Sessions often have an agenda, goals are explicit, and clients practice between sessions.

The consultant uses guided discovery, asking Socratic questions about the evidence for and against an automatic thought so the client reaches a more balanced view on their own rather than being told it is wrong.

Behavioral experiments test beliefs directly: the client makes a prediction, tries the feared action in a planned way (often while dropping a safety behavior), and compares what happened with what they expected. In assessment, the consultant asks what the client was thinking in key moments.
Unlicensed CMPCs apply these methods to performance; they don't diagnose or treat disorders.

cards.title: Person-centered and humanistic core conditions
points: Client as expert; actualizing tendency
Congruence, unconditional positive regard, accurate empathy
Empathy is shown through reflections, not reassurance or advice
Nondirective; the relationship drives change
cards.examNote: Expect items asking which response conveys empathy or which condition is missing. Reassurance and advice-giving are common distractors.
body: Carl Rogers proposed that change happens through the relationship.

The client, not the consultant, is the expert on their own experience and has a natural tendency toward growth when the conditions are right. Of the conditions he described, three are provided by the helper.

Congruence (genuineness) means the consultant's outward behavior matches what they actually feel, with no professional façade. Unconditional positive regard means accepting the person regardless of what they report or achieve; warmth that rises after wins and cools after losses is conditional regard.

Accurate empathic understanding means sensing the client's inner world and communicating that understanding back, usually through reflections of feeling and meaning rather than reassurance, advice or fact-finding.

In performance work, a person-centered consultant explains the process as client-directed, follows the client's lead when something important comes up mid-session, and treats the relationship itself as the main vehicle of change.

cards.title: ACT and the Mindfulness-Acceptance-Commitment (MAC) approach
points: Six processes: acceptance, defusion, present moment, self-as-context, values, committed action
Target is the relationship to thoughts, not their content
Suppression and avoidance are seen as experiential avoidance
MAC: accept internal states and commit to task-focused, values-driven action
cards.examNote: Distractors are often control strategies (thought stopping, relaxation "until the nerves are gone") or CBT evidence-weighing. Those are inconsistent with ACT and MAC.
body: Acceptance and commitment therapy aims for psychological flexibility: being in contact with the present moment and acting on what matters even while unpleasant thoughts and feelings are present.

Six interrelated processes support this. Acceptance is willingness to have internal experiences without fighting them. Cognitive defusion means seeing thoughts as passing mental events rather than literal truths, as in "I'm having the thought that I'm too old."

Present-moment contact is flexible, nonjudgmental attention to the here and now. Self-as-context is a stable observing perspective that is distinct from any single thought. Values are freely chosen directions, and committed action is behavior guided by them.
ACT reads thought suppression and avoidance of situations as experiential avoidance, which tends to maintain the problem. Gardner and Moore's MAC approach applies these ideas to performance.
The goal shifts from controlling or eliminating anxiety to noticing it while attending to task-relevant cues and committing to values-driven performance behavior.

cards.title: Solution-focused approach
points: Future- and strengths-focused; little time on problem origins
Exception questions: when is the problem absent or smaller?
Scaling questions point to the next small, observable step
Miracle question defines the preferred future
cards.examNote: Problem-history questions ("When did it start?") and searching for negative thoughts are the usual wrong answers when a solution-focused approach is specified.
body: Solution-focused brief therapy, developed by Steve de Shazer, Insoo Kim Berg and colleagues, is future-oriented and strengths-based. It spends little time analyzing where a problem came from.

Instead it clarifies what the client wants instead and builds on what already works. Exceptions are times when the problem was absent or smaller, such as the games when a pitcher settled after a walk.
The consultant asks what was different then and helps the client do more of it. Scaling questions ("Where are you from 1 to 10?") turn vague goals into steps.
Typical follow-ups are what puts the rating where it is rather than lower, and what one point higher would look like in concrete, observable behavior.

The miracle question asks the client to imagine the problem resolved overnight and describe what they would notice first, which helps define a preferred future. The client is treated as resourceful, and the consultant uses the client's own language and existing strengths rather than importing new techniques first.

cards.title: Feminist approaches
points: The personal is political: distress in sociocultural context
Egalitarian relationship; demystify the process; values are not hidden
Empowerment and collaborative advocacy rather than taking over
Examine power and gender rather than defaulting to self-blame
cards.examNote: Correct answers share power and examine context. Wrong answers present the consultant as the expert, claim value-neutrality, pathologize reactions to real inequity, or have the consultant take over without the client's agreement.
body: Feminist approaches start from the view that the personal is political.
Individual distress is understood within its sociocultural context, including gender, power and other social structures, rather than located only inside the client. The relationship is egalitarian.

The consultant demystifies the process by explaining methods and their rationale, invites the client to question them, shares decisions about goals, and is open about their own values instead of claiming neutrality. In conceptualization, the consultant asks how the environment contributes.

Examples include a culture that brushes off a woman's ideas, or unequal access to facilities. This guards against simply accepting a client's self-blame. In delivery, the emphasis is empowerment: validating real inequities and helping clients recognize and use their own power, including collective advocacy through appropriate channels.

The consultant does not reframe inequities away, and does not take over without the client's collaboration; advocacy agreed with the client is compatible. These approaches address gender-role socialization for clients of any gender.

cards.title: Systems and ecological approaches
points: Teams, families and organizations are interacting systems
Circular, not linear, causality; target the pattern
Ecological view: nested, interacting settings around the athlete
Involving stakeholders requires consent and clear confidentiality limits
cards.examNote: Choose answers that look at interactions across people or settings. Answers that "fix" a single individual, or blame a single cause, reflect linear thinking.
body: Systems theory treats a family, team or organization as a set of interacting parts. A change in one part ripples through the others. Causality is circular rather than linear.
A coach yells, defenders tighten up, more shots reach the goalie, the goalie's anxiety rises, and the coach yells more.

Each behavior is both cause and effect, so the consultant asks what pattern keeps the problem going rather than who is to blame, and intervenes on the interaction pattern. The person labeled as the problem may be where strain shows most, though individual concerns still need assessment.

Bronfenbrenner's ecological model adds nested contexts: the immediate settings of family, school and club; the links between them; settings that affect the athlete indirectly, such as a parent's workplace or a sport federation; and surrounding cultural values.

A systems-oriented consultant explains early that key adults or stakeholders may be part of the work, with consent and clear confidentiality limits. Assessment asks how changes at home, school and in sport connect.

cards.title: Transtheoretical model (stages of change)
points: Precontemplation → contemplation → preparation → action → maintenance
Match the strategy to the stage
Decisional balance is key early; self-efficacy grows across stages and supports action and maintenance
Relapse is normal; people recycle through stages
cards.examNote: Identify the stage from the client's words, then reject action-stage tactics for early-stage clients and passive waiting for anyone.
body: Prochaska and DiClemente's transtheoretical model describes readiness for change in stages. In precontemplation, the person has no intention to change, often because they see no problem.

In contemplation, they intend to change within roughly six months but feel ambivalent. In preparation, they intend to act soon and have taken small steps. In action, they are actively changing. In maintenance, they are sustaining the change and preventing relapse.

The practical lesson is to match strategies to the stage. With precontemplators, build rapport and raise awareness without pushing. With contemplators, explore pros and cons (decisional balance) and build confidence. With people in preparation, make concrete plans.

In action and maintenance, use behavioral strategies such as cues, scheduling, support and relapse-prevention planning. Mismatching, such as handing a detailed action plan to someone who sees no reason to change, can increase resistance, although research support for strict stage-matching is mixed.
Relapse is common and people often recycle through stages. It is normalized, and the consultant re-engages strategies that fit current readiness.

cards.title: Theory of planned behavior
points: Attitudes + subjective norms + perceived behavioral control → intention → behavior
Perceived behavioral control can also influence behavior directly
Assess all three determinants and intention
Intervene on a weak determinant that matters for the behavior
cards.examNote: Don't confuse TPB with stages of change (TTM), SDT's basic needs, or the health belief model's susceptibility and severity.
body: Ajzen's theory of planned behavior explains deliberate behaviors such as attending training, doing an injury-prevention warm-up, or exercising regularly.

Three determinants shape intention, and intention is the most immediate predictor of behavior. The first is attitude toward the behavior: is it good, worthwhile, enjoyable? The second is subjective norms: do important others expect it, and do I care what they think?

The third is perceived behavioral control: how easy or possible is it for me, given time, skill and barriers? Perceived control can also predict behavior directly when it reflects real control. For consultants, the model works as a diagnostic map. Assessment asks about all three determinants plus intention.

Planning then targets a determinant that is weak and matters for that behavior. If people already value exercise and feel supported but believe they cannot fit it in, a benefits campaign or more endorsements miss the point.
Protected time, short sessions and barrier planning address the real problem, which is low perceived control.

cards.title: Philosophy of practice and models of performance excellence
points: Core beliefs → paradigm → model and role → goals → techniques
Consistency across layers is the mark of a sound philosophy
Orlick and Partington: commitment, quality practice, mental readiness, evaluation
Gould et al.: champion characteristics are developed, not simply innate
cards.examNote: When asked what explains differences between consultants, or which plan fits a stated philosophy, trace back to core beliefs and pick the option consistent across the layers.
body: Poczwardowski, Sherman and Ravizza describe a professional philosophy as layered. At the base are core beliefs and values about people and change.

On top of these sit a theoretical paradigm, then a model of practice and the consultant's role, then intervention goals, and finally techniques. Two consultants using the same techniques may relate to clients very differently because their deeper beliefs differ.

Good practice is consistent: a consultant who values self-reliance takes an educational role and hands responsibility to athletes, and a consultant with a cognitive view plans work on interpretations. A clear philosophy also lets consultants describe their approach honestly so clients can judge fit.

Models of excellence inform what consultants build. Orlick and Partington's study of Olympians highlighted commitment, quality practice, mental preparation and focus plans, distraction control and post-competition evaluation.

Gould, Dieffenbach and Moffett found that Olympic champions showed characteristics such as anxiety control, confidence, focus, goal setting and optimism, developed over years through parents, coaches and the sport environment.

cards.title: Case conceptualization (formulation)
points: Integrates multi-source data, including life outside sport
Tentative and testable; refined collaboratively with the client
Disagreement between sources is a clue, not noise
Identifies when referral is needed
cards.examNote: Expect vignettes where one source (often a coach's label) conflicts with others; the best answer integrates all the data into a tentative explanation rather than adopting one view.
body: A case conceptualization is the consultant's working explanation of what is happening for a client and why.

It pulls together everything gathered in assessment: the reason for consulting, performance history and demands, strengths, health and self-care, injury, motivation and readiness for change, and cultural and contextual factors inside and outside the performance environment.

It links these to the presenting concern and points toward goals and an intervention plan. A good formulation draws on several methods (interview, observation, questionnaires, stakeholder input, performance data), treats discrepancies between sources as information, and is held as a hypothesis.

It is shared and refined with the client and revised as new data arrive. It should also flag when the picture suggests a concern outside the consultant's competence or scope, which calls for referral.

cards.title: Motivational interviewing: OARS and change talk
points: OARS: open questions, affirmations, reflections, summaries
Change talk: desire, ability, reasons, need, commitment
Respond to sustain talk with reflection, not argument
Avoid the righting reflex with reluctant or referred clients
cards.examNote: A likely scenario asks for the best response to an ambivalent client or which statement is change talk; the key reflects or evokes the client's own motivation, never confronts.
body: Motivational interviewing (MI) is a collaborative, person-centered way of talking with someone who is ambivalent about change. Its core skills are OARS: Open questions, Affirmations, Reflections, and Summaries.

During assessment, MI helps the consultant gauge readiness and hear the client's own reasons for change. Change talk is the client's language in favor of change: desire ("I want..."), ability ("I could..."), reasons, need, and, later, commitment and taking steps. Sustain talk argues for staying the same.
The consultant evokes and reflects change talk and responds to sustain talk with reflection rather than argument. A double-sided reflection that ends on the change side is a common tool.
The "righting reflex," also called the "fixing reflex" (pushing, persuading, confronting, or jumping to fix) tends to increase resistance, especially with clients referred by a coach.

cards.title: Socratic questioning
points: Open, evidence-seeking, non-leading questions
Guided discovery: the client reaches the conclusion
Not reassurance, arguing, or lecturing
Useful in assessment for mapping beliefs
cards.examNote: When asked which response "reflects Socratic questioning," pick the open question that invites the client to examine evidence, not the one that reassures or corrects.
body: Socratic questioning uses open, curious questions that help clients examine their own thoughts and reach their own conclusions instead of being told what to think.
In assessment it shows what a belief is, how firmly it is held, and what evidence the client draws on, which feeds the formulation. Later it supports cognitive restructuring through guided discovery.

Typical questions ask for evidence ("What have you seen happen when...?"), alternatives ("How else could you read that?"), consequences ("What does believing this do to your preparation?"), and perspective ("What would you tell a teammate?").

Socratic questioning is not the same as reassurance, lecturing, labeling a thought as "irrational," or asking closed yes/no questions. The rationale is that conclusions clients reach themselves are likely to feel more convincing.

cards.title: Performance profiling
points: Performer generates the qualities, then rates current vs. ideal
Builds awareness and ownership of goals
Coach ratings can be compared, not substituted
Re-rate the same profile over time to monitor progress
cards.examNote: Choose profiling when the stem stresses the client's own view of what matters or buy-in; in Domain V, re-rate the same qualities against the baseline.
body: Performance profiling, developed by Butler and Hardy from personal construct theory, asks the performer to name the qualities (mental, physical, technical, tactical) they believe matter for top performance in their role.

They then rate their current level on each, often alongside an ideal or target rating. The gaps show priorities in the performer's own terms, which builds awareness, ownership, and motivation for goal setting.

It suits clients who resist standardized questionnaires or feel "handed a checklist," and it adapts to teams, positions, and non-sport performers. Coaches can rate the same qualities so perceptions can be compared and discussed.
For evaluation, the performer re-rates the same qualities later and compares them with the baseline; this tracks perceived change and guides plan revisions.

cards.title: Selecting, administering, and debriefing questionnaires
points: Match state vs. trait to the question; check population, age, language
Consent defines who sees results and how they are used
Consistent administration; secure storage; anonymity or coding for team measures
Debrief collaboratively; never rely on one score
cards.examNote: A likely scenario turns on appropriate use rather than the instrument itself: wrong population norms, a coach wanting individual scores, or a screener treated as a diagnosis.
body: Start with the question, then choose the instrument. Is the interest a state (how someone feels before this event) or a trait (a general tendency)?

Does the instrument have validity and reliability evidence for this population, age, and language? Norms only apply to the groups they were built on, and ad hoc translations lack validity evidence. Obtain informed consent that says who will see the results and for what purpose.

For minors, get guardian permission plus the minor's assent. Administer under consistent conditions: state measures depend on timing, and anonymity or confidential coding matters for team measures. Store data securely. Give feedback as a collaborative conversation that treats scores as hypotheses to check against the client's experience.

Never base a decision on a single score, and never use results for purposes, such as selection, that the instrument and consent do not support. Clinical screeners may be used only with appropriate training, policy, and a referral pathway; they flag rather than diagnose.

cards.title: Anxiety instruments: CSAI-2 and SAS-2
points: CSAI-2: state cognitive anxiety, somatic anxiety, self-confidence
CSAI-2 timing: close to competition; repeat under similar conditions
SAS-2: trait somatic anxiety, worry, concentration disruption
SAS-2 suits youth and adults
cards.examNote: Decide state vs. trait from the stem ("right now, before this race" vs. "usually, across competitions") and check the client's age; then pick the CSAI-2 or the SAS-2.
body: The Competitive State Anxiety Inventory-2 (CSAI-2) measures state cognitive anxiety, somatic anxiety, and self-confidence.

It was built from multidimensional anxiety theory and is designed to be completed shortly before competition (traditionally about an hour before). Because it captures a moment, it is ideal for tracking pre-competition states across events.

Comparisons are meaningful only when timing and the type of event are kept similar. Later work added directional scales asking whether symptoms feel facilitative or debilitative, and concerns about factor structure led to a revised form (CSAI-2R).
The Sport Anxiety Scale-2 (SAS-2) measures trait sport performance anxiety: somatic anxiety, worry, and concentration disruption. It was developed for children as well as adults.
Use it to describe a general tendency, such as an athlete who is nervous before every competition regardless of stakes, or as a pre/post measure of change in that tendency.

cards.title: Skills and attention inventories: TOPS, ACSI-28, TAIS
points: TOPS: skill use, separately for practice and competition
ACSI-28: broad sport coping skills profile
TAIS: attentional width/direction and overload, plus interpersonal style
ACSI-28 concentration is not the same as attentional style
cards.examNote: Practice-vs-competition gaps point to the TOPS; broad/narrow or internal/external attention problems point to the TAIS.
body: The Test of Performance Strategies (TOPS) measures how often athletes use psychological skills and strategies, with separate practice and competition sections.

Practice-section scales include goal setting, imagery, self-talk, relaxation, activation, emotional control, automaticity, and attentional control; the competition section includes negative thinking. This makes it a good fit when performance differs between training and competition.

The Athletic Coping Skills Inventory-28 (ACSI-28) gives a broad picture of psychological coping skills in sport, such as coping with adversity, peaking under pressure, concentration, confidence and achievement motivation, and coachability. It does not separate settings.

The Test of Attentional and Interpersonal Style (TAIS), based on Nideffer's model, profiles attentional width (broad–narrow) and direction (internal–external), including overload tendencies, plus interpersonal style. Choose it when the question is the type of attention, not just how well someone concentrates.
Interpret it cautiously, because evidence for its factor structure and validity is mixed.

cards.title: Other instruments, observation, and multi-source data
points: SIQ = imagery use; MIQ-3 = imagery ability
POMS trends flag possible overreaching; route to coaching and medical staff
GEQ: anonymous, aggregate reporting
Observation: defined behaviors, real-time records, multiple contexts
cards.examNote: Expect instrument-matching vignettes and items on reassessing with the same method and conditions as the baseline, plus triangulation when sources disagree.
body: TEOSQ: task vs. ego goal orientation, that is, whether success is defined as improvement or as beating others.

SIQ: how often imagery is used for cognitive and motivational functions (imagery use). MIQ-3: ease of generating external visual, internal visual, and kinesthetic movement images (imagery ability). AIMS: the strength and exclusivity of athletic identity, relevant to injury and transition.

POMS: mood states; repeated monitoring can show responses to training load, such as an inverted "iceberg" with high fatigue and low vigor. Mood profiles flag issues; they do not diagnose overtraining. GEQ: task and social cohesion. Collect it anonymously and report at team level.

Beyond questionnaires, systematic observation defines target behaviors, records them as they happen, and samples several contexts. Coach and stakeholder input (with consent) is most useful as specific, observable examples. Performance metrics, video, and wearables add objective data, but each measures something specific.
Triangulate sources and explore disagreements with the client.

cards.title: Chelladurai's Multidimensional Model of Leadership
points: Required (situation), preferred (athletes), and actual (leader) behavior
Often summarized: actual–required congruence → performance; actual–preferred congruence → satisfaction
LSS dimensions: training and instruction, democratic, autocratic, social support, positive feedback
Target the specific gap, not the coach's entire style
cards.examNote: Expect vignettes where a coach matches what athletes like but not what the situation needs, or the reverse; predict the outcome or pick the specific behavior to adjust.
body: Chelladurai's model explains leadership effectiveness as the fit among three kinds of leader behavior. Required behavior is what the situation demands, given the sport, level, team size, and organizational constraints.
Preferred behavior is what athletes want, shaped by their age, gender, skill, experience, and personality. Actual behavior is what the leader really does, shaped by the leader's own characteristics.
It is often summarized this way: when actual behavior matches required behavior, performance is expected to benefit; when it matches preferred behavior, satisfaction; and when all three align, both.

The Leadership Scale for Sports (LSS) measures five dimensions (training and instruction, democratic behavior, autocratic behavior, social support, and positive feedback) in versions for athletes' preferences, athletes' perceptions, and coaches' self-ratings, so specific gaps can be identified.

For consultants, the model is a practical lens: use gaps to target one behavior rather than critiquing a coach's whole style, and remember that athletes' preferences are not the only criterion, because the situation's requirements matter too.

cards.title: Transformational Leadership
points: Four I's: idealized influence, inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, individualized consideration
Transactional: contingent reward and management by exception
Laissez-faire is the least effective style in the full-range model
Transformational behaviors build on transactional ones
cards.examNote: A likely scenario describes a coach who relies on rewards or on correcting errors; the best answer usually adds one of the four I's, such as individualized consideration.
body: Transactional leaders work through exchanges: rewards for meeting standards (contingent reward) and correcting deviations (management by exception). Transformational leaders also inspire followers to look beyond self-interest and exceed expectations.
Bass's full-range model places these styles on a continuum, with laissez-faire leadership (avoiding leadership responsibilities) as least effective.

Transformational leadership has four components, often called the four I's: idealized influence (role modeling that earns trust), inspirational motivation (a compelling vision and high, optimistic expectations), intellectual stimulation (inviting people to question assumptions and solve problems), and individualized consideration (attending to each person's needs and growth).

Transformational behaviors add to effective transactional ones rather than replacing them. In sport, transformational coaching and athlete leadership are associated with greater effort, satisfaction, cohesion, and intrinsic motivation. Athlete-centered and servant approaches share this emphasis on developing the person and serving the group.
Consultants can help coaches and captains add specific behaviors, such as one-on-one check-ins or involving athletes in problem-solving.

cards.title: Mastery-Oriented Coach Training (CET and MAC)
points: Mistake-contingent encouragement plus corrective instruction
Positive reinforcement of effort and improvement; reduce punitive behavior
Mastery definition of success; preseason parent meeting
Reported outcomes: more enjoyment, less performance anxiety, lower dropout
cards.examNote: When a coach punishes errors or praises only outcomes, the best answer usually applies encouragement plus corrective instruction and a mastery definition of success.
body: Coach Effectiveness Training (CET), developed by Smith, Smoll, and colleagues, and its successor, the Mastery Approach to Coaching (MAC), teach youth coaches a small set of evidence-based behavioral guidelines.

Success is defined as effort, improvement, and enjoyment, not just winning. Coaches give frequent positive reinforcement for effort and progress, respond to mistakes with encouragement followed by corrective instruction delivered supportively, give technical instruction in a positive way, and cut punitive and hostile behaviors.
They set team rules with athletes' input and work with parents, for example through a preseason parent meeting. Coaches also self-monitor their own behavior.

Athletes of trained coaches have reported more enjoyment, more liking for coaches and teammates, gains in self-esteem among those who started low, and lower dropout; reduced performance anxiety has been reported for both programs.
For consultants, CET and MAC model good train-the-trainer work: a few concrete behaviors, practiced with feedback and backed by self-monitoring.

cards.title: Coach–Athlete Relationship (3+1Cs)
points: Closeness: trust, respect, liking
Commitment: intention to maintain the relationship
Complementarity: cooperative, corresponding behaviors
Co-orientation: shared and accurately perceived views
cards.examNote: Vignettes describe a dyad strong on some Cs and weak on one; identify the weak C and choose the intervention that targets it.
body: Jowett's model describes the coach–athlete relationship in terms of the partners' linked feelings, thoughts, and behaviors. Closeness is the emotional tie: mutual trust, respect, liking, and appreciation.

Commitment is each partner's intention to maintain the relationship over time. Complementarity is cooperative, corresponding behavior; for example, the coach instructs and the athlete responds, or the athlete asks and the coach provides input.

Co-orientation, the '+1', is how far coach and athlete share views and perceive each other accurately, including actual similarity, assumed similarity, and empathic understanding. The CART-Q measures closeness, commitment, and complementarity.
Strong relationships are associated with satisfaction, motivation, and performance, and problems often sit in one C rather than all of them.

Consultants can use the model to locate the weak dimension (trust is high but sessions are uncoordinated, or each partner assumes an agreement that doesn't exist) and design facilitated conversations that target it.

cards.title: Cultural humility vs. cultural competence
points: Competence: awareness, knowledge, skills; ongoing, never 'finished'
Humility: client as expert on their own identity; lifelong self-reflection
Treat group-level knowledge as a hypothesis to check, not a conclusion
'I treat everyone the same' is not humility; it ignores what matters to the client
cards.examNote: Keys usually show the consultant asking what an identity means to this client, or examining their own assumptions, rather than applying generalizations or avoiding culture altogether.
body: Cultural competence is usually framed as awareness of one's own assumptions, knowledge of other worldviews, and culturally appropriate skills.
Read as a destination, it can slide into the idea that learning facts about a group lets you predict an individual.

Cultural humility is an ongoing, other-oriented stance: the client is the expert on which identities matter to them and what those identities mean, and the consultant stays curious, self-reflective, and open to being wrong. The two work together.

Group knowledge is useful as a tentative hypothesis that you check with the person in front of you, never as a script. Humility also means owning mistakes: when a remark lands badly, listen without defending, acknowledge the impact, and repair the relationship.

cards.title: Contextual intelligence
points: Read culture, structure, power, and unwritten rules before intervening
Developed through experience, observation, mentoring, and reflection
Ask stakeholders what they need rather than leading with expertise
Mandated attendance or borrowed insider jargon can undermine trust
cards.examNote: In entry and new-setting scenarios, the best first step is usually learning the culture and asking about needs, not presenting credentials or a ready-made program.
body: Contextual intelligence is the ability to read the setting you work in (its culture, history, structure, power relationships, unwritten rules, and the goals of key stakeholders) and to adjust how you deliver services to fit.
The same mental skills program can succeed in one organization and fail in another because of who holds influence, how outsiders are viewed, or what the group values.

Consultants entering a new setting, such as moving from college sport to a professional club or to a fire department, build contextual intelligence by observing before intervening, learning the group's language and routines, finding mentors who know the system, asking what people need, and reflecting deliberately on what they learn.
Credentials and research rarely substitute for this understanding.

cards.title: Consultant identity, bias, and cultural praxis
points: Self-reflexivity: examine how your own identities and privilege shape judgments
Praxis links reflection, theory, and action; reflection should change practice
Check frustrations and deficit labels against your own background
Use supervision and peer consultation to surface blind spots
cards.examNote: When a consultant's judgment of a client seems shaped by their own background, the key is usually to reflect (often with supervision) and adapt, not to refer out or impose rules.
body: Consultants bring their own identities (race, gender, class, nationality, religion, sexuality, ability, athletic background) into every relationship. These shape what consultants notice, what seems 'normal,' and how they interpret behavior.

Cultural praxis, drawn from cultural sport psychology, asks practitioners to be self-reflexive: to examine how their own social positions and privileges influence their judgments, to listen for voices that dominant sport culture marginalizes, and to let that reflection change their practice.
A warning sign is a judgment about a client, such as 'not committed' or 'low confidence,' that rests on the consultant's own experience or norms.
Supervision, peer consultation, and reflective journaling are the practical tools, and the result should be adapted practice, such as flexible scheduling or re-checked interpretations.

cards.title: Microaggressions
points: Three forms: microassaults, microinsults, microinvalidations
Attend to impact even when intent was benign
In groups: name it briefly, tie it to norms, follow up privately
Don't make the targeted person educate the group
cards.examNote: Distractors include ignoring the comment, lecturing at length, explaining intent, or asking the targeted person to explain; the key is brief, non-shaming acknowledgment plus repair.
body: Sue and colleagues described racial microaggressions as brief, everyday verbal, behavioral, or environmental slights, intentional or not, that communicate hostile, demeaning, or invalidating messages to people of color.
The term has since been extended to other marginalized identities.

The authors described three forms: microassaults (explicit, usually deliberate attacks), microinsults (subtle snubs that demean a person's identity), and microinvalidations (comments that negate a person's experiences, such as 'I don't see color' or treating a U.S.-born person as a foreigner).

Because microinsults and microinvalidations are often unintentional, their impact is easy to dismiss, yet repeated experiences add up. In a group, a consultant should address a microaggression promptly and briefly, without shaming, linking it to agreed norms and checking in with the person targeted.
When the consultant is the source, the repair is to listen without defending, acknowledge the impact, apologize, and reflect.

cards.title: Athletic identity and career transitions
points: Strong, exclusive athletic identity: risk factor for difficult transitions
Normative vs. non-normative transitions; multiple interacting life levels
Involuntary exit (deselection, injury) usually means harder adjustment
Pre-retirement planning and social support aid adjustment
cards.examNote: Expect scenarios where the best action is starting transition planning early or broadening identity, not waiting until the career is over.
body: Athletic identity is the degree to which a person identifies with the athlete role.

A strong identity can support commitment, but when it is also exclusive, injuries, deselection, and retirement can threaten the person's whole sense of self. The Athletic Identity Measurement Scale (AIMS) assesses it.

Wylleman and Lavallee's developmental model frames transitions across athletic, psychological, psychosocial, and academic or vocational levels that interact over the lifespan. Transitions may be normative (junior to senior, retirement) or non-normative (injury, deselection).

Adjustment tends to be harder when exit is involuntary, identity is exclusive, and there is little planning or support. Pre-retirement planning, a broader identity, and social support help, and planning can begin while the athlete is still competing.
Stigma about seeking help can keep struggling athletes from using support.

cards.title: DEIB at the organizational level
points: Culture lives in leadership, policy, practices, and everyday norms
One-off sessions alone are unlikely to change climate; favor sustained, leadership-backed work
Design around access barriers (schedule, transport, language) with community input
Be transparent about competence; partner with DEI specialists when needed
cards.examNote: Keys favor honest scoping, stakeholder co-design, and system-level change over quick fixes or public-relations gestures.
body: Diversity, equity, inclusion, and belonging work happens at individual, team, and organizational levels.

At the organizational level, culture is shaped by leadership behavior, policies, selection and scheduling practices, and everyday norms, such as praising athletes who play hurt or running programs only in one language at times families cannot attend.

An ecological view reminds consultants that athletes are influenced by nested systems: family, team, institution, and community. A single workshop after an incident is unlikely on its own to change climate.

Integrity requires being honest about what a one-off session can achieve, recommending assessment of climate and sustained, leadership-backed processes, designing programs around real access barriers with community input, and recognizing the limits of one's own competence by partnering with qualified DEI professionals when needed.

cards.title: Principle: Competence
points: Practice within the limits of your training, experience and credentials
Keep skills current through continuing education
Consult, seek supervision or refer when a need exceeds your competence
Cultural awareness is part of competence
cards.examNote: Competence underlies many scenario answers: when a client presents something outside mental performance training (e.g., signs of a clinical disorder), the best move is usually to recognize the limit and refer, not to try a new technique.
body: The competence principle asks consultants to offer only the services their education, training, supervised experience and credentials actually support.
It is not a one-time achievement: competence has to be kept current as research, methods and client populations change. It also means being honest with yourself about where your skills stop.

A mental performance consultant may be excellent at teaching imagery or goal setting yet have no training in treating an eating disorder or depression. Working at the edge of your training calls for extra study, consultation or supervision, and working beyond it calls for referral.
Competence also includes cultural competence, meaning awareness of how a client's background, identity and context shape what an effective, respectful service looks like.
When a client's needs exceed what you can responsibly offer, the competent response is to say so and connect the client with someone who can help.

cards.title: Principle: Integrity
points: Accurate representation of credentials and services
No guarantees of performance outcomes
Be transparent about roles, who pays and potential conflicts
Avoid deception and misrepresentation
cards.examNote: Shows up in marketing and role-clarity scenarios: the best answer corrects or avoids misleading claims (e.g., implying CMPC is a license or promising results) and openly clarifies roles.
body: Integrity means being honest, fair and transparent in everything a consultant does: practice, teaching, research and self-promotion.

Consultants describe their qualifications accurately, don't overstate what their services can achieve, and don't make promises about results such as guaranteed wins or rankings. Integrity also means being clear about roles.
If you are both a team's consultant and a faculty member, or you are paid by an organization while working with its athletes, you are open about those arrangements and how they might affect the work.

Consultants avoid deception, keep their commitments, and don't steal or misrepresent other people's work. When a conflict between interests arises, integrity points toward naming it openly rather than quietly managing it in a way that serves the consultant.
Clients and organizations should be able to trust that what a consultant says about themselves and their services is true.

cards.title: Principle: Professional and Scientific Responsibility
points: Base practice on theory and evidence
