Take responsibility for your conduct and for those you supervise
Cooperate with other professionals in the client's interest
Address colleagues' ethical problems appropriately
cards.examNote: Tends to decide questions about evidence-based practice, supervision of trainees, and what to do when a colleague behaves unethically (address it, usually informally first).
body: This principle concerns the consultant's accountability to the profession and to the science behind it.

Consultants uphold professional standards of conduct, take responsibility for their own behavior, and ground their work in theory and evidence rather than fads or personal preference. They are accountable for the people they supervise and the services delivered under their name.

Professional responsibility also extends to colleagues: when a consultant becomes aware that another professional may be acting unethically, they don't simply ignore it, and they address it in an appropriate way.

Consulting with peers and making referrals that serve the client are expressions of this principle, as is cooperating with other professionals such as athletic trainers, physicians and licensed mental-health providers.
The aim is to protect clients and the public, and to maintain trust in the field of sport and performance psychology.

cards.title: Principle: Respect for People's Rights and Dignity
points: Privacy, confidentiality and self-determination
Informed, voluntary participation
Respect for individual and cultural differences; guard against bias
Extra protections for people with limited autonomy (minors: guardian permission plus assent)
cards.examNote: Underpins consent, confidentiality and diversity scenarios; the best answer preserves the client's autonomy and privacy even when a coach or parent wants otherwise.
body: Consultants respect the worth of every person and protect clients' rights to privacy, confidentiality and self-determination.
Clients have the right to understand the services offered and to decide freely whether to take part, which is the foundation of informed consent.

Respect also means recognizing and valuing differences in age, gender and gender identity, race, ethnicity, culture, national origin, religion, sexual orientation, disability, language and socioeconomic status, and working to reduce the influence of personal biases.

Extra care is needed for people whose ability to make independent decisions is limited, such as minors (who need guardian permission plus their own assent) or athletes facing pressure from coaches or organizations.
Respecting dignity does not mean the consultant decides what is best for the client; it means supporting the client's own choices while being honest about risks and options.

cards.title: Principle: Concern for Others' Welfare
points: Benefit clients and avoid harm
Client wellbeing comes before performance and before the consultant's interests
Be aware of power differences; never exploit them
Resolve competing interests in the way that minimizes harm
cards.examNote: Often the tiebreaker when performance and wellbeing conflict: the best answer protects the athlete's health and safety rather than satisfying the coach or the result.
body: Consultants try to benefit the people they work with and to avoid harming them.
In practice this means putting the client's wellbeing ahead of the consultant's own interests and ahead of performance goals that would cost the client their health.
Consultants stay alert to the power they hold, since athletes, students and trainees may feel unable to refuse a request, and they never use that power to exploit anyone.

When conflicts arise between the interests of different parties, such as a coach who wants an injured athlete back quickly, the consultant works to resolve them in a way that minimizes harm. Concern for welfare also covers research participants, supervisees and the organization's members.
Sometimes it requires uncomfortable action, such as raising a safety concern, arranging a referral, or ending a service that is no longer helping.

cards.title: Principle: Social Responsibility
points: Contribute to the welfare of communities and society
Educate the public accurately
Advocate for safe, inclusive and accessible sport and performance settings
Consider pro bono or reduced-cost services
cards.examNote: A likely scenario involves public education, advocacy for athlete safety (e.g., youth abuse prevention), and widening access to services.
body: Social responsibility reaches beyond the individual client to the communities where consultants work and to society at large.

Consultants share knowledge in ways that contribute to human welfare, support policies and practices that make sport and performance settings safer and more inclusive, and avoid uses of their work that could cause social harm.

This can mean contributing some services for little or no cost, educating the public accurately about what sport psychology can and cannot do, and advocating for athlete welfare, for example by supporting abuse-prevention policies in youth sport.

It also means being mindful of how sport systems can disadvantage some groups and working to widen access to services. Socially responsible consultants comply with laws and regulations while working to change rules that are unjust or that harm the people the profession serves.

cards.title: Applicability of the Ethics Code
points: Covers professional roles and activities, including online ones
Conflict with law or an employer: state the Code commitment and try to resolve it
Never use law or organizational demands to justify human-rights violations
Not knowing a standard is not a defense
cards.examNote: A likely scenario: an employer asks for something that conflicts with ethics (e.g., sharing session notes with a coach). The deciding move is to explain the ethical obligation and seek a resolution, not to comply silently.
body: The Code applies to a consultant's professional roles and activities: consulting, teaching, supervising, research, public speaking, writing and online professional presence.

It doesn't govern purely private conduct, but private behavior that spills into professional roles (for example, posting about clients) falls within its scope. The Code applies across delivery formats, whether in person, by phone or video, or through social media.

When the Code conflicts with law, regulations or an employer's demands, consultants make their commitment to the Code known and take reasonable steps to resolve the conflict in a way consistent with its principles. They never use law or organizational demands to justify violating human rights.
Ignorance or misunderstanding of a standard is not a defense, so consultants are expected to know the Code.

cards.title: Boundaries of Competence
points: Stay within training, experience and credentials
Recognize mental-health concerns and refer to licensed professionals
New populations or emerging areas: get training, consultation or supervision
Emergencies: immediate safety support and connection to services; scope does not expand
cards.examNote: A likely scenario is an athlete showing clinical warning signs during performance work; the best answer is to discuss concerns and refer (with consent unless there is imminent risk), while continuing performance work if appropriate, not to treat or to ignore it.
body: Consultants provide services, teach and do research only within areas where they have appropriate education, training, supervised experience or professional credentials.
For a CMPC who is not a licensed mental-health professional, this means teaching mental performance skills while not diagnosing or treating mental disorders.

A key competence skill is recognizing warning signs, such as disordered eating, depression, substance misuse or suicidal thoughts, and referring to an appropriately licensed professional, normally with the client's consent and continued support where appropriate; imminent risk calls for immediate emergency or crisis help, with or without consent.

Working with a new population (for example, para athletes or a performing-arts company) or in an emerging area where standards are still developing calls for relevant training, consultation or supervision, plus reasonable steps to protect clients while competence is built.
In an emergency, good practice is immediate safety support while connecting the person to emergency or licensed services; this does not expand scope.

cards.title: Maintaining Expertise
points: Ongoing continuing education and engagement with research
Peer consultation and supervision support competence
Update practice when evidence changes
CMPC recertification depends on continuing education
cards.examNote: A likely scenario: a consultant uses outdated methods or enters a new area; the best answer involves targeted training and consultation rather than either refusing all new work or proceeding untrained.
body: Competence decays if it isn't maintained.

Consultants have an ongoing obligation to keep their knowledge and skills current through continuing education, reading research, attending workshops and conferences, peer consultation and supervision. This matters because the evidence base in sport and performance psychology keeps changing, as do technologies, laws and the populations consultants serve.

The CMPC credential itself requires recertification through continuing education, which reflects this expectation. Maintaining expertise also means updating practice when evidence shows that a commonly used method is ineffective or harmful.

A consultant who learned a technique years ago and never revisited the literature may be delivering outdated or poorly supported services. Self-assessment helps here: periodically reviewing which areas of practice feel shaky and seeking targeted learning in those areas.

cards.title: Basis for Scientific and Professional Judgments
points: Combine research, professional expertise and client context
Be able to state the rationale for interventions
Be cautious with unsupported techniques and commercial claims
Tell clients when evidence is limited; monitor effectiveness
cards.examNote: Typical scenario: a coach wants a trendy, unproven intervention. The best answer explains the evidence and offers a supported alternative or monitors carefully, rather than adopting it uncritically.
body: Consultants base their work on established scientific and professional knowledge.
This is often described as evidence-informed practice: combining the best available research with professional expertise and the client's characteristics, culture and preferences.
It does not mean every intervention needs a randomized trial behind it, but it does mean consultants can explain the theoretical and empirical rationale for what they do.

They avoid promoting techniques with no credible support, and they are cautious about claims made by commercial products such as neurofeedback devices or brain-training apps unless the evidence is sound. When evidence is limited, consultants tell clients so and monitor whether the service is helping.
Conclusions in reports or public statements should go no further than the data support.

cards.title: Describing the Nature and Results of Services
points: Explain services and expected outcomes in plain language
Explain assessment results and findings understandably
Agree in advance on who receives results
Tell clients at the outset if feedback will be limited
cards.examNote: A likely scenario combines informed consent and assessment: the best answer gives clear, jargon-free explanations and feedback and avoids promising specific performance outcomes.
body: Before and during services, consultants explain in language the client can understand what the services involve, how they will be delivered, what is realistically expected, and how information will be used.

When a consultant works with a group or team, they explain this to everyone involved. After assessments or interventions, consultants explain findings and results in an understandable way, avoiding jargon and avoiding overstatement.

If someone other than the client receives results (for example, a coach receiving a team-level summary), the arrangement should have been agreed in advance and the information shared should stay within what was consented to.

When services are delivered on behalf of an organization in a way that limits explaining results to individuals, consultants say so at the outset. The goal is that clients never feel surprised by what happened or by who learned what.

cards.title: Respect and Nondiscrimination
points: No unfair discrimination on any protected characteristic
Examine your own biases; seek training or consultation
Adapt services to be culturally responsive and accessible
Don't impose personal values on clients
cards.examNote: Appears in scenarios where a consultant feels uncomfortable with a client's identity or values; the best answer is self-reflection and consultation, not refusing service on discriminatory grounds.
body: Consultants do not engage in unfair discrimination based on age, gender, gender identity, race, ethnicity, culture, national origin, religion, sexual orientation, disability, language, socioeconomic status or any other protected characteristic.

Beyond avoiding discrimination, they treat everyone with respect and work to understand how identity and context shape a client's experience in sport, such as the pressures faced by a first-generation college athlete or an athlete who is the only one of their identity on a team.

Consultants examine their own biases and assumptions and seek training or consultation when working with groups they know less about. Good practice includes using a client's chosen name and pronouns and adapting services so they are accessible.

When a consultant's personal values could interfere with serving a client, they seek consultation or supervision rather than imposing those values; referral is for limits of competence, not for discomfort with a client's identity.

cards.title: Sexual and Other Harassment
points: No sexual harassment of anyone in professional roles
No harassment or demeaning behavior based on identity
Applies online and during travel
Don't retaliate against people who make complaints
cards.examNote: A likely scenario is a boundary problem in a travel or team setting; the right answer protects the person affected and follows reporting policy (including SafeSport where it applies).
body: Consultants do not engage in sexual harassment, meaning unwelcome sexual advances, requests or comments, or sexual conduct that is offensive or creates a hostile environment, whether as a single severe act or as repeated conduct.

They also don't engage in other harassment or demeaning behavior based on a person's identity or characteristics. This applies to clients, students, supervisees, research participants, colleagues and organizational staff, and it applies online as well as in person.

Because sport settings involve close contact, travel and significant power differences, consultants are especially careful about boundaries and, as good practice, avoid comments about bodies or appearance. Within the U.S. Olympic and Paralympic movement, the SafeSport Code also prohibits sexual misconduct and other forms of abuse and harassment.
With minors in any setting, child-abuse reporting law and organizational policy also apply. Consultants also treat people who file harassment complaints fairly and don't retaliate against them.

cards.title: Personal Problems and Conflicts
points: Monitor your own functioning and practice self-care
Don't start work you're too impaired to do competently
If impaired: seek help, limit or suspend work, arrange transfers
Protect continuity of care when stepping back
cards.examNote: Typical scenario: a consultant is going through a personal crisis or burnout. The deciding move is to seek consultation or help and adjust or pause the caseload with proper referrals, not to keep going unchanged or to abandon clients abruptly.
body: Consultants avoid starting work when they know, or should know, that personal problems such as illness, grief, burnout, substance use or a major life crisis are likely to keep them from doing the work competently.

Self-awareness and self-care are part of the job: consultants monitor their own functioning, set reasonable workloads and seek support early. When a consultant notices that personal problems are affecting their work, they take appropriate steps.

These might include getting professional help or consultation, limiting their practice, temporarily stepping back, or arranging for clients to be transferred or referred with appropriate continuity of care. Personal conflicts count too.
For example, a strong emotional reaction to a particular client, or a dispute with the client's coach, can cloud judgment. The duty is to protect clients from impaired service, not to be perfect.

cards.title: Avoiding Harm
points: Avoid foreseeable harm; minimize unavoidable harm
Consider how others might use your recommendations or data
Don't participate in or condone abusive practices
End services thoughtfully, with referrals as needed
cards.examNote: A likely scenario: a coach or organization pressures the consultant; choose the option that prevents foreseeable harm to the athlete (e.g., not handing over individual data that could be used to cut players).
body: Consultants take reasonable steps to avoid harming clients, students, supervisees, research participants, organizations and others they work with, and to minimize harm where it is foreseeable and unavoidable.

Harm can be physical, psychological, social or financial. In sport settings it can come from encouraging an athlete to play through an injury, keeping them in a service that isn't helping, or disclosing information that damages their place on a team.

Consultants consider how their recommendations might be used, for example whether a coach could use assessment results to cut players. They do not participate in or tolerate abusive coaching practices or emotional abuse, and they follow reporting obligations when they suspect abuse.
Ending services appropriately is part of avoiding harm: when services are no longer helpful, consultants discuss termination and offer referrals rather than abandoning clients.

cards.title: Misuse of Influence
points: Be aware of the influence your role and expertise carry
Guard against personal, financial or organizational pressures
Don't use influence for self-benefit at the client's expense
Correct misuse of your work by others
cards.examNote: Shows up when a consultant has a financial or organizational interest (e.g., selling products to clients, referring to their own programs); the best answer avoids or discloses the conflict and puts the client's interests first.
body: Consultants often hold influence through their expertise, their relationship with coaches and administrators, and the trust athletes place in them.
This standard asks them to be alert to personal, financial, social, organizational or political factors that could lead to that influence being misused, and to guard against it.

Examples include pressuring a client to buy a product the consultant sells, steering a young athlete toward a program in which the consultant has a financial stake, or using access to an athlete's private information to gain standing with a coach.

Consultants also avoid allowing their work to be used by others in misleading or harmful ways. If they learn that their findings or recommendations are being misused, they take reasonable steps to correct or limit that misuse.

cards.title: Multiple Relationships
points: Not all multiple relationships are unethical; avoid those risking impairment or exploitation
When unavoidable: clarify roles, discuss boundaries, document, consult, monitor
Social media connections can be multiple-relationship issues
Have a written social media policy
cards.examNote: A likely scenario is a consultant who also coaches, teaches, or knows the client socially. The deciding move is to clarify roles and boundaries and consult, or decline if the risk is high, not to assume it is automatically fine or forbidden. Romance with a current client is always forbidden.
body: A multiple relationship exists when a consultant has a professional role with someone and also another role with them or someone close to them, such as being a team's consultant and also its assistant coach, a professor grading the athlete, or a friend of the athlete's parent.

Multiple relationships aren't automatically unethical, and in sport and small communities some are unavoidable. The problem arises when the second relationship could impair objectivity or effectiveness, or risk exploitation or harm. Consultants refrain from relationships reasonably likely to do so.

Sexual or romantic relationships with current clients are never acceptable, nor with former clients for at least two years. When a lesser overlap is unavoidable, good practice is to clarify roles, discuss confidentiality and boundaries openly, document, consult a colleague, and monitor it.
Social media counts as well: friending or messaging clients can blur boundaries, so good practice is a clear policy, such as no personal connections with current clients.

cards.title: Exploitative Relationships and Sexual Intimacies
points: Never sexual intimacy with a current client
Former clients: at least two years after services end, and only if not exploitative
No sexual relationships with students or supervisees under one's authority
Burden of showing non-exploitation is on the consultant
cards.examNote: A likely scenario is a straightforward boundary question: any romantic involvement with a current client is a violation; with a former client, look for whether two years have passed and whether exploitation is possible.
body: Consultants do not exploit anyone over whom they have supervisory, evaluative or other authority, such as clients, students, supervisees or athletes.

Sexual intimacy with a current client is never acceptable, and good practice also rules out intimacy with a current client's close relatives, guardians or significant others. Consultants also don't accept as clients people with whom they have had a prior sexual relationship.
For former clients, sexual intimacy is prohibited for at least two years after services end, and even after that it is permitted only in rare circumstances where it is clearly not exploitative.

Relevant factors include how long and intense the work was, the client's history and vulnerability, how services ended, and whether a romantic relationship was discussed during services. The consultant carries the burden of showing there was no exploitation.

cards.title: Barter and Gifts
points: Barter only if not contraindicated and not exploitative; never tied to performance
Small, occasional token gifts are generally acceptable
Expensive or repeated gifts raise boundary concerns
Consider culture, value, timing and motive; consult and document
cards.examNote: A likely scenario offers barter or a gift from an athlete or family; the best answer weighs the conditions, usually accepts only modest tokens, declines arrangements that blur roles, and always declines payment tied to results.
body: Barter means accepting goods or services instead of money as payment, for example free gym access in exchange for consulting.

Because barter can create conflicts of interest, exploitation and blurred roles, consultants accept it only when it isn't contraindicated for the work and isn't exploitative. Good practice adds fair, clear terms agreed in advance, ideally in writing.

Payment in any form, including barter, is never contingent on the client's performance, and barter that creates an ongoing business relationship is especially risky. Gifts call for similar good-practice judgment.
A small token of appreciation such as a team shirt at season's end is usually fine, while expensive gifts, repeated gifts, or gifts that seem meant to change the relationship are not.
Consultants consider the gift's value, the timing, the client's motives and cultural meaning, and they consult and document when unsure.

cards.title: Consultation and Referral
points: Consult colleagues or mentors on difficult situations
Refer when needs exceed competence or role
Get consent; share only what is needed; de-identify when consulting
Coordinate with other providers in the client's interest
cards.examNote: Referral is the right answer when the scenario clearly signals a need outside CMPC scope; consultation is often the right first step when the consultant faces an ethical gray area.
body: Consultants seek consultation from colleagues, supervisors or mentors when they face difficult ethical or professional situations, and they refer clients to other professionals when the client's needs fall outside their competence or role.

Good referrals are made thoughtfully: the consultant explains the reason to the client, gets their consent (for a minor, guardian permission plus assent), provides names of appropriate providers (licensed mental-health professionals, physicians, registered dietitians and others), and where appropriate stays involved for the performance work while coordinating with the other provider.
When consulting colleagues about a case, consultants protect confidentiality by sharing only what is needed and, where possible, removing identifying details unless the client has consented.

Cooperating with other professionals involved with a client, such as the athletic trainer or team physician, serves the client and should happen with the client's permission, unless an emergency or reporting duty requires otherwise.

cards.title: Third-Party Requests for Services
points: Clarify at the start who the client is
Explain your role and how information will be used
Agree on limits of confidentiality with all parties
Revisit agreements if circumstances change
cards.examNote: A likely scenario: a coach or organization refers an athlete and wants updates; the best first step is to clarify roles, the client and confidentiality limits with all parties before starting work.
body: In sport, services are often requested by someone other than the person receiving them.
A coach asks you to work with a struggling player, a parent books sessions for a teenager, or a university or professional club hires you for its athletes.

In these cases the consultant clarifies at the outset, with everyone involved, who the client is, what the consultant's role will be, what information will be shared and with whom, how it may be used, and where confidentiality ends.

For example, it should be clear whether the coach will receive anything beyond attendance or general themes. These agreements should be settled before services start and revisited if circumstances change.
Clarity protects the athlete's trust and the consultant's integrity, and it prevents later conflicts when the paying party expects information the athlete never agreed to share.

cards.title: Delegation and Supervision of Others
points: Delegate only what the person can do competently
The supervisor remains responsible for delegated work
Clients should know when a trainee is involved
Set clear expectations and give timely, fair evaluation
cards.examNote: Typical scenario: a supervisee is about to work beyond their training or without disclosing trainee status. The deciding move is to ensure appropriate supervision, competence and client awareness.
body: Consultants who delegate work to employees, interns, graduate students or other supervisees remain responsible for that work.

They delegate only tasks the person can be expected to perform competently given their training and experience, and they provide adequate supervision. They don't delegate to someone whose multiple relationship with the client is likely to cause exploitation or loss of objectivity.

Supervisors give timely, specific feedback, evaluate supervisees on relevant performance requirements set out at the start, and ensure clients know when a trainee is involved and who is supervising. Supervisors also model ethical behavior and help supervisees develop their own ethical reasoning.

In mentored experience toward certification, the supervisor and supervisee should agree on expectations, the format and frequency of meetings, how evaluation will work and how disagreements will be handled.

cards.title: Documentation and Records
points: Keep accurate, relevant and timely records
Store securely and control access
Retain per applicable law or policy; plan for practice closure
Dispose of records in ways that protect confidentiality
cards.examNote: A likely scenario involves leaving a position, storing notes on shared drives, or a coach asking to see files; the best answer protects record security and confidentiality.
body: Consultants create and maintain records of their work to support continuity of services, accountability, billing and legal requirements. Records should be accurate, timely and limited to what is relevant.
Consultants store records securely, whether on paper (locked storage) or electronically (encryption, password protection, secure platforms), and they control who has access.

They keep records for the period required by applicable law, regulation or organizational policy, and good practice is to plan for what happens to records if they leave a job, close a practice, become incapacitated or die.
When records are no longer needed, they dispose of them in a way that protects confidentiality, for example by shredding or secure deletion.
In team and organizational settings, consultants clarify in advance who owns records and who can see them, so that coaches or administrators can't access session notes without consent.

cards.title: Fees and Financial Arrangements
points: Agree on fees and arrangements early, ideally in writing
Don't misrepresent fees; discuss financial limits early
Never contingent on performance outcomes (e.g., prize money, win bonuses)
Give notice before any collection action
cards.examNote: A likely scenario: an athlete or agent offers a share of winnings or a bonus for a medal; the right answer declines any fee contingent on future achievement and sets a standard fee.
body: Consultants and clients (or the paying organization) agree on fees and billing arrangements as early as possible in the relationship, covering rates, cancellation policy, payment schedule and what happens if payment stops.

Consultants don't misrepresent their fees, and when financial limits are foreseeable they discuss them early. If a client stops paying, the consultant follows an agreed process and gives notice before taking collection steps. A key sport-specific rule is that fees are never contingent on future achievement.

A consultant should not accept a percentage of prize money, a bonus for winning, or a share of a future contract, because tying payment to results creates conflicts of interest and pressure that can harm the client and compromise the consultant's objectivity.
Pro bono or reduced-fee work is acceptable when the terms are clear.

cards.title: Public Statements, Advertising and Titles
points: No false, deceptive or misleading statements
CMPC is a certification, not a license
Use "psychologist" only where local law permits
Correct misrepresentations made by others; no outcome guarantees
cards.examNote: A likely scenario: a bio or website calls a non-licensed CMPC a "sport psychologist" or a "licensed" professional. The best answer corrects the wording to match the person's actual credentials and local law.
body: Consultants don't make false, deceptive or misleading public statements about their training, credentials, services, fees, affiliations or results.

This covers websites, social media, interviews, presentations and bios written by others on their behalf. If someone else, such as a team's media office, misrepresents them, they take reasonable steps to correct it.
A key point is that the CMPC is a certification, not a license, so consultants never describe it as a license or imply it authorizes clinical practice.

The title "psychologist" is regulated by law in many jurisdictions; consultants use it only if local law permits, which usually requires a license. Media comments should be grounded in evidence, should avoid diagnosing public figures, and should not imply a personal professional relationship.
Advertising should also avoid guarantees of performance outcomes.

cards.title: Testimonials
points: No testimonials from current clients
Avoid requests to anyone vulnerable to undue influence
Former-client testimonials: freely given, consented, accurate
Naming a client publicly is a disclosure requiring consent
cards.examNote: A likely scenario: a consultant wants to post a quote from an athlete they are currently working with. The correct answer is not to solicit or use it while the athlete is a current client.
body: Testimonials are endorsements from clients used to promote a consultant's services.

Consultants don't solicit testimonials from current clients, or from others who are vulnerable to undue influence because of their circumstances, such as a young athlete who depends on the consultant's good opinion or an athlete still in services.
The concern is that a client who is currently receiving help may feel unable to refuse, and that public endorsement can compromise confidentiality and the working relationship.

If a consultant uses testimonials from former clients, they should be freely given with informed consent, accurate, and should not imply guaranteed results. Consultants also think about confidentiality: naming a well-known athlete as a client is a disclosure that requires the athlete's explicit, informed permission.
Paying for endorsements or offering discounts in exchange for them is likewise problematic.

cards.title: Informed Consent
points: Capacity, information, voluntariness, documentation
Ongoing: revisit when services or circumstances change
Minors: guardian permission plus the minor's assent
Specific consent for recording, sharing and research
cards.examNote: A likely scenario involves a minor or a first session. For a minor, the best answer obtains guardian permission and the athlete's assent; for any client, it covers confidentiality limits and the right to withdraw before starting.
body: Informed consent is an ongoing process, not just a signature.

Valid consent has four parts: capacity (the person can understand and decide), information (the nature and purpose of services, fees, risks and benefits, the consultant's role and credentials, confidentiality and its limits, and the right to stop at any time), voluntariness (free of coercion, which matters when a coach or team arranges services), and documentation.

Consent is revisited when services, roles or circumstances change. For minors or others who cannot legally consent, the consultant obtains permission from a parent or legal guardian and also seeks the minor's assent, explaining things in age-appropriate terms and taking the young person's preferences seriously.
Specific consent is obtained for recording sessions, taking part in research, and sharing information with others, except where law or safety requires disclosure.

cards.title: Confidentiality and Privacy
points: Explain confidentiality limits up front, especially in team work
Disclose only with consent or as required or permitted by law
Exceptions include imminent danger and suspected child abuse
Share the minimum necessary
cards.examNote: A likely scenario: a coach asks what an athlete said; the best answer refers to the agreement made at the outset and shares nothing beyond it without consent, unless a legal or safety exception applies.
body: Consultants protect information obtained through their work and discuss the limits of confidentiality at the start, before sensitive information comes up.

In team and organizational work these limits must be especially clear. Clients should know what, if anything, the coach or organization will receive, that group members may not keep each other's disclosures private, and how data will be stored.
Consultants disclose confidential information only with the client's consent or when disclosure is required or permitted by law.

Examples include imminent danger to self or others, suspected abuse of a minor (reported promptly to child protective services or police, and also to SafeSport in Olympic/Paralympic sport), or a court order. When disclosure is necessary, consultants share only what the purpose requires.

They avoid discussing clients in public spaces or on social media, and they include only necessary information in reports. Privacy also covers where sessions happen, such as a crowded team facility; one-on-one sessions with minors stay observable and interruptible.

cards.title: Technology-Mediated Services
points: Verify client identity
Use secure platforms; explain technology risks in consent
Follow laws where both parties are located
Plan for emergencies: client location, local resources, backup contact
cards.examNote: A likely scenario: starting video work with an athlete in another state or country. The best answer verifies identity, uses secure platforms, checks jurisdictional rules and sets up an emergency plan.
body: Consultants who work by video, phone, text, apps or online platforms apply the same ethical standards as in person, plus some specific safeguards.

They verify the client's identity, especially at the start and for minors. They use secure, privacy-protecting communication platforms and explain the risks and limits of technology, such as data breaches or someone overhearing, as part of informed consent.
They learn and follow the laws and regulations that apply where both the consultant and the client are located, which matters most for licensed professionals working across state or national borders.

They plan for emergencies in advance: knowing the client's location for each session, having local emergency contacts and resources, and agreeing on what to do if the connection drops during a crisis.
Consultants also need competence in the technology and should judge whether remote delivery suits the particular client.

cards.title: Assessment
points: Use tools validated for the population and language
Multi-method assessment, not a single score
Consent, understandable feedback and secure storage
Use only tools you are competent to use
cards.examNote: A likely scenario involves a coach wanting test scores for selection or a tool used outside its validated population; the best answer protects the athlete, uses validated multi-method assessment and keeps results confidential.
body: Consultants use assessment tools only for purposes they are suited for and only with populations and languages for which they have evidence of reliability and validity.

Using a scale validated only on adult athletes with a youth team, or with athletes in a language it hasn't been validated in, calls for caution and acknowledgment of the limits. Good assessment is multi-method, combining interviews, observation and questionnaires instead of relying on a single score.

Consultants obtain informed consent for assessment (for minors, guardian permission plus assent), explaining its purpose and who will see the results, and they give clients understandable feedback. They store results securely and don't release raw data to people unqualified to interpret it.
They use only tools they are competent to administer and interpret, and they don't use assessments to make team selection decisions unless that use is supported and agreed in advance.

cards.title: Resolving Ethical Issues
points: Informal resolution first when appropriate and confidentiality allows
Escalate: supervisor or mentor, AASP Ethics Committee, licensing boards
Cooperate with ethics processes; no frivolous complaints
Mandatory reporting (e.g., abuse) overrides informal resolution
cards.examNote: A likely scenario: you see a colleague misrepresent credentials. The best first step is usually to speak with them directly; escalate if that fails, is inappropriate, would breach confidentiality, or the harm is serious.
body: When a consultant believes a colleague may have acted unethically, the usual first step is to raise the concern with that person informally, provided this is appropriate and does not violate anyone's confidentiality.

Many issues can be resolved this way, for example a colleague's misleading website. If informal resolution is not appropriate, doesn't work, or the violation is serious or has caused substantial harm, the consultant takes further action.
That might mean consulting a supervisor or mentor, or referring the matter to the AASP Ethics Committee, a licensing board or the relevant organization.

Consultants cooperate with ethics investigations and proceedings, and they do not file complaints that are frivolous or meant to harm someone rather than protect the public. Good practice also means not penalizing someone simply because a complaint has been made against them or by them.
Reporting duties, such as suspected abuse, override informal approaches.

cards.title: CMPC scope compared with other professionals
points: Mental disorder diagnosis and treatment: licensed clinicians
Injury care and return-to-play clearance: medical team
Training programs: strength coach; meal plans: registered dietitian
General education is fine; individualized medical, clinical, nutrition, or training assessment or prescription is not
cards.examNote: A likely scenario offers a tempting option where the consultant does another professional's job (clears an athlete to play, writes a meal plan, treats a disorder). Choose the option that stays in scope while still helping, usually by sharing general information and coordinating or referring.
body: A CMPC teaches and applies mental performance skills such as focus, confidence, arousal regulation, goal setting, and team dynamics.

Many neighboring jobs overlap with that work, so scope questions arise naturally. Licensed clinicians (such as psychologists, counselors, social workers, psychiatrists) diagnose and treat mental disorders as their licenses allow; a CMPC without such a license does not.

Athletic trainers, physicians, and physical therapists evaluate and treat injuries, and the designated medical authority (often the team physician) decides return to play. Strength and conditioning coaches design physical training. Registered dietitians write individualized nutrition plans and provide medical nutrition therapy.
Executive coaches work on leadership and organizational issues under a title anyone can use.

The working rule: a CMPC may share general, evidence-based information in these areas, but leaves assessment, diagnosis, and prescription to the right professional, and coordinates with them (with the client's consent) as part of a team.

cards.title: SafeSport Code and MAAPP essentials
points: Report suspected abuse of a minor promptly to CPS or police, and also to the Center in Olympic/Paralympic sport
Don't investigate, confront, or promise secrecy
One-on-one with minors: observable and interruptible, in person or online
Electronic messages with minors: professional and open, e.g., parent copied
cards.examNote: Abuse disclosures override the usual consulting sequence. The best answer reports promptly to both outside authorities and, in the Olympic movement, the Center; options that first verify the story or talk to the coach are wrong.
body: In the U.S. Olympic and Paralympic movement, the U.S. Center for SafeSport has authority over sexual misconduct reports, may take other abuse cases, and sets abuse-prevention rules.

Adults in the movement must report suspected child abuse, including sexual abuse, to law enforcement or child protective services as the law requires, and to the Center. Reporting requires reasonable suspicion, not proof.

The adult who hears a disclosure should listen calmly, avoid promising secrecy, attend to safety, and report promptly. They should not investigate, gather evidence, or confront the alleged perpetrator.

The Minor Athlete Abuse Prevention Policies (MAAPP) limit risky situations: one-on-one interactions with minors must be observable and interruptible (with narrow exceptions, such as emergencies), and electronic communication with minors must be professional and transparent, for example by copying a parent or guardian.
Other MAAPP areas include travel, locker rooms, and massage or athletic training modalities.

cards.title: Ethical decision-making models
points: Identify the issue, the facts, and every stakeholder
Check the Code, the law, and policy; consult a colleague or mentor
Generate options and weigh consequences for each stakeholder
Act, evaluate the outcome, and document the reasoning
cards.examNote: Expect scenarios where a consultant is pressured to act fast. Look for the option that follows the structured process, often consulting a colleague or mentor before acting, rather than deferring to the payer or acting on instinct.
body: Ethical decision-making models give consultants a structured process to replace gut reaction when standards, loyalties, or stakeholders conflict.

The models share a common core: recognize that an ethical issue exists; gather the facts and identify every stakeholder, including who the client is; identify the relevant Ethics Code standards, laws, and organizational policies; consult a trusted colleague or mentor while protecting identities; generate possible courses of action; weigh each option's likely consequences for everyone affected, guided by principles such as respecting autonomy, doing good, avoiding harm, fairness, and keeping commitments; choose and carry out the action; then evaluate the outcome and document the reasoning.
The models don't produce automatic answers, but they make decisions more defensible and less driven by pressure, especially from people with power or money in the situation.

cards.title: The CMPC credential, titles, and educating consumers
points: CMPC = certification, never a license
Follow local law on "psychologist"; never imply licensure you lack
Explain scope clearly to clients, parents, and organizations
Advertising must be accurate: no guarantees, no overstated evidence
cards.examNote: Wrong options often call the CMPC a license, use "psychologist" without licensure, or claim the credential permits treating disorders. The best option describes the credential accurately and points to licensed care when needed.
body: The Certified Mental Performance Consultant (CMPC) credential from AASP shows that a practitioner has met standards for graduate education, specified coursework, mentored applied experience, and a certification exam, and keeps the credential through continuing education and recertification.
It is a professional certification, not a state license. It doesn't authorize anyone to diagnose or treat mental disorders, and it doesn't make the holder a psychologist.

Many jurisdictions restrict the title "psychologist" (sometimes including "sport psychologist") to licensed psychologists, so consultants must follow local law and describe themselves accurately, for example as a Certified Mental Performance Consultant with their actual degree.

Educating consumers is part of the job: athletes, parents, coaches, and organizations should understand what a CMPC does, how that differs from licensed mental health care, and when a referral is appropriate.

cards.title: Kirkpatrick's four levels of evaluation
points: Reaction → Learning → Behavior → Results
Behavior = transfer of skills to the real performance environment
Transfer needs a supportive climate (leaders, schedules, norms)
Results are multi-causal: claim a contribution, not sole credit
cards.examNote: Expect a stakeholder's question or a data pattern (e.g., high satisfaction and good quiz scores but no on-the-job use) and be asked which level it reflects, what to measure, or what to do next.
body: Kirkpatrick's model evaluates a training program at four levels. Reaction asks how participants felt about it: satisfaction, engagement, perceived relevance.

Learning asks what knowledge, skills, or attitudes they gained, measured with quizzes, skill demonstrations, or confidence ratings. Behavior asks whether they actually use what they learned in the real performance setting (the field, the stage, the job), usually weeks later, through observation, logs, or coach and supervisor reports.

Results asks what changed in the outcomes the organization cares about, such as performance, retention, injuries, or revenue. The levels form a chain of evidence, not substitutes: liking a program does not guarantee learning, and learning does not guarantee transfer.

Behavior change also depends on the environment; if schedules, leaders, or norms do not support skill use, transfer stalls. Choose the levels and measures during planning, matched to what each stakeholder needs to know, and be cautious about crediting results-level outcomes, which have many causes.

cards.title: Evaluating the consultant: methods and effective characteristics
points: Use structured, preferably anonymous, forms plus coach and client input
Effective: fits in, trustworthy, accessible, good listener, practical and individualized
Tends to count against: too theoretical, poor fit, weak interpersonal skills
Turn recurring feedback into goals via supervision or peer consultation
cards.examNote: Items give a feedback pattern (e.g., 'knowledgeable but hard to apply') and ask what to change, or ask how to collect candid feedback; practical, individualized help and anonymous structured forms are the usual answers.
body: Consultants evaluate themselves as well as their programs.

Common methods are structured consultant evaluation forms, such as the form Partington and Orlick developed, on which athletes and coaches rate the consultant's characteristics and the usefulness of the service; interviews with clients and coaches; and the process and outcome data gathered for the program.

Anonymous completion, or collection by someone other than the consultant, reduces pressure to give socially desirable answers. Evaluations of Olympic consultants link effectiveness with fitting in with the team, being accessible and trustworthy, listening well, and giving clear, practical strategies individualized to the athlete.

Poor fit, too much theory, or weak interpersonal skills or sport understanding tend to count against a consultant. Consultants interviewed about their own effectiveness stress the quality of the consulting relationship.
Feedback becomes growth when the consultant takes it to supervision, mentoring, or peer consultation and turns it into specific development goals.

cards.title: Reflective practice: Gibbs, Kolb, and Schön
points: Gibbs: description, feelings, evaluation, analysis, conclusion, action plan
Kolb: experience → reflective observation → abstract conceptualization → active experimentation
Schön: reflection-in-action (during) vs. reflection-on-action (after)
Structured post-session reflection plus supervision or peer consultation
cards.examNote: Expect a consultant's journal entry or in-session adjustment and a question about which stage or type of reflection it shows, or which stage is missing or comes next.
body: Reflective practice is the structured habit of learning from one's own consulting experiences, and it is a core part of self-evaluation for applied sport psychologists.

Gibbs's reflective cycle has six stages: description (what happened), feelings, evaluation (what was good and bad), analysis (why it happened, using theory and context), conclusion (what else could have been done), and action plan (what to do next time).

Skipping evaluation and analysis produces vague plans like 'do better'. Kolb's experiential learning cycle runs from concrete experience to reflective observation, then abstract conceptualization (making sense of it with theory), then active experimentation (testing a revised approach), which becomes a new experience.

Schön distinguished reflection-in-action, thinking and adjusting while a session is unfolding, from reflection-on-action, reviewing afterward. Practical tools include post-session notes or journals, structured reflection templates, and discussing reflections with a supervisor, mentor, or peer.

cards.title: Measuring progress and program evaluation designs
points: Plan measures and collect a stable baseline before intervening
Pair outcome measures with process measures of the targeted skill
A–B change at the phase change suggests, not proves, an effect; staggered starts strengthen inference
Social validation: importance, acceptability, meaningfulness
cards.examNote: Likely scenarios: what to do before starting an intervention (baseline), how to read a graph whose baseline was already trending, how to handle conflicting data sources, and how to describe a team's win honestly.
body: Decide how progress will be measured while building the plan, before intervening.

Match measures to the goals and include process measures of the targeted skill (routine use, communication quality, focus ratings), not only outcomes such as wins, which have many causes. Triangulate sources: client self-report, coach or stakeholder reports, observation, and performance data.
When sources disagree, explore the discrepancy and add targeted measures rather than picking one source. Single-case designs fit applied work.

In an A–B design, the target is measured repeatedly during a baseline until it is stable, and then after the intervention starts; a change in level, trend, or variability at the phase change is consistent with an effect, though A–B alone cannot rule out other causes.

A trend already present in the baseline that simply continues is not evidence of an effect. A multiple-baseline design staggers the start across athletes, behaviors, or settings, which strengthens inference. Social validation asks clients and stakeholders whether goals were important, procedures acceptable, and results meaningful. Attribute outcomes realistically.

cards.title: Concluding a consultation
points: Plan ending from the outset; review progress together at the end
Consolidate skills, plan for relapse and generalization, build independence
Teams: closing session, staff handoff, confidentiality-respecting report
Poor fit or departure: open discussion, alternatives, consented handoff
cards.examNote: Expect 'which focus for the final sessions' or 'how to end' questions; the best answer builds independence and continuity and avoids both abrupt endings and open-ended dependence.
body: Ending is planned, ideally discussed from the start as part of informed consent (expected length, how ending will be decided).
Consultations end when goals are met, when the client is no longer benefiting or the fit is poor, or for external reasons such as a contract ending or the consultant relocating.

Good endings review progress with the client, consolidate the skills that work rather than adding new ones, and plan for generalization and relapse: anticipate high-risk situations and rehearse self-directed coping so the client can work independently.

Agree on any follow-up or booster contact and an open-door policy without fostering dependence. With teams and organizations, hold a closing session, build staff capacity to sustain routines, and report only what confidentiality agreements allow.

When a client is not benefiting despite revision, discuss it openly and help them find a better-fitting provider. When the consultant must leave, give timely notice and arrange a consented handoff. Abrupt consultant-initiated endings without notice, referral, or transition planning can amount to abandonment.

cards.title: Multidimensional Anxiety Theory
points: Predicted: cognitive anxiety negative linear with performance
Predicted: somatic anxiety inverted-U; self-confidence positive linear
Cognitive anxiety builds early; somatic anxiety spikes near the start and then dissipates
Measured with the CSAI-2; supports matching technique to anxiety type
cards.examNote: Expect a CSAI-2 profile or anxiety log and a question about which component to prioritize or when to intervene. Don't treat moderate somatic anxiety as a problem.
body: Multidimensional anxiety theory splits competitive state anxiety into separate parts that relate to performance in different ways.

Cognitive anxiety (worry, negative expectations) is predicted to have a negative linear relationship with performance: more worry, worse performance. Somatic anxiety (perceived bodily activation such as butterflies, tension, racing heart) is predicted to follow an inverted-U, so moderate levels are best.
Self-confidence is predicted to relate positively and linearly to performance. Research support for these performance predictions is mixed.

The components also follow different timelines: cognitive anxiety rises early and stays fairly steady before an event, while somatic anxiety stays low until shortly before the start, peaks at the start, and fades once performance begins. The CSAI-2 was built to measure these three components.
In practice, the theory tells a consultant which component to target, when to intervene, and why matching the technique to the type of anxiety makes sense.

cards.title: Individual Zones of Optimal Functioning (IZOF)
points: Optimal zones are individual and can be at any intensity
Includes pleasant and unpleasant emotions that can be functional or dysfunctional
Assessed by recalling best and worst performances, not by comparing to norms
Intervention moves the athlete toward their own zone, up or down
cards.examNote: IZOF is usually the answer when athletes differ in their best-performance states, or when an athlete plays best while highly anxious. Watch for distractors that impose a moderate target or group norms.
body: Hanin's IZOF model holds that each performer has a personal range, or zone, of emotional intensity in which they perform best.
That zone can sit at low, moderate, or high intensity, so there is no universal ideal level of anxiety or arousal.

Later versions of the model expanded from anxiety to a full emotional profile that includes pleasant and unpleasant emotions, each of which can be functional (helpful) or dysfunctional (harmful) for a given person.
Tension or irritation may be part of one athlete's optimal profile, while calm contentment may come before another athlete's worst performances.

Assessment is idiographic: athletes recall emotions before their best and worst performances, often using their own descriptors, and these zones are then checked against ratings before upcoming competitions. Interventions help the athlete move into and stay in their own zone, which might mean energizing rather than calming.

cards.title: Catastrophe Model
points: Low cognitive anxiety: arousal has a gradual, mild effect
High cognitive anxiety: arousal past a threshold causes a sudden, large drop
Hysteresis: recovery is not a simple reversal of the collapse
In practice: lower arousal substantially, address worry, then rebuild
cards.examNote: Look for abrupt collapses that happen only when worry is high, or an athlete whose small calming efforts fail mid-competition. The inverted-U, which ignores cognitive anxiety and predicts smooth change, is the usual distractor.
body: The catastrophe model (Hardy and colleagues) describes how cognitive anxiety and physiological arousal interact to affect performance.

When cognitive anxiety is low, rising physiological arousal has a mild, inverted-U effect, so performance changes gradually. When cognitive anxiety is high, increasing arousal can improve performance up to a point, after which performance drops suddenly and steeply rather than tapering off: the catastrophe.

The model also predicts hysteresis: once a collapse occurs, slightly lowering arousal does not restore performance along the same path. In practice, recovery usually means bringing arousal down well below the collapse point and dealing with worry before rebuilding toward an optimal state.

The model implies that neither arousal nor cognitive anxiety is harmful in itself: cognitive anxiety can even help when arousal is low. The risk lies in combining high worry with high arousal. Research support is mixed.

cards.title: Directional Interpretation of Anxiety
points: Same intensity can be facilitative or debilitative
Direction is measured with a rating added to intensity scales
Elite performers more often interpret anxiety as facilitative
Reinterpretation can be trained; intensity reduction isn't always the goal
cards.examNote: When high anxiety scores coexist with strong performance, or two athletes with equal anxiety perform differently, the answer usually involves assessing or changing direction.
body: Jones's directional perspective adds a second question to how much anxiety a performer feels: is it experienced as helpful or harmful?
The same intensity of cognitive or somatic symptoms can be interpreted as facilitative (a pounding heart means I'm ready) or debilitative (it means I'm about to fall apart).

Research using direction scales added to intensity measures such as the CSAI-2 has found that direction often separates better from poorer performers, and elite performers more often report facilitative interpretations. Self-confidence appears to help protect a facilitative reading.

In assessment, measure direction as well as intensity before deciding that high anxiety is a problem. In intervention, cognitive strategies such as restructuring, self-talk, and imagery can help performers reinterpret symptoms rather than only lowering intensity, as Hanton and Jones described with elite swimmers.

cards.title: Cue Utilization Theory
points: Low arousal: attention too broad, irrelevant cues get in
Moderate arousal: irrelevant cues are filtered out (helpful)
High arousal: relevant cues are lost too (harmful)
Adjust arousal in either direction to restore the best attentional width
cards.examNote: Missing a relevant peripheral cue only under peak pressure points to over-narrowing; noticing everything except the task in a low-stakes moment points to under-arousal.
body: Easterbrook's cue utilization theory explains how arousal changes the range of cues a performer attends to.

At low arousal, attention is broad and lets in irrelevant cues such as crowd noise or the scoreboard, so the performer is easily distracted. As arousal rises to a moderate level, attention narrows and irrelevant cues drop out, which improves performance.

If arousal keeps rising, attention narrows further and relevant cues, often peripheral ones like an open teammate or a second threat, begin to be missed, and performance declines. The theory offers one explanation for the inverted-U pattern between arousal and performance.
Practically, it implies raising activation for under-aroused, distractible performers, lowering it for over-aroused ones, and training scanning of relevant cues under gradually increasing stress.

cards.title: Nideffer's Attentional Styles
points: Broad-external: assess the situation
Broad-internal: analyze and plan
Narrow-internal: rehearse or center
Narrow-external: execute on a target; TAIS assesses attentional style
cards.examNote: Items describe a performer stuck in one focus and ask which shift a routine or refocusing cue should train. Match the focus type to the demand of that moment.
body: Nideffer describes attention along two dimensions: width (broad to narrow) and direction (external to internal). Together they produce four types of focus, each suited to a different demand.

Broad-external focus assesses the environment quickly, as when a point guard reads the defense. Broad-internal focus analyzes and plans, as when choosing a strategy. Narrow-internal focus rehearses or centers, such as feeling a movement or taking a calming breath.
Narrow-external focus locks onto a target for execution, such as the rim or the ball.

Effective performers shift between these types as the situation changes; problems arise when someone gets stuck in the wrong type, such as analyzing at the moment of execution or ruminating internally while missing information around them.
The Test of Attentional and Interpersonal Style (TAIS) was developed to assess attentional tendencies.

cards.title: Achievement Goal Theory and Motivational Climate
points: Task orientation: self-referenced improvement; ego orientation: beating others
High ego plus low perceived ability is the highest-risk profile
Mastery climate: improvement, effort, and cooperation are recognized
Performance climate: rankings, comparison, and results-only praise
cards.examNote: Coach-behavior vignettes usually test climate (what to change), while athlete-profile vignettes test orientation plus perceived ability (who is at risk). Assess both the person and the environment.
body: Achievement goal theory explains motivation by how people define success. With a task orientation, success means improving, learning, and giving effort, judged against one's own past performance.
With an ego orientation, success means beating others or doing as well with less effort. The orientations are independent, so a person can be high in both.

The most vulnerable profile is high ego orientation with low perceived ability: when winning is the only route to feeling competent and the person doubts they can win, they tend to avoid challenges, withdraw effort, and drop out. A strong task orientation tends to protect motivation.

The motivational climate created by coaches and leaders also matters. A task-involving (mastery) climate recognizes individual improvement, effort, and cooperation; an ego-involving (performance) climate emphasizes public comparison, rankings, and praise mainly for top performers. Orientation is often measured with the TEOSQ.

cards.title: Self-Determination Theory
points: Needs: autonomy, competence, relatedness
Continuum: amotivation → external → introjected → identified → integrated → intrinsic
Controlling rewards can undermine intrinsic motivation
Autonomy support: choice within limits, rationale, acknowledgment, input
cards.examNote: Identify the regulation type from a quote (guilt means introjected), or find which need is unmet and match the fix to it. Rewards and pressure are common distractors.
body: Self-determination theory (Ryan and Deci) proposes three basic psychological needs: autonomy (feeling volitional and having a say), competence (feeling effective), and relatedness (feeling connected and cared for).
Satisfying these needs supports more autonomous motivation and well-being; thwarting them pushes motivation toward control or amotivation.

Motivation falls along a continuum: amotivation, external regulation (rewards and punishments), introjected regulation (guilt, shame, ego pressure), identified regulation (valuing the outcome), integrated regulation (fully aligned with one's identity), and intrinsic motivation (doing it for the activity itself).

Cognitive evaluation theory, part of SDT, explains why expected tangible rewards that feel controlling can undermine intrinsic interest, whereas informational feedback can support competence. In practice, consultants and coaches use autonomy support: offering choices within limits, giving rationales, acknowledging feelings, and inviting input.

cards.title: Self-Efficacy and Its Sources
points: Mastery experiences are the strongest source
Vicarious experience works best with similar models
Verbal persuasion is weaker and must be credible
Physiological states matter through interpretation; collective efficacy is the group-level version
cards.examNote: If persuasion or modeling has failed, the answer is usually graded mastery experiences. For bodily signals, look for reinterpretation rather than more encouragement.
body: In Bandura's social cognitive theory, self-efficacy is a person's belief in their capability to carry out a specific task in a specific situation. It predicts choice, effort, persistence, and performance.

Efficacy draws on four main sources. Performance accomplishments (mastery experiences) are the strongest. Vicarious experience, watching others succeed, has the most impact when the model is similar to the observer, and a coping model who struggles and then succeeds can be especially helpful for fearful learners.

Verbal persuasion is weaker and loses credibility when it contradicts experience. Physiological and emotional states matter through how they are interpreted: a racing heart read as incapacity lowers efficacy. Sport researchers have also emphasized imaginal experiences.
Collective efficacy, a group's shared belief in its joint capability, develops from the same sources, especially shared mastery.

cards.title: Attribution Theory
points: Dimensions: locus of causality, stability, controllability
Stability drives future expectancy
Internal, stable, uncontrollable failure attributions are most damaging
Retraining shifts attributions toward effort and strategy
cards.examNote: Classify a quote on the three dimensions, then pick the response that moves failure attributions toward controllable, changeable causes. Blaming luck or officials is a tempting but unhelpful distractor.
body: Attribution theory, especially Weiner's model, explains how the causes people give for success and failure shape their emotions, expectations, and future effort. Attributions vary on three main dimensions.

Locus of causality (internal or external) is tied mainly to pride and self-esteem. Stability (stable or unstable) shapes expectations of future success: stable causes for failure predict more failure. Controllability (controllable or uncontrollable) shapes emotions such as guilt or shame and willingness to keep trying.

Explaining failure with an internal, stable, uncontrollable cause, such as lack of natural ability, is linked to low expectations, reduced effort, and helplessness. Attribution retraining helps performers explain setbacks with unstable, controllable causes such as effort, strategy, and preparation.
Consultants and coaches can guide attributions in debriefs by steering discussion toward factors the person or team can change.

cards.title: Vealey's Sport-Confidence Model
points: Trait vs. state sport confidence; competitive orientation
Later work identified multiple sources of sport confidence
Controllable sources (mastery, preparation) are thought to be sturdier
Confidence that relies on others' approval tends to be fragile
cards.examNote: Vignettes describe confidence that swings with feedback, results, or disrupted training. The best answer rebuilds it from mastery and preparation rather than more praise or lower goals.
body: Vealey defined sport confidence as an athlete's belief or degree of certainty about their ability to be successful in sport.

Her original model separated trait sport confidence (a general disposition) from state sport confidence (confidence in a particular moment) and included competitive orientation, meaning whether an athlete defines success by performing well or by winning.
Trait confidence and competitive orientation were proposed to shape state confidence, which in turn influences performance.

Later work took a multidimensional approach and identified sources of sport confidence, including mastery, demonstration of ability, physical and mental preparation, physical self-presentation, social support, vicarious experience, coaches' leadership, environmental comfort, and situational favorableness.

Sources athletes control, such as mastery and preparation, are thought to give a sturdier foundation than sources that depend on others' evaluations or on circumstances. Consultants help athletes broaden confidence toward these controllable sources and reconnect with evidence of their preparation.

cards.title: Cohesion, the GEQ, Group Development, and Shared Mental Models
points: Task vs. social cohesion; GEQ: ATG-T, ATG-S, GI-T, GI-S
Team building: goals, roles, norms, distinctiveness, interaction
Tuckman: forming, storming, norming, performing, adjourning
Shared mental models drive coordination among skilled individuals
cards.examNote: Read GEQ profiles by dimension, recognize storming as normal rather than failure, and choose shared-mental-model work when skilled individuals coordinate poorly.
body: Carron describes cohesion as a dynamic process, seen in a group's tendency to stay together while pursuing its goals and meeting members' needs.

Task cohesion concerns working together toward goals; social cohesion concerns liking one another. The Group Environment Questionnaire (GEQ) measures four parts: individual attractions to the group–task and –social, and group integration–task and –social. Interpret each dimension separately; high social cohesion does not offset low task cohesion.

Team building targets task cohesion with shared goals, role clarity, and standards, and in exercise groups with distinctiveness, norms, and member interaction. Tuckman's model of group development runs forming, storming (conflict over roles and influence), norming, and performing, with adjourning added later for groups that disband.
Shared mental models, team members' overlapping knowledge of roles, cues, and procedures, support coordination and are built through briefs, rehearsal, and debriefs.

cards.title: Resilience and Stress Appraisal
points: Primary appraisal: what's at stake; secondary appraisal: can I cope
Same demands, different appraisals, different stress
Protective psychological factors promote challenge appraisals
Resilience develops through challenge with support
cards.examNote: If people face equal demands but respond differently, the answer involves appraisal. For resilience programs, reject options that remove all stressors or treat resilience as a fixed trait.
body: Lazarus's transactional model holds that stress comes from appraisal, not from demands alone. Primary appraisal asks what is at stake; secondary appraisal asks whether one's coping resources are adequate.

Demands appraised as exceeding resources produce threat and distress; demands seen as manageable can be appraised as challenges. This explains why two people facing identical demands respond differently, and it points interventions toward both the meaning of the demand and the person's resources.

Fletcher and Sarkar's grounded theory of resilience in Olympic champions found that psychological factors (positive personality, motivation, confidence, focus, and perceived social support) protected performers from the potential negative effects of stressors, partly by promoting challenge appraisals and helpful meta-cognitions.
Resilience is a process that can be developed; their later work on mental fortitude training emphasizes manageable challenge combined with support, not removing all adversity.

cards.title: Fitts and Posner's Stages of Learning
points: Cognitive → associative → autonomous
Novices: few simple cues and demonstrations; external focus often helps at any level
Experts: conscious control of mechanics can disrupt performance
Technique changes bring a temporary regression
cards.examNote: Match the intervention to the stage: simplify for novices, avoid step-by-step mechanical focus during expert execution, and progress new mental skills from calm to pressured practice.
body: Fitts and Posner described three stages of motor learning.

In the cognitive stage, learners work out what to do; performance is inconsistent and effortful, errors are large, and the task consumes attention, so instruction should be simple, with demonstrations and one or two key cues.

In the associative stage, learners refine how to do it; errors become smaller and more consistent, and learners start detecting their own mistakes. In the autonomous stage, the skill runs largely automatically, freeing attention for tactics and the environment; step-by-step attention to mechanics can disrupt it.

Research on attentional focus adds that an external focus on movement effects often aids learning and performance more than an internal focus on body parts. Rebuilding an established technique sends a performer back toward earlier stages, often with a temporary dip.
Mental skills can be viewed the same way: a new breathing technique or routine is effortful at first and should be practiced in calm settings before it is used under pressure.

cards.title: Practice Scheduling and Contextual Interference
points: Random practice typically: worse acquisition, better retention and transfer
Blocked practice inflates practice performance
Desirable difficulties: spacing, interleaving, variability, retrieval
Learning is judged by retention and transfer, not practice performance
cards.examNote: Look for athletes who look great in repetitive practice but fail in competition; the answer is usually random or variable, game-like practice.
body: Blocked practice repeats one task many times before moving on; random practice mixes tasks in an unpredictable order. Contextual interference is the disruption caused by switching between tasks.

Shea and Morgan's classic finding is that random practice produces worse performance during acquisition but better retention and transfer than blocked practice. Proposed explanations include elaboration (comparing tasks) and reconstruction (re-planning each action).

Variable practice, which changes parameters of one skill such as distance or target, similarly supports transfer. This is one example of the learning–performance distinction: practice performance can mislead, and conditions that make practice harder (desirable difficulties such as spacing, interleaving, variability, and retrieval) often produce more durable learning.

The effect is clearest in laboratory tasks and less consistent in applied sport; complete beginners may benefit from some blocked practice first. For consultants, the principle extends to mental skills: rehearse routines on every repetition in varied, game-like contexts, and spread sessions out instead of massing them.

cards.title: Feedback and the Guidance Hypothesis
points: Frequent feedback helps acquisition but creates dependence
Faded, bandwidth, and summary feedback can improve retention; effects vary
Let learners self-assess before giving input
Fade feedback on mental skills too
cards.examNote: If a skill holds up only when the coach or consultant is present, the best answer usually reduces or fades feedback and builds self-evaluation.
body: Augmented feedback, meaning knowledge of results (outcome) and knowledge of performance (movement pattern), supplements what learners sense for themselves.

The guidance hypothesis (Salmoni, Schmidt, and Walter) proposes why more is not always better. Frequent, immediate feedback guides performance during practice, but learners come to depend on it, neglect their own error detection, and overcorrect normal variability, so retention and performance without feedback can suffer.
Effects vary across tasks and studies.

Ways to reduce dependence include faded feedback (frequent early, less over time), bandwidth feedback (given only when error exceeds a set tolerance, so silence signals acceptable performance), summary feedback after several attempts, a short delay that lets the learner self-assess first, and letting learners request feedback.

Beginners need more guidance than experienced performers; the key is to taper it. The same logic applies when consultants teach mental skills: biofeedback displays and comments on a routine should be faded so athletes can self-regulate in competition, where no one is giving feedback.

cards.title: Deliberate Practice and the DMSP
