points: Deliberate practice: effortful, goal-directed, feedback-rich, not inherently fun
Sampling (~6–12), specializing (~13–15), investment (~16+), or recreational
Deliberate play dominates the sampling years
Early specialization carries burnout and dropout risks in most sports
cards.examNote: Expect parents pushing early specialization or athletes logging hours without improvement; the answers favor sampling with deliberate play, or focused work on weaknesses with feedback.
body: Ericsson and colleagues defined deliberate practice as effortful, structured activity designed to improve specific aspects of performance, with clear goals, feedback, and repetition with refinement.

It demands concentration, is described as not inherently enjoyable, and is limited by how long effort can be sustained, so it accumulates through limited sessions over years; hours of mere repetition don't count. Côté's Developmental Model of Sport Participation (DMSP) adds a developmental view.

In the sampling years (about ages 6–12), children try several sports with plenty of deliberate play (informal, intrinsically motivating games, often modified by the children) and some structured practice.

In the specializing years (about 13–15), they focus on one or two sports with more deliberate practice; in the investment years (about 16 and older), deliberate practice dominates. A recreational pathway emphasizes enjoyment and health.
Early specialization may suit sports with peak performance before maturity, but for most sports it has been linked to burnout, dropout, and injury.

cards.title: Cognitive and Emotional Development and the Adolescent Brain
points: Young children: concrete, brief, playful instruction
By about age 12, most see effort and ability as separate
Prefrontal maturation continues into the mid-20s
Teens' risk-taking tends to rise in emotional ('hot') moments, often with peers
cards.examNote: Choose age-matched delivery: games and concrete images for young children, and calm-state planning and self-regulation tools for adolescents who act impulsively around peers.
body: Children's thinking moves from concrete toward abstract, which shapes how mental skills should be taught.

Young children learn best through concrete images, brief explanations, demonstrations, and games; abstract talk about physiology or thought patterns loses them. Children also change how they judge competence. Younger children tend to equate effort with ability.

Peer comparison grows during childhood, and by about age 12 most separate effort from ability, so needing high effort can feel like proof of low talent. Adolescents can reason abstractly and reflect on their own thinking, making tools such as cognitive restructuring, journaling, and goal plans more usable.

Brain development is uneven: reward and emotion systems become highly reactive around puberty, while the prefrontal cortex, which supports planning, impulse control, and emotion regulation, keeps maturing into the mid-20s. Teens may reason well when calm yet take more risks in emotional moments, often with peers.
Strategies prepared in calm states, such as if-then plans, adult structure, and self-referenced goals, help bridge the gap.

cards.title: Goal types and goal-setting principles
points: Outcome = result vs. others; performance = own standard; process = how you execute
Combine types; process goals drive daily practice and in-event focus
Specific, challenging-but-attainable goals with feedback generally beat vague 'do your best' goals
Set goals collaboratively so the performer owns them
cards.examNote: Expect a vignette where an athlete has only an outcome goal and anxiety about rivals; the best plan keeps the outcome goal but adds controllable performance and process goals.
body: Goals come in three types. Outcome goals concern results that depend partly on others, such as winning or placing.

Performance goals concern the performer's own standard, judged against a personal baseline, such as a split time or a shooting percentage. Process goals concern the actions that produce performance, such as a relaxed grip or an early call-out.

Outcome goals can motivate long-term effort, but on their own they are less controllable and can raise anxiety. Performance and process goals are more controllable, and process goals in particular are linked to better focus, self-efficacy, and control of cognitive anxiety.

Most plans combine all three, with process goals guiding the day-to-day work. Goal-setting research supports goals that are specific and measurable, challenging but attainable, set over short and long time frames, written down, and paired with regular feedback.
Specific, challenging goals generally beat 'do your best' goals when there is commitment and feedback; sport findings are more mixed.

cards.title: The goal-setting process and monitoring
points: Assess first, then prioritize a few goals collaboratively
Plan measurement up front: baseline plus repeated measures of use, process, and outcome
Review regularly; adjust difficulty based on progress
Check practice adherence before judging whether a strategy works
cards.examNote: Evaluation items often hinge on adjusting rather than abandoning: revise unrealistic goals, and check whether a skill was practiced before concluding it failed.
body: Goal setting is a cycle, not a one-time event. It starts with assessment, such as a performance profile, interview, or baseline data, so that goals target what matters most.
The consultant and performer then prioritize a small number of goals together, since trying to fix everything at once spreads practice too thin.
Each goal needs a plan of action, a time frame, and an agreed way to measure progress, ideally with a baseline taken before the intervention begins. Progress is reviewed regularly.
If a goal is met easily, it can be raised; if it is repeatedly missed despite real improvement, it should be revised to a challenging but attainable step rather than kept unchanged or abandoned.

Monitoring also checks whether the planned practice is actually happening, because a skill that was never practiced has not been tested. Common pitfalls include too many goals, vague goals, outcome-only goals, and no follow-up.

cards.title: Building self-awareness
points: Awareness comes before regulation
Tools: performance profiling, self-monitoring logs, video review, debriefs, biofeedback
Performer-generated assessments build ownership as well as insight
Treat conflicting data sources as something to explore
cards.examNote: When a performer can't describe their strengths or misreads their own stress response, look for the option that has them generate or review their own data.
body: Self-awareness, meaning the ability to notice one's own thoughts, emotions, bodily states, and performance patterns, is the foundation for most mental skills.

A performer cannot regulate arousal they do not notice or change self-talk they cannot hear. Assessment and awareness-building often overlap. Performance profiling asks the performer to name the qualities that matter and rate themselves, which builds both insight and ownership.

Self-monitoring logs and journals track thoughts, feelings, and skill use across practice and competition. Video review, post-performance reflection, and structured debriefs help link internal states to outcomes.

Physiological measures such as heart rate or biofeedback can reveal a gap between what a performer feels and what the body is doing. When self-report and observation disagree, the discrepancy is itself useful information and a starting point for exploration rather than a reason to choose one source.

cards.title: Delivery factors in mental performance training
points: Teach new skills early; refine familiar ones close to competition
One-off sessions introduce; repeated practice builds
Virtual delivery needs structured independent practice and review
Agree on team vs. individual scope and reporting with coaches and sponsors
cards.examNote: Look for the option that fits the program to its time of season, contact time, and format, and that sets honest expectations about what that format can achieve.
body: The same skill is delivered differently depending on context.

Season timing: the off-season and preseason suit introducing and practicing new skills; in-season work should be brief, focused on priorities, and built into existing practice; the days before a major event are for refining familiar strategies, not learning new ones.

Program length: a single workshop can raise awareness and introduce a tool but rarely produces durable change, so multi-session programs with practice between sessions are preferred, and expectations should match the time available.
Format: virtual delivery can work well but needs structured between-session practice, recorded guidance, and a way to review practice, plus attention to privacy and identity.
Level: individual work allows tailoring; team work suits shared needs and common language; organizational work needs clear agreement with sponsors on purpose, reporting, and what is realistic.

cards.title: Building confidence with self-efficacy sources
points: Mastery experiences are the strongest source
Vicarious experience works best with similar models
Verbal persuasion helps but is weaker alone
Reinterpreting arousal and successful imagery also contribute
cards.examNote: If a coach plans to rely on praise or video of elite performers, the better answer usually builds graded mastery experiences.
body: Bandura's self-efficacy theory gives a practical map for building confidence in a specific task.

Performance accomplishments, meaning mastery experiences, are the strongest source: a performer who repeatedly succeeds has direct evidence of capability. Plans therefore build graded tasks that start where success is likely and progress in difficulty, often in practice before competition.

Vicarious experience, such as watching a similar peer succeed, helps, especially when the model resembles the performer. Verbal persuasion from coaches, teammates, or oneself (self-talk) can support efforts but is weaker and fades without real success behind it.

Physiological and emotional states matter too: helping a performer interpret arousal as readiness supports confidence. Imagery of successful performance adds a further, imaginal source in sport. Vealey's work on sport confidence adds that confidence also draws on preparation, social support, and coaching.

cards.title: Performing under pressure and pressure training
points: Pressure can narrow attention and trigger inward focus on mechanics
Teach coping skills, then practice them under graded pressure
Add evaluation, consequences, audiences, or time limits step by step
Debrief pressure drills to reinforce what worked
cards.examNote: For 'great in practice, poor in competition' scenarios, the best plan typically adds graded, realistic pressure to practice while performers use coping skills.
body: Performers often execute well in relaxed practice but struggle when evaluation, consequences, or audiences are added.

Pressure can raise anxiety, narrow attention, and pull focus inward onto mechanics, which disrupts well-learned skills. Preparation works on two fronts. First, performers learn coping skills such as breathing, routines, refocusing cues, and reappraisal of arousal as readiness.

Second, practice is made more competition-like in planned stages: scoring, consequences, time limits, observers, noise, or fatigue are added gradually so performers rehearse their coping skills under realistic demands. This graded exposure is the core of pressure training and resembles the application phase of stress inoculation training.

It can build confidence that skills will hold up. Simply adding repetitions in relaxed conditions, or telling performers the moment does not matter, is unlikely on its own to build this capacity. Pressure should be raised in manageable steps, with debriefs to reinforce what worked.

cards.title: Values and committed action in performance
points: Values = chosen directions; goals = concrete steps toward them
Committed action happens with discomfort present
Experiential avoidance is a common target
Thought suppression and 'wait until the fear is gone' contradict ACT/MAC
cards.examNote: When an athlete avoids actions because of fear, an acceptance-based plan sets values-linked committed actions practiced with the fear present.
body: Acceptance-based approaches, including acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT) and the Mindfulness-Acceptance-Commitment (MAC) approach applied to sport, shift the aim from controlling or eliminating uncomfortable thoughts and feelings to acting on what matters while they are present.

Values are chosen, ongoing directions, such as being a bold competitor or a reliable teammate; unlike goals, they are never finished. Committed action means taking concrete, goal-directed steps in the direction of those values, even when fear or doubt shows up.

Experiential avoidance, such as avoiding risky shots to escape the fear of failing, often narrows performance and moves people away from their values. Plans therefore pair values clarification with specific behavioral commitments and practice in willingness, defusion, and present-moment focus.
Strategies built on suppressing thoughts, or waiting for anxiety to disappear before acting, run against this approach.

cards.title: Facilitation and debriefing (experiential learning)
points: Kolb: experience → reflection → conceptualization → experimentation
Debrief: what? so what? now what?
Use open questions and link insights to concrete next actions
No debrief often means fun without transfer
cards.examNote: After an activity or workshop, the best facilitation choice usually involves a guided reflective debrief that ends with specific application, not a lecture or moving straight on.
body: Kolb's experiential learning cycle describes how people learn from doing: a concrete experience, reflective observation on what happened, abstract conceptualization of what it means, and active experimentation that applies the lesson to the next experience.

Good facilitation of mental skills sessions and team-building activities follows this cycle rather than ending when the activity does. Debriefing is where much of the learning happens. A simple structure asks what happened, so what it means, and now what to do next.

The facilitator asks open questions, invites several voices, links observations to the mental skill or team goal, and helps participants commit to a specific application in training or competition. Psychological safety, clear ground rules, and attention to confidentiality limits in groups support honest reflection.
Activities without a debrief, or debriefs where the facilitator simply lectures, tend to produce enjoyment without transfer.

cards.title: Imagery and the PETTLEP model
points: Functional equivalence: make imagery as performance-like as possible
Physical, Environment, Task, Timing, Learning, Emotion, Perspective
Real-time speed by default; slow motion only for isolated elements
Imagery ability (vividness, controllability) is trainable
cards.examNote: Vignettes describe imagery done lying down, relaxed, slowed, or in an unrealistic setting; the best answer adjusts the specific PETTLEP element that is mismatched with real performance.
body: Imagery is the deliberate creation or re-creation of an experience in the mind, ideally using all relevant senses, especially kinesthetic feel.

Holmes and Collins' PETTLEP model is built on functional equivalence: imagery works best when it draws on neural and psychological processes that overlap with actual performance, so it should resemble the real thing as closely as possible.

The seven elements are Physical (posture, clothing, holding equipment), Environment (the real venue or realistic cues from it), Task (content matched to the skill and the performer's level), Timing (real-time speed, with slow motion used only selectively), Learning (content updated as the skill develops), Emotion (the feelings and arousal of real performance), and Perspective (internal or external, chosen to fit the task).

In delivery, consultants assess imagery ability, start with simple familiar scenes, build controllability (rewind and replay errors), add response propositions to scripts, and schedule short, regular practice.

cards.title: Imagery functions (Paivio/Hall framework)
points: CS = skills; CG = strategies and routines
MS = goals and outcomes
MG-A = arousal and emotion; MG-M = confidence and coping
Match imagery content to the desired outcome
cards.examNote: Items give a purpose (learn a new play, regain confidence, calm down) and ask which imagery type fits; watch the confidence-versus-goal distinction between MG-M and MS.
body: Paivio proposed that imagery serves cognitive and motivational functions, each operating at a specific or general level.

Hall and colleagues expanded this into five functions measured by the Sport Imagery Questionnaire. Cognitive-specific imagery rehearses individual skills (a serve, a turn). Cognitive-general imagery rehearses strategies, game plans, set plays, and routines. Motivational-specific imagery focuses on goals and goal-related outcomes, such as winning or achieving a target.

Motivational general–arousal imagery regulates arousal, relaxation, stress, and emotion (psyching up or calming down). Motivational general–mastery imagery depicts being confident, focused, mentally tough, and in control, especially in difficult situations, and is the function most closely tied to self-confidence and self-efficacy.
In practice, the consultant chooses imagery content to match the purpose: the 'what you image' should follow from 'why you are imaging,' and athletes often use several functions within one session.

cards.title: Self-talk
points: Instructional suits precision and technique; motivational is often used for effort and endurance
Cues: brief, personal, task-linked, practiced in training first
Restructuring: identify, test against evidence, replace
Affirmations must be believable to help
cards.examNote: Expect task-matching vignettes (putting, archery versus sprinting, lifting, rucking) and items where a consultant-imposed generic cue fails and the fix is a performer-created, task-specific cue.
body: Self-talk is what performers say to themselves, aloud or silently, and it can direct attention, regulate effort and emotion, and shape confidence. Interventions sort self-talk by function.

Instructional self-talk ('elbow high,' 'pendulum') supports precision, fine-motor, and technical tasks and is especially useful during learning. Motivational self-talk ('drive,' 'keep pushing') supports strength, power, endurance, and effort. Meta-analytic evidence shows self-talk interventions improve performance, with larger effects for fine and novel tasks and when self-talk is trained.

Instructional self-talk is better for fine tasks; support for matching motivational self-talk to gross tasks is mixed. Effective cues are brief, specific, meaningful to the performer, and ideally created with them.

For unhelpful self-talk, consultants help the performer notice it and its triggers, then use cognitive restructuring: test the thought against evidence and replace it with a realistic, constructive statement.
Thought-stopping on its own and unrealistic affirmations are weaker options, and acceptance-based approaches offer an alternative by defusing from thoughts rather than disputing them.

cards.title: Relaxation and the matching hypothesis
points: Somatic anxiety → somatic techniques (PMR, breathing)
Cognitive anxiety → cognitive techniques (restructuring, self-talk)
Crossover effects exist; multimodal packages are common
Assess type, intensity, and interpretation before choosing
cards.examNote: Vignettes describe a performer with mainly bodily or mainly worry symptoms and ask which technique fits best; read carefully for which component dominates.
body: Anxiety has cognitive components (worry, negative expectations, catastrophic predictions) and somatic components (racing heart, muscle tension, butterflies, nausea).

The matching hypothesis proposes that an anxiety-management technique works best when it matches the dominant type of anxiety: somatic techniques such as progressive muscle relaxation, breathing, and biofeedback for somatic anxiety, and cognitive techniques such as restructuring, self-talk, and mindfulness or meditation for cognitive anxiety.
Because the two components interact, techniques have crossover effects, and many performers benefit from multimodal packages, so matching is a starting principle rather than a rule.

Applying it requires assessment first: ask what the performer notices in body and mind, and consider whether symptoms are interpreted as facilitative or debilitative. Consultants should also remember that some performers need to raise rather than lower activation, so relaxation is not always the goal.

cards.title: PMR and breathing techniques
points: PMR: full tense–release → shortened → release-only → cue-controlled
Differential relaxation: relax what the task doesn't need
Slow, diaphragmatic breathing, often with an extended exhale
Practice when calm first, then under simulated stress
cards.examNote: A likely scenario asks for the next step after full PMR has been learned (abbreviated, cue-controlled forms) or explain why an untrained technique failed under pressure.
body: Jacobson's progressive muscle relaxation teaches performers to recognize the contrast between tension and relaxation by systematically tensing and releasing muscle groups.

Later abbreviated protocols start with longer sessions covering many muscle groups, then progress to combined groups, release-only relaxation, cue-controlled relaxation (pairing a word with the relaxed state), and differential relaxation (relaxing muscles not needed for the task while performing).

The goal is a quick relaxation response that can be used in performance settings. Breathing techniques are the most portable regulation tools. Slow diaphragmatic breathing, often with a longer exhale than inhale, can lower physiological arousal; a single centering breath can anchor a routine.

Like any skill, breathing and PMR must be overlearned in calm conditions and then rehearsed under progressively realistic stress before they will hold up under pressure. Rapid, forced breathing raises arousal and can cause hyperventilation symptoms.

cards.title: Biofeedback and HRV
points: Displays a physiological signal so it can be self-regulated
Resonance breathing: about six breaths per minute, individually identified
Fade the feedback to promote transfer
Requires specific training to use competently
cards.examNote: Look for the first phase of HRV training (find the resonance rate, practice daily) and for transfer problems, where the answer is to fade the device rather than add more feedback.
body: Biofeedback uses instruments to display physiological signals—heart rate, heart rate variability (HRV), muscle tension (EMG), skin conductance, skin temperature, or brain activity—so performers can learn to change them.
HRV reflects beat-to-beat variation in heart rate and is influenced by breathing and autonomic balance.

In resonance frequency HRV biofeedback (Lehrer and colleagues), the practitioner identifies each person's breathing rate, typically around six breaths per minute and ranging roughly from 4.5 to 7, at which HRV oscillations peak, and the person then practices slow, paced breathing at that rate regularly.
Biofeedback is scaffolding: the aim is self-regulation without the device, so feedback is faded and the skill is rehearsed without the display, then in practice and competition settings.

Consultants need specific training to use biofeedback equipment competently and should interpret HRV data cautiously, since readings are affected by sleep, illness, training load, and measurement conditions.

cards.title: Pre-performance and between-play routines
points: Purpose: arousal regulation, attentional focus, readiness
A few functional elements; flexible, not ritualistic
Rehearse with disruptions in practice
Between-play: release, recover, refocus, commit
cards.examNote: Expect a routine that collapses when interrupted; the best answer streamlines it to core elements and practices it amid simulated disruptions, not a longer routine or abandoning it.
body: A pre-performance routine is a systematic sequence of thoughts and actions a performer uses before executing a self-paced skill such as a serve, free throw, putt, kick, or dive.
Routines help regulate arousal, focus attention on task-relevant cues, block distractions, and trigger well-learned movements.

Research favors routines built around a few functional elements, such as a centering breath, a focus cue or brief image, a target, and a commitment, in a consistent sequence (evidence for strict timing is mixed), rather than rigid ritualistic counts, which break down under interruptions and can drift into superstition.
Routines should be developed with the performer, practiced in training, and rehearsed under realistic disruptions such as delays, timeouts, and noise.

Between-play routines serve sports with short breaks, like tennis points or baseball pitches: the performer responds to and releases the last play, recovers physically, then plans and commits to the next one.

cards.title: Attention control, focus cues, and refocusing
points: Width × direction: four attentional styles
Train planned shifts with situation-linked cues
Refocusing plans: anticipate, prepare if-then responses, rehearse
Focus on the present, controllable task
cards.examNote: Items ask which attentional style or shift a situation demands, or what to do about recurring distractions; prepared and rehearsed refocusing plans usually beat 'block everything out.'
body: Attention control means directing focus to task-relevant cues, holding it as needed, and shifting it as situations change.

Nideffer's model describes attention along width (broad to narrow) and direction (external to internal), producing four styles: broad-external to read the environment, broad-internal to analyze and plan, narrow-internal to rehearse or center, and narrow-external to execute on a target.

Many tasks require planned shifts between styles—for example, a goalkeeper scanning broadly and narrowing as an attack develops. Focus cues, such as brief words, images, or physical triggers tied to game situations, make those shifts deliberate.

Because distractions are inevitable, Orlick's work emphasizes refocusing plans: identify likely internal and external distractions in advance, prepare an if-then response for each (a breath, a cue, a return to the next task), and rehearse them in simulation so recovery becomes quick and automatic.
Suppressing all stimuli or holding a narrow focus indefinitely is unrealistic.

cards.title: Mindfulness in performance
points: Notice and allow, rather than control or suppress
MAC applies ACT processes to performance
Mind-wandering is expected; returning is the practice
Values guide committed action despite discomfort
cards.examNote: When a vignette names a mindfulness or acceptance approach, distractors are usually change-based techniques (thought-stopping, disputing, suppression); the key involves noticing, defusing, and refocusing on the task.
body: Mindfulness is paying attention to present-moment experience, on purpose and nonjudgmentally.

Rather than trying to eliminate anxiety or negative thoughts, mindfulness- and acceptance-based approaches teach performers to notice internal experiences, allow them, and redirect attention to task-relevant cues and valued action.

Gardner and Moore's Mindfulness-Acceptance-Commitment (MAC) approach applies this to performance, drawing on ACT processes: acceptance, cognitive defusion, present-moment contact, self-as-context, values, and committed action. A key rationale is that effortful suppression of thoughts often backfires, making them more intrusive.

In delivery, consultants use brief formal practices (breath or body scans) and informal ones (mindful warm-ups), normalize mind-wandering—noticing and returning is the repetition that trains attention—and link practice to performance situations.
Values work helps performers take committed action, such as entering an audition or competition, while making room for fear rather than waiting for it to disappear.

cards.title: Team building (Carron & Spink framework)
points: Environment (distinctiveness, proximity) and structure (roles, norms)
Processes (sacrifice, communication, cooperation) → cohesion
Indirect delivery: consultant trains the coach or leader
Role clarity and acceptance support task cohesion
cards.examNote: Items ask which framework component a strategy targets or how a consultant with limited contact should deliver team building; the indirect, coach-implemented approach is often best.
body: Carron and Spink's team-building framework treats cohesion as the output of a linear process.

Inputs are the group environment (distinctiveness, such as a name, shirts, or shared identity, and togetherness or proximity, meaning members spending time physically together) and group structure (norms, roles and positions, and leadership).
These feed group processes (sacrifice, cooperation, interaction, and communication, including group goals), which in turn build task and social cohesion.

The approach is typically indirect: the consultant educates the coach or leader, who then implements strategies within regular sessions, which suits consultants with limited contact time and may help sustain effects. Role clarity and role acceptance are central structural levers, linked to task cohesion.

Direct interventions led by the consultant, such as team goal setting or structured mutual-sharing sessions, require psychological safety, voluntary participation, and careful debriefing. One-off outings rarely produce lasting cohesion without reinforcement in the team environment.

cards.title: Energy Systems and Arousal
points: Phosphagen (~10 s), glycolytic (~10 s–2 min), oxidative (longer efforts)
Power tasks tolerate higher activation; precision tasks often benefit from lower (individuals differ)
Slow breathing: slow rate, comfortable depth, often a longer exhale
Rehearse regulation under competition-like physiology
cards.examNote: Items ask you to match arousal strategies to the task's demands and to practice them in realistic physiological states, not just at rest.
body: Three energy systems resynthesize ATP. The phosphagen (ATP-PCr) system powers maximal efforts of roughly 10 seconds, such as a lift, a jump, or a sprint start.

Anaerobic glycolysis contributes heavily to intense efforts of roughly 10 seconds to 2 minutes, with the aerobic share growing with duration. The oxidative (aerobic) system supports longer, lower-intensity work. All three operate together, and an event's duration and intensity determine the mix.

Arousal is general physiological and psychological activation, driven by the sympathetic nervous system (raised heart rate, breathing, muscle tension, adrenaline) and countered by parasympathetic activity.

Tasks differ in optimal activation: brief, gross-motor power tasks tolerate or benefit from higher activation, while fine-motor precision tasks such as shooting or putting often benefit from lower activation, with large individual differences. Some events, such as biathlon, combine both.

Slow-paced breathing (about six breaths per minute) at a comfortable depth, often with a longer exhale, tends to increase parasympathetic influence. Consultants match arousal strategies to task demands and rehearse them under realistic physiological conditions.

cards.title: Periodization and Mental-Skills Timing
points: Macrocycle → mesocycles → microcycles
Preparatory, competitive (taper), and transition phases
Learn new skills in preparation; rehearse only during the taper
Review and plan during the transition phase
cards.examNote: Timing questions favor teaching new mental skills early in preparation and avoiding anything new close to a peak competition.
body: Periodization organizes training into cycles: the macrocycle (often a season or year), mesocycles (blocks of several weeks with a particular emphasis), and microcycles (usually about a week).

A typical annual plan moves through a preparatory phase (general, then specific preparation), a competitive phase that includes a taper of reduced training before key events, and a transition phase of rest and active recovery. Mental skills training can follow the same logic.

New skills are taught in the preparatory phase, when there is time to make errors; they are refined and tested in lower-priority competitions; and during the taper and peak they are rehearsed, not changed.

Tapers often bring restlessness and doubts about fitness, so preparing athletes for those sensations helps. Heavy training blocks can temporarily lower mood and concentration, which affects both session design and how monitoring data should be read. The transition phase suits evaluation, reflection, and planning.
Consultants align with the coach's plan but never prescribe training loads.

cards.title: Overreaching, Overtraining, and RED-S
points: Functional overreaching: short-term, recovers with rest
Overtraining syndrome: months of decline despite rest; diagnosis of exclusion
RED-S (now also written REDs): problematic low energy availability affecting health and performance
Recognize, share concerns, and coordinate with medical and nutrition staff
cards.examNote: Distinguish expected training fatigue (reassess after recovery) from prolonged decline or energy-deficiency signs (coordinate medical care); the consultant never diagnoses or prescribes.
body: Training deliberately creates fatigue. Functional overreaching is a short-term performance drop after intense training that leads to improvement once the athlete recovers.

Nonfunctional overreaching is a longer decline, lasting weeks to months, with psychological and hormonal disturbance but eventual full recovery. Overtraining syndrome is a prolonged maladaptation in which performance and wellbeing stay depressed for months despite rest; it is diagnosed by excluding other causes, so medical evaluation is required.

Mood monitoring can flag worrying trends. Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (RED-S, now also written REDs) results from problematic (prolonged or severe) low energy availability: too little dietary energy left for body functions after exercise, intentionally or not.

It extends the female athlete triad to all athletes and affects bone health, hormonal and menstrual function, metabolism, immunity, psychological health, and performance. Warning signs include stress fractures, missed periods, persistent fatigue, and restrictive eating.
CMPCs recognize these patterns, share concerns, and coordinate with physicians and registered dietitians; they don't diagnose, change training, or design meal plans.

cards.title: Sleep and Recovery
points: Teens ~8–10 h; adults (18–64) ~7–9 h
Assess sleep before attributing attention problems to mental skills
Teach habits and share needs with coaches and parents
Refer for signs of a sleep disorder; no medication advice
cards.examNote: A likely scenario has sleep as the hidden cause of focus or mood problems; the best answer assesses or educates within scope rather than prescribing.
body: Sleep is a primary recovery tool that supports tissue repair, consolidation of newly learned skills, mood, and attention.

The National Sleep Foundation recommends about 9–11 hours for school-age children (6–13), 8–10 hours for teenagers (14–17), and 7–9 hours for adults aged 18–64. Many athletes fall short because of early training, travel, competition schedules, screens, and pre-competition worry.
Insufficient sleep is linked to slower reactions, poorer decisions, lower mood, and, in some studies, higher injury and illness risk.

Consultants can include sleep in initial assessment, for example with sleep logs, teach sleep-supportive habits (consistent schedules, wind-down routines, screens out of bed, relaxation for pre-sleep worry), and share sleep needs with coaches and parents who control schedules. Recommending sleep medications or supplements is outside CMPC scope.
Signs of a possible sleep disorder, such as loud snoring or pauses in breathing, persistent insomnia despite adequate opportunity, or excessive daytime sleepiness, warrant referral to a physician.

cards.title: Andersen & Williams stress–injury model
points: Inputs: personality, history of stressors, coping resources
Stress response: appraisal and physiological/attentional changes, in both directions
Attentional narrowing and muscle tension are proposed injury pathways
Interventions target appraisal and physiological/attentional responses
cards.examNote: This model is about predicting and preventing injury; post-injury reactions belong to the integrated model.
body: Andersen and Williams proposed that psychosocial factors raise injury risk through the stress response.

When an athlete faces a potentially stressful situation, the response has two linked parts: cognitive appraisal of demands, resources, and consequences, and the physiological and attentional changes that follow, such as increased muscle tension, narrowing of peripheral vision, and greater distractibility.

Three sets of factors shape the size of that response: personality, history of stressors (major life events, daily hassles, previous injuries), and coping resources (including social support). History of stressors, especially negative life events, has been among the most consistent predictors.

The model points prevention at two targets: the appraisal (for example, cognitive restructuring and confidence building) and the physiological and attentional response (for example, relaxation and attention training).

cards.title: Integrated model of response to injury (and stage models)
points: Appraisal ↔ emotional response ↔ behavioral response, cycling toward recovery
Personal and situational factors shape appraisals
Adherence is a behavioral response influenced by appraisals and emotions
Stage/grief models are poorly supported; don't wait for 'acceptance'
cards.examNote: Distractors often invoke grief stages or claim physical healing alone resolves psychological responses; the key ties appraisal to emotions and behavior.
body: Wiese-Bjornstal and colleagues' integrated model explains what happens after injury.

Pre-injury factors from the stress–injury model feed into a post-injury cycle in which cognitive appraisal (such as how the athlete interprets the injury, their ability to cope, and their recovery), emotional response (frustration, fear, depressed mood, hope), and behavioral response (adherence, effort, use of social support) influence one another and drive physical and psychological recovery outcomes.

Personal factors (injury severity, history, identity, personality) and situational factors (sport context, social support, rehab environment) shape appraisals. Stage or grief models, which assume a fixed sequence like denial, anger, and acceptance, are poorly supported: responses vary widely between athletes and over time.
In practice, the appraisal is a key place to intervene.

cards.title: Psychological readiness and return to sport
points: Physical clearance ≠ psychological readiness
Return continuum: participation → sport → performance
Key concerns: re-injury anxiety, performance doubts, isolation, pressure
Consultant informs and supports; the medical team clears
cards.examNote: Keys typically name the gap between clearance and readiness and support a graded return, without overriding medical decisions or oversharing.
body: Medical clearance means that tissue healing and functional criteria are met; it does not guarantee that the athlete is psychologically ready.
Return to sport is better seen as a continuum, from return to participation, to return to sport, to return to performance, with decisions shared among the athlete, medical staff, and coaches.

Common return concerns include re-injury anxiety, doubts about regaining prior performance, feeling isolated from the team, and pressure to come back early. Signs of low readiness include avoidance of contact or specific movements, hesitation, and vivid worry about re-injury.

CMPCs can help with graded exposure through imagery and progressive drills, confidence building, re-entry goals, and keeping the athlete connected to teammates. Consultants communicate about readiness only within the athlete's consent and do not make clearance or selection decisions.

cards.title: Interdisciplinary roles and mental skills in rehabilitation
points: Medical team: diagnosis, treatment, clearance; CMPC: psychological adjustment and skills
Share information only within the athlete's consent (safety and legal limits aside)
Mental skills complement, never replace, prescribed rehab
Concussion and clinical-level distress go to the right professionals
cards.examNote: Watch for distractors where the consultant gives medical advice, changes rehab prescriptions, overshares with staff, or treats possible concussion with mental skills.
body: Injury care is a team effort.

Physicians diagnose and decide on treatment and clearance; athletic trainers handle immediate care, injury management, and day-to-day rehab; physical therapists design and progress rehabilitation; coaches manage involvement and selection; and the CMPC supports the athlete's psychological adjustment and mental skills.

All sharing of information runs on the athlete's informed consent, except where safety or law requires otherwise. Concussion assessment and return-to-play decisions belong to the medical team, so possible symptoms go to them right away.

Mental skills are adjuncts to medical care: short-term process goals tied to rehab milestones can support adherence; imagery may support skill maintenance, coping, and re-entry; relaxation and attention strategies help with expected discomfort; and self-talk addresses unhelpful appraisals.
When distress looks clinical, such as persistent hopelessness or loss of interest, refer to a licensed professional.

cards.title: The working alliance (Bordin)
points: Three components: goals, tasks, bond
Negotiate goals first; tasks must serve agreed goals
Diagnose the strained component: task problem means renegotiate the task, not the goal
Repair ruptures with immediacy: name the shift and invite feedback
cards.examNote: Expect a scenario where one component is strained (for example, homework is skipped but the goal and bond are intact) and you must pick the response that targets that component.
body: Bordin described the working alliance as a pantheoretical account of what makes any helping relationship work, whatever the helper's model.
It has three parts: agreement between consultant and client on the goals of the work, agreement on the tasks used to pursue those goals, and an emotional bond of trust and mutual respect.
The parts depend on one another: a client who trusts the consultant may still disengage from a task that feels pointless, and a well-chosen technique fails if it serves a goal the client never chose.

In practice, the consultant negotiates goals before choosing tasks, checks agreement regularly, and diagnoses which part is strained when engagement drops. Strains or ruptures (withdrawal, quiet compliance, or open disagreement) are normal. Addressing them openly and nondefensively often strengthens the relationship.

cards.title: Building rapport and trust
points: Rogers: empathy, unconditional positive regard, congruence
Be specific and honest about confidentiality limits; never promise total secrecy
Fit in and be present before formal interventions
Clear, consistent boundaries support trust
cards.examNote: A likely scenario asks for the first step: clarifying the role and building rapport come before assessment or technique; answers that overpromise confidentiality or impose mandatory contact are distractors.
body: Rapport is the foundation of the consulting sequence; it begins before assessment or intervention and continues throughout.

Rogers's core conditions (accurate empathy, unconditional positive regard, and congruence, or genuineness) describe the helper's stance. Research with athletes, coaches, and consultants points to trustworthiness, keeping confidences, being approachable and easy to relate to, fitting in with the team's culture, and practical, sport-relevant help.

Trust grows from transparency: explaining exactly what the consultant does, who receives what information, and where confidentiality ends, without overpromising. In team settings, being visible at practices and in informal moments lets athletes judge the consultant before they commit.
Boundaries are part of trust, not opposed to it: consistent, warmly explained limits around contact, travel, and social media make the relationship safer and more dependable.

cards.title: Counseling microskills (Ivey)
points: Paraphrase = content; reflection of feeling = emotion
Summary = several themes integrated and checked
Confrontation = neutral "on one hand… on the other"
Self-disclosure: brief, relevant, client-focused, then return the focus
cards.examNote: Items quote a client and ask which response best demonstrates a named skill; distractors are usually other real microskills (a paraphrase offered as a reflection of feeling, a "why" question offered as an open question).
body: Ivey's microskills break effective helping conversations into learnable behaviors.
Attending behavior, meaning culturally appropriate eye contact, body language, vocal qualities, and verbal tracking, comes first; on video it must be made visible.

The basic listening sequence follows: open questions ("what" and "how" invite elaboration; "why" can sound accusatory) and closed questions (for specific facts), encouragers, paraphrasing (restating content), reflection of feeling (naming the emotion beneath the words), and summarizing (pulling several themes together and checking accuracy).
Confrontation is a supportive challenge that lays two discrepant statements side by side without judgment.

Other skills include immediacy, which addresses what is happening between consultant and client right now, and self-disclosure, which helps when it is brief, relevant, for the client's benefit, and followed by a return of focus to the client.

cards.title: Role clarity with multiple stakeholders
points: Identify the client and the consultant's role at the outset
Agree in advance what each stakeholder receives
Payment or referral alone does not equal access to content
Minors: parental permission plus the athlete's assent
cards.examNote: A likely scenario has a third party asking for information: prefer an upfront joint agreement on role and information-sharing over either full disclosure to the payer or total refusal to share.
body: Consultants often work in triangles: a parent, coach, athletic director, sports medicine team, agent, manager, or HR sponsor arranges or pays for services delivered to someone else.

Before services begin, the consultant clarifies who the client is, what role the consultant will and will not play (for example, whether they will offer any input on selection), what information each party receives (often attendance and broad progress, not session content), and the exceptions, such as safety.
Everyone affected, especially the athlete, hears the same arrangement before disclosing anything. With minors, parents give permission and the young athlete gives assent.

Paying for services or making a referral does not by itself entitle anyone to session content, though guardians of minors may have legal access rights, so clarify this at the outset. Sharing with medical staff or coaches happens with consent, except where safety or law requires disclosure.
When a stakeholder misstates the consultant's role, the consultant corrects it promptly and respectfully.

cards.title: Psychological safety
points: Shared belief that interpersonal risk-taking is safe
Linked to team learning behavior (Edmondson)
Built through clear confidentiality limits, co-created norms, and modeling
Protect it in the moment when a norm is broken
cards.examNote: Look for answers that set or reinforce norms transparently; distractors overpromise confidentiality, ignore the breach, or shame the offender publicly.
body: Edmondson defined team psychological safety as a shared belief that the team is safe for interpersonal risk-taking: people can admit mistakes, ask questions, and raise concerns without fear of embarrassment or punishment.

In her research, psychologically safe teams showed more learning behavior, such as seeking feedback and discussing errors. Psychological safety is not the same as comfort or low standards; it enables candor in demanding environments.

Consultants build it in team work by being transparent about what leaves the room, co-creating group norms (including the right to pass), and modeling curiosity about mistakes. Leaders' reactions to bad news strongly shape it, so the consultant often works through the coach or commander.
When a norm is broken in the room, such as a teammate ridiculing an admitted error, the consultant addresses it briefly in the moment so the group sees that candor is protected.

cards.title: Inclusive practice in the relationship
points: Invite names and pronouns; correct mistakes briefly
Learn para-sport context, including classification
Ask clients what they need; don't assume
Identity is not a reason to refer; build competence
cards.examNote: Identity is never the trick: the right answer is the respectful, competent process (ask, adapt, follow the client's lead), not an assumption about the person.
body: Inclusive practice means treating each client's identity as part of who they are, not as the presenting problem.

With names and pronouns, the consultant models sharing their own, invites (rather than requires) clients to share theirs, uses them consistently, and handles a slip by correcting it briefly, apologizing simply, and moving on.

With para athletes, the consultant learns the sport's context, including classification, which groups athletes by how their impairment affects performance in that sport and can shape selection and lineups, and treats athletes as experts on their own experience.

Adaptations such as imagery built around a racer's own pushing stroke, or a qualified interpreter for a Deaf client, are chosen with the client. Cultural humility means being honest about what one does not know and staying curious.
A client's identity alone is not a reason to refer; consultants work within their competence and build cultural competence through education and consultation.

cards.title: Online consulting: jurisdiction, consent, identity, emergencies
points: Follow the laws where both consultant and client are located
Consent covers technology risks, disconnection, and messaging rules
Verify identity; confirm the client's location each session
Emergency plan: backup number, local contact, local crisis resources
cards.examNote: "First step" items in virtual settings usually favor identity verification and emergency preparedness (location, local contacts, backup plan) before intake content. Emergency calls go to services where the client is, not where the consultant is.
body: APA's telepsychology guidelines (written for psychologists, since revised) offer useful guidance. Before technology-mediated work begins, the consultant checks the laws and regulations where both parties are located.
These cover who may provide the service, which titles are allowed, and data protection; licensed professionals must also consider licensure in the client's jurisdiction.

Informed consent covers the usual elements plus technology-specific ones: the risks of the platform (breaches, recording, interception), what happens if the connection fails, how and when to use messaging, response times, and the fact that remote work may not suit every concern.

At the first session the consultant verifies the client's identity. At the start of each session, the consultant confirms where the client is physically located, because emergency services must be local to the client.

An emergency plan includes a backup phone number, a local emergency contact, and local crisis resources, so a dropped call has a clear next step. With minors, get guardian permission plus assent and keep one-on-one sessions observable and interruptible.

cards.title: Confidentiality, HIPAA basics, and secure platforms
points: HIPAA applies to covered entities and their business associates
Ethical confidentiality duties apply regardless of HIPAA
Use encrypted, access-restricted platforms; tell clients how data are handled
Technology can't guarantee group members' discretion
cards.examNote: Distractors claim HIPAA applies to everyone, or that being outside HIPAA removes privacy duties, or that a "HIPAA compliant" label is sufficient. The best answer pairs accurate HIPAA scope with the ethical requirement for secure communication.
body: The ethical duty to protect confidentiality applies to every consultant, whatever the technology.

HIPAA's Privacy and Security Rules are federal regulations that apply to covered entities (health plans, health care clearinghouses, and health care providers who conduct certain transactions electronically, such as insurance billing) and to their business associates. Whether HIPAA applies therefore depends on the practice.
Those it covers need safeguards for electronic health information and business associate agreements with vendors that handle it.

Either way, consultants should use secure, encrypted platforms with access controls for video, messaging, assessment, and storage, avoid ordinary email or consumer apps for sensitive content, and tell clients how their data are handled.
In group or team sessions online, encryption can't stop members from sharing what they hear, so agreed norms and honest limits of confidentiality still matter.

cards.title: Documentation and records with technology
points: Document modality, client location, disruptions, and emergency actions
Encrypted, access-restricted storage; secure devices
Recordings and app or wearable data need consent and protection
Follow legal and policy retention, then dispose securely
cards.examNote: When an organization asks for open access to notes or data, the best answer explains the confidentiality conflict and works toward restricted access, rather than complying, splitting records, or dropping documentation altogether.
body: Technology changes where records live and who can reach them, but not the obligation to keep accurate records and store them securely.

For remote sessions, guidelines written for psychologists offer a useful model: document the delivery mode, the client's location, who else was present, technical disruptions, and any emergency steps taken.

Records belong in encrypted, password-protected systems with access limited to people the client has agreed may see them, not on a shared organizational drive open to coaches or on an unsecured personal device. Devices that hold client information need passcodes, encryption, and automatic locking.
Messages, recordings, app data, and wearable data that bear on services need the same care, and recordings require informed consent covering purpose, viewers, storage, and deletion.
Records should be kept for the period required by law and policy, disposed of securely, and planned for if the consultant leaves or becomes unable to practice.

cards.title: Social media and professional conduct online
points: Decline personal connections with clients; have a written social media policy
Don't identify anyone as a client online without explicit consent
Comment generally; never speculate about a specific person's mental health
Keep professional and personal accounts separate
cards.examNote: Look for options that set a clear, explained boundary (not silent ignoring) and that protect the existence of the consulting relationship. "It's already public" is never a reason to disclose that someone is a client.
body: The Ethics Code's standards on confidentiality, multiple relationships, accurate public statements, and testimonials all apply online.

Accepting friend or follow requests from current clients on personal accounts can create a social relationship alongside the professional one, so consultants usually decline, explain why, and put a written social media policy into informed consent.
Merely working with someone is confidential, so posting about a client (even a public win) or a photo that implies the connection requires the client's explicit consent.
Public commentary should share general, evidence-based information and never speculate about whether a specific person, especially someone the consultant has never assessed, has a mental disorder.
Professional accounts should be kept separate from personal ones, marketing must be accurate, and testimonials from current clients are off limits even if they consent.
